profile.summary: The Plant Genomic Benchmark (PGB) is the set of eight supervised plant genomics tasks released with AgroNT, a DNA language model trained on 48 plant genomes. The tasks cover polyadenylation sites, splice sites, long non-coding RNA, promoter strength, terminator strength, chromatin accessibility, tissue-specific gene expression and an intergenic enhancer set, over 32 datasets in the paper's Table 1 (31 in the released dataset card's size table) with sequences from 101 to 6000 base pairs. It is for comparing deep learning methods on plant sequence prediction, in a field the authors say lacked a shared benchmark.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Introduction and Table 1. Dataset card: Dataset Overview

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a model can predict functional annotations and quantitative measurements from plant DNA sequence. The eight tasks span regulatory features, RNA processing and gene expression: binary classification of polyadenylation sites, splice sites, long non-coding RNA and intergenic enhancer regions; regression on promoter and terminator strength; multi-label classification of chromatin accessibility; and multi-output regression of tissue-specific gene expression. The authors' stated aim is a shared assessment for deep learning methods in plant genomics, with attention to species that are little studied.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction, Table 1. Dataset card: Dataset Overview

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Each task is a reuse or a rebuild of published data. Table 1 names the source of each: polyadenylation, lncRNA, gene expression and the enhancer set were compiled for this study, splice sites come from Baten et al., promoter strength from Jores et al., terminator strength from Gorjifard et al. and chromatin accessibility from Zhao et al. Polyadenylation sequences are 400 bp with the poly(A) site at position 301, and negatives were made by shifting that position by 1 to 50 bases, giving twice as many negatives as positives. The lncRNA negatives are mRNA sequences matched to each lncRNA on length and GC content. Promoter sequences are the 170 bp windows from -165 to +5 around annotated transcription start sites, measured by STARR-seq in two systems, tobacco leaves and maize protoplasts; terminators are 170 nucleotides from -150 to +20 around a cleavage and polyadenylation site, and the terminator study also added randomised sequences of varying GC content. For promoters, terminators and chromatin accessibility the authors downloaded the original studies' own train and test sets so their numbers can be compared with the original models.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Methods, Polyadenylation site prediction, Splicing site prediction, lncRNA prediction, Promoter and terminator strength prediction, Chromatin profiles prediction

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is a fine-tuned model's predictions on each task's held-out test split, scored with the metric the task's source study used. The authors report AUROC and AUPRC for the imbalanced classification tasks (splice sites, polyadenylation, lncRNA, chromatin accessibility), the coefficient of determination R2 for promoter and terminator strength, and for gene expression the R2 of a linear model between predicted and observed levels on held-out genes. Fine-tuning in the paper uses IA3, which injects re-scaling vectors at the model's activations and updates about 1% of the parameters. The dataset card's size table gives the train, validation and test counts for each of the 31 datasets it lists; several tasks have no validation split, and the card notes that lncRNA fine-tuning was done on all six species datasets together because each is small.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Fine-tuning strategy, Splicing site prediction, Promoter and terminator strength prediction, Chromatin profiles prediction; Fig. 5 caption. Dataset card: Dataset Sizes

sections.title: Promoter and terminator strength tasks
sections.body: These two tasks are regression on STARR-seq activity of 170 bp sequences from Arabidopsis thaliana, Zea mays and Sorghum bicolor, measured separately in tobacco leaves and in maize protoplasts, with terminator data covering Arabidopsis thaliana and Zea mays and over 50,000 terminators. The dataset card splits each task into a leaf and a protoplast dataset: 7154 and 7595 test sequences for promoter strength, 4806 and 4811 for terminator strength. The paper reports R2 of 0.7 in the maize system and 0.73 in the tobacco system for promoters, and 0.67 and 0.77 for terminators. Figure 3e and 3f compare AgroNT with the two CNN models from the original studies across plant species: on promoters AgroNT was ahead in every species and system, by 3 R2 points on average, and on terminators it matched or beat the CNN in 5 of 6 datasets.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Promoter and terminator activity prediction; Fig. 3 caption; Methods, Promoter and terminator strength prediction. Dataset card: Dataset Sizes

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The benchmark is distributed as a Hugging Face dataset with one configuration per dataset, loaded by name with the datasets library. The AgroNT weights are published separately on Hugging Face and through the InstaDeep nucleotide-transformer repository. No scoring script is published with the data, so the metrics have to be computed by the user, and the paper states that the pre-training code is proprietary and not released.
sections.source_locator: Dataset card: Example Usage. Paper: Data availability and Code availability

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Eight tasks. Table 1 of the paper, and the summary table on the dataset card, list 32 datasets with six for gene expression; the dataset card's size table lists 31 datasets, with five gene expression datasets (Glycine max, Oryza sativa, Solanum lycopersicum, Zea mays, Arabidopsis thaliana). Table 1 gives the number of datasets per task: polyadenylation 6, splicing site 2, lncRNA 6, promoter strength 2, terminator strength 2, chromatin accessibility 7, gene expression 6, enhancer region 1. Sequence lengths run from 170 bp (promoters and terminators) and 398 to 400 bp (splice and poly(A) sites) to 1000 bp (chromatin accessibility and enhancers) and 6000 bp (gene expression), with lncRNA sequences from 101 to 6000 bp. Test counts per dataset range from 360 (lncRNA in cassava) to 377,873 (Arabidopsis donor splice sites).
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1. Dataset card: task table and Dataset Sizes

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Fixed train, validation and test counts per dataset on the dataset card, with the split rule differing by task. Polyadenylation and lncRNA test sets are restricted to sequences from a single sampled chromosome per species, with chromosomes 1A, 1B and 1D for Triticum aestivum; the splice site test set is chromosome 5 of Arabidopsis thaliana; chromatin accessibility uses the same validation and test chromosomes as the Zhao et al. study; promoter, terminator and chromatin accessibility reuse the original studies' train and test sets. Polyadenylation, splicing and lncRNA have no validation split on the card.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Polyadenylation site prediction, Splicing site prediction, lncRNA prediction, Chromatin profiles prediction. Dataset card: Dataset Sizes

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Per task, with higher better in every case. AUROC and AUPRC for polyadenylation, splice site, lncRNA and chromatin accessibility; the coefficient of determination R2 for promoter and terminator strength; for gene expression the R2 of a linear model between predicted and observed levels on held-out genes; AUC for the cassava intergenic enhancer set.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Splicing site prediction, lncRNA prediction, Promoter and terminator strength prediction, Chromatin profiles prediction; Results, in silico mutagenesis; Fig. 5 caption

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The models from the source studies, task by task: two CNN models for promoter and terminator strength (Figure 3e and 3f), the Zhao et al. chromatin accessibility predictions, and lncRNA-LSTM for the Zea mays lncRNA dataset of Meng et al., where AgroNT reached an AUC of 0.991 against the reported 0.9934. The paper also compares its gene expression results with two earlier models for Arabidopsis thaliana and Zea mays and reports up to a three-fold improvement.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Fig. 3 caption; Results, lncRNA prediction and gene expression; Methods, Chromatin profiles prediction

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Chromosome-level separation on the tasks the authors built: the polyadenylation and lncRNA test sets hold only sequences from one sampled chromosome per species, and the splice site test set is chromosome 5. Chromatin accessibility reuses the validation and test chromosomes of the source study. The lncRNA negatives are matched to the positives on length and GC content so that length alone cannot solve the task. No sequence identity cut-off between train and test is described, and nothing is said about overlap between the test sequences and the 48 genomes used for pre-training.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Polyadenylation site prediction, Splicing site prediction, lncRNA prediction, Chromatin profiles prediction

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Only for the lncRNA task. There the authors resampled the matched mRNA negatives five times per species and report the spread: the median range of the difference in AUROC across resamplings is 1.6 to 3.9 points and in AUPRC 2.5 to 4.6 points. No seeds, replicates or confidence intervals are described for the other tasks.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, lncRNA prediction; Results, lncRNA prediction

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a DNA sequence window with a label or a measured value: a 400 bp window centred on a candidate poly(A) site, a 398 bp splice site window, an lncRNA or mRNA transcript sequence, a 170 bp promoter or terminator with its STARR-seq strength, a 1000 bp window labelled for open chromatin or enhancer activity, or a 6000 bp gene-proximal window with expression levels across tissues.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Methods, Polyadenylation site prediction, Chromatin profiles prediction. Dataset card: task table

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Edible and model plants, plus one alga. Named across the tasks: Arabidopsis thaliana, Oryza sativa (japonica and indica), Zea mays, Sorghum bicolor, Setaria italica, Brachypodium distachyon, Glycine max, Solanum lycopersicum, Triticum aestivum, Medicago truncatula, Trifolium pratense, Manihot esculenta (cassava) and Chlamydomonas reinhardtii. The promoter and terminator assays were read out in tobacco leaves and maize protoplasts rather than in the source species.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Polyadenylation site prediction, Chromatin profiles prediction, Promoter and terminator strength prediction. Dataset card: Dataset Sizes

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: STARR-seq for promoter and terminator strength, ATAC-seq for chromatin accessibility, RNA-seq for tissue-specific gene expression, and PRO-seq based intergenic enhancer calls in cassava. The polyadenylation labels come from the curated PlantAPAdb catalogue of alternative polyadenylation sites, the splice site labels from an existing annotated dataset, and the lncRNA labels from the GreeNC database.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Promoter and terminator strength prediction, Chromatin profiles prediction, gene expression prediction, Polyadenylation site prediction. Dataset card: Dataset Sizes and ISM section

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: DNA sequence only. Every task gives a fixed-length nucleotide window, and the paper's own model reads a sequence of up to about 6000 bp tokenised into 6-mers. No alignment, structure or annotation input is described as part of a task.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Fig. 1 caption. Dataset card: task table

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Supervised fine-tuning on each task's training split. The paper fine-tunes with IA3, a parameter-efficient method that updates about 1% of the model's parameters, and notes that for lncRNA the six species datasets were fine-tuned together in a single training run because each is small. The benchmark itself does not restrict the adaptation method.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Fine-tuning strategy. Dataset card: note under Dataset Sizes

strengths.text: The data are published in one place with a DOI and with per-dataset train, validation and test counts, loadable by task name, which makes the splits reusable rather than something each user rebuilds.
strengths.source_locator: Dataset card: Dataset Sizes and Example Usage. Hugging Face API record: tags

strengths.text: On the tasks the authors built, test sets are separated by chromosome rather than at random, and for the lncRNA task the negative mRNA sequences are matched to the positives on length and GC content.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Polyadenylation site prediction, Splicing site prediction, lncRNA prediction

strengths.text: Where a task comes from an earlier study, the authors kept that study's train and test sets and its metric, so a new result can be put beside the original model's.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Promoter and terminator strength prediction, Chromatin profiles prediction

strengths.text: The benchmark covers more than one model species: twelve plants and one alga appear across the tasks, including under-studied crops such as cassava, which the authors give as a reason for the work.

limitations.text: The data licence is non-commercial and share-alike: the Hugging Face repository is marked cc-by-nc-sa-4.0, so commercial use is not permitted even though the paper itself is CC BY 4.0.
limitations.source_locator: Hugging Face API record: cardData.license and tags. Dataset card: front matter

limitations.text: The benchmark was assembled by the authors of the model it was first used to evaluate, and in the paper AgroNT is the method that wins on it.

No evaluation code or leaderboard comes with the data. The dataset card gives only a loading example, the paper says the pre-training code is proprietary, and the headline comparisons in Figure 3e and 3f are figures, so a reader has to take the per-species values from the figure data files rather than from a table.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Code availability; Fig. 3 caption. Dataset card: Example Usage and Data source for Figures 2-8

limitations.text: Three tasks have no validation split on the dataset card (polyadenylation, splicing and lncRNA), so any model selection on those tasks has to come out of the training data.

steps.explanation: The dataset card's example imports load_dataset from the datasets library; this line installs it. No version is given by the sources.

steps.title: Load one task
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from datasets import load_dataset

task_name = 'terminator_strength.protoplast'  # one of the task names from the dataset card table

dataset = load_dataset("InstaDeepAI/plant-genomic-benchmark", task_name=task_name)
print(dataset)
PY
steps.explanation: The three lines inside the heredoc are the dataset card's own example, with the heredoc and the print added here so the step runs on its own. Any name from the card's size table can replace the task name, for example promoter_strength.leaf or lncrna.z_mays.

profile.summary: BacBench is a multi-task benchmark for machine-learning models of bacterial genomics. A model embeds genomes or their genes and proteins, and the embeddings are scored on five active tasks: essential gene prediction, operon identification from long-read RNA sequencing, protein-protein interaction, antibiotic resistance prediction and phenotypic trait prediction; a sixth task, strain clustering, is deprecated but kept in the repository. The datasets are published on Hugging Face in DNA and protein-sequence form, and the repository holds the embedding and evaluation scripts for each task. It is for developers of bacterial genome, DNA and protein language models who want one comparison across tasks and across the bacterial tree of life.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening paragraphs; Task overview

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Each task asks whether a model's representation of a genome carries a particular kind of biological information. Essential gene prediction and protein-protein interaction are per-gene or per-protein questions answered from gene or protein embeddings. Operon identification asks whether neighbouring genes belong to one transcriptional unit, from per-gene embeddings grouped by contig. Antibiotic resistance and phenotypic traits are whole-genome questions answered from a pooled genome embedding. The tasks therefore test different granularities of the same representation.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Task overview

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The datasets are curated from public databases and published on Hugging Face, each in DNA and protein-sequence form: essential genes from the Database of Essential Genes, operons from long-read RNA sequencing, protein-protein interaction labels from STRING, antibiotic resistance and phenotypic traits from genome collections. Sizes differ by orders of magnitude, from 59.2 MB for the essential-gene protein sequences to 38.8 GB for the antibiotic-resistance protein sequences, so the README recommends streaming the large ones. The splits ship inside the data: the essential-gene and PPI parquet files carry a split column with train, validation and test values, while the operon dataset has a test split only. Row counts on the dataset cards are genomes: 37 train, 9 validation and 9 test genomes for essential genes, 159, 49 and 53 for the small PPI set, and 5 test genomes for operons. As of 2026-05-13 the essential-gene and PPI tasks use a phylogeny-aware split by genus. The package also includes functions to download genomes from NCBI or GenBank and preprocess GBFF, GFF and FNA files into the required format.
sections.source_locator: README.md: News, Datasets, Download and preprocess genomes; PPI README: Data; Hugging Face dataset cards

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Running a task has two stages. First a model embeds the dataset: run_embed_prot_seqs.py or run_embed_dna.py writes a parquet file of embeddings, with options for whole-genome aggregation and a pooling method for the genome-level tasks. Then a per-task script reads that parquet file and scores it. Reading the scripts rather than their names: the essential-gene script takes the split straight from the parquet file's split column, trains a classifier, computes AUROC and average precision per genome with torchmetrics, reports the median across genomes for validation and test, selects the checkpoint on validation AUROC, and repeats the whole run for random states 1, 2 and 3, writing one parquet file of results. The operon script is unsupervised: it explodes the data by contig, scores each adjacent gene pair by the cosine similarity of the two embeddings rescaled to 0 to 1, sets the score to zero when the two genes are on different strands, concatenates the pairs of a strain, and computes ROC AUC and average precision per strain with scikit-learn, printing the mean and standard deviation. The antibiotic-resistance script defaults to split = genus with 0.7, 0.1 and 0.2 train, validation and test proportions, falling back to stratified or plain shuffled splits when a group split cannot be made, and reports classification metrics or, in regression mode, the coefficient of determination and the Pearson correlation. PPI is binary classification with STRING combined scores thresholded at 0.6 by default, scored per genome by AUROC and average precision.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Embedding genomes, Model evaluation; run_train_cls.py; run_evaluation_long_read_rna_seq.py; train_and_predict_linear.py; PPI README

sections.title: What the operon score actually computes
sections.body: The operon task is worth reading closely because it is not a trained probe. For each contig the script turns the annotated operon membership into a binary label per adjacent gene pair, one when the two genes share an operon. The prediction is the cosine similarity between the two genes' embeddings, mapped from minus one to one onto zero to one, with one exception: when the two genes lie on different strands the score is set to zero, a strand veto. Scores and labels are then pooled per strain and scored by ROC AUC and average precision. Intergenic distances are computed in the script but are not used in the prediction.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Install the package from a clone, optionally with the fast-attention extra on a GPU machine. Load the task's dataset from Hugging Face, streaming the large ones. Embed it with the protein or DNA script, naming the model checkpoint and, for the genome-level tasks, adding whole-genome aggregation and a pooling method. Then run the task's evaluation script on the resulting parquet file. The README notes that embedding and most full benchmark runs need GPU hardware and task-specific input files, and the task READMEs give the per-task dataset and label-file locations.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Five active task datasets on Hugging Face, each in DNA and protein-sequence form, with sizes the README prints: essential genes (59.2 MB protein, 92.2 MB DNA), operon identification (15.3 MB protein, 24 MB DNA), protein-protein interaction (792 MB protein and 985 MB DNA for the 261-genome small version, 58 GB for the large protein-only version with more than 10k genomes), antibiotic resistance (38.8 GB protein, 54.9 GB DNA) and phenotypic traits (36 GB protein, 51.1 GB DNA). The dataset cards give genome counts: 37 train, 9 validation and 9 test for essential genes; 159, 49 and 53 for the small PPI set; 5 test genomes for operons.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Datasets; Hugging Face dataset cards

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Per task, and carried in the data. The essential-gene and PPI parquet files hold a split column with train, validation and test values, which the scripts read directly; since 2026-05-13 those two tasks use a phylogeny-aware split by genus. The operon dataset has a test split only and its evaluation trains nothing. The antibiotic-resistance and phenotypic-trait scripts make their own splits at run time, defaulting to split = genus with proportions 0.7 train, 0.1 validation and 0.2 test, and falling back to a stratified or plain shuffled split when a group split cannot be made.
facts.source_locator: README.md: News; run_train_cls.py; train_and_predict_linear.py; PPI README: Data; operon dataset card

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: AUROC and average precision (AUPRC), higher is better, are the metrics for the essential-gene, operon and PPI tasks, computed per genome or per strain and then summarised: the essential-gene script reports the median across genomes, the operon script the mean and standard deviation across strains. The antibiotic-resistance script adds a regression mode reporting the coefficient of determination and the Pearson correlation (higher is better for both).

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The benchmark publishes no numeric results of its own; its reference points are the supported models, which the README lists with checkpoint, objective, parameter count, dimension and maximum context: Mistral-DNA, DNABERT-2, Nucleotide Transformer, ProkBERT, Evo, Evo2, ESM-2, ESM-C, ESMPlusPlus, ProtBert, gLM2, BacLM, Bacformer and Bacformer Large. A model leaderboard for each task is on the to-do list.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Benchmarked models; To-do-list

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: A phylogeny-aware split by genus for the essential-gene and PPI tasks since 2026-05-13, and split = genus as the default group for the antibiotic-resistance and phenotypic-trait scripts, so genomes of one genus do not appear in both training and test. The group split has fallbacks that drop to a stratified or plain shuffled split when it cannot be made, which removes the control for that run. No sequence-identity cut-off is described.
facts.source_locator: README.md: News; train_and_predict_linear.py: _split_indices

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Repeated runs and per-genome spread, task by task. The essential-gene script runs the whole training and test cycle for random states 1, 2 and 3 and keeps the random state in the output. The antibiotic-resistance and phenotypic-trait scripts accept a list of seeds and default to one seed. The operon script prints the standard deviation across strains. No confidence intervals are computed.
facts.source_locator: run_train_cls.py; train_and_predict_linear.py; run_evaluation_long_read_rna_seq.py

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: Depends on the task: a gene or protein for essential-gene prediction, an adjacent gene pair within a contig for operon identification, a protein pair for PPI, and a whole genome for antibiotic resistance and phenotypic traits. Dataset rows are genomes, with gene-level fields nested inside and exploded by the scripts.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Task overview; run_train_cls.py; run_evaluation_long_read_rna_seq.py

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Bacteria, across the bacterial tree of life; the essential-gene dataset card carries species, genus and family fields per genome, and the genus is what the phylogeny-aware splits group on. No individual species list is printed in the files read.
facts.source_locator: README.md: opening paragraph; essential-gene dataset card features

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Public database annotations rather than one assay: gene essentiality from the Database of Essential Genes, operon structure from long-read RNA sequencing, interaction labels from the STRING database's combined score, and antibiotic resistance and phenotypic trait labels from genome collections. Inputs are assembled genome sequences and their annotated genes and proteins.
facts.source_locator: README.md: opening paragraph, Datasets; PPI README

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: DNA sequence or protein sequence, whichever modality a model takes, with the datasets published in both; mixed-modality models (gLM2, BacLM) can use either but not both at once in the current implementation. Embedding granularity is set by flags: per-gene or per-protein embeddings, or whole-genome aggregation with a pooling method for the genome-level tasks. Context limits are the model's own, listed in the model table.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Datasets, Embedding genomes, Benchmarked models

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Three settings appear. Zero-shot: the operon task and the PPI unsupervised evaluation score embeddings directly with no training. Linear or shallow probes: a classifier is trained on frozen embeddings for essential genes, PPI, antibiotic resistance and phenotypic traits. End-to-end fine-tuning: the essential-gene folder also holds fine-tuning scripts for protein, DNA and mixed-modality language models, which load the Hugging Face datasets directly.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Model evaluation, Task overview; run_evaluation_long_read_rna_seq.py; essential-gene folder listing in the task README

strengths.text: One pipeline covers many model families: fourteen checkpoints across DNA, single-protein, whole-genome protein and mixed-modality models are supported by the same embedding scripts, with their parameter counts, dimensions and context lengths tabulated.
The splits are shipped in the data rather than left to the user for the essential-gene and PPI tasks, and are grouped by genus, so the same split can be reused across models.
The datasets are published under Apache-2.0 on Hugging Face in both DNA and protein form, and the repository code is Apache-2.0, so both halves of a run are redistributable.

The package also covers getting the data in: it can download genomes from NCBI or GenBank by taxid or assembly id and extract protein and DNA information from GBFF, GFF and FNA files into the format the models expect.

limitations.text: The repository prints no numeric results and no leaderboard: a model leaderboard for each task and dataset details in the repository are both on the to-do list, so any comparison has to be run by the reader or taken from a paper.

The model table contradicts itself on size: Bacformer and Bacformer Large are both listed at 27 M parameters while differing in dimension (480 against 960), so the parameter column cannot be relied on for the large variant.

Protocols changed on 2026-05-13: the essential-gene and PPI tasks moved to genus splits and strain clustering was deprecated, so results from before that date are not on the current protocol. The strain clustering scripts remain in the repository.

Two tasks are small and one has no training split: essential genes has 9 test genomes and the operon dataset card lists 5 genomes in a test split only, so per-genome medians and means rest on few genomes. The genome-level tasks are the opposite problem, at 36 to 55 GB per modality, needing streaming and a GPU.
limitations.source_locator: Hugging Face dataset cards; README.md: Datasets, Requirements

run_guide.summary: Install BacBench, embed a task's dataset with the model you want to test, then run that task's evaluation script on the embedding parquet file.
prerequisites: Python 3.10, PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers and PyTorch Lightning; the repository was developed in python=3.10.
A GPU and considerable disk space: embedding and most full benchmark runs need GPU hardware, and the genome-level datasets run to tens of gigabytes.
Optionally the faesm extra, which needs flash-attention and a CUDA GPU, for fast ESM-2, ESM-C and Bacformer inference.
The code and the task datasets are Apache-2.0.

steps.title: Install the package
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/macwiatrak/BacBench.git
cd BacBench
git checkout --detach 64b7d45823b2ff2ef88458e3aa235caa461a12aa
pip install .
steps.explanation: The README's clone, cd and install lines. The checkout line was added here to pin the commit this page was read at. On a CUDA machine the README also recommends pip install ".[faesm]".

steps.title: Embed the task dataset
steps.shell:
python bacbench/modeling/run_embed_prot_seqs.py \
    --dataset-name macwiatrak/bacbench-essential-genes-protein-sequences \
    --output-filepath <output-dir>/essential_genes_esmc_embeddings.parquet \
    --model-path Synthyra/ESMplusplus_small \
    --batch-size 64
steps.explanation: The README's example for the essential-gene task with an ESM-C reimplementation. The script downloads the dataset from Hugging Face and writes one parquet file of per-protein embeddings. For the genome-level tasks the README adds --agg-whole-genome, --genome-pooling-method and --streaming.
steps.source_locator: README.md: Embedding genomes, Essential genes prediction task

steps.title: Score the embeddings for the essential-gene task
steps.shell:
python bacbench/tasks/essential_genes/run_train_cls.py \
    --input-df-file-path <input-dir>/essential_genes_esmc_embeddings.parquet \
    --output-dir <output-dir> \
    --lr 0.005 \
    --max-epochs 100 \
    --model-name esmc
steps.explanation: The README's example. Reading the script: it takes the train, validation and test rows from the parquet file's split column, selects the checkpoint on validation AUROC, computes AUROC and average precision per genome and reports the median, and repeats the run for random states 1, 2 and 3.

steps.title: Or score the operon task, which trains nothing
steps.shell:
python bacbench/tasks/operon/run_evaluation_long_read_rna_seq.py \
    --input-filepath <input-dir>/operon_identification_bacformer_embeddings.parquet \
    --output-filepath <output-filepath>
steps.explanation: The README's example. Reading the script: it labels adjacent gene pairs by shared operon membership, scores each pair by the cosine similarity of the two embeddings rescaled to 0 to 1 with a zero for genes on different strands, pools per strain, and prints the mean and standard deviation of ROC AUC and average precision, writing the per-strain table to the output file.

outputs: For the essential-gene task, a parquet file of results named after the model, with one row per genome and seed.
For the operon task, printed mean and standard deviation of AUROC and AUPRC across strains, and a CSV of the per-strain values when an output path is given.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
The detached checkout line was added here; the README does not pin a commit.
The antibiotic-resistance and phenotypic-trait scripts also need a separate labels CSV, whose location the task READMEs give and which this guide does not cover.
The repository prints no reference numbers, so a run's output cannot be checked against a published baseline from these files.

name: SEQC2 HCC1395 somatic CNV benchmark
description: Benchmark of six somatic CNV callers on a hyper-diploid cancer cell line.

attributes.task: Somatic copy-number gain, loss and LOH detection in tumour/normal WGS and WES
attributes.scope_note: Callers ascatNgs 4.2.1, CNVkit 0.9.1, Control-FREEC 11.6, DRAGEN 4.0.x, FACETS 0.6.0, HATCHet 1.0.4. Accuracy is reported in figures only; no results extracted.
limitations: No per-caller accuracy table in the article or Additional file 1

profile.summary: A SEQC2 study that built a high-confidence set of somatic copy number gains, losses and loss-of-heterozygosity (LOH) regions for the hyper-diploid breast cancer cell line HCC1395, and used it to score six CNV callers on whole-genome and whole-exome tumour and normal sequencing under varied conditions. The truth set comes from agreement across 21 WGS replicates and six callers (five for LOH), checked against microarrays and Bionano. It is useful to cancer genomics groups choosing a CNV caller or validating a somatic CNV pipeline.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results, 'Study design' and 'Establishment of CNV reference call set'

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How reproducibly and accurately somatic CNV callers detect copy gain, copy loss and LOH in a cancer genome whose ploidy is not two (HCC1395 ploidy 2.85), and how sequencing centre, WGS versus WES, FFPE fixation, tumour purity, read coverage, DNA input and library protocol change the result.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Background; Results, 'Study design'

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: For gains and losses, six callers were run on 21 fresh tumour and matched normal WGS replicates from six sequencing centres, giving 126 call sets. LOH calls come from the five callers that report LOH (CNVkit, Control-FREEC, DRAGEN, FACETS, HATCHet), giving 105 call sets, with their own score cut-offs for the confidence levels. Overlapping calls were split into disjoint intervals and scored for reproducibility within centre, across centres and across callers, then given strong, medium, weak or neutral confidence. The benchmark keeps strong-evidence calls and medium or weak calls supported by at least two of three orthogonal technologies (Affymetrix CytoScan, Illumina BeadChip, Bionano); neutral calls are excluded. The paper reports 346 gain calls (1525.6 Mb), 33 loss calls (87.9 Mb) and 320 LOH calls (1490.4 Mb). The deposited BED file holds 307 gain intervals (1503.9 Mb, counted from the saved file) against the paper's 346; its 33 loss and 320 LOH rows match the paper.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, 'Establishment of CNV reference call set' and 'Validation of CNV call sets'; Methods

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A call set is scored by genomic overlap with the high-confidence set: precision is the fraction of called CNV regions that match, recall the fraction of high-confidence regions that are called, and F1 their harmonic mean, computed with BEDTools. Reproducibility between call sets uses the Jaccard index of region lengths. Chr6p, chr16q, chrX and gap regions are excluded. The authors state that only the qualitative class (gain, loss, LOH) is benchmark-grade; copy number values and breakpoints are not.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, 'Reproducibility calculation' and 'Calculation of precision, recall, and F1 score'; Discussion

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: SEQC2 HCC1395 tumour and HCC1395BL normal data: 21 WGS and 12 WES replicates, plus purity and coverage (SPP), library and DNA input (LBP) and FFPE datasets. The paper reports 346 gain, 33 loss and 320 LOH calls; the deposited BED file has 307 gain, 33 loss and 320 LOH rows.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: None: one cell line, and every query call set is scored against the whole truth set. The truth set was itself derived from the same callers' WGS calls.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Region-based precision, recall and F1 (higher is better) against the truth set; Jaccard index for reproducibility between call sets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Six callers: ascatNgs, CNVkit, FACETS, DRAGEN, HATCHet and Control-FREEC.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, 'Study design'

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None in the machine learning sense. The truth set is built from the same callers that are then scored (six for gains and losses, five for LOH), with orthogonal array and Bionano support required for medium and weak calls.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Replicates across centres and callers are the main measure of variability; precision and recall are shown per replicate in figures. No confidence intervals are given for caller accuracy.

facts.value: A genomic interval called as copy gain, copy loss or LOH.

strengths.text: The truth set combines agreement across 21 WGS replicates from six centres and six callers (five for LOH) with three orthogonal technologies.
It tests conditions labs meet in practice: FFPE, low tumour purity, low coverage and low DNA input.
The truth set and raw call sets are on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0, and the sequencing data are on the NCBI FTP site.
strengths.source_locator: Zenodo record 10081398; Paper: Availability of data and materials

limitations.text: The truth set is built from the same callers it is used to score (six for gains and losses, five of them for LOH), which can favour callers that agree with the consensus.
Only the class of each call is trusted; copy number values and breakpoints are not suitable as a gold standard.
One cell line, with few loss calls (33), and chr6p, chr16q and chrX excluded.
Caller accuracy is reported in figures only; no per-caller table, and no leaderboard.

The paper and the deposited truth set file disagree on gain calls. The paper reports 346 high-confidence gain calls spanning 1525.6 Mb, while the deposited ngs_benchmark_cnvs_gain_loss_loh.bed has 307 gain intervals spanning 1503.9 Mb (counted from the saved file); the loss (33) and LOH (320) counts agree. A user who downloads the file will score against 307 gain intervals.

sections.body: ATOM3D evaluates predictions from molecular structures using eight separate tasks. It supplies task-specific reference labels and partitions, ranging from random small molecules to held-out protein families and future structure-prediction targets. Each task has its own metric and representation-matched baseline; the suite is not a single universal structure score.

instructions.title: Compute embeddings
instructions.code:
import os, sys
current_path = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
parent_dir = os.path.dirname(current_path)
sys.path.append(parent_dir)
from model.utrlm.modeling_utrlm import UtrLmModel
from tokenizer.tokenization_opensource import OpenRnaLMTokenizer

tokenizer = OpenRnaLMTokenizer.from_pretrained('./checkpoint/opensource/utr-lm-mrl', model_max_length=1026, padding_side="right", use_fast=True,)
model = UtrLmModel.from_pretrained('./checkpoint/opensource/utr-lm-mrl')     
sequences = ["AUUCCGAUUCCGAUUCCG"]
output = tokenizer.batch_encode_plus(sequences, return_tensors="pt", padding="longest", max_length = 1026, truncation=True)
input_ids = output["input_ids"]
attention_mask = output["attention_mask"]

embedding = model(input_ids=input_ids,attention_mask=attention_mask)[0] # shape [bz,length, hidden_size]
print(embedding.shape)

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: BEND asks whether DNA representations support realistic human-genome annotation across short and long contexts. Frozen embeddings feed a small CNN for supervised tasks, while variant-effect prediction compares reference and alternate embeddings without fitting a task predictor. Whole-chromosome or sequence-identity partitions and specialist baselines make the tested capability explicit.

run_guide.summary: Run the official gene-finding downstream example with BEND's own ResNet-LM and AWD-LSTM embedders, fetching only the gene-finding inputs. This is one BEND task, not the entire suite.
prerequisites: Git and a conda environment with Python 3.10; the README recommends this Python version.
curl and wget on the PATH: the download step uses curl, and BEND's embedders call wget to fetch their checkpoints.
About 3.7 GB of disk: 3.5 GB for the gene-finding inputs and 166 MB for the two checkpoints, plus room for the embeddings.
Internet access to the official data host, sid.erda.dk. Preserve the downloaded data directory structure.

steps.title: Check out the reviewed code
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/frederikkemarin/BEND.git
cd BEND
git checkout --detach 58ad41011125cfca339d511e9b8eb536a54b582a
steps.explanation: The clone command comes from the README; the detached checkout selects commit 58ad410, the first revision with working checkpoint links (BEND PR #79).
steps.source_locator: README.md at 58ad410, lines 39-40; pinned repository revision

steps.title: Install and download the gene-finding data
steps.shell:
pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install -e .
S=https://sid.erda.dk/share_redirect/aNQa0Oz2lY
mkdir -p data/genomes data/gene_finding
for f in GRCh38.primary_assembly.genome.fa GRCh38.primary_assembly.genome.fa.fai; do
  curl -fL -o "data/genomes/$f" "$S/data/genomes/$f"
done
for f in gene_finding.bed gene_finding.hdf5; do
  curl -fL -o "data/gene_finding/$f" "$S/data/gene_finding/$f"
done
steps.explanation: Run within the prepared Python 3.10 environment. From commit 58ad410 requirements.txt includes lxml, h5py and pysam, which earlier revisions lacked. The curl loop replaces python scripts/download_bend.py, which downloads the whole share (7,251,859,341 bytes listed on 2026-11-17). Gene finding reads only the GRCh38 reference and the gene_finding bed and hdf5 files, 3,509,054,493 bytes with the index. The README asks for the data folder structure to be kept, which these paths do.
steps.source_locator: README.md at 58ad410, lines 41-43 and 48; requirements.txt at 58ad410, lines 14-19; conf/embedding/embed.yaml at 58ad410, lines 39 and 106-109

steps.title: Precompute the gene-finding embeddings
steps.shell: python scripts/precompute_embeddings.py model=resnetlm,awdlstm task=gene_finding
steps.explanation: Adapted from the README example, with the task list narrowed to gene_finding because only those inputs are fetched. When pretrained_models/convnet/ or pretrained_models/awd_lstm/ is missing, ConvNetEmbedder and AWDLSTMEmbedder download the checkpoints with wget from ERDA share aNQa0Oz2lY. The resnetlm configuration loads pretrained_models/convnet, which the maintainer confirmed holds the paper's dilated ResNet; the resnetlm folder on the share is empty. To fetch the checkpoints ahead of time, call bend.utils.download.download_model('convnet', destination_dir='./pretrained_models/convnet/') and the same for 'awd_lstm'. With its default destination_dir the function writes the files directly into ./pretrained_models/, where the configuration does not look.
steps.source_locator: README.md at 58ad410, line 58; conf/embedding/embed.yaml at 58ad410, lines 40 and 77-82; commit 58ad410, bend/utils/download.py and bend/utils/embedders.py

steps.title: Train and evaluate gene finding
steps.shell: python scripts/train_on_task.py --config-name gene_finding embedder=resnetlm,awdlstm
steps.explanation: Run after gene-finding embeddings are present in data/gene_finding/<embedder>/. Task-specific Hydra configuration supplies the data, model and evaluation settings.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: DART-Eval separates regulatory sequence discrimination, motif sensitivity, cell-type specificity, quantitative accessibility and variant effects. It uses matched controls and consistent chromosome partitions where models are fitted. A result therefore needs its precise task and adaptation setting, rather than a single regulatory-intelligence score.

instructions.title: Schedule prepared scoring with site-specific resources
instructions.code:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
# Set these for your cluster; no performance or resource estimate is implied.
: "${REWIRE_ACCOUNT:?Set your Slurm account}"
: "${REWIRE_PARTITION:?Set your Slurm partition}"
: "${REWIRE_CPUS:?Set the requested CPU count}"
: "${REWIRE_MEMORY:?Set the requested memory}"
: "${REWIRE_WALLTIME:?Set the requested time limit}"
: "${REWIRE_JOB_ROOT:?Set a shared absolute directory with prepared data and SIF}"
export REWIRE_JOB_ROOT
sbatch --account="$REWIRE_ACCOUNT" --partition="$REWIRE_PARTITION" \
  --cpus-per-task="$REWIRE_CPUS" --mem="$REWIRE_MEMORY" \
  --time="$REWIRE_WALLTIME" --export=ALL <<'REWIRE_JOB'
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
cd "$REWIRE_JOB_ROOT"
mkdir -p runs
apptainer run --cleanenv --containall \
  --bind "$PWD/prepared-dart-task1:/prepared:ro" \
  --bind "$PWD/predictions:/predictions:ro" \
  --bind "$PWD/runs:/outputs:rw" \
  rewirebench-core.sif evaluate \
  --prepared /prepared --predictions /predictions/predictions.json \
  --output /outputs/dart-task1-rescore
REWIRE_JOB

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: FLIP evaluates sequence-to-fitness models under protein-engineering distribution shifts. It separates landscapes from their partitions: the same assay can test random interpolation, higher mutation counts, higher fitness or transfer across sequence groups. Comparisons are meaningful within the same landscape and split.

name: Gene-MTEB
description: Genomic embedding evaluations covering sequence classification and clustering. Accuracy and V-measure remain separate metrics and each source task retains its own comparison.

attributes.source_locator: METAGENE-1 Section 5.3; Table 3

run_documentation.source_locator: Section 5.3
run_documentation.summary: The paper describes frozen embedding probes and references Gene-MTEB. Rewire has no maintained runner for this published evaluation. Original split hashes, checkpoint revisions and evaluator revision are not established.

profile.summary: Gene-MTEB asks how useful a model's frozen sequence embeddings are on metagenomic data. It was introduced with METAGENE-1 as a genomics version of MTEB: eight classification tasks scored by accuracy and eight clustering tasks scored by V-measure, built from Human Microbiome Project sequences, human virus reference sequences and held-out parts of the METAGENE-1 pretraining corpus. A model is used only as an encoder, so it suits someone choosing a frozen genomic encoder for a lightweight downstream model.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Section 5.3 and Table 3. README.md: introduction and Quick Tour

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The quality of representations a model produces without being trained for the task. The authors say such representations matter for building light predictive models on a frozen foundation model, for interpretability work with sparse autoencoders and for anomaly detection. The classification tasks ask whether an embedding separates labels carried by the sample: which human-infecting virus a read comes from, and the disease status, sex and body source behind an HMP sample. The clustering tasks ask whether embeddings of reference sequences group by taxonomy.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 5.3. Task metadata in HumanVirusClassification.py, HumanMicrobiomeProjectDemonstrationClassification.py and HumanVirusReferenceClustering.py

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The paper names eight classification tasks (Human-Virus-1 to 4, HMPD-single, HMPD-disease, HMPD-source, HMPD-sex) and eight clustering tasks (HVR and HMPR, each as p2p, s2s-align, s2s-small and s2s-tiny). The data come from the Human Microbiome Project and from held-out portions of the authors' own metagenomic dataset, and the paper points to the project Hugging Face page for access. In the code each task loads one of four Hugging Face dataset repositories at revision main: HumanVirusInfecting, HumanMicrobiomeProjectDemonstration, HumanVirusReference and HumanMicrobiomeProjectReference. Clustering tasks rename a sequence column to sentences and a taxonomy column to labels, then drop the top taxonomic level as trivial. Every task's metadata records its licence as not specified.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 5.3. Task files: dataset blocks, dataset_transform and metadata

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model is used as an encoder only. The paper takes embeddings for all models by mean pooling the last hidden state, fits logistic regression on top of the embeddings for every classification task and runs mini-batch k-means for every clustering task, reporting accuracy and V-measure. The code confirms the rest: each classification task sets its method to logReg, makes one shuffled, unstratified split of the loaded train set whose training fraction is 8 divided by the count of the rarest label, so the rarest label gets about 8 training examples and commoner labels get proportionally more (the code comment says 8 samples per label), with everything else as the test split, and evaluates on test with accuracy as the main score. The clustering tasks evaluate on test with V-measure as the main score, hold the clustering to a maximum label depth of 5, and cap how many documents are embedded, which is what separates the p2p, align, small and tiny variants of the same dataset. All splitting is seeded at 42.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 5.3. Task files: __init__, load_data, metadata main_score, class attributes

sections.title: Classification tasks
sections.body: Seven of the eight sit in two files: four Human-Virus tasks, each loading a different configuration (class-1 and its siblings) of the HumanVirusInfecting dataset, and three HMP demonstration tasks for disease, sex and source. All seven are single-sentence tasks scored by accuracy on a test split from one random split whose training fraction is 8 divided by the count of the rarest label. The repository also adds one multi-label classification task on the HMP demonstration sequences, which was not read for this page; the paper's eighth classification row is HMPD-single, printed in the paper as MHPD-single.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Quick Tour. HumanVirusClassification.py and HumanMicrobiomeProjectDemonstrationClassification.py: class definitions. Paper: Section 5.3 and Table 3

sections.title: Clustering tasks
sections.body: Eight tasks, four on human virus reference sequences and four on HMP reference sequences. Each clustering task splits its data with test_size 0.9 (p2p) or 0.995 (align, small, tiny), seed 42, evaluates on the test split only, and caps the number of documents embedded at the variant's max_document_to_embed. The variants differ in how many documents may be embedded: for the virus reference set 40 (p2p), 147 (align, the size of the train split), 40 (small) and 3 (tiny); for the HMP reference set 27, 2198, 27 and 3. The tiny limit of 3 is described in the code as simulating the 3-mer in DNA sequence processing.
sections.source_locator: HumanVirusReferenceClustering.py and HumanMicrobiomeProjectReferenceClustering.py: class attributes and load_data

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: Table 3 of the METAGENE-1 paper compares five models: DNABERT-2, DNABERT-S, NT-2.5b-Multi, NT-2.5b-1000g and METAGENE-1. METAGENE-1 has the highest global average, 0.590 against 0.545 for the next model, and the paper singles out the Human-Virus group, where its average of 0.775 is more than 6 points above the others. The spread is not uniform: on HVR-p2p METAGENE-1 scores 0.466 while NT-2.5b-1000g scores 0.650, and both METAGENE-1 and NT-2.5b-Multi reach 1.000 on HVR-s2s-tiny.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Table 3 and Section 5.3

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Install the repository's fork of MTEB, wrap your model in an encode method that returns one vector per sequence, and run the sixteen named tasks through the MTEB runner. The repository's own example wraps METAGENE-1 with a Hugging Face AutoModel, tokenises with padding and truncation to 512 tokens, takes the mean of the last hidden state over tokens, fixes the seed at 42, and passes the list of sixteen task names to mteb.get_tasks before calling evaluation.run.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Installation; Example Using METAGENE-1

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Sixteen tasks over four Hugging Face dataset repositories: HumanVirusInfecting (four classification tasks), HumanMicrobiomeProjectDemonstration (three classification tasks plus one multi-label task), HumanVirusReference (four clustering tasks) and HumanMicrobiomeProjectReference (four clustering tasks). The paper gives no row or sequence counts for any task, and the files read print only the per-task document limits, not dataset sizes.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 5.3. README.md: Quick Tour. Task files: dataset blocks

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Each task cuts its own test split from a single loaded train set, with the seed fixed at 42. Classification: one shuffled, unstratified split with training fraction 8/M, where M is the count of the rarest label, so the rarest label gets about 8 training examples and commoner labels more; the rest becomes the test split. Clustering: the p2p tasks use test_size 0.9 and the align, small and tiny tasks use test_size 0.995. Every task evaluates on the test split only.
facts.source_locator: Task files: load_data and metadata eval_splits

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Accuracy for the classification tasks and V-measure for the clustering tasks, higher better in both cases; the task metadata names accuracy and v_measure as each task's main score. Table 3 also prints a mean per group (Human-Virus, HMPD, HVR, HMPR) and a global average, but the paper does not say how the global average is weighted.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 5.3 and Table 3. Task metadata main_score

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Four other models alongside METAGENE-1: DNABERT-2, DNABERT-S, NT-2.5b-Multi and NT-2.5b-1000g.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 3 column headings

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: One is described and it is weak: the paper says the task data come from the Human Microbiome Project and from held-out portions of its own metagenomic dataset. No sequence identity cut-off, time split or held-out taxonomic group is described, and the baselines' own pretraining corpora are not discussed in this context.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 5.3

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: None is reported: Table 3 prints one value per model and task with no interval or replicate. The code fixes the seed at 42 before loading and splitting each task, so a repeated run uses the same split rather than giving a spread.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 3. Task files: load_data

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a nucleotide sequence. In the classification tasks it carries a sample-level label; in the clustering tasks the sequence column is renamed to sentences and its taxonomy becomes the label list.
facts.source_locator: README.md: introduction. HumanVirusReferenceClustering.py: dataset_transform

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human-associated: viruses that infect a human host, human virus reference sequences, and bacterial and other sequences from human microbiome samples. The tasks' metadata records the domain as Medical, and the task descriptions name the human host.
facts.source_locator: README.md: introduction. Task metadata: description and domains

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: None. The labels are not experimental measurements: they are metagenomic sequencing samples with metadata (disease status, sex, body source, virus of origin) or reference sequences with a taxonomy, and each task's metadata records its annotations as derived.
facts.source_locator: Task metadata: annotations_creators, sample_creation, description

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Sequence only. A model is called as an encoder over a list of sequences and must return one vector each; the paper takes every model's embedding by mean pooling the last hidden state, and the repository's example truncates to 512 tokens.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 5.3. README.md: Example Using METAGENE-1

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Frozen embeddings only. The paper calls this a zero-shot assessment of representations: the model is not fine-tuned, and the only fitting is the logistic regression trained on a small split for the classification tasks (training fraction 8 divided by the count of the rarest label), with mini-batch k-means for the clustering tasks.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 5.3. HumanVirusClassification.py: __init__ and load_data

strengths.text: The tasks are released as code in a fork of MTEB, with each task's dataset, split rule, evaluation split and main score written in its metadata, so the protocol can be read rather than inferred, and the repository's example lists the sixteen task names needed to reproduce the table.
strengths.source_locator: README.md: Example Using METAGENE-1. HumanVirusClassification.py: TaskMetadata

strengths.text: All models are embedded the same way, by mean pooling the last hidden state, so the comparison does not mix pooling conventions.

Both classification and clustering are included, and the clustering variants vary the number of documents embedded within the same dataset, which exposes how a model behaves at different amounts of context.

limitations.text: The benchmark was introduced by the authors of one of the models compared on it, and in the paper METAGENE-1 has the best global average. Part of the task data is drawn from held-out portions of METAGENE-1's own metagenomic dataset.

Several tasks are very small. The clustering tasks embed at most 40 documents (virus reference) or 27 (HMP reference) in their p2p and small variants and only 3 in their tiny variants, and the classification tasks fit on a split sized to give about 8 examples of the rarest label. Two models already score 1.000 on HVR-s2s-tiny.
limitations.source_locator: Task files: class attributes and load_data. Paper: Table 3

limitations.text: No per-task uncertainty is published, and because each task splits its data once under a fixed seed, repeating a run does not produce a spread to compare small differences against.

The data terms are unstated. Every task's metadata records its licence as not specified, and the dataset repositories are pinned only to the moving revision main, so a later run may not use the same data.

steps.title: Run the sixteen tasks with a model wrapper
steps.shell:
cat > run_gene_mteb.py <<'PY'
import mteb
from mteb.encoder_interface import PromptType
import numpy as np
from tqdm import tqdm
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer
from transformers.trainer_utils import set_seed
import torch


class LlamaWrapper:
    def __init__(self, model_name, seed, max_length=512):
        self.seed = seed
        self.tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
        self.model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
            model_name,
            torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
            trust_remote_code=True,
            device_map="cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "auto")
        self.model.config.pad_token_id = self.tokenizer.pad_token_id
        self.max_length = max_length
        self.model.eval()

    def encode(self, sentences, task_name=None, prompt_type=None, **kwargs):
        set_seed(self.seed)
        batch_size = kwargs.get("batch_size", 32)
        embeddings = []
        for i in tqdm(range(0, len(sentences), batch_size)):
            batch = sentences[i:i + batch_size]
            inputs = self.tokenizer(
                batch, padding=True, truncation=True,
                max_length=self.max_length, return_tensors="pt").to(self.model.device)
            if "token_type_ids" in inputs:
                del inputs["token_type_ids"]
            with torch.no_grad():
                outputs = self.model(**inputs)
                batch_embeddings = outputs.last_hidden_state.mean(dim=1)
            embeddings.extend(batch_embeddings.cpu().to(torch.float32).numpy())
        return np.array(embeddings)


model = LlamaWrapper(model_name="metagene-ai/METAGENE-1", seed=42)
tasks = mteb.get_tasks(tasks=[
    "HumanVirusClassificationOne",
    "HumanVirusClassificationTwo",
    "HumanVirusClassificationThree",
    "HumanVirusClassificationFour",
    "HumanMicrobiomeProjectDemonstrationClassificationDisease",
    "HumanMicrobiomeProjectDemonstrationClassificationSex",
    "HumanMicrobiomeProjectDemonstrationClassificationSource",
    "HumanMicrobiomeProjectDemonstrationMultiLabelClassification",
    "HumanVirusReferenceClusteringP2P",
    "HumanVirusReferenceClusteringS2SAlign",
    "HumanVirusReferenceClusteringS2SSmall",
    "HumanVirusReferenceClusteringS2STiny",
    "HumanMicrobiomeProjectReferenceClusteringP2P",
    "HumanMicrobiomeProjectReferenceClusteringS2SAlign",
    "HumanMicrobiomeProjectReferenceClusteringS2SSmall",
    "HumanMicrobiomeProjectReferenceClusteringS2STiny",
])
evaluation = mteb.MTEB(tasks=tasks)
results = evaluation.run(model)
PY
python run_gene_mteb.py

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: GENEB compares frozen genomic model representations under standardized probe and sample-budget settings. It keeps preprocessing, partitions and random seeds consistent across models and summarizes several biological task categories. Organism and dataset coverage are uneven, so category-specific results remain necessary.

run_recipes.title: Score your own classifier with rewirebench
run_recipes.summary: Prepare a downloaded dataset and score an adapter on accuracy and F1 over the packaged test split.
inputs: The dataset directory the genomic-benchmarks package downloaded.
An adapter returning a class index, or a probability for a binary dataset.
outputs: A local report with accuracy, F1, the coverage and the digest of the sequences it read.

requirements.data: Whatever the package downloaded locally, read from its train and test directories.
requirements.weights: Whatever your own model needs; the runner supplies none.
requirements.licence: Runner code is MIT. The benchmark's own data terms are upstream and unreported here.
requirements.software: Python 3.11 with the pinned rewirebench environment.
requirements.hardware: CPU for scoring. Your own model decides what it needs.

instructions.title: Prepare a dataset
instructions.code:
rewirebench prepare genomic-benchmarks-v2 \
  --source ./genomic_benchmarks --options '{"dataset": "human_nontata_promoters"}' \
  --output ./prepared-promoters
instructions.source_locator: docs/genomic-benchmarks.md at aecb9e79, Prepare, run and score, lines 51-53

instructions.title: Run and score an adapter
instructions.code:
rewirebench run --prepared ./prepared-promoters \
  --adapter my_models.dna:MyAdapter \
  --model-name 'my model' --training-overlap 'unreported' \
  --output ./scored-promoters
instructions.source_locator: docs/genomic-benchmarks.md at aecb9e79, Prepare, run and score, lines 61-64

limitations: Quoted from the runner's documentation and not executed by this repository.
Scoring follows the benchmark's own evaluator; running it does not by itself reproduce a published number.
Class labels are assigned from the sorted class name, because upstream takes them from filesystem order, which differs between machines. Compare class names, not indices.
For the one dataset with three classes the paper does not say which F1 averaging it used, so macro and weighted are both reported and neither is the paper's number.
Genomic Benchmarks v1 prepared artifacts exposed class information in row IDs and must be discarded. V2 uses opaque IDs and label-independent ordering; prepare the dataset again.
This scores a hashed local data copy; it does not certify the official cohort or reproduce a published experiment.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: GUE combines genome sequence classification tasks with supplied partitions and task-specific metrics. Models are fine-tuned on labelled training examples, selected with validation data and scored on test data. Random partitions occur in the suite, so a high score does not automatically demonstrate transfer to unrelated genomes.

sections.body: HEST-Benchmark connects histology patches to spatially measured gene expression. A patch encoder supplies features to a regression model, which predicts highly variable genes. sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The released MassSpecGym MS/MS/molecule dataset, with task-specific inputs and candidate sets. MCES molecular clusters are grouped into fixed training, validation and test folds, stratified by acquisition metadata. Cross-fold molecular bond-edit distance is at least 10; all spectra follow the assigned molecular fold. Task evaluators distinguish molecular exact match/structural similarity, candidate-retrieval hit rate and spectrum similarity. These are separate readouts, not interchangeable scores. Maximum common edge subgraph (MCES) clustering keeps molecules connected by a bond-edit distance below 10 in the same fold. The split additionally balances instrument, collision-energy, adduct and molecule-frequency metadata; this is stronger than simply separating 2D InChIKeys.

steps.title: Run the documented CPU training and test example
steps.shell:
cat > massspecgym_retrieval_example.py <<'PY'
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import pytorch_lightning as pl
from pytorch_lightning import Trainer

from massspecgym.data import RetrievalDataset, MassSpecDataModule
from massspecgym.data.transforms import SpecTokenizer, MolFingerprinter
from massspecgym.models.base import Stage
from massspecgym.models.retrieval.base import RetrievalMassSpecGymModel

class MyDeepSetsRetrievalModel(RetrievalMassSpecGymModel):
    def __init__(
        self,
        hidden_channels: int = 128,
        out_channels: int = 4096,  # fingerprint size
        *args,
        **kwargs
    ):
        """Implement your architecture."""
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)

        self.phi = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(2, hidden_channels),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden_channels, hidden_channels),
            nn.ReLU(),
        )
        self.rho = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(hidden_channels, hidden_channels),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(hidden_channels, out_channels),
            nn.Sigmoid()
        )

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        """Implement your prediction logic."""
        x = self.phi(x)
        x = x.sum(dim=-2)  # sum over peaks
        x = self.rho(x)
        return x

    def step(
        self, batch: dict, stage: Stage
    ) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
        """Implement your custom logic of using predictions for training and inference."""
        # Unpack inputs
        x = batch["spec"]  # input spectra
        fp_true = batch["mol"]  # true fingerprints
        cands = batch["candidates"]  # candidate fingerprints concatenated for a batch
        batch_ptr = batch["batch_ptr"]  # number of candidates per sample in a batch

        # Predict fingerprint
        fp_pred = self.forward(x)

        # Calculate loss
        loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(fp_true, fp_pred)

        # Calculate final similarity scores between predicted fingerprints and retrieval candidates
        fp_pred_repeated = fp_pred.repeat_interleave(batch_ptr, dim=0)
        scores = nn.functional.cosine_similarity(fp_pred_repeated, cands)

        return dict(loss=loss, scores=scores)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Init hyperparameters
    n_peaks = 60
    fp_size = 4096
    batch_size = 32

    # Load dataset
    dataset = RetrievalDataset(
        spec_transform=SpecTokenizer(n_peaks=n_peaks),
        mol_transform=MolFingerprinter(fp_size=fp_size),
    )

    # Init data module
    data_module = MassSpecDataModule(
        dataset=dataset,
        batch_size=batch_size,
        num_workers=4
    )

    # Init model
    model = MyDeepSetsRetrievalModel(out_channels=fp_size)

    # Init trainer
    trainer = Trainer(accelerator="cpu", devices=1, max_epochs=5)

    # Train
    trainer.fit(model, datamodule=data_module)

    # Test
    trainer.test(model, datamodule=data_module)
PY
python massspecgym_retrieval_example.py

instructions.title: Embed and evaluate
instructions.code:
import torch

import mrna_bench as mb
from mrna_bench.embedder import DatasetEmbedder
from mrna_bench.linear_probe import LinearProbeBuilder

device = torch.device("cuda")

dataset = mb.load_dataset("go-mf")
model = mb.load_model("Orthrus", "orthrus-large-6-track", device)

embedder = DatasetEmbedder(model, dataset)
embeddings = embedder.embed_dataset()
embeddings = embeddings.detach().cpu().numpy()

prober = (LinearProbeBuilder(dataset)
    .fetch_embedding_by_embedding_instance("orthrus-large-6", embeddings)
    .build_splitter("homology", species="human", eval_all_splits=False)
    .build_evaluator("multilabel")
    .set_target("target")
    .build()
)

metrics = prober.run_linear_probe(2541)
print(metrics)

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: DMS assays and human clinical variants, with substitution and indel collections kept separate. Five-fold random, contiguous-position and modulo-position cross-validation are separate supervised DMS regimes. The original clinical analysis uses available ClinVar labels with explicit overlap warnings; zero-shot scoring does not fit on assay labels. Zero-shot DMS: Spearman, NDCG, AUC, MCC and top-K recall; supervised DMS: Spearman/MSE; clinical: AUC. Aggregation first groups assays by UniProt ID, then averages functional categories. Supervised DMS evaluations distinguish five-fold random, contiguous-position and modulo-position partitions. The original clinical benchmark explicitly warns that supervised methods may overlap ClinVar labels and that population-frequency training can leak information into benign-variant evaluation.

facts.value: In the original supervised single-substitution analysis, random folds assign mutants, contiguous folds group sequence positions into segments, and modulo folds assign positions by remainder. Five folds are usual; the paper excepts F7YBW8_MESOW and SPG1_STRSG, which have four mutated positions. The pinned supervised scorer uses random splits only for indels; substitution schemes remain separate. Zero-shot scoring does not fit assay labels.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Zero-shot DMS: Spearman, NDCG, AUC, MCC and top-K recall; supervised DMS: Spearman/MSE; clinical: AUC. Aggregation first groups assays by UniProt ID, then averages functional categories.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The README distinguishes sequence-only baselines such as ESM-1v, alignment-based approaches such as DeepSequence/EVE, and sequence-plus-structure approaches such as SaProt; clinical baselines use dbNSFP 4.4a.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Supervised DMS evaluations distinguish five-fold random, contiguous-position and modulo-position partitions. The original clinical benchmark explicitly warns that supervised methods may overlap ClinVar labels and that population-frequency training can leak information into benign-variant evaluation.
facts.source_locator: Sections on supervised DMS and clinical benchmarking

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: For DMS substitution summaries at revision 144fe22, the zero-shot scorer bootstraps 10,000 times within functional categories after averaging by UniProt and category, and reports the standard deviation of differences from the model with the highest aggregate metric. The supervised scorer also reports bootstrap differences, using ProteinNPT as its default reference. These errors are not absolute per-model confidence intervals or variation across model-training seeds.

profile.summary: scIB is an atlas-level single-cell integration benchmark study covering RNA, chromatin-accessibility and simulated datasets. It compares batch removal with preservation of biological variation. The scib Python package and scib-pipeline implement its evaluation workflow.
profile.summary_source_locator: Primary paper Abstract; Results: Single-cell integration benchmarking (scIB), Figure 1 and Table 1; Methods: Datasets and preprocessing; Code availability. Pinned scib README lines 7-33, 62-100.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The published scIB study compares integration methods on 13 atlas-level tasks spanning RNA, chromatin-accessibility and simulated data. Each task defines its batches and biological annotations. Four preprocessing choices combine scaled or unscaled values with full features or highly variable features for the RNA comparisons. Metrics measure batch correction and biological conservation separately. Label-assisted methods must retain that additional-input distinction. The scib package computes metrics and the separate scib-pipeline coordinates integrations; neither software package is itself a fixed dataset or a universal train/test split.

from tdc import BenchmarkGroup
group = BenchmarkGroup(name = 'ADMET_Group', path = 'data/')
predictions_list = []

for seed in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]:
    benchmark = group.get('Caco2_Wang')
    # all benchmark names in a benchmark group are stored in group.dataset_names
    predictions = {}
    name = benchmark['name']
    train_val, test = benchmark['train_val'], benchmark['test']
    train, valid = group.get_train_valid_split(benchmark = name, split_type = 'default', seed = seed)

        # --------------------------------------------- #
        #  Train your model using train, valid, test    #
        #  Save test prediction in y_pred_test variable #
        # --------------------------------------------- #

    predictions[name] = y_pred_test
    predictions_list.append(predictions)

results = group.evaluate_many(predictions_list)

profile.summary: The read classification part of Hall and Coin 2024: label each non-human read in a sputum-like metagenome as Mycobacterium tuberculosis or not. Kraken2 and minimap2 are each run with three databases, standard and custom, on simulated and artificial real Nanopore and Illumina data. It is for people building culture-free tuberculosis sequencing pipelines who need to choose a classifier and database, including on a laptop.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, Classification of Mycobacterium reads

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How accurately each tool and database labels reads as M. tuberculosis, with as few false positives and false negatives as possible, and what it costs in runtime and memory. The authors frame this as a step toward sequencing directly from sputum, where contamination is higher than in culture.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results; Discussion

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Simulated reads mimic sputum: 46% bacteria, 46% human, 6% M. tuberculosis complex and 1% each virus and NTM, 4.5 gigabases of Nanopore and 0.9 of Illumina. The artificial real set combines real reads from three 1000 Genomes people, an M. tuberculosis isolate and the ZymoBIOMICS HMW standard, so each read's true taxon is known. Classification uses the non-human reads left after host removal: 100,733 simulated Nanopore reads, 1,417,015 simulated Illumina pairs, 915,209 real Nanopore reads and 21,172,961 real Illumina pairs. Simulation genomes were kept out of the custom kraken Mycobacterium database.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Kraken2 uses the standard, standard-8 and a custom Mycobacterium database; minimap2 uses an M. tuberculosis database, the Clockwork decontamination database and a Mycobacterium genus database. A true positive is an M. tuberculosis read classified as M. tuberculosis. Each configuration is scored by sensitivity, specificity and Youden's index with Wilson score 95% intervals, plus mean runtime and peak memory over 10 runs with 4 threads.
