profile.summary: This is a benchmark of taxonomic classification and profiling tools, not of models. Eleven methods, five of them written for long reads, were run on public mock community datasets sequenced with PacBio HiFi, Oxford Nanopore and Illumina, where the species present and their intended abundances are known. Each method is scored on how many reads it uses, how precisely and completely it detects the known species, and how close its abundance estimates are to the manufacturer's specification.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Materials and methods

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Three things per method and dataset. Read utilisation: what fraction of the reads the method assigns. Detection: precision, recall and F-score for the known species or genera, where a true positive is a mock community taxon whose read count passes a threshold and a false positive is any taxon not in the community. Abundance accuracy: the L1 distance between estimated and theoretical abundances, with a chi-squared goodness of fit test against the manufacturer's specification.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Detection metrics and Relative abundance estimates

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The datasets are public, empirical sequencing runs of commercial mock communities, chosen over simulations because simulations do not capture real error profiles, read length spread or extraction and library effects. They include a PacBio HiFi run of ATCC MSA-1003 (20 bacterial species in staggered abundances from 18% down to 0.02%; 2.4 million HiFi reads, median length 8.3 kb, 20.54 Gb) and a PacBio HiFi run of ZymoBIOMICS D6331 (17 species including one archaeon and two yeasts, staggered from 14% down to 0.0001%; 1.9 million reads, median 8.1 kb, 17.99 Gb), plus Oxford Nanopore R10 and Q20 runs of ZymoBIOMICS D6300 and Illumina runs of both communities. The truth is the species list and the manufacturer's stated genomic DNA abundances.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Mock community datasets; Relative abundance estimates

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Presence or absence is scored against a minimum percentage of the dataset's total reads, not a fixed read count, because the datasets differ in size. Three thresholds are used: 0.001% (mild), 0.1% (moderate) and 1% (heavy); Table 3 gives the resulting read counts per dataset, for example 24 reads at 0.001% and 24,190 at 1% for HiFi ATCC MSA-1003. Scoring is done at both species and genus level. Abundances are normalised with all false positives summed into an 'Other' category, which is compared against a theoretical abundance of zero, and the chi-squared test uses a Bonferroni correction over the 11 methods, so the altered alpha is 0.0045.

run_guide.summary: Download one mock community dataset and run the paper's own Kraken2 and Bracken commands on it.
prerequisites: Kraken2 version 2.1.1 and Bracken version 2.6.0, the versions the paper used.
The pre-built PlusPF database (RefSeq archaea, bacteria, viruses, plasmid, human, protozoa and fungi, released 27 January 2021).
One mock community dataset, for example HiFi ATCC MSA-1003 from NCBI SRX6095783, converted to FASTA.

steps.title: Get a dataset
steps.shell:
# HiFi ATCC MSA-1003: NCBI PRJNA546278, run SRX6095783
# download with your preferred SRA client and convert to SAMPLE.fasta
steps.explanation: The paper names the accession for each dataset in its availability statement but gives no download command, so this step is an instruction rather than a command.

steps.title: Classify the reads with Kraken2
steps.shell: kraken2 --db PlusPF --threads 24 –report SAMPLE.kreport.txt SAMPLE.fasta > SAMPLE.kraken
steps.explanation: The paper's Kraken2 command, copied as printed. Note that the report flag as printed in the article uses a non-standard dash character.

steps.title: Estimate species abundances with Bracken
steps.shell: bracken -d PlusPF -i SAMPLE.kreport.txt -o SAMPLE.bracken -r 50 -l S -t 10
steps.explanation: The paper's Bracken command, which reads the Kraken2 report and gives species-level abundances.

outputs: A Kraken2 report (SAMPLE.kreport.txt) and read assignments (SAMPLE.kraken), then a Bracken species abundance table (SAMPLE.bracken). The authors' own kreport outputs for all methods and datasets are on the OSF project.
limitations: These commands were read from the paper and have not been executed by Rewire.
They cover two of the eleven methods; the paper gives separate commands and databases for the rest.

profile.summary: A clinical comparison of two metagenomic workflows for detecting microbes in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid: short-read sequencing on MGI and host-depleted nanopore sequencing (HD-ONT). On 62 BALF specimens, each workflow's organism calls are scored against culture, clinical microbiological tests and a composite reference standard by positive and negative percent agreement. It is for clinical microbiology labs weighing short-read against rapid nanopore metagenomics for pneumonia diagnostics.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods, Clinical performance evaluation

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether each sequencing workflow finds the organisms that reference methods find in a patient's BALF, and how many extra organisms it reports. The paper also studies mock communities, but the store's protocols cover only the 62 clinical specimens.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Study design

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Residual BALF specimens with traceable culture results were sequenced with the MGI short-read workflow (MGISEQ-200, single-end 50 bp) and the HD-ONT workflow (nuclease and saponin host depletion, GridION R9.4.1). Reads were host-filtered against GRCh38 and classified against a curated database of 20,484 genomes or sequences. A species was called when normalised reads passed RP20M of at least 3 (short read) or RP10K of at least 1 (HD-ONT).
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, NGS and TGS workflows; Bioinformatic processing; Reference database; Read normalization

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each workflow's organism calls are compared with three references: routine culture; clinical microbiological tests (culture plus qPCR or GeneXpert verification where residual volume allowed); and a composite reference standard that adds organisms detected by both sequencing workflows. Agreement is assessed per organism and summarised as PPA and NPA, restricted to bacteria and fungi. Against the composite standard, the paper reports PPA of 93.3% (NGS) and 90.7% (TGS), and NPA of 77.6% and 83.3%.

name: Plasma mcfDNA sequencing for predicting and diagnosing bloodstream infection in high-risk leukaemia (Wolf et al. 2026)
description: Episode-level sensitivity against blood-culture organisms before and at bloodstream infection onset, and specificity in afebrile control samples.

attributes.task: Detect the blood-culture organism in plasma cell-free DNA before and at bloodstream infection onset
attributes.source_locator: Methods 'Outcomes' and 'Statistical analysis'
attributes.scope_note: Day-by-day sensitivity (Figure 2 and appendix) and the appendix tables were not extracted.
limitations: One commercial assay; no comparator workflow.

profile.summary: This is one prospective cohort study's evaluation of a single commercial test, not a reusable suite. Plasma microbial cell-free DNA metagenomic sequencing (mcfDNA-Seq) was run on leftover plasma from children and young people treated for high-risk leukaemia at one hospital, and asked whether it names the organism a blood culture would later grow. The measures are predictive sensitivity in the 3 days before bloodstream infection onset, diagnostic sensitivity on the day of or after diagnosis, and specificity in control samples from the same patients when they had no fever or infection. It tells a reader how far ahead of a positive culture a plasma sequencing test can call the pathogen, and at what false-positive cost.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Summary, Background and Methods; Methods, Procedures and Outcomes

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a plasma sequencing test can detect the causative organism of a bloodstream infection before the patient has symptoms, which is what a pre-emptive treatment strategy would need. The authors state that no validated screening test exists for this. Three quantities are reported: predictive sensitivity over day minus 3 to day minus 1, diagnostic sensitivity over day 0 to day 1, and specificity in control samples, where specificity means that no bacterium or yeast was reported at all.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Summary, Background; Methods, Procedures and Outcomes

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Leftover clinical plasma was collected prospectively, up to once a day, from patients under 25 receiving leukaemia care at St Jude Children's Research Hospital between 9 August 2017 and 28 February 2022, who were at high risk of bloodstream infection and expected to stay at least 7 days. Blood collected for routine haematology was held at 4 degrees C, processed to plasma and frozen at minus 80 degrees C. A bloodstream infection was defined by the National Healthcare Safety Network laboratory-confirmed classification, with onset set at the collection time of the first positive blood culture. Samples from 7 days before to 1 day after onset were tested, with up to two control samples per episode from patients with no fever or infection within 7 days either side. 158 participants were enrolled; of 127 bloodstream infection episodes, 94 in 60 participants had at least one evaluable sample, and there were 162 evaluable control episodes. 19 episodes had already been reported in the study's pilot phase, and the numbers here are consolidated across both phases.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Study design and participants, Procedures; Results. ClinicalTrials.gov record: design and status modules

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Testing was done in one accredited laboratory (Karius, Redwood City, California), which reported, for each organism found against a proprietary reference genome database, a DNA fragment concentration in molecules per microlitre of plasma. Samples were tested in batches and the laboratory was masked to whether a sample came from an infection episode or a control. An episode counts as a hit only if every culture-confirmed organism was detected, including in polymicrobial episodes, which is why polymicrobial infections score lower. Each episode was treated as an independent event. The study followed Simon's optimal two-stage design with a favourable sensitivity of 50% and a target of 100 evaluable episodes, and results are given both on raw data and with logical imputation of missing values. Exploratory analyses restricted results to bacteria or to common bloodstream infection pathogens, which are the genera accounting for more than 1% of central line-associated bloodstream infections in children with cancer in a national database, and applied a post-hoc concentration cutoff of 140 molecules per microlitre chosen from a receiver operating characteristic analysis with an area under the curve of 0.73.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Procedures, Outcomes and Statistical analysis; Results

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: Consolidated predictive sensitivity over day minus 3 to minus 1 was 51.9% (95% CI 40.5 to 63.1) across all episodes, from 42 positives among 81 evaluable episodes, and 53.8% (42.2 to 65.2) for bacterial infections. Diagnostic sensitivity on day 0 or 1 was 81.3% (71.0 to 89.1), from 65 of 80 evaluable episodes, and 83.1% (72.9 to 90.7) for bacterial infections. Sensitivity was lowest at day minus 7 and rose daily towards diagnosis. Specificity in the 162 control episodes was 82.7% (76.0 to 88.2) for any organism, 88.9% (83.0 to 93.3) when restricted to common bloodstream infection pathogens, and 93.8% (88.9 to 97.0) with both that restriction and the 140 molecules per microlitre cutoff. Sensitivity was higher in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia than acute myeloid leukaemia (adjusted odds ratio 11.1, 1.7 to 74.2) and lower in polymicrobial infections (0.0, 0.0 to 0.2). Clinical false positives were associated with gastrointestinal disturbance alone (p=0.037) and with gastrointestinal disturbance plus recent high-dose cytarabine (p=0.012). Of 80 episodes with an evaluable sample at diagnosis, 29 (36%) carried an extra organism not grown in culture, but an untreated organism was detected in only 8 (10%).
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results; Tables 2 and 3; Summary, Findings

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One cohort at one hospital. 158 participants enrolled, 94 evaluable bloodstream infection episodes in 60 participants out of 127 episodes, and 162 evaluable control episodes. Table 2 gives the evaluable counts per analysis: 81 episodes for the predictive period and 80 for the diagnostic period on raw data, 91 of the 94 episodes being bacterial. The registry records 160 participants as the actual enrolment.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results; Table 2. ClinicalTrials.gov record: enrollmentInfo

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: There is no train and test split: this is a diagnostic accuracy study, and every evaluable sample contributes to the estimate. The division is by time window relative to culture-confirmed onset (day minus 7 to minus 4, day minus 3 to minus 1, day 0 to 1) and by case against control. Results are also reported as a pilot phase and a completion phase, consolidated here; the 140 molecules per microlitre cutoff was derived from the consolidated data after the fact rather than on a held-out set.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Procedures and Statistical analysis; Results

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Sensitivity and specificity with 95% confidence intervals, higher better. Predictive sensitivity is the proportion of evaluable episodes with at least one predictive sample in which every organism grown in blood culture was also detected by mcfDNA-Seq in at least one sample from that window; diagnostic sensitivity is the same over day 0 to 1; specificity is the proportion of control samples with no bacterium or yeast reported. A generalised linear mixed model gives adjusted odds ratios for clinical factors.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Procedures and Statistical analysis; Tables 2 and 3

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: No comparator workflow was run. The reference standard is clinical blood culture, collected from all lumens of indwelling central venous catheters and, at clinician discretion, peripheral blood, in patients with new fever or clinical concern. The only external comparison is in the Research in context panel, which cites two small earlier studies with 16 predictive episodes each reporting predictive sensitivity of 87.5% in adults in intensive care and 75.0% in children with leukaemia, the latter being this study's own pilot phase. The study's prespecified favourable sensitivity of 50% acts as the threshold the result is judged against.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Procedures and Statistical analysis; Research in context, Evidence before this study

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Masking rather than data separation, as suits a diagnostic study. The testing laboratory was masked to whether a sample was from an infection episode or a control, and samples were tested in batches. Control samples were required to have no fever or infection within 7 days either side. The organism definition and the onset time come from an external classification (National Healthcare Safety Network) rather than from the test under evaluation. The 140 molecules per microlitre cutoff, by contrast, was derived from the same consolidated data it is then reported on.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Procedures; Results

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: 95% confidence intervals on every sensitivity and specificity, and on the adjusted odds ratios; p values for the clinical false-positive associations. Each result is also given twice, on raw data and with logical imputation of missing values, which is the study's way of showing the effect of missing samples: for example predictive sensitivity 51.9% raw against 51.2% imputed. There are no replicate runs of the assay, and the paper notes no missing data for the variables in the mixed model.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Tables 2 and 3; Results; Methods, Statistical analysis

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A bloodstream infection episode for the sensitivity measures, scored from the plasma samples available in a time window, and a control episode or sample for specificity. The paper also reports per-day results, where the unit is a single plasma sample on a given day relative to onset.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Statistical analysis; Results

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human patients, with bacterial and fungal pathogens as the detection targets. 91 of the 94 episodes were bacterial; specificity for any organism is defined over bacteria and yeast and excludes Burkholderia species, moulds, viruses and parasites. Participants were people younger than 25 receiving leukaemia therapy.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 2 and Table 3 footnotes; Methods, Study design and participants

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Plasma microbial cell-free DNA metagenomic sequencing, run as a commercial clinical test by Karius in an accredited laboratory, which reports each organism's DNA fragment concentration in molecules per microlitre against a proprietary reference genome database. The comparator measurement is clinical blood culture. Plasma came from leftover clinical haematology samples.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Procedures

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: A plasma sample, and nothing else at the point of the test: the laboratory was masked to sample status, so no clinical context was available to it. Clinical variables (leukaemia type, counts, gastrointestinal disturbance, cytarabine, transplant) enter only the later modelling of what drives sensitivity and false positives, not the detection itself.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Procedures; Results

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: None of the machine learning kind: the test is a fixed commercial assay with a proprietary database and was not trained or tuned on this cohort. The only parameter fitted to these data is the post-hoc 140 molecules per microlitre reporting cutoff, chosen from a receiver operating characteristic analysis of the consolidated results.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Procedures; Results

strengths.text: The design is prospective, registered and masked: samples were collected daily in advance of any infection, the study is registered as NCT03226158, and the testing laboratory did not know which samples came from infection episodes.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Study design and participants and Procedures. ClinicalTrials.gov record

strengths.text: The success criterion is strict and stated in advance: every culture-confirmed organism in an episode had to be detected, the predictive window was defined a priori, and the target sensitivity of 50% and sample size of 100 episodes were set by a two-stage design before the data were read.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Procedures and Statistical analysis

strengths.text: Every headline figure carries a confidence interval and is reported both on raw data and with imputation for missing samples, and the exploratory cuts (bacteria only, common pathogens, concentration cutoff) are labelled as exploratory or post-hoc.

limitations.text: One assay and no comparator. The test is a single commercial product whose reference database is proprietary, so a reader cannot tell which part of performance comes from the laboratory process, the database or the reporting threshold, and no alternative workflow was run on the same samples.

One centre and one patient group: people under 25 treated for leukaemia at a single hospital, with study disruptions for staffing in 2018 to 2019 and for pandemic restrictions in 2020. Predictive sensitivity also differed sharply by leukaemia type, so the pooled figure should not be read as applying to every patient.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Study design and participants; Results

limitations.text: Nothing can be re-run or re-analysed by a third party. The study protocol is in the appendix, but individual participant data are not available, and no sequencing data, code or sample-level table is released.

The concentration cutoff that gives the best specificity was derived from the same consolidated data it is reported on, so the 93.8% figure is not an out-of-sample estimate. Specificity also depends on a definition that excludes Burkholderia species, moulds, viruses and parasites.

profile.summary: The evaluation from the BERTax paper: assign 1,500 nt genome fragments to superkingdom, phylum and, in one dataset, genus. BERTax is compared with Kraken2, sourmash, MMseqs2, minimap2 and DeepMicrobes, all given the same reference or training data, on a closely related split and a genus-held-out split. It is for people choosing a taxonomic classifier, especially for sequences without close relatives in reference databases.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Comparison to Other Classification Approaches

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How well a method assigns the taxonomic origin of a DNA fragment when close relatives are, or are not, in the reference data. The distantly related dataset simulates unknown sequences by holding out whole genera.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Significance; Three Evaluation Datasets

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Genomes of archaea, eukaryotes, bacteria and viruses were taken from NCBI, and 1 million 1,500 nt fragments per superkingdom were extracted, then clustered at 80% identity. Fine-tuning data keep phyla with at least 10,000 fragments: 30 phylum classes and 2,328,584 samples. The closely related dataset tests on 2,000 random samples per phylum; the distantly related dataset tests on whole held-out genera, balanced to 1,780 samples per phylum; the final model dataset adds 2 million eukaryotic and bacterial fragments and has 5 superkingdom, 44 phylum and 156 genus classes, split like the closely related dataset. In every case 95% of the rest is training and 5% validation.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Data, Pretraining Dataset, Preparing Data for Fine-Tuning, Three Evaluation Datasets

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each tool is scored by macro average precision (AveP) at superkingdom and phylum, and at genus for the final dataset. Database tools get only the training partition as reference, default parameters are used, and MMseqs2 is also run with taxonomy parameters to obtain a confidence for precision-recall curves. DeepMicrobes is trained on the same data. The share of sequences each tool classifies is reported alongside, since database tools leave some unclassified.

profile.summary: This is the evaluation published with MetageNN, a long-read taxonomic classifier. Six tools assign Oxford Nanopore reads from 81 verified bacterial isolates to a genus, all of them indexing the same 516 reference genomes, in two settings: when the read's own species is in the database, and when it is not. The same tools are then run on 30 pseudo-mock communities built from the out-of-database isolates, and Table 1 records each tool's database size and classification speed. It is useful to someone choosing a read classifier and wanting to know how each behaves when the species is missing from the reference set.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results summary; Methods, Test datasets and Databases; Table 1

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a tool can put a long read in the right genus, and what happens when the read's species has no genome in the reference database. The authors set the problem up around that gap: the SRA has Nanopore data for only 489 unique bacterial species while RefSeq had complete genomes for more than 6800, so a classifier is often asked about a species it has never seen. The second question is cost: how much disk the database needs and how many reads per second the tool classifies.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, MetageNN model; Results for Species out of the database settings; Table 1

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The test data are real Nanopore reads with a checked ground truth. The authors searched the SRA for R.9.4.1 Nanopore datasets from bacterial isolates whose species had a RefSeq genome, confirmed the strain name matched, then assembled each read set with Flye and two rounds of medaka polishing and required average nucleotide identity above 99% to the reference. That left 81 strains, subsampled to about 20,000 reads each. The 47 strains whose genome is in the reference set form the Species in the database set and the remaining 34 form the Species out of the database set. The main database is the 47 genomes expanded about tenfold with randomly chosen RefSeq representative genomes, giving 516 genomes across 505 species and 311 genera; the repository's list of those assemblies has 516 lines. A smaller 47-genome database was used only for model and hyperparameter choices and for the comparison against other deep learning classifiers.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Test datasets and Databases. Repository: data/main_database_list_of_genomes.txt

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Every tool indexes the same main database, and the non-machine-learning tools are run at their default settings. Reads are classified at genus rank and scored by sensitivity, precision and F1 per bacterial isolate, then averaged across isolates within a dataset; differences against MetageNN are tested with a Wilcoxon rank sum test. Error bars in the figures are the standard deviation across isolates. MetageNN itself was trained on 8x coverage of the main database genomes, about 17 million 1 kbp sequences, with 200 validation sequences per genome, and classifies a read by splitting it into non-overlapping 1 kbp chunks and taking a majority vote, accepting a call only at probability 0.5 or above. GeNet was given a matched parameter count and the same training data so that the difference between the two is mainly how they encode a long read.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Databases; Evaluation metrics; Experimental setup; Fig. 3 caption

sections.title: The community-level test
sections.body: Thirty pseudo-mock communities were assembled from the reads of the out-of-database isolates, each with a random number of species between 20 and 34 and up to 100,000 reads log-distributed across them. Two things are reported: the percentage of reads a tool classifies, and sensitivity, precision and F1 for the presence or absence of a genus at cumulative read thresholds of 0.001%, 0.1% and 1% of the reads in the dataset, which is about 1, 100 and 1000 reads. GeNet was dropped from this comparison because of its performance in the read-level test. MetageNN classified 93.26% of the reads, ahead of MMseqs2 at 85.49%, Kraken2 at 64.90%, MEGAN-LR at 53.06% and MetaMaps at 37.30%.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Experimental setup for the pseudo-mock analysis; Read classification results

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: The two settings separate the tools. When the species is in the database, Kraken2, MetaMaps and MEGAN-LR have the best average F1, sensitivity and precision and beat MetageNN. When it is not, MetageNN has the highest sensitivity along with MMseqs2, improving on MetaMaps, Kraken2, GeNet and MEGAN-LR by 100%, 23%, 17% and 36%; its precision is slightly lower than MetaMaps, Kraken2 and MMseqs2, and only the gap to MEGAN-LR is significant. Over both sets together MMseqs2 is first on F1 and sensitivity with 0.85 and 0.81, then Kraken2 with 0.83 and 0.79. Every tool does worse when three or fewer species share the tested genus. Table 1 gives database size and speed: MetageNN uses 0.839 GB at 1424 reads per second, against 3.7 GB for Kraken2, 5.1 GB for MEGAN-LR and 27.8 GB for MMseqs2.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results for all genomes; Results for Species in the database settings; Results for Species out of the database settings; Table 1

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository publishes the model code, the genome and isolate lists and the hyperparameter files, not the benchmark harness. Requirements are installed by a shell script. Sequences are turned into canonical 6-mer profiles with the Phylopythia k-mer counter, fasta2kmers2, and training is one command that reads a settings JSON. Only the small-database training set, at 1x coverage, is offered for download, through a link in the data folder; the main-database training data and the test read sets are not in the repository, only lists of the SRA identifiers and RefSeq assemblies they come from.
sections.source_locator: Repository: README.md, Requirements, Counting k-mers, Settings and Training; data/README.txt

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Three test sets plus one reference database. Species in the database: Nanopore reads from 47 bacterial isolates, about 20,000 reads each. Species out of the database: reads from the remaining 34 isolates. Mock, Species out of DB: 30 pseudo-mock communities of 20 to 34 species each with up to 100,000 reads. The shared main database holds 516 genome assemblies covering 505 species and 311 genera; the repository's list of those assemblies has 516 lines. A separate small database of the 47 genomes was used for parameter choices only.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Test datasets and Databases; Experimental setup for the pseudo-mock analysis. Repository: data/main_database_list_of_genomes.txt

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: The split is by whether the test species is in the reference database, not by random sampling. Training sequences are 1 kbp windows sampled from the database genomes (8x coverage of the main database, about 17 million samples; 1x coverage of the small database, about 235,000 sequences), validation is 200 sequences per genome drawn the same way with different seeds, and the test reads are real Nanopore reads from isolates. The 34 out-of-database isolates have no genome in the database at all.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Test datasets and Databases; Experimental setup

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Sensitivity, precision and F1 at genus rank, higher better, averaged across bacterial isolates for the read-level tests and across the 30 communities for the community-level test, where presence of a genus is decided at cumulative read thresholds of 0.001%, 0.1% and 1%. The community test also reports the percentage of reads classified, higher better. Table 1 reports database memory in GB, lower better, and speed in reads per second, higher better.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Evaluation metrics; Experimental setup for the pseudo-mock analysis; Table 1

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Five classifiers beside MetageNN: MetaMaps and MEGAN-LR (alignment based, with minimap2 alignments for MEGAN-LR), MMseqs2 with a nucleotide database, Kraken2 for k-mer matching, and GeNet as the deep learning representative. DeepMicrobes and GeNet were also compared on the small database for training and inference cost and for robustness to simulated errors; GeNet was dropped from the community-level test.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Baselines (both sections); Results; Experimental setup for the pseudo-mock analysis

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Two. The Species out of the database setting removes the test species' genome from the reference set altogether, and the results are further stratified by how many species share the tested genus (exactly one, two or three, more than three), which separates the easy cases from the hard ones. Within the model's own data, validation sequences are drawn with different seeds from the training sequences. Test reads are real reads whose identity was confirmed by assembly and an average nucleotide identity above 99% to the reference, so the ground truth does not come from the classifier under test.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Test datasets; Results for Species out of the database settings; Experimental setup

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Spread across isolates and a significance test, but no repeated runs. Figure error bars are the standard deviation across the ONT bacterial isolates, and MetageNN is compared with each baseline by Wilcoxon rank sum test with significance marked on the figures. No seeds, repeated trainings or confidence intervals for the aggregate numbers are reported.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Evaluation metrics; Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 captions

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is an Oxford Nanopore sequencing read, classified to a genus; MetageNN works on non-overlapping 1 kbp chunks of that read and votes. For the community-level test the unit is instead a pseudo-mock community, and the call is whether a genus is present in it.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Experimental setup; Experimental setup for the pseudo-mock analysis

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Bacteria only. 81 bacterial strains provide the reads, and the main database holds 516 bacterial genome assemblies across 505 species and 311 genera from RefSeq. No host, virus, fungus or archaeon is part of the evaluation.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Test datasets and Databases. Repository: data/README.txt

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Oxford Nanopore whole-genome sequencing of bacterial isolates on R.9.4.1 flow cells, taken from the SRA. The labels are not an assay readout: each read's true genus follows from the isolate it was sequenced from, after the strain match was confirmed by assembly and average nucleotide identity. Simulated reads from the BadReads tool were used separately to test robustness at 95%, 90% and 80% median accuracy.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Test datasets; Experimental setup for the small-database experiments

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Nucleotide sequence and the shared reference database, nothing else. Every tool indexes the same 516 genomes; MetageNN reads only canonical 6-mer profiles of 1 kbp windows, which the authors chose because short k-mer profiles are less disturbed by sequencing errors and are read-length agnostic.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Databases and MetageNN model. Repository: README.md, Counting k-mers

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Mixed by tool, which is part of the comparison. The learned models (MetageNN, GeNet, DeepMicrobes) are trained from scratch on sequences sampled from the database genomes, with early stopping on validation loss and hyperparameters tuned on the 1x dataset; MetageNN took three days on four GPUs and GeNet about six. The alignment and k-mer tools are not trained: their indices are built from the same genomes and they run at default settings.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Experimental setup (both sections). Repository: settings/MetageNN_settings_main_database.json

strengths.text: Every tool queries the same 516-genome database and the non-learned tools run at their defaults, so the comparison is not confounded by different reference sets.
The ground truth is checked rather than assumed: each isolate's strain match was confirmed by assembling its reads and requiring average nucleotide identity above 99% to the reference genome.
The missing-genome case is tested directly and then stratified by how many species share the tested genus, which shows that all tools degrade when three or fewer references are available.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results for Species out of the database settings

strengths.text: Cost is reported beside accuracy: Table 1 gives each tool's database memory and reads per second on the same data, so a reader can see what a given accuracy costs.

limitations.text: The benchmark was designed and run by the developers of one of the tools in it, and MetageNN is the tool it is built to show, including the choice to drop GeNet from the community-level comparison.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results summary; Experimental setup for the pseudo-mock analysis

limitations.text: The reference database is small by clinical standards: 516 genomes over 505 species, where the authors note RefSeq had complete genomes for more than 6800 bacterial species. A tool's behaviour here need not carry over to a full-size index.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Databases and MetageNN model

limitations.text: Scope is narrow: bacterial isolates only, genus rank only, one sequencing chemistry (R.9.4.1 Nanopore), and the authors call the model itself a proof of concept.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Test datasets and Experimental setup. Repository: README.md

limitations.text: The per-tool sensitivity, precision and F1 values live only in bar plots (Figures 3 and 4), and no result table or file of them is published, so a reader cannot read exact numbers for most comparisons. The repository ships the model code and the data lists, not a runner for the benchmark, and only the 1x small-database training set is offered for download.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Fig. 3 and Fig. 4 captions; Availability of data and materials. Repository: README.md, Data; data/README.txt

run_guide.summary: Install the repository's requirements, turn genome segments into 6-mer profiles, and train MetageNN on the small database with its published settings file.
prerequisites: The dependencies installed by the repository's install_requirements.sh.
The Phylopythia k-mer counting tool, fasta2kmers2, from the kmer_counting repository the README references.
The small-database training set at 1x coverage, downloaded through the link in the repository's data folder.
The saved main-database settings file sets gpus to 0; the small-database settings file was not read. The paper trained MetageNN on four GPUs.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/csb5/MetageNN
cd MetageNN
git checkout --detach d7c858cee1b88bf78fb1ea7d120b3be180a52b69
steps.explanation: The repository address is the one the paper's availability note gives. The clone and checkout lines were added here to pin the version these steps were read from.
steps.source_locator: Paper: Availability of data and materials

steps.title: Install the requirements
steps.shell: bash install_requirements.sh
steps.explanation: The single command the README gives under Requirements.

steps.title: Count canonical 6-mers for the sampled sequences
steps.shell: fasta2kmers2 -i path_to_file/genome_segments.fasta -j 6 -k 6 -s 0 -l 0 -n 1 -f k_mers_counted.6mer
steps.explanation: The README's own k-mer counting command, with its save_file variable substituted into the -i flag. It counts canonical 6-mers of a FASTA file of sequences sampled from genomes; the paper used 1 kbp sequences.
steps.source_locator: Repository: README.md, Counting k-mers. Paper: Methods, Experimental setup

steps.title: Train on the small database
steps.shell: python code/MetageNN_train.py -s settings/MetageNN_settings_small_database.json
steps.explanation: The README's training command. The settings file holds the hyperparameters and the paths the loader expects; the main-database file, read here, sets a layer width of 3000, a 6144-dimensional k-mer input, 500 epochs, a learning rate of 0.001, a batch size of 1024 and the training arrays it loads.

outputs: A trained model written to the folder named by save_folder in the settings file, which is models.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.

The main-database training data and the isolate read sets are not distributed: the repository gives only the lists of RefSeq assemblies and SRA identifiers, and only the small-database 1x training set is downloadable.
The repository states no licence.

profile.summary: This is a molecular identification test: given one tandem mass spectrum, a model predicts a molecular fingerprint, and that fingerprint is used to rank a pool of candidate molecules drawn from PubChem for the spectrum's molecular formula. The pool and the fingerprints come from the MIST codebase and its public CANOPUS data set, which the MIST authors have since renamed NPLIB1. The record holds the version of this evaluation reported by the DreaMS paper, whose Extended Data Table 1 prints retrieval accuracy at top 1 to top 200 and the cosine similarity between predicted and true fingerprints for feed-forward, MIST and DreaMS models. It is useful to anyone comparing methods that annotate untargeted metabolomics spectra by database lookup.
profile.summary_source_locator: DreaMS: Results (Transfer learning to MS/MS spectrum annotation tasks), Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction), Extended Data Table 1; MIST README.md: Data

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The capability under test is structure annotation from a single spectrum without a reference spectrum of the same molecule. A model reads the spectrum, outputs a molecular fingerprint, and the fingerprint is compared with the fingerprints of candidate molecules to rank them. What is scored is whether the true molecule appears near the top of that ranking, which is the question a metabolomics analyst actually faces. The evaluation also reports how close the predicted fingerprint is to the true one, which is a different thing: the DreaMS authors note that their model does better at retrieval while scoring lower on fingerprint cosine similarity than MIST, and that the same pattern was reported for SIRIUS against MIST.
sections.source_locator: DreaMS: Results (Transfer learning to MS/MS spectrum annotation tasks); Extended Data Table 1 footnote

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The spectra are the public CANOPUS data set, extracted from GNPS and prepared for the 2021 CANOPUS methods paper, which the MIST repository calls canopus_train and has since renamed NPLIB1. The DreaMS paper describes it as covering 8,000 spectra from 7,000 unique molecules. The candidate pools are built by the MIST codebase: one pool per spectrum, holding positive candidates, which are PubChem molecules sharing the first 14 characters of the InChI key with the true molecule, including the true molecule, and negative candidates, which are molecules with the same molecular formula. The MIST repository stores these pools in an HDF5 file that is not part of the data download because it is larger than 5 GB, and says it is built with the relevant isomers for the data set. Splits are shipped as tables of split name and category with the values train, validation, test or exclude, and the README recommends three named split files for future comparisons.
sections.source_locator: DreaMS: Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction); MIST README.md: Data, Experiments

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model must produce a fingerprint for each test spectrum. The MIST retrieval script computes a distance between the predicted fingerprint and each candidate's fingerprint, cosine distance being one of the options, sorts the candidates by that distance and keeps the top k. The analysis script then finds the rank of the true molecule in each list and reports, for k in 1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 500, the fraction of spectra whose true molecule is within the first k candidates, so higher is better. Where two candidates tie in distance the script takes the worse of the two positions, which the README describes as a change from the earlier optimistic reporting. The DreaMS paper reports accuracy at top k for k up to 200, in per cent, counting a hit for any candidate that shares the first 14 characters of the true molecule's InChI key, together with the cosine similarity between predicted and true fingerprints, and notes that this cosine similarity is the inverted test loss. The DreaMS authors state that for this benchmark they did not use their own Murcko histogram split rule for deciding when to stop fine-tuning, as they did for their other tasks, but kept the split of the benchmark established by the MIST authors.
sections.source_locator: DreaMS: Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction), Results, Extended Data Table 1 footnote; retrieval_fp.py: get_dist_fn and rank_indices; analyze_rankings.py: run_analysis; MIST README.md: Change log

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Install the MIST environment, download the public CANOPUS data, rebuild the retrieval HDF5 file from PubChem because it is not shipped, train a fingerprint model on the data set, then run retrieval and the analysis. The README gives one script for each of these steps in the public data retrieval section, and the analysis step calls analyze_rankings.py on the saved ranking files.
sections.source_locator: MIST README.md: Install and setup, Data, Experiments (Public data retrieval analysis); eval_retrieval.py

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: The public CANOPUS spectra data set in the MIST repository, called canopus_train there and renamed NPLIB1 by its authors, extracted from GNPS and prepared for the 2021 CANOPUS methods paper. The DreaMS paper describes the whole benchmark as 8,000 spectra from 7,000 unique molecules. The candidate molecules come from PubChem and are kept in a retrieval HDF5 file over 5 GB that the repository does not ship.
facts.source_locator: DreaMS: Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction); MIST README.md: Data

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: The MIST repository's own splits, kept as tables of split name against the categories train, validation, test or exclude, with three split files the README recommends for comparisons. The DreaMS paper states that for this benchmark it kept the split established by the MIST authors rather than its own Murcko histogram split, which it used for its other tasks. No saved file gives the number of spectra in the test fold.
facts.source_locator: MIST README.md: Data, Experiments (CSI fingerprint comparison); DreaMS: Results (Transfer learning to MS/MS spectrum annotation tasks)

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Retrieval accuracy at top k, higher is better, reported in per cent by DreaMS for k of 1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100 and 200: the share of test spectra for which a positive molecule falls in the first k ranked candidates. The MIST analysis script reports top k accuracy for the same values of k plus 500, but counts a hit only for the exact InChI key from the labels file rather than the 14-character prefix. The secondary metric is the cosine similarity between the predicted and the true fingerprint, higher is better, which DreaMS describes as the inverted test loss.
facts.source_locator: DreaMS: Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction), Extended Data Table 1 footnote; analyze_rankings.py: run_analysis

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Five reference methods in DreaMS Extended Data Table 1: a feed-forward network predicting fingerprints, with top 1 accuracy 17.309, a feed-forward contrastive model, MIST predicting fingerprints, top 1 29.368, MIST contrastive, and MIST contrastive plus fingerprint, top 1 30.703. DreaMS fingerprint, the paper's own model, reports top 1 32.731. The contrastive variants train with batches of PubChem molecules of the same molecular formula and a noise contrastive estimation loss.
facts.source_locator: DreaMS: Extended Data Table 1 and its footnote

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The split files mark molecules as train, validation, test or exclude, and the MIST README states that test set molecules must be kept out of the augmented training spectra. The DreaMS authors criticise structure-disjoint splitting of spectral libraries as leaky for fingerprint prediction, because closely similar structures end up in different folds, and that is why they designed their Murcko histogram splits, which they did not apply to this benchmark. No saved file states a structural similarity cut-off used for the CANOPUS split itself.
facts.source_locator: MIST README.md: Change log; DreaMS: Methods (Murcko histograms algorithm for splitting molecular datasets)

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: None reported. DreaMS Extended Data Table 1 prints a single number per method and metric, with no error bars, seeds or repeated runs, and the MIST README says ensembles were removed from the updated code. The MIST analysis script writes one metric value per k from one ranking file.
facts.source_locator: DreaMS: Extended Data Table 1; MIST README.md: Change log; analyze_rankings.py

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One tandem mass spectrum with a candidate pool. Each example is a single MS/MS spectrum of one molecule, together with the pool of PubChem candidates assembled for it, and the prediction is a molecular fingerprint used to rank that pool.
facts.source_locator: DreaMS: Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction)

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Not applicable in the usual sense: the examples are small molecules and their spectra, not sequences from an organism. The spectra come from GNPS and the candidates from PubChem, and no saved file attributes the data to particular species.
facts.source_locator: MIST README.md: Data; DreaMS: Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction)

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Tandem mass spectrometry. The labels are the known molecular structures of library spectra, from which Morgan fingerprints are computed as the prediction target, and the candidate labels are PubChem structures matched by InChI key prefix or molecular formula.
facts.source_locator: DreaMS: Results (Transfer learning to MS/MS spectrum annotation tasks); Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction)

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The spectrum, and whatever derived features a method chooses. DreaMS predicts fingerprints from the raw spectrum in a single forward pass and notes that this avoids assigning chemical formulas to peaks or building fragmentation trees, while MIST is built on molecular formulas assigned to individual peaks and the repository also feeds in subformula and MAGMa annotations. The retrieval step needs the candidate pool for the spectrum's molecular formula.
facts.source_locator: DreaMS: Results (Transfer learning to MS/MS spectrum annotation tasks); MIST README.md: Data

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Supervised fine-tuning or training on the benchmark's training split. DreaMS fine-tunes its pre-trained network end to end with a cosine similarity loss on the fingerprints; MIST trains its fingerprint model on the same data, optionally with a contrastive model on top and with augmented spectra from a forward model. There is no zero-shot setting.
facts.source_locator: DreaMS: Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction); MIST README.md: Training models, Experiments

strengths.text: The scoring is the question an analyst asks: whether the right structure is in the top k of a candidate list, rather than how close a predicted fingerprint is. The DreaMS authors show these two can disagree, their model ranking better while scoring lower on fingerprint similarity.

The code is public under the MIT licence and the data are publicly downloadable, though no licence is stated for the CANOPUS spectra in the files read here; the candidate pools are built by a published script, and the repository names the split files to compare against, so another group can reproduce the same setup.

Ties are scored conservatively. The current analysis script takes the worst position among candidates tied at the same distance, which the MIST authors adopted in place of their earlier optimistic reporting.
strengths.source_locator: MIST README.md: Change log; analyze_rankings.py: run_analysis

limitations.text: It is small. The DreaMS authors state the benchmark covers 8,000 spectra from 7,000 unique molecules and, citing an assessment of how MIST generalises after training on it, describe their own fine-tuning result as a proof of concept rather than a production-ready fingerprint predictor.

The split is the MIST authors' own, and the DreaMS authors argue in the same paper that structure-disjoint splits of spectral libraries leak for fingerprint prediction, since near-identical structures can fall in different folds. They applied their own stricter split rule to their other tasks but not to this one.
limitations.source_locator: DreaMS: Results (Transfer learning to MS/MS spectrum annotation tasks); Methods (Murcko histograms algorithm for splitting molecular datasets)

limitations.text: Rerunning it is heavy and not fully packaged. The retrieval candidate file is over 5 GB and is not distributed, so it has to be rebuilt from PubChem, and the comparison numbers in DreaMS come with no repeats or error bars.
limitations.source_locator: MIST README.md: Data; DreaMS: Extended Data Table 1

limitations.text: The counting rule is not identical between the two sources read here. DreaMS counts a hit when a candidate sharing the first 14 characters of the InChI key is in the top k, while the MIST analysis script looks for the full InChI key from the labels file, so a page or a score should say which rule produced it.
limitations.source_locator: DreaMS: Methods (Molecular fingerprint prediction); analyze_rankings.py: run_analysis

name: Brandes et al. 2023 clinical missense pathogenicity benchmarks (ClinVar and HGMD/gnomAD)
description: Global ROC-AUC and balanced PRC-AUC of variant effect predictors for pathogenic versus benign missense variants on primary UniProt isoforms.

attributes.task: Missense variant pathogenicity classification
attributes.scope_note: Two labelled sets (ClinVar; HGMD disease-causing versus gnomAD common). Extracted: the common-variant comparison of the 19 methods eligible for clinical benchmarking (Supplementary Table 2 columns AUC_AUROC and AUC_Balanced_AUPRC) and the ESM1b versus EVE ROC-AUCs quoted in the Results.
attributes.source_locator: Results paragraphs 1, 2 and 5 of 'ESM1b outperforms other VEP methods...'; Supplementary Table 2 'Contents'

profile.summary: These are the two clinical missense benchmarks from the ESM1b variant effect paper. One labels variants from ClinVar as pathogenic or benign; the other treats HGMD disease-causing variants as positives and gnomAD variants with allele frequency above 1% as negatives. Predictors are scored by a global ROC-AUC over all variants together, plus a class-balanced PRC-AUC, and only methods that avoid clinical-database training and allele frequency features are included in the main comparison.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results, ESM1b outperforms other VEP methods; Methods, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a variant effect predictor separates harmful from harmless missense variants across the whole genome, not within one gene. The authors argue a global score matters because diagnosis means comparing variants in different genes, so the scores must be comparable between genes; they also report the gene-average ROC-AUC used by the EVE paper for contrast.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: ClinVar labels come from ClinVar's variant summary file, with only high-confidence variants kept. In the ESM1b versus EVE comparison the ClinVar set has 19,925 pathogenic and 16,612 benign variants across 2,765 genes, and the HGMD and gnomAD set has 27,754 disease-causing and 2,743 common variants across 1,991 genes; the paper does not say whether the full sets are larger. A separate ClinVar benchmark with EVE scores came from the EVE portal. Predictions for most of the compared methods were downloaded from dbNSFP 4.3a, with VARITY and MTBAN added separately. HGMD is a private resource, so that half of the benchmark cannot be redistributed.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results; Methods, Other VEP methods; Data availability; README.md: Data Availability

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Global ROC-AUC over the pooled variants is the main metric. The balanced PRC-AUC downsamples each dataset to an equal number of pathogenic and benign variants, taking 80% of the minority class, and averages over 100 such draws. Two comparison modes are reported: all 19 eligible methods on the variants that all of them score, and head-to-head comparisons where ESM1b is compared with each method on that method's own set of scored variants, with the percentage of variants used shown. Differences are tested by permutation, shuffling scores between variants over 2,000 iterations.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, AUC metrics and Testing for significant performance differences; Fig. 2 legend

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository holds the processed benchmark files with every method's predictions, except the HGMD variants, plus command line tools that score missense or multi-residue mutations with ESM1b. Install the dependencies, clone the repository, then run esm_score_missense_mutations.py on a FASTA file to get a score for every possible missense mutation.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Repository Contents, Installation, Usage

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Two sets, ClinVar and HGMD with gnomAD. The paper gives counts for the variants in the ESM1b versus EVE comparison (Fig. 2b): ClinVar, 19,925 pathogenic and 16,612 benign missense variants in 2,765 genes (36,537 in total); HGMD and gnomAD, 27,754 disease-causing and 2,743 common variants in 1,991 genes (30,497 in total). The paper does not state whether the full sets are larger.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results; Fig. 2 legend

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No split: both sets are evaluation data only, and the compared predictors are external published methods.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Other VEP methods

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Global ROC-AUC across all variants pooled (higher is better) and a class-balanced PRC-AUC averaged over 100 downsamplings (higher is better). A gene-average ROC-AUC is reported for contrast.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: 46 variant effect predictors were collected, mostly from dbNSFP 4.3a, with VARITY (two versions) and MTBAN added. Of these, 19 including ESM1b and EVE qualify for the clinical benchmarks. LINSIGHT and three cell-line versions of fitCons were excluded.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Other VEP methods

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Eligibility rules rather than data filtering: a method may enter the clinical comparison only if it was not trained on clinical databases such as ClinVar or HGMD, does not use features from methods trained on such data, and does not use allele frequency, since allele frequency is used to curate variants as benign. Results for the excluded methods are still reported in Supplementary Table 2.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results; Methods, Other VEP methods

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: The balanced PRC-AUC is averaged over 100 downsamplings. Differences between methods are tested by permutation over 2,000 iterations, reported as P < 0.001 when no permutation reaches the observed difference. Bootstrapped means and standard deviations are used for the stop-gain analysis, not for the missense benchmarks.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, AUC metrics; Testing for significant performance differences

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A missense variant on a curated human protein isoform, labelled pathogenic or benign.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results; Data availability

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: No assay: labels are clinical assertions from ClinVar and HGMD, and population allele frequency from gnomAD. The paper's separate deep mutational scanning benchmark, which does use assays, is a different evaluation.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Whatever each published predictor uses; for the clinical comparison, methods using allele frequency features are excluded. ESM1b itself reads the protein sequence only, with a sliding window for long proteins.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results; Methods, Handling long sequences

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: None: published predictors are scored as they are. ESM1b is used zero-shot, scoring a variant by the log-likelihood ratio against the wild type.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results; README.md: Usage

strengths.text: Explicit eligibility rules exclude predictors trained on clinical labels or using allele frequency, so the main comparison is less affected by circularity than a typical ClinVar comparison.
Two comparison modes are reported: a common variant set for all 19 methods, and head-to-head sets per method with the fraction of variants used stated.
The processed benchmarks with every method's predictions are published in the repository, apart from the HGMD variants.

limitations.text: The HGMD half cannot be redistributed: HGMD is a private resource and access must be requested from its curators, so that benchmark cannot be reproduced from public files.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Data availability; README.md: Data Availability

limitations.text: The negative class is population frequency, not demonstrated benignity: gnomAD variants above 1% allele frequency are assumed benign.
The global ROC-AUC rewards scores that are comparable between genes; by the gene-average metric used in the EVE paper the ordering of ESM1b and EVE reverses on the ClinVar subset.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification

limitations.text: It is one paper's evaluation, run by the authors of the method being promoted, with no leaderboard or ongoing submission route.

name: Brandes et al. 2023 ClinVar in-frame indel and stop-gain pathogenicity benchmarks
description: ROC-AUC of ESM1b-based scores, CADD and simple baselines for pathogenic versus benign ClinVar in-frame indels and stop-gain variants.

attributes.task: Pathogenicity classification of in-frame indels and stop-gain variants
attributes.scope_note: Two ClinVar-derived labelled sets built by the authors. Only CADD among published predictors is compared on indels, because most indel predictors are trained on ClinVar; no published predictor is compared on stop-gains.
attributes.source_locator: Results 'ESM1b can predict the effects of multiresidue variants' and Fig. 6 legend; Methods 'Generalized effect scores for indels and stop-gain variants', 'Baseline scores of indel and stop-gain variant effects'; Supplementary Methods 'Indels and stop gain ClinVar benchmarks'

profile.summary: These are the two labelled sets Brandes et al. built to test whether a protein language model can score coding variants that are not single amino acid substitutions. One holds 3,470 in-frame insertions, deletions and deletion-insertion combinations from ClinVar, 1,791 pathogenic and 1,679 benign; the other holds 36,000 or so ClinVar stop-gain variants, split by whether the new stop codon is expected to trigger nonsense-mediated decay. Both are scored by ROC-AUC for separating pathogenic from benign. They are useful to anyone asking whether a sequence model's likelihood scores transfer from missense variants to indels and truncations.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results, ESM1b can predict the effects of multiresidue variants; Fig. 6 legend. Repository: the indel benchmark table

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether an effect score separates pathogenic from benign variants in two classes of coding variant that most variant effect predictors cannot handle: in-frame indels, which change the length of the protein, and stop gains, which truncate it. The authors' point is that a protein language model can be applied to any amino acid sequence, so it can score these as well as missense variants. The stop-gain set is further split by nonsense-mediated decay, because a truncation often acts at the transcript level rather than through the protein sequence a language model sees.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, ESM1b can predict the effects of multiresidue variants

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Both sets are drawn from ClinVar, with labels downloaded from the ClinVar variant_summary table, and the authors say only high-confidence variants were included, with the processing described in the Supplementary Methods. The published indel table holds 3,470 rows against RefSeq NM transcripts, each with the wild-type and mutated sequence, the affected window, the number of amino acids affected and the length difference, labelled 1 for 1,791 variants and 0 for 1,679; its mut_type column gives 2,248 deletions, 937 insertions and 285 delins. The stop-gain set is partitioned with the 50 base pair rule, which treats a transcript as likely to undergo decay only if the new stop codon falls more than 50 bases upstream of the last exon junction in the coding region, applied using exon annotations from the human genome.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Data availability; Methods, Baseline scores of indel and stop-gain variant effects; Fig. 6 legend. Repository: the indel benchmark table and README

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A method supplies one score per variant and the whole set is treated as a single classification task, scored by global ROC-AUC rather than averaged per gene; the authors argue a global figure is more informative for clinical use because variants are compared across genes. For indels the model score is the pseudo-log-likelihood ratio between the mutated and wild-type sequences, in three variants: plain, weighted by sequence length, and absolute valued. For stop gains the score is the lowest log-likelihood ratio among all possible missense variants in the region lost after the new stop codon. Differences between methods are tested by a permutation test over 2,000 iterations, shuffling the scores between variants, with one-tailed empirical p values and a floor of p below 0.001. Uncertainty on the stop-gain figures comes from bootstrapping 140 pathogenic and 140 benign variants from each group over 20 iterations.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Generalized effect scores for indels and stop-gain variants, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification, Testing for significant performance differences

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: On the indel set the absolute-valued score reaches ROC-AUC 0.874, ahead of the plain 0.869 and the weighted 0.861, and all three beat CADD at 0.835; on delins variants alone the gap is wider, 0.887 against 0.671. The three sequence-similarity baselines are near or below 0.6: edit distance 0.501, pairwise alignment 0.586, BlastP 0.581. On stop gains, ESM1b scores 0.734 on variants not expected to undergo decay but only 0.565 on those that are, and on the non-decay group it beats the number of residues lost (0.649) and the fraction of the protein lost (0.599). The authors also estimate from the score distribution that 52% of in-frame indel variants of uncertain significance in ClinVar are pathogenic.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, ESM1b can predict the effects of multiresidue variants

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository publishes both benchmark tables with every method's scores already in them, so a comparison can be reproduced from the files alone. To score new variants, install the listed dependencies and run the multi-residue scoring script, which takes a CSV of wild-type sequence, mutated sequence and start position; a separate script scores all possible missense substitutions in a FASTA file, which is the route used for stop gains.
sections.source_locator: Repository: README.md, Repository Contents, Installation and Usage

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Two ClinVar-derived sets. In-frame indels: 3,470 variants, 1,791 pathogenic and 1,679 benign, which the published table splits into 2,248 deletions, 937 insertions and 285 delins. Stop gains: 36,034 pathogenic and 345 benign variants in the Fig. 6d legend, split into 3,672 pathogenic with 147 benign not expected to undergo nonsense-mediated decay and 32,362 pathogenic with 198 benign expected to undergo it.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Fig. 6 legend. Repository: the indel benchmark table, label and mut_type columns

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No train, validation or test split: each set is evaluated whole as a single classification task, which the authors can do because the method is unsupervised. The only partitioning is by variant class for reporting: deletions, insertions and delins for the indel set, and the 50 base pair decay rule for the stop-gain set.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification; Discussion; Fig. 6 legend

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Global ROC-AUC on pathogenic versus benign, higher better, computed over the whole set rather than averaged per gene. Elsewhere in the paper a label-balanced PRC-AUC is also used, obtained by downsampling each class to 80% of the minority class 100 times and averaging, but the indel and stop-gain figures are reported as ROC-AUC.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification; Results

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: On indels, one published predictor and three simple scores: CADD, plus Levenshtein edit distance, a pairwise alignment score (match 2, mismatch minus 1) and BlastP with BLOSUM62 and gap penalties. On stop gains, no published predictor at all, and three simple scores: number of residues lost, percentage of residues lost, and the binary 50 base pair rule. The authors state why: nearly all indel and stop-gain predictors are trained on clinical databases, which would make evaluation on ClinVar circular, and CADD is the exception they could use.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Baseline scores of indel and stop-gain variant effects

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The main control is the choice of comparators, not a data split. Because the evaluated method is unsupervised, the authors argue there is no leakage from training into these ClinVar sets, and they exclude predictors trained on clinical databases to avoid circularity, which is why only CADD appears on indels and nothing on stop gains. The sets themselves are restricted to high-confidence ClinVar variants. No sequence identity cut-off between the indel set and anything else is described.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Discussion; Methods, Baseline scores of indel and stop-gain variant effects; Results

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Bootstrapped standard deviations on the stop-gain figures and permutation p values on the indel comparison. For Fig. 6d, 140 pathogenic and 140 benign variants were sampled from each group over 20 iterations, and the error bars are the standard deviation of the resulting ROC-AUCs. For Fig. 6b, one-tailed p values from 2,000 permutations are reported for the difference between CADD and each ESM1b score, with p below 0.001 when no permutation matched the observed gap. No error bars are reported for the indel ROC-AUCs themselves.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification and Testing for significant performance differences; Fig. 6 legend

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One coding variant in a human protein-coding transcript, labelled pathogenic or benign. For the indel set the published row carries the wild-type and mutated protein sequence, the start and end position, the reference and alternative alleles, the number of amino acids affected and the length difference, against RefSeq NM transcripts. For the stop-gain set the variant is a substitution creating a premature stop codon.
facts.source_locator: Repository: the indel benchmark table header and seq_source column. Paper: Fig. 6 legend

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human only. The variants come from ClinVar, the scoring is against human protein isoforms, and the 50 base pair rule was applied using exon annotations in the human genome.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Baseline scores of indel and stop-gain variant effects; Data availability

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: None. The labels are clinical assertions from ClinVar, restricted to high-confidence entries, not experimental measurements. Deep mutational scanning data are used elsewhere in the same paper, but not in these two sets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Data availability; Results

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Protein sequence for the evaluated method: the wild-type and mutated amino acid sequences, with no alignment or structure. Where a sequence exceeds the model's 1,022 amino acid limit, the score is computed on a window containing the affected region with 511 residues of context before it and enough after to fill the limit. The stop-gain score needs the position of the new stop codon, and the 50 base pair rule needs exon annotations, which is transcript-level information used for the partition rather than by the model.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Generalized effect scores for indels and stop-gain variants. Repository: README.md, Usage

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot. The scores are likelihood ratios from a pretrained protein language model with no fitting to these labels; the only choices are which of the three pseudo-log-likelihood ratio forms to use for indels, and taking the minimum missense score over the lost region for stop gains. CADD, the one published comparator, is a supervised method.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results and Fig. 6 legend; Discussion

strengths.text: Both labelled sets are published as tables with every compared method's scores in them, so the reported ROC-AUCs can be recomputed without rerunning any model, and the counts check out: the indel file has 3,470 rows, 1,791 labelled 1 and 1,679 labelled 0.
strengths.source_locator: Repository: README.md, Benchmarks; the indel benchmark table. Paper: Fig. 6 legend

strengths.text: The authors exclude comparators that were trained on ClinVar rather than reporting flattering comparisons, and say so explicitly, which is why only CADD appears on indels.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Baseline scores of indel and stop-gain variant effects

strengths.text: The stop-gain set is split by expected nonsense-mediated decay, which exposes where a protein-sequence model fails: 0.734 on variants not expected to undergo decay against 0.565 on those that are. The authors report the weak half rather than only the aggregate.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results, ESM1b can predict the effects of multiresidue variants; Fig. 6 legend

strengths.text: Simple sequence-similarity baselines are included, which gives a floor for the indel task: edit distance scores 0.501, close to chance, so the task is not solved by noticing that the sequence changed.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results and Methods, Baseline scores of indel and stop-gain variant effects

limitations.text: The stop-gain set is extremely unbalanced: 345 benign against 36,034 pathogenic overall, and only 147 benign in the non-decay group that the headline 0.734 is computed on. ROC-AUC on such a set rests on a few hundred negatives, which is why the authors bootstrap 140 of each class rather than reporting a single number.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Fig. 6 legend; Methods, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification

limitations.text: Almost nothing can be compared against. On stop gains no published predictor is evaluated at all, and on indels only CADD, so these sets rank one model against three simple scores rather than against the field.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Baseline scores of indel and stop-gain variant effects

limitations.text: The labels are clinical assertions, so the benchmark inherits ClinVar's biases, and the rule for what counts as high confidence is in the Supplementary Methods rather than the article. The stop-gain partition also depends on the 50 base pair rule being correct, which is a heuristic rather than a measurement.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results; Methods, Baseline scores of indel and stop-gain variant effects

limitations.text: The two counts given for the stop-gain groups do not agree between the Fig. 6d legend and the Methods: the legend says 32,362 pathogenic in the decay group and 36,034 overall, while the bootstrapping description says 32,441 and 36,113. A user should check the published stop-gain file before quoting either.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Fig. 6 legend; Methods, AUC metrics for pathogenicity classification
