profile.summary: CACHE #3 is a blinded prospective challenge: 23 computational teams each picked up to 100 commercially available compounds for the macrodomain 1 of SARS-CoV-2 Nsp3, the organisers had them synthesised and assayed, and a separate hit evaluation committee scored the confirmed binders for quality and chemical novelty. The 1739 selected compounds all went through a fluorescence displacement screen and crystal soaking, and subsets went on to dose response and surface plasmon resonance, and teams whose compounds bound could then nominate up to 50 analogues each in a second round. It shows what current hit-finding workflows achieve on a target whose answers were not known in advance.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Introduction; Results 'Compounds Were Drug-like and Chemically Diverse' and 'Selection and Experimental Testing of Round 2 Compounds'

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: CACHE is a series of challenges meant to show, prospectively and under a time limit, what computational hit-finding can do and what machine learning adds. Teams submit compound selections before any testing, so no retrospective tuning is possible. For CACHE #3 the target was Nsp3-Mac1, and the brief was stricter than binding alone: participants were asked for compounds with a novel chemical scaffold and no carboxylic acid. What is measured is therefore both whether a workflow finds confirmed binders and whether those binders are chemically new.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results 'Discovering Chemically Novel Ligands Was Challenging'

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: A new protein target is nominated every few months and applications are ranked by double-blind peer review, each applicant scoring five others' proposed methods, with the ranking reviewed by an independent Applications Review Committee; the top 25 applicants are then invited to submit, within three months, a list of 100 drug-like ligand candidates from Enamine REAL. For CACHE #3, 23 of the 25 participants submitted within the required two-month window, and their selections, ranging from 41 to 99 molecules each, came to 1739 compounds, which Enamine synthesised and shipped. The library is therefore made by the participants, not by the organisers, and the labels come from the assays that follow. For reference, 161 Nsp3-Mac1 ligands had been published before the challenge.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results 'Computational Workflows Were Diverse' and 'Compounds Were Drug-like and Chemically Diverse'

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Round 1: all 1739 compounds were tested at 100 micromolar in a homogeneous time-resolved fluorescence (HTRF) assay measuring displacement of an ADP-ribose conjugated peptide. 302 compounds that reduced the binding signal by 30% or more in at least one of two duplicates, or gave ambiguous data, went to a limited three-point dose response at 25, 50 and 100 micromolar, leading to 166 compounds tested by surface plasmon resonance (SPR); 28 compounds from nine participants were confirmed in a six-point SPR dose response and advanced. In parallel all 1739 compounds were soaked with crystallised Nsp3-Mac1, giving complex structures for 44, all binding at the ADP-ribose site; three of those were rescued as hits but not advanced. Round 2: 296 analogues of the 28 advanced compounds, from nine teams, were synthesised and tested; after HTRF and dynamic light scattering for solubility, 158 compounds plus 16 crystallography-rescued Round 1 molecules went to six-point SPR, giving 84 confirmed hits, each then counter-screened against the macro 1 domain of PARP14 to check specificity. Each of the 28 Round 1 hits, and the three rescued with a measurable dissociation constant, was given an activity score for signal quality and chemical soundness, and three chemists on the Hit Evaluation Committee voted a separate novelty score from 0 to 3. Teams were also asked to predict the actives in the merged library of all 1739 Round 1 compounds, which puts every workflow on the same library; confirmed hits scoring above 15 were grouped into four chemically novel Tier 1 compounds and 25 Tier 2 compounds judged not novel, and each workflow's selection was normalised as the aggregated score of its predicted actives divided by the number it predicted.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results 'Discovering Chemically Novel Ligands Was Challenging', 'Selection and Experimental Testing of Round 2 Compounds', 'Evaluation of Experimental Data and Computational Workflows'; Figure 6 caption

sections.title: What the organisers concluded
sections.body: Over 85% of the designed molecules were chemically novel, but the best confirmed hits were structurally similar to previously published compounds, and the active molecules largely mimicked the adenine ring of ADP-ribose. Nine of the 23 workflows delivered at least one Round 1 compound scoring above 15, and only four of those produced a compound the committee judged novel. The paper classifies the seven best-performing workflows two ways. The Introduction says two included a deep learning step, one used a random forest classifier as a preliminary filter and the remaining four were purely physics-based. The abstract says two used compounds selected by physics-based screening to train machine learning models and four used exclusively physics-based approaches, and that three pharmacophore searches and one fragment growing strategy were also part of the seven. The organisers conclude that machine learning augments but does not consistently outperform physics-based methods, and that there is no single best method for rapid computational hit-finding.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Introduction; Results 'Evaluation of Experimental Data and Computational Workflows'; Conclusion

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: No fixed library: the data are made during the challenge. Round 1 is the 1739 compounds the 23 participating teams selected from Enamine REAL and Enamine synthesised, with 41 to 99 molecules per team. Round 2 is 296 analogues of the 28 advanced compounds. The merged Round 1 library of all 1739 compounds is also used as a common prediction set.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results 'Compounds Were Drug-like and Chemically Diverse', 'Selection and Experimental Testing of Round 2 Compounds'; Figure 6 caption

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No train, validation or test split. The design is prospective and blinded: predictions are submitted before any compound is made or tested, within a time limit (three months in the general format, and the CACHE #3 participants submitted within the required two-month window).
facts.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results 'Computational Workflows Were Diverse'

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Expert scores rather than a single statistic, all higher is better: an activity score per confirmed hit for signal quality and chemical soundness, a novelty score from 0 to 3 voted by three chemists, the best and aggregated Round 1 score per team, and for the merged-library prediction the aggregated score of the compounds a workflow predicted active divided by the number it predicted.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results 'Evaluation of Experimental Data and Computational Workflows'; Figure 6 caption

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The reference points are the other teams' workflows and the previously published chemistry: 161 Nsp3-Mac1 ligands were in the literature before the challenge, the 10 published carboxylate-free ligands with a Ki below 100 micromolar all shared a bi- or tricyclic adenine-mimetic ring, and five of those had Ki values in a similar range to the new hits. The organisers also compare against the earlier CACHE #1 and #2 rounds.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results 'Discovering Chemically Novel Ligands Was Challenging'; Introduction

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The design is the control: targets and libraries are set by the organisers and every prediction is submitted before testing, so there is nothing to memorise. It is not a control against prior knowledge of the target: the organisers note that the binding features of the ADP-ribose site were well documented at the outset and that 161 ligands had been published, and the confirmed hits largely reused the known adenine-mimetic chemotype.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results 'Discovering Chemically Novel Ligands Was Challenging' and 'Trends and Strategies from the Best Performing Computational Workflows'

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Experimental replication rather than statistical intervals: the primary HTRF screen was run in two duplicates, compounds were taken through dose response and then an orthogonal SPR assay, Round 2 resupplied 17 parent molecules to check that a signal was not limited to one batch, and hits were counter-screened against PARP14. No confidence intervals or seeds are reported for the computational workflows.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results 'Discovering Chemically Novel Ligands Was Challenging' and 'Selection and Experimental Testing of Round 2 Compounds'; Introduction

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A commercially available compound selected by a team, later labelled by assay; the unit of comparison is a workflow, and chemical series group the confirmed compounds.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results 'Selection and Experimental Testing of Round 2 Compounds'

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: The target protein is viral: macrodomain 1 of SARS-CoV-2 Nsp3, with human PARP14 used as the antitarget in the counter-screen. Constructs were expressed in Escherichia coli.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods 'Protein Expression and Purification'

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Homogeneous time-resolved fluorescence displacement of an ADP-ribose conjugated biotin peptide as the primary screen; limited three-point and six-point dose response; surface plasmon resonance on a Biacore 8K with dissociation constants from 1:1 steady-state affinity; dynamic light scattering for compound solubility; and X-ray crystallography by ligand soaking, with coordinates deposited in the Protein Data Bank under group deposition G_1002327.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Homogeneous Time-Resolved Fluorescence (HTRF)', 'Surface Plasmon Resonance (SPR)', 'Dynamic Light Scattering', 'Crystallography'

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Anything the team chooses, as long as the compounds come from the Enamine REAL catalogue and the selection is submitted in time. All 23 workflows used docking at some point; 17 included a machine learning step, eight molecular dynamics, five binding free energy methods, four pharmacophore searches guided by multiple PDB-bound molecules, and two quantum mechanics. Participants were also asked, though not required, to check their molecules against the badapple chemical liability filter.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results 'Computational Workflows Were Diverse' and 'Compounds Were Drug-like and Chemically Diverse'

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Inapplicable as a model setting: this is a prospective human-and-software competition, not a fixed dataset a model is trained or probed on. Teams built whatever workflow they chose, several trained machine learning models on docking scores from their own physics-based screens, and the organisers note that most top teams also inspected the selected molecules by eye.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Discussion

strengths.text: It is prospective and blinded: compounds are chosen before synthesis and testing, so a workflow cannot be tuned to known answers, and every selection is actually made and assayed.

Confirmation is layered: a primary displacement assay in duplicate, dose response, an orthogonal SPR measurement, solubility by light scattering, crystal soaking of all 1739 compounds, an analogue round to test whether a scaffold holds, and a counter-screen against a related protein.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results 'Discovering Chemically Novel Ligands Was Challenging' and 'Selection and Experimental Testing of Round 2 Compounds'

strengths.text: The merged-library prediction puts every workflow on the same 1739 compounds, which allows a comparison that the teams' own differing selections do not.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results 'Evaluation of Experimental Data and Computational Workflows'

strengths.text: All molecular structures with their properties and activities are published in machine-readable supplementary tables, and the crystal structures are deposited in the Protein Data Bank.

limitations.text: Scores are expert judgements, not a reproducible statistic: an activity score set by a Hit Evaluation Committee and a novelty score voted by three chemists. No per-workflow hit rate is published in the text read.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results 'Evaluation of Experimental Data and Computational Workflows'

limitations.text: The chemical space is bounded by one catalogue: participants could select only within the Enamine catalogue, and the organisers say either that catalogue lacks alternative templates for this site or in silico workflows cannot find the ones present, and suggest other libraries may hold novel scaffolds.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results 'Discovering Chemically Novel Ligands Was Challenging'; Discussion

limitations.text: One target, one round: the numbers describe Nsp3-Mac1 only, nine of 23 teams produced a high-scoring Round 1 compound and only four a novel one, and the Tier 1 set is four compounds, so differences between workflows rest on very few confirmed molecules.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results 'Evaluation of Experimental Data and Computational Workflows'

limitations.text: Some outcomes depended on practicalities rather than method quality: three compounds rescued by crystallography were not advanced to Round 2 for lack of time, one top novel molecule could not be confirmed because the follow-up compounds chosen were not analogues, and two of the 25 invited teams did not submit.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results 'Discovering Chemically Novel Ligands Was Challenging'; Figure 5 caption; Results 'Computational Workflows Were Diverse'

name: DEKOIS 2.0
description: Virtual-screening benchmark that scores a method on how well it ranks experimentally validated actives above property-matched decoys for each of its targets.

attributes.task: Protein-ligand virtual screening (library ranking)
attributes.scope_note: As described by Shen et al. 2025: 81 structurally diverse targets, each with 40 experimentally validated actives from BindingDB and 1200 property-matched decoys selected from ZINC, an actives-to-decoys ratio of 1:30. Data at http://www.dekois.com.
attributes.source_locator: Methods 'Datasets'; Data availability
limitations: The decoys are synthetic property-matched molecules, not measured inactives, so enrichment factors on this benchmark are not comparable with benchmarks whose negatives were assayed.

The set was released over ten years before Shen et al. 2025 and its template protein structures may overlap substantially with the training data of the co-folding models scored on it (Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset').

version.note: The DEKOIS 2.0 primary paper (doi 10.1021/ci400115b) is closed access and was not retrieved; the composition recorded here is as Shen et al. 2025 describe it

profile.summary: DEKOIS 2.0 is a virtual screening benchmark: for each target it asks how well a method ranks experimentally validated active compounds above property-matched decoys. The official page offers 81 target sets for download; Shen et al. describe each set as 40 actives from BindingDB and 1200 decoys selected from ZINC. It is used by developers of docking, scoring and co-folding methods to compare enrichment of actives.
profile.summary_source_locator: dekois.com page: list of targets; Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The benchmark measures early recognition in structure-based virtual screening: given a protein target and a library of 40 known actives mixed with 1200 decoys, can a method place the actives near the top of its ranking. Because the decoys are chosen to match the actives' physicochemical properties, a method cannot succeed simply by preferring, for example, heavier or more lipophilic molecules. Shen et al. use it as their primary reference set for comparing AlphaFold3-like co-folding methods with conventional docking programs.
sections.source_locator: Shen et al.: Introduction; Results 'Evaluation of AF3's built-in confidence scores on DEKOIS2.0 dataset'; Methods 'Datasets'

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Each target set pairs actives taken from BindingDB with decoys selected from ZINC and matched on molecular properties, giving an actives-to-decoys ratio of 1 to 30. The official page lists 81 targets, spread across kinases, proteases, nuclear receptors, GPCRs and other enzyme families, and offers the target sets in three download parts plus a ligands download. The page does not print a version string, a licence or a construction protocol; the construction details on this page come from Shen et al.'s description. Shen et al. also used the protein templates and initial ligand conformers that come with the dataset rather than preparing their own.
sections.source_locator: dekois.com page: downloads and list of targets; Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets' and 'Complex structure prediction'

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is a ranking of each target's library. Shen et al. score rankings with the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), BEDROC with alpha = 80.5, which weights the top 2% of the ranking to 80% of the score, and enrichment factors at 0.5%, 1% and 5%. Per-target values are then summarised across targets, with the mean marked in their box plots. Their comparison runs on 79 of the 81 targets, because two targets (pygl-in and pygl-out) were dropped as too costly to model; values for one tool, SurfDock, were taken over from earlier work and cover all 81 targets. There is no central leaderboard: each paper publishes its own numbers.
sections.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Evaluation metrics'; Methods 'Datasets'; Fig. 1 caption

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: 81 target sets on the official download page, each described by Shen et al. as 40 actives and 1200 decoys. Shen et al.'s own comparison uses 79 of them.
facts.source_locator: dekois.com page: list of targets; Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: None. The benchmark is a screening set only: every compound of a target is ranked and scored, with no train, validation or test division.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets' and 'Evaluation metrics'

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: AUROC, BEDROC (alpha = 80.5) and enrichment factors at 0.5%, 1% and 5%, as used by Shen et al.; higher is better for all of them. AUROC runs from 0 for complete failure through 0.5 for random to 1 for perfect classification.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Evaluation metrics'

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: As reported by Shen et al.: five docking programs (Glide SP, AutoDock Vina, GOLD CHEMPLP, Surflex-Dock, LeDock) and five machine-learning docking tools (Gnina, TankBind, KarmaDock, CarsiDock, SurfDock), with the values for all but AF3, Protenix, Boltz-2 and Gnina taken over from earlier studies.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Results 'Evaluation of AF3's built-in confidence scores on DEKOIS2.0 dataset'; Fig. 1 caption

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None in the benchmark itself, and Shen et al. warn that it is a problem here: the set was released over ten years before their study and its template structures may overlap AlphaFold3's training data, so they built the separate GPCRrecent set. They also say Boltz-2's affinity numbers on DEKOIS2.0 are likely over-estimated, because Boltz-2 took affinity data from the same public databases that DEKOIS 2.0 draws on. In place of a split control they computed, for each active compound, its minimum Tanimoto similarity (ECFP4) to any PDB ligand, as the paper words it, and re-calculated the metrics at varying similarity thresholds.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'; Results on ligand similarity

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: No replicates or intervals are asked for. Shen et al. report the spread across targets with box plots and mark the mean; the co-folding predictions were run with one fixed random seed (seed = 1).
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Fig. 1 caption; Methods 'Complex structure prediction'

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A compound in a target's screening library, labelled active or decoy; one score is produced per target.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Not stated in the files read. The official page lists protein targets by name, including human proteins and pathogen proteins such as HIV-1 protease and the SARS coronavirus 3C-like protease, but no species column is printed.
facts.source_locator: dekois.com page: list of targets

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: The actives carry measured binding or inhibition data from BindingDB. The decoys are not assayed: they are library compounds matched on properties, which Shen et al. call artificially generated decoys.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Results 'Performance on a subset of LIT-PCBA dataset'

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Not fixed by the benchmark. The dataset ships protein templates and initial ligand conformers, so methods may use the 3D structure; Shen et al. note that co-folding methods take only one-dimensional protein and ligand sequences, while some baselines need 3D structural information.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot screening in practice: in Shen et al. the methods are run as released, with default or recommended settings, and nothing is trained on the benchmark.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Complex structure prediction'

strengths.text: The actives are experimentally validated measurements from BindingDB, and the decoys are matched on physicochemical properties, so simple property bias does not by itself produce enrichment.

81 target sets spanning many protein families are downloadable from the official page, with the protein templates and ligand conformers included, so methods that need a prepared structure can be run without extra preparation.
strengths.source_locator: dekois.com page: downloads; Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'

strengths.text: Shen et al. describe it as widely used for both physics-based and machine-learning docking tools, which is why results from different papers can be put side by side; they take ten tools' values from earlier work.
strengths.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Fig. 1 caption

limitations.text: The negatives are property-matched library compounds, not assayed inactives. Shen et al. report that a reviewer raised this as a possible bias, which is why they added a LIT-PCBA subset where actives and inactives are both measured.
limitations.source_locator: Shen et al.: Results 'Performance on a subset of LIT-PCBA dataset'

limitations.text: Age makes training overlap likely for recent models: Shen et al. state the set was released over ten years earlier and that its template protein structures may overlap AlphaFold3's training data, and they treat Boltz-2's affinity numbers on it as a reference only.
limitations.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Results on DEKOIS2.0

limitations.text: The official site is a temporary download page: it carries no version string, no licence, no per-target composition table and no leaderboard, so terms of use and the exact file contents cannot be read from it.

Published figures may be on different target counts: Shen et al. score 79 targets, but the SurfDock values they carry over were computed on all 81, so numbers from different papers are not automatically on the same set.
limitations.source_locator: Shen et al.: Fig. 1 caption; Methods 'Datasets'

profile.summary: DUD-E is a virtual screening benchmark: for each of 102 protein targets it supplies a set of known active compounds and, for every active, 50 decoy molecules chosen to match it on physico-chemical properties while being topologically dissimilar. A docking program or scoring model ranks the pooled library for a target, and the benchmark measures how far the actives rise above the decoys, reported as an adjusted logarithmic area under the ROC curve and an enrichment factor at 1 per cent. The actives come from ChEMBL09, or the literature for AmpC beta-lactamase, with affinities of 1 micromolar or better, molecular weight under 600 and fewer than 20 rotatable bonds, clustered to 22,886 ligands, and the decoys from ZINC. It is used to compare docking programs and scoring functions, and a later study shows that machine learning models trained on it can score well without learning anything about binding.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Characteristics of DUD-E, Methods (Automated Decoy Generation, Docking Metrics); DUD-E home page

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Ligand enrichment: whether a method puts known binders near the top of a library that is otherwise full of molecules that look like them but are not known to bind. The decoys are the point. They are matched to each active on six physico-chemical properties, so a method cannot win by preferring heavy or greasy molecules, and they are topologically dissimilar to the actives, so the task is not fingerprint matching. The target list was chosen for diversity, adding classes such as G protein coupled receptors and ion channels that the original DUD lacked. What the benchmark does not measure, as the authors of a later study showed, is whether a model has learned protein-ligand interaction physics.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Results; Chen et al. 2019: Introduction and Discussion; DUD-E home page

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Actives come from ChEMBL09: compounds assigned to a protein target with a confidence score of at least 4 and an affinity of 1 micromolar or better. Raw ligands also had to have a molecular weight under 600 and fewer than 20 rotatable bonds, which gives 66,695 raw ligands. For AmpC beta-lactamase the ChEMBL09 ligands are covalent, so its ligands were compiled by hand from the literature instead. Molecules with no measurable affinity at 30 micromolar or worse are kept as experimental decoys, and the in-between cases are kept separately as marginal. Each target's ligands are clustered to leave 22,886 clustered ligands for chemotype diversity. Targets are defined by UniProt gene prefix with species pooled, and each target gets one X-ray structure, chosen by an automated docking campaign over thousands of PDB entries with preference for resolution, enrichment and the human orthologue, with manual intervention where the automated preparation failed. Decoys are drawn from ZINC: for each unique set of six properties of a protonated ligand, molecular weight, estimated log P, rotatable bonds, hydrogen bond acceptors and donors and net charge, a pool of a few thousand candidates is gathered by widening or narrowing property windows in seven steps, ECFP4 fingerprints are computed, the pool is sorted by maximum Tanimoto similarity to any ligand, the most dissimilar quarter is kept, duplicates are spread evenly over the ligands, and 50 decoys are picked at random. That gives 1,411,214 computational decoys in all.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Characteristics of DUD-E; Methods (ChEMBL and RCSB PDB Data Extraction, Target Selection Docking, Target Preparation, Ligand Clustering, Automated Decoy Generation)

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A method ranks the library for one target, actives and decoys together, and the ranking is scored. The paper's primary measure is the adjusted LogAUC at 0.001, which is the area under the ROC curve on a semi-logarithmic x-axis spanning three decades, with the random curve's 14.462 per cent subtracted so that random performance is 0 per cent and higher is better. The ROC-based enrichment factor at 1 per cent is also reported: the percentage of ligands found by the point where 1 per cent of the decoys have been found, which the authors prefer to a traditional enrichment factor. Plain ROC AUC is noted as a common alternative. The authors' own numbers come from docking with DOCK 3.6 using solvent-excluded volume ligand desolvation, with conformations from Omega, and they report per-target LogAUC and enrichment factor values in their target table. Scores are per target; the benchmark defines no single aggregate.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Docking Metrics, Docking Calculations); Table 2

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The data are downloaded from the benchmark's own site, either target by target, by subset such as the G protein coupled receptor or kinase groups, or as one package, and the site says the files can also be browsed directly under its db directory without JavaScript. Each target ships the chosen receptor structure and the active and decoy sets, in mol2 and SDF formats. There is no scoring server: a user docks or scores the molecules with their own program and computes the enrichment metrics themselves. The site also runs a decoy generation service, so the same protocol can be applied to a user's own ligand list for a target that is not in the set.
sections.source_locator: DUD-E home page; Paper: Online Tools for Automated Generation of Further Ligand and Decoy Sets

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One set, split by target: 102 proteins, 22,886 clustered ligands from ChEMBL09 and, for AmpC beta-lactamase, the literature, out of 66,695 raw ligands, an average of 224 ligands per target on the project page, 50 property-matched decoys per active, and 1,411,214 computational decoys in all. Experimental decoys, molecules measured as inactive, number 9,219. Each target also has one chosen X-ray structure.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Abstract and Characteristics of DUD-E table; DUD-E home page

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: None. DUD-E is a test set, not a train and test division: each target is an independent screening problem with its own actives and decoys, and the authors say targets are independent of one another so that they can be added, deleted or replaced. Methods that train on DUD-E, as machine learning work does, have to invent their own split, and Chen et al. show that the usual choice, separating targets by sequence similarity, rests on an untested assumption about their actives.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Online Tools section; Chen et al. 2019: Methods and Discussion

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Adjusted LogAUC at 0.001, higher is better: the ROC area in semi-logarithmic space over three decades, with the random curve's 14.462 per cent subtracted so random is 0. Alongside it the ROC-based enrichment factor at 1 per cent, higher is better, the percentage of ligands recovered when 1 per cent of the decoys have been recovered. Plain ROC AUC is named as a common metric and is what later machine learning work reports.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Docking Metrics; Chen et al. 2019: Introduction

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The authors' own docking runs with DOCK 3.6 and solvent-excluded volume ligand desolvation, reported per target as LogAUC and enrichment factor at 1 per cent, and a comparison against the original DUD on the 37 directly comparable targets. A random background calculation is also described, seeding the DUD-E ligands into a ChEMBL subset of ZINC of 273,375 ligands.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Docking Calculations, Original DUD Comparison); Table 2

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Within a target, two. Ligands are clustered by Bemis-Murcko frameworks so that near-identical analogues do not dominate, and decoys are filtered to be topologically dissimilar to the actives, keeping only the most dissimilar quarter of the candidate pool by ECFP4 Tanimoto similarity. There is no control across targets, and no control for a model trained on DUD-E: Chen et al. report that models can separate actives from decoys from the ligand alone, with no receptor, which they attribute to analogue bias among each target's actives and to the way the decoys were chosen.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Ligand Clustering, Automated Decoy Generation); Chen et al. 2019: Results and Discussion

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: No replicates or intervals are defined by the benchmark: a target's score is a single ranking of a fixed library. The authors do provide a way to probe one source of variance, since the final decoy pick is random where possible, so several decoy sets can be generated for the same ligands to test whether a method is overfitted to the canonical decoys.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Online Tools for Automated Generation of Further Ligand and Decoy Sets; Methods, Docking Metrics

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A molecule paired with a target: one example is a compound in a target's library, labelled active or decoy, to be scored against that target's single chosen receptor structure. Decoys belong to a specific active, one decoy to one ligand, so filtering a ligand removes its decoys.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Online Tools section, Methods; DUD-E home page

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Mixed and pooled. Targets are defined by UniProt gene prefix with the data from each species combined into one set, and the structure choice gave preference to the human orthologue, so a target can carry ligands measured against several species' proteins. The saved files give no species breakdown.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Methods (Target Preparation)

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Binding and activity measurements from the literature, as collected by ChEMBL: half maximal inhibitory and effective concentrations, inhibition and dissociation constants and their logarithmic variants. An active needs 1 micromolar or better; an experimental decoy needs no measurable affinity at 30 micromolar or worse. The receptor structures are X-ray crystal structures from the PDB.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, ChEMBL and RCSB PDB Data Extraction

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The target's receptor structure and the molecules. Each target ships one prepared X-ray structure and its ligand and decoy sets in mol2 and SDF form, so a method may use the protein structure, the ligand structures, or only the ligands. Chen et al. exploit exactly that freedom, training a ligand-only model as a control.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods; DUD-E home page; Chen et al. 2019: Methods

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: As published, none: DUD-E was built for docking programs, which are not trained on it, and the paper describes using it to test method variants such as a new desolvation model. Later work does train on it, and Chen et al. describe building training and test subsets of DUD-E for convolutional networks, which is the use their study criticises.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Applications to Docking Optimization and Testing; Chen et al. 2019: Introduction and Methods

strengths.text: The decoys are hard by construction. They match each active on six properties including net charge, and only the quarter least similar to the actives by ECFP4 fingerprint is kept, so neither property bias nor fingerprint similarity gives an easy win.

The target list is broader than the benchmark it replaced, adding classes such as G protein coupled receptors and ion channels, and each target's receptor structure was chosen through a systematic docking campaign rather than by hand alone.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods, Target Selection Docking and Target Preparation

strengths.text: It is extensible rather than frozen. The decoy generation protocol is offered as a service for a user's own ligand list, the raw unclustered sets are published so a different clustering can be used, and the random final pick lets several decoy sets be made for the same ligands to test overfitting.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Online Tools for Automated Generation of Further Ligand and Decoy Sets; DUD-E home page

strengths.text: The metric is designed for screening rather than for overall ranking: the adjusted LogAUC weights the top of the list and is shifted so that random performance reads as zero.

limitations.text: Scores from models trained on DUD-E can be meaningless. Chen et al. report that convolutional network models reach high area under the curve without using the receptor at all, and attribute this to analogue bias among each target's actives and to how the decoys were selected, so performance on DUD-E is not evidence that such a model has learned protein-ligand binding.
limitations.source_locator: Chen et al. 2019: Introduction, Results, Conclusions

limitations.text: The decoys are presumed inactive, not measured inactive. Only 9,219 experimental decoys exist against 1,411,214 computational ones drawn from ZINC, so almost every negative label is an assumption.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Characteristics of DUD-E table; Methods, Automated Decoy Generation

limitations.text: Each target is one receptor structure and one pooled set of species, chosen in part because it already enriched known ligands under automated docking. That selection, which the authors describe, favours targets and structures that docking handles well.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Target Selection Docking and Target Preparation

limitations.text: There is no leaderboard, no submission route and no stated data licence: the project page says only that the set is free to use and provided by the laboratories at UCSF, and it points to a newer version, DUDE-Z, at another address.

profile.summary: GPCRrecent is a virtual screening set of 16 G protein-coupled receptors whose first crystal structures were determined after 2022, built by Shen et al. so that the targets postdate AlphaFold3's training data. Each target pairs actives taken from BindingDB with decoys generated by a conditional recurrent neural network at one active to fifty decoys, and a method is scored on how early it ranks the actives. It is for testing whether a structure prediction or docking method still enriches actives on targets it cannot have seen as structures.
profile.summary_source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Zenodo record 16826965

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The set measures early enrichment in virtual screening on targets that are new as structures. Shen et al. built it because DEKOIS2.0 had been released over ten years earlier and its template protein structures might overlap AlphaFold3's training data, so good scores there may reflect memorised structures. Here every target's first crystal structure was released after 2022, which the authors say guarantees temporal separation from AlphaFold3's training samples.
sections.source_locator: Shen et al.: Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'; Methods 'Datasets'

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: UniProt and BindingDB were queried for targets whose first crystal structure was released after 2022 and which have ligands in BindingDB, giving 47 eligible UniProt entries, mostly GPCRs, and the analysis was then limited to the GPCRs. Actives were taken from BindingDB with IC50, EC50, Ki or Kd below 10 micromolar, excluding peptide-like inhibitors and natural products above 600 molecular weight, and keeping EC50 entries rather than dropping them. After standardisation with RDKit the actives were clustered on Murcko scaffolds and only the most potent member of each cluster was kept; targets with many actives were cut to at most 300 diverse scaffolds by ECFP4 fingerprint, and targets with fewer than 200 actives were removed, leaving 16 GPCRs. Decoys come from a streamlined implementation of TocoDecoy, a conditional recurrent neural network that synthesises property-matched decoys, at one active to fifty decoys. For the protein side, the lowest-resolution structure for each UniProt entry was taken from the PDB and prepared in Schrodinger, and ligands were prepared with LigPrep.
sections.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Zenodo record 16826965

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A method ranks each target's library and is scored with AUROC, BEDROC with alpha = 80.5, and enrichment factors at 0.5%, 1% and 5%; distributions across the 16 targets are compared in box plots. Shen et al. also report a six-target subset: Boltz-2 used a training cutoff of 2023-6, so only the six targets whose first crystal structures were released after that date (O15552, P0DMS8, P13945, P35348, P46098, Q96RJ0) are temporally clean for it. They warn that the six-target subset is too small for firm statistical conclusions. They also plot how BEDROC changes with each active's minimum Tanimoto similarity to PDB ligands, dropping targets with no actives above the threshold. There is no leaderboard; the authors' own scores are in their Zenodo source data.
sections.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Evaluation metrics'; Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'; Fig. 5 caption; Data availability

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One dataset of 16 GPCR targets, published as a single archive gpcr.tar.gz on Zenodo record 16826965. Shen et al. also score a six-target subset of it, for Boltz-2's training cutoff. Per-target active and decoy counts are in the paper's Table S1, which was not retrieved.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Zenodo record 16826965

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No train, validation or test split: the whole library of each target is ranked and scored. The temporal rule is the selection rule rather than a split: only targets whose first crystal structure was released after 2022, and for the Boltz-2 comparison only the six whose first structures came after 2023-6.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: AUROC, BEDROC (alpha = 80.5) and enrichment factors at 0.5%, 1% and 5%, higher is better for all. BEDROC with alpha = 80.5 gives the top 2% of the ranking 80% of the score.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Evaluation metrics'; Fig. 5 caption

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: As reported by Shen et al.: new docking runs with Glide SP and Gnina (Vina score, CNNscore, CNNaffinity), against Protenix and Boltz-2 confidence scores and rescoring schemes. On this set the methods scored are Protenix and Boltz-2, chosen for their lower memory needs than AlphaFold3; Boltz-2's affinity module is excluded.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Scoring schemes'; Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: A temporal cut on structures: every target's first crystal structure postdates 2022, which the authors say separates them from AlphaFold3's training samples, and a six-target subset handles Boltz-2's later cutoff. The control does not cover binding data: the authors exclude Boltz-2's affinity module because its training sources, such as BindingDB, overlap this benchmark's own composition, and they say the set cannot show the generalisation of affinity prediction models. They also plot performance against each active's minimum Tanimoto similarity to PDB ligands.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'; Fig. 5 caption

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: None requested. Shen et al. report distributions across targets as box plots and means across targets, with structure prediction run under one fixed random seed (seed = 1); for the six-target subset they say the number of targets precludes robust statistical conclusions.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Fig. 5 caption; Methods 'Complex structure prediction'; Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A compound in a target's screening library, labelled active (from BindingDB) or decoy (generated); one score per target.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Not stated in the files read. The targets are named by UniProt accession rather than species.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Actives carry measured IC50, EC50, Ki or Kd values below 10 micromolar from BindingDB. The decoys are not assayed: they are synthesised by a conditional recurrent neural network to match the actives' properties.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Not fixed by the benchmark. Co-folding methods take one-dimensional protein and ligand sequences; docking baselines need a prepared 3D structure, and Shen et al. took the lowest-resolution PDB structure per UniProt entry and prepared it in Schrodinger, with the binding box set from the crystallised ligand.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets' and 'Scoring schemes'

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot screening: the methods are run as released, with default or recommended settings, and nothing is trained on the benchmark.
facts.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Complex structure prediction'

strengths.text: The targets are selected by a date rule on structures, so a co-folding model cannot have seen their crystal structures in training; the authors state this gives complete temporal separation from AlphaFold3's training samples.

The curation rules are printed in full: the activity cut-off, the exclusions, Murcko scaffold clustering with the most potent representative, at most 300 scaffolds per target, a floor of 200 actives, and a fixed one to fifty actives-to-decoys ratio.
The dataset is on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0, and the authors' own scores and statistics are published as a separate Zenodo record, so their numbers can be checked.
strengths.source_locator: Zenodo records 16826965 and 17568813; Shen et al.: Data availability

limitations.text: The decoys are generated by a conditional recurrent neural network, not assayed inactives, so enrichment here is not comparable with benchmarks whose negatives were measured. Shen et al. report that a reviewer raised this for both DEKOIS2.0 and GPCRrecent.
limitations.source_locator: Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'; Results 'Performance on a subset of LIT-PCBA dataset'

limitations.text: Temporal separation covers structures only. The authors exclude Boltz-2's affinity module because its training data overlap this set's composition, and say the set cannot reflect the generalisation of affinity prediction models.
limitations.source_locator: Shen et al.: Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'

limitations.text: It is small and narrow: 16 GPCR targets, or six for a model with a 2023-6 cutoff, and the authors say the six-target subset precludes robust statistical conclusions. Its results also do not carry over from DEKOIS2.0, because dataset composition and decoy generation differ.
limitations.source_locator: Shen et al.: Results 'Performance on GPCRrecent dataset'

limitations.text: The per-target composition is in the paper's Table S1, part of the supplementary information, which was not retrieved, and the Zenodo record gives only one archive with a one-line description.

name: LIT-PCBA
description: Virtual-screening benchmark whose actives and inactives are both experimentally measured, taken from high-confidence PubChem BioAssay dose-response data.

attributes.task: Protein-ligand virtual screening (library ranking)
attributes.version: Full data and AVE-unbiased data as published on the official page; no version string is printed
attributes.scope_note: 15 target sets. The official page states 7761 actives and 382674 unique inactives from high-confidence PubChem BioAssay data, with per-target counts and an AVE-unbiased split published alongside the full data; Shen et al. 2025 state 10030 confirmed actives and 2798737 confirmed inactives for the full set. Because the inactives are measured rather than synthetic, and because the actives-to-inactives ratio reaches about 1:18000 for ADRB2, enrichment factors on LIT-PCBA sit far below those on property-matched decoy benchmarks.

limitations: Huang, Knight and Naprienko 2025 audit the benchmark and report extensive leakage between its splits: 323 active training-validation analogue pairs at ECFP4 Tanimoto at or above 0.6 in ALDH1 alone, and 2491 2D-identical inactives shared between training and validation across targets. They conclude that a parameter-free memorisation baseline matches or exceeds published deep-learning and 3D-similarity results, that nearly all published LIT-PCBA results are undermined, that zero-shot evaluations are also affected by analogue leakage into the query set, and that the benchmark in its current form does not measure recovery of novel chemotypes.
The official page and Shen et al. 2025 give different active and inactive totals and neither reconciles them.
The LIT-PCBA primary paper (doi 10.1021/acs.jcim.0c00155) is closed access and was not retrieved.

profile.summary: LIT-PCBA is a virtual screening benchmark of 15 protein target sets whose actives and inactives both come from measured PubChem BioAssay dose-response data, rather than from synthetic decoys. The official page states 7761 actives and 382674 unique inactives, publishes per-target counts, and offers the full data and an AVE-unbiased version. Method developers use it to test whether a model ranks measured actives above measured inactives at a realistic class imbalance.
profile.summary_source_locator: Official page: header and data content table; audit paper: Section 2

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The benchmark asks whether a method can pick measured actives out of a large library of measured inactives for each of 15 targets. Because the negatives were assayed rather than generated, the ratio of actives to inactives is as lopsided as a real screen: ADRB2 has 17 actives against 311748 inactives, while ALDH1 has 5363 actives against 101874 inactives. The audit paper describes the intended capability as recovering novel chemotypes, that is finding actives whose chemistry differs from what the model has already seen.
sections.source_locator: Official page: data content table; audit paper: Abstract and Introduction

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Each target set is drawn from a PubChem BioAssay identifier and holds measured actives and inactives plus one or more PDB templates; the official table gives the assay identifier, the target, whether the ligands are agonists, antagonists or inhibitors, the active and inactive counts and the number of PDB templates. The audit paper describes three components per target: query ligands taken from co-crystal structures, a training set and a validation set, with training and validation partitioned by the asymmetric validation embedding (AVE) protocol. Its Table 1 prints the per-target split sizes, for example 4020 training and 1343 validation actives for ALDH1. The official page offers both the full data and an AVE-unbiased version.
sections.source_locator: Official page: data content table and download links; audit paper: Section 2 and Table 1

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission ranks each target's library, and the ranking is scored for early enrichment. The audit paper describes the usual protocol: the co-crystal query ligands are the fixed inputs, the LIT-PCBA validation split is treated as the held-out test set, and the ranking is scored with measures such as normalised EF1%, average precision, ROC AUC and BEDROC; single-ligand evaluation scores one query at a time and reports the mean across queries, while multi-ligand evaluation ranks by the maximum similarity over all queries, the max-pooling the original paper adopts. Because the active-to-inactive ratio varies so much across targets, both the audit paper and Shen et al. normalise the enrichment factor by each target's theoretical maximum (nEF1% or NEF). There is no central leaderboard; each paper publishes its own numbers.
sections.source_locator: Audit paper: Section 2 and Section 3.1.1; Shen et al.: Methods 'Evaluation metrics'

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: 15 target sets. The official page states 7761 actives and 382674 unique inactives from high-confidence PubChem BioAssay data, with per-target counts; Shen et al. state 10 030 confirmed actives and 2 798 737 confirmed inactives for the full set. Neither source reconciles the two figures.
facts.source_locator: Official page: header; Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Per target: query ligands from co-crystal structures, a training set and a validation set, with training and validation partitioned by the AVE protocol. The audit paper's Table 1 gives the per-target sizes, for example FEN1 with 269 training and 91 validation actives and 263 771 training and 86 947 validation inactives. The official page also publishes an AVE-unbiased version of the data.
facts.source_locator: Audit paper: Section 2 and Table 1; official page: download links

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Enrichment at the top of the ranking, higher is better. The audit paper names nEF1%, average precision, ROC AUC and BEDROC as the ranking metrics in use and argues for reporting mean, median and the normalised nEF1%. Shen et al. use AUROC, BEDROC (alpha = 80.5), EF at 0.5%, 1% and 5%, and the normalised enrichment factor NEF for this benchmark.
facts.source_locator: Audit paper: Section 2 and Section 3.1.1; Shen et al.: Methods 'Evaluation metrics'

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Not published by the benchmark itself in the sources read. The audit paper supplies a parameter-free memorisation baseline built from 4096-bit ECFP4 fingerprints against the training actives, reaching a median raw EF1% of 4.15 on the validation set under the multi-ligand protocol, and compares it with the CHEESE EspSim and ShapeSim encoders, ECFP4, ROCS and SFX. Shen et al. use Glide and Gnina as baselines on their five-target subset.
facts.source_locator: Audit paper: Section 3.1 and Table 2; Shen et al.: Results 'Performance on a subset of LIT-PCBA dataset'

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The AVE protocol is the benchmark's own control, and the audit paper reports that it does not hold. It finds 2,491 unique inactives shared between training and validation across the 15 targets, 323 active training-validation pairs at ECFP4 Tanimoto at or above 0.6 in ALDH1 alone, query ligands that also appear in the training or validation set, and near-duplicate query ligands within a set. It concludes that the benchmark in its current form does not measure the ability to recover novel chemotypes and that zero-shot evaluations are also affected.
facts.source_locator: Audit paper: Abstract; Sections 5.1.1 and 5.1.2

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: The benchmark asks for none in the sources read. The audit paper argues that a single summary statistic is not enough and that mean, median and nEF1% should all be reported, because one outlier target can move the result.
facts.source_locator: Audit paper: Section 3.1.1

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A compound in a target's library, labelled active or inactive from a dose-response assay; query ligands are compounds taken from co-crystal structures.
facts.source_locator: Audit paper: Section 2; official page: data content table

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Not stated in the files read. The target list names human proteins such as the beta2 adrenergic receptor, estrogen receptor alpha and cellular tumor antigen p53, but no species column is printed.
facts.source_locator: Official page: data content table

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: PubChem BioAssay dose-response data: both actives and inactives are measured. Shen et al. describe the compounds as derived from real-world screening campaigns and both classes as experimentally verified.
facts.source_locator: Official page: header; Shen et al.: Results 'Performance on a subset of LIT-PCBA dataset' and Methods 'Datasets'

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Not fixed by the benchmark. Each target ships PDB templates and query ligands, so ligand-based methods may use the query ligands and structure-based methods the templates; Shen et al. picked one of the recommended PDB entries per target for their docking baselines.
facts.source_locator: Audit paper: Section 2; Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Both are in use. The benchmark provides a training set, so a model may be fitted on it and tested on the validation split; methods may also be run zero-shot from the query ligands or the structures, as Shen et al. do with co-folding methods run at default settings.
facts.source_locator: Audit paper: Section 2; Shen et al.: Methods 'Complex structure prediction'

strengths.text: Both classes are measured: actives and inactives come from high-confidence PubChem BioAssay data, so enrichment is not an artefact of generated decoys. Shen et al. turned to it for that reason after a reviewer questioned decoy-based sets.
strengths.source_locator: Official page: header; Shen et al.: Results 'Performance on a subset of LIT-PCBA dataset'

strengths.text: The per-target composition is published on the official page, with the assay identifier, actives, inactives and number of PDB templates for each of the 15 sets, so a reader can see the class imbalance before choosing a metric.
An AVE-unbiased version of the data is published alongside the full data, so the AVE-debiased split can be used without rebuilding it.

limitations.text: Huang, Knight and Naprienko audit the benchmark and conclude it is compromised by leakage: 2,491 unique inactives shared between training and validation, 323 active training-validation analogue pairs at ECFP4 Tanimoto at or above 0.6 in ALDH1 alone, and query ligands repeated in other splits. They report that a parameter-free memorisation baseline matches or exceeds published results and say nearly all published LIT-PCBA results are undermined.

The official page and Shen et al. print different totals for the full set (7761 actives and 382674 unique inactives against 10 030 actives and 2 798 737 inactives), and neither explains the difference.
limitations.source_locator: Official page: header; Shen et al.: Methods 'Datasets'

limitations.text: Raw EF1% is not comparable across targets here, because the active-to-inactive ratio varies by orders of magnitude; the audit paper and Shen et al. both normalise it, and published numbers using raw EF1% can invert a ranking.
limitations.source_locator: Audit paper: Section 3.1.1 and 3.1.2; Shen et al.: Results 'Performance on a subset of LIT-PCBA dataset'

limitations.text: Published results are often on subsets, not the 15 targets: Shen et al. scored five targets with fewer than 100 000 compounds each and dropped MTORC1 despite it meeting the size rule, because its recommended structures have ambiguous binding sites.

profile.summary: MF-PCBA is a set of 60 drug screening data sets assembled from PubChem BioAssay, each pairing two measurement qualities for the same project: a large, noisy primary screen at a single concentration, and the much smaller dose-response confirmation of the compounds that came through it. The prediction task is regression on the dose-response values, and the point of the benchmark is whether a model can use the hundreds of thousands of primary measurements to predict the few thousand confirmatory ones better than it could from the confirmatory data alone. The collection holds over 16.6 million unique compound and target interactions and over 1.1 million unique compounds, with five fixed random splits per data set. It is for people building molecular property prediction methods, particularly transfer learning between cheap and expensive measurements.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Methods (MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification, Assay Overlap and Size Considerations); README.md: Abstract

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether low-quality data helps. In a real screening campaign a library is tested once at a single dose, then the hits are retested over a dose range to get a reliable potency. Machine learning work usually models only the second, small set and throws the first away. MF-PCBA keeps both and asks for predictions of the dose-response values, so a method is judged on whether it can turn hundreds of thousands of noisy single-dose measurements into better predictions of a few thousand reliable ones. The authors describe the training sets for the confirmatory-only task as typically fewer than 2000 instances, against primary screens orders of magnitude larger. They also point out that the relationship between the two is not simply strong: the per-data-set correlation between paired single-dose and dose-response values is printed for every one of the 60 sets, and it includes weak and negative values.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction, Methods (MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification, Evaluation Strategies), Table 1; README.md: Abstract

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The 60 projects were found by hand, searching PubChem BioAssay for primary and confirmatory screening terms, because the two halves of a campaign may sit in one assay or in two and the formats differ. The assays date from 2008 to 2018. Everything after the selection is automated through PubChem's REST interface: the assay rows are downloaded by identifier, SMILES strings are fetched per compound, replicate primary measurements are averaged by mean, with a median option in the code, and dose-response values reported as half maximal concentrations or their logarithms are converted to pXC50. Four RDKit filtering steps follow: sanitisation, keeping the largest fragment to drop counterions, removing stereochemistry and then deduplicating on SMILES, which makes the task modelling racemic mixtures, and neutralising charges. The paper reports how many compounds each step removed on average. Each finished data set holds the compound identifier, the SMILES string and the single-dose and dose-response activity values, with PubChem's binary activity labels included, and five random 80, 10, 10 splits of the dose-response data are provided with their seeds published.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Data Acquisition, Filtering Steps, MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification), Results (Effects of Filtering); README.md: General, Random seeds

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: One model per data set: the authors say they consider only single-task learning, so a separate model is trained for each of the 60 sets. The recommended comparison is between a dose-response-only model, trained on confirmatory data alone, and a model that also uses the primary data, so that any gain can be attributed to the extra modality. The paper's own evaluation uses two ways of adding the primary information: appending the measured single-dose value to the compound's feature vector, and training a graph neural network on all the primary data and appending the embedding it produces, which also works for molecules it never saw. For the dose-response regression the authors recommend the coefficient of determination together with an error metric, mean absolute error or root mean square error; for the classification form of the task, the Matthews correlation coefficient together with the area under the ROC curve. Their reported numbers come from random forests, support vector machines and graph neural networks for the confirmatory step, with graph networks for the primary step, over the five provided splits.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Assay Overlap and Size Considerations, Evaluation Strategies and Multifidelity Modeling)

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The data are not distributed as a file: the repository downloads and rebuilds them from PubChem. Install Python 3.9 or later with pandas, numpy, rdkit, tqdm and scipy, then call the retrieval script with the primary assay identifier, the names of the columns holding the single-dose and dose-response values, the transformation to apply to the dose-response values, the confirmatory assay identifier when it is a separate assay, and an output directory. Ready-made scripts for all 60 data sets are in the retrieve-scripts directory, and the authors note they can be run in parallel. A notebook then splits the dose-response data into train, validation and test sets five times using the published seeds, writing one numbered directory per split. The paper reports that rebuilding one data set of 335,445 primary molecules took 554.52 seconds on the machine described.
sections.source_locator: README.md: General, Provided scripts, Random seeds, Requirements, Example workflow; Paper: Data Availability

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: 60 multifidelity data sets, each a primary single-dose screen paired with its dose-response confirmation, drawn from PubChem BioAssay with assay dates from 2008 to 2018. In total over 16.6 million unique compound and target interactions and over 1.1 million unique compounds. Table 1 of the paper lists every data set with its assay identifiers, assay type, measurement types, unfiltered sizes and the correlation between the paired measurements; primary screen sizes there run to the hundreds of thousands and confirmatory sets to the hundreds or low thousands. The collection is also split into MF-PCBA-23, the previously analysed subset, and the disjoint MF-PCBA-37.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1, Methods (Data Acquisition, Assay Overlap and Size Considerations), Results

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Five random splits per data set, 80 per cent train, 10 per cent validation and 10 per cent test, drawn over the dose-response data only. The seeds are published in the repository as a JSON file with a notebook that applies them, so the same five splits can be reproduced. The primary single-dose data are not split: they are available in full as the low-fidelity source.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification; README.md: Random seeds, Example workflow

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: For the regression task, the authors recommend the coefficient of determination together with mean absolute error or root mean square error. For the classification form, using PubChem's binary activity labels, the Matthews correlation coefficient together with the area under the ROC curve. Higher is better for the coefficient of determination, the Matthews coefficient and the area under the curve; lower is better for the error metrics. The benchmark defines no single aggregate score across the 60 data sets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Evaluation Strategies and Multifidelity Modeling

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The paper's own evaluation: random forests, support vector machines and graph neural networks for the dose-response step, each run as a confirmatory-only model and as a multifidelity model, with a graph neural network trained on the primary data to produce the embeddings for the second augmentation. The authors report this for all 60 data sets, focusing their analysis on the 37 that were new in this work.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Evaluation Strategies and Multifidelity Modeling; Results

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Deduplication and an overlap check, but no structural split. Stereochemistry is removed and molecules are deduplicated on SMILES within a data set, so the same structure cannot appear twice. The splits are random over compounds, not by scaffold or by cluster, so analogues can fall on both sides. The authors do check overlap with other collections: no assay in common with the 128 assays of PCBA, 27 confirmatory assays in common with the 1310 assays of an earlier ChEMBL-derived set, and no overlap in primary assays. Overlap between the 60 data sets themselves is limited, with over 75.6 per cent of values missing if all compounds are matched against all primary screens.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Filtering Steps, MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification, Assay Overlap and Size Considerations)

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Five splits per data set, whose seeds are published, so a result is reported over five runs rather than one. The paper reports its filtering effects as means with standard deviations, and Table 1 gives a p value alongside each data set's correlation between the paired measurements. The benchmark does not ask for multiple model seeds beyond the five splits.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification; Results, Effects of Filtering on Dataset Size; Table 1

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A molecule in one screening project. Each row is a compound, identified by its PubChem compound identifier and a SMILES string, carrying a single-dose activity value, a dose-response value, or both, for that project's target. Stereochemistry is stripped, so a row stands for a racemic mixture.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification; Filtering Steps

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Mostly inapplicable: the examples are small molecules and the labels are activity against a target or in a cell or organism assay, not sequences from a species. The paper says the assays span biochemical inhibition through to phenotypic experiments on whole organisms, and Table 1 marks each data set's assay type, but no saved file gives a species list.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data Acquisition and Table 1

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: High-throughput screening data from PubChem of two kinds. Primary screens are single-concentration measurements, reported as percent inhibition, percent activity or a B-score at a stated concentration, sometimes with replicates, which are averaged. Confirmatory screens are dose-response measurements reported as half maximal inhibitory, activity or effective concentrations, or their logarithms, all converted to pXC50. Assay types in Table 1 include biochemical, cell-based and whole-organism readouts.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data Acquisition; Table 1

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The molecular structure, plus the primary screening data as the extra modality. The authors say any algorithm that works on fixed-dimension vectors applies, naming fingerprints, physical and chemical descriptors and atom and bond encodings, and the multifidelity augmentations add either the measured single-dose value or an embedding learned from the primary screen. No protein structure or sequence is provided.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification; Evaluation Strategies

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Training from scratch, one model per data set. The authors state they consider only single-task learning, with a separate model for each data set, and the multifidelity setting adds a transfer step: a model trained on the primary screen supplies embeddings to the confirmatory model. There is no zero-shot or pretrained-and-frozen setting defined by the benchmark.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Assay Overlap and Size Considerations; Evaluation Strategies

strengths.text: It keeps the part of screening data that other collections discard. Each data set pairs the full primary screen with its dose-response confirmation, which is what a real campaign produces, and the authors state no earlier collection explicitly considered screening data of different fidelities.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Assay Overlap and Size Considerations; README.md: Abstract

strengths.text: The splits are fixed and published. Five random 80, 10, 10 splits per data set with their seeds in the repository, and a notebook that writes them out, so two groups can score on the same test sets.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification; README.md: Random seeds

strengths.text: The curation is reproducible and documented step by step: the filtering is four named RDKit operations, the paper reports how many compounds each removed, and the MIT licensed code rebuilds every data set from PubChem rather than shipping a snapshot.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Filtering Steps; Results, Effects of Filtering; README.md: Provided scripts; LICENSE

strengths.text: The authors state a recommended comparison, confirmatory-only against multifidelity models, and recommended metrics for both the regression and the classification form, which makes two papers' numbers more likely to mean the same thing.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Evaluation Strategies and Multifidelity Modeling

limitations.text: The test sets are small and the splits are random over compounds, not structural. Confirmatory training sets are typically fewer than 2000 molecules, a 10 per cent test split is therefore in the hundreds, and nothing stops close analogues from sitting on both sides of a split.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Evaluation Strategies; MF-PCBA Format and Problem Specification

limitations.text: Chemical information was deliberately thrown away for consistency: stereochemistry is removed and molecules are then merged on their flat structure, so the labels describe racemic mixtures and a method cannot be credited for handling stereochemistry.

The selection was manual and the sources are heterogeneous. The authors had to search PubChem by hand because formats and conventions differ, primary screens come at different concentrations and with different readouts, and units for confirmatory values are not always consistent, so comparability across the 60 data sets is limited.

There is no leaderboard and no distributed data file. Every user rebuilds the data from PubChem with the scripts, which takes minutes per data set and depends on PubChem's current contents, and the benchmark defines no aggregate score over the 60 sets.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Data Availability; README.md: Provided scripts

run_guide.summary: Rebuild one or all of the 60 data sets from PubChem and write the five published splits of the dose-response data.
prerequisites: Python 3.9 or later with pandas, numpy, rdkit, tqdm and scipy.
An internet connection: the data are downloaded from PubChem, and the paper reports 554.52 seconds for a data set with 335,445 primary molecules on the machine it describes.
The code is MIT licensed. No licence is stated for the assembled data; the measurements come from PubChem.

steps.title: Get the code
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/davidbuterez/mf-pcba
cd mf-pcba
git checkout --detach 776cb013a5ab9949adfc9c11a212cd7ad7dada7a
steps.explanation: The paper's data availability statement names this repository as the way to download, filter and assemble the data sets. The clone and the detach at the commit read for this page were added here.

steps.title: Install the requirements
steps.shell: pip install pandas numpy rdkit tqdm scipy
steps.explanation: The README lists these libraries and a minimum of Python 3.9. The pip line was written here from that list; the README prints the names, not a command.

steps.title: Rebuild one data set
steps.shell: python pubchem_retrieve.py --AID "1445" --list_of_sd_cols "Primary Inhibition" "Primary Inhibition Rep 2" "Primary Inhibition Rep 3" --list_of_dr_cols "IC50" --transform_dr "pXC50" --save_dir retrieved
steps.explanation: The README's first worked invocation, for the case where the primary and confirmatory data are in a single PubChem assay. For a project split across two assays the README's second example adds --AID_DR with the confirmatory identifier. Scripts for all 60 data sets are in retrieve-scripts.

steps.title: Write the five splits
steps.shell: jupyter notebook split_DR_with_random_seeds.ipynb
steps.explanation: The README says this notebook splits the dose-response data five times using the published seeds, writing train, validation and test CSV files into one numbered directory per split. The jupyter command was added here; the notebook name and its behaviour are the README's.
