profile.summary: This is the evaluation the HyCell technical report runs: frozen, zero-shot embeddings of eleven pretrained single-cell models, plus PCA of the counts, scored on seven human atlases that were excluded from HyCell's pretraining corpus. Each embedding is scored for biological conservation and batch correction with scIB metrics and for annotation transfer to a held-out batch, combined into one score S. Every model was rerun by the authors on the same cells with one scoring implementation, so the figures are comparable within this report.
profile.summary_source_locator: Report: Abstract; Section 3.1; README.md: Recorded result

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The question is whether a pretrained model's frozen embedding of a cell is useful without further training: does it separate the curated cell types, does it mix cells from different donors, laboratories and chemistries, and can a simple classifier trained on some batches annotate a held-out batch from it. The report motivates this by noting that independent evaluations find zero-shot embeddings often separate cell types no better than PCA of the counts, so PCA fitted to each atlas is included as a reference without pretraining.
sections.source_locator: Report: Section 1; Section 3.1

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Seven atlases with raw integer counts and curated cell-type labels are used: the integer-count parts of the scIB integration benchmarks for human immune cells (32,484 cells, 9 batches, 16 cell types), pancreas (10,963 cells, 5 batches, 14 types) and lung (9,701 cells, 4 batches, 11 types); peripheral blood mononuclear cells from two 10x runs (12,039 cells, 2 batches, 9 types); the healthy donors of the MultiVINE human brain vasculature atlas (21,155 cells, 10 donors, 14 types); a stratified 40,322-cell sample of the cross-tissue immune atlas spanning 17 tissue sites, 12 donors and three 10x chemistries, with 45 cell types; and a 41,140-cell sample of the Asian Immune Diversity Atlas (5 sites, 32 types). Batches are the unit held out in annotation transfer and the label the batch metrics use. Every dataset and collection contributing cells to these atlases, and to a separate development set of eight tissues used for the design choices, was removed from HyCell's pretraining corpus, taking the Census from 95.0 million cells in 555 datasets down to 79.5 million in 532.
sections.source_locator: Report: Section 3.1 and Table 2; Section 2.5

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: All embeddings are scored by one implementation built on scib-metrics, on the absolute scale with no rescaling across methods. Biological conservation is the mean of seven scIB metrics: isolated-label score, NMI and ARI of k-means and of Leiden clusters against the cell types, cell-type silhouette and cLISI. Batch correction is the mean of five: batch silhouette, iLISI, kBET, graph connectivity and principal-component regression. Annotation transfer holds out each batch in turn, trains a logistic-regression classifier and a 15-nearest-neighbour classifier on the remaining batches, and reports macro-F1 averaged over held-out batches. The composite score is S = 0.3 Bio + 0.2 Batch + 0.25 LR + 0.25 kNN, which weights the scIB total (0.6 Bio + 0.4 Batch) and annotation transfer equally. Atlases are weighted equally in all averages.
sections.source_locator: Report: Section 3.1, Metrics

sections.title: Which systems are compared, and under what conditions
sections.body: Ten published models are compared with HyCell: Stack, SCimilarity, scFoundation, UCE, Tahoe-x1, TranscriptFormer, scGPT, Geneformer V2, STATE and scPRINT, each run by the authors with its released weights and default inference settings on the same cells, plus PCA fitted to each atlas. The conditions are not identical, and the report says so: Stack encodes sets of 256 cells and the authors encode each batch together, so Stack uses batch labels at inference; SCimilarity and scPRINT were trained with cell-type labels; PCA is fitted to each atlas; and HyCell embeds each cell from its counts alone. The report marks these cases in its tables and states that Stack also draws on the other cells of a sample at inference, which helps sample-level tasks that this benchmark does not include.
sections.source_locator: Report: Section 3.1 Models; Section 3.2; README.md: Recorded result

sections.title: Downstream analyses on one atlas
sections.body: Beyond the scores, the report applies the frozen embeddings to the cross-tissem immune atlas, where cells of the same state come from 12 donors, 17 tissue sites and three chemistries. The 2,778 CD4 T cells (1,343 naive or central-memory, 1,435 effector or effector-memory) are split in two by k-means on each embedding; with HyCell the groups are 85% naive and 96% effector (ARI 0.64) and nearly independent of chemistry, while every other embedding reaches at most ARI 0.031 and seven of them follow chemistry instead. Diffusion pseudotime on the 3,751 cells of four B-cell to plasma-cell states (1,440, 572, 618 and 1,121) is correlated with stage at Spearman 0.937 for HyCell, the highest of all embeddings, and eight of the ten published models order the stages less faithfully than PCA. The decoder is used to read gene programs back from embeddings, with decoded and counted fold changes correlated at Spearman 0.81 over the 12,879 genes detected in at least 1% of either state.
sections.source_locator: Report: Sections 4, 4.1, 4.2, 4.3

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The hycell package installs from the repository subdirectory with pip, and its weights (64 MB) ship inside the package, so it runs without network access once installed. Embedding is one call on an AnnData object of raw counts, or one command-line call on an h5ad file, and the embedding can then be used as any representation in scanpy. Decoding and fine-tuning have their own calls, and four example scripts plus a 512-cell test file from the scIB lung atlas come with the package. The report's own scores are reproduced bit for bit on a CUDA GPU with flash-attn, verified on all seven evaluation atlases, 167,804 cells. What the package does not provide is the benchmark harness itself: the scIB and annotation-transfer scoring of the eleven models is not among the published scripts.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Install, Embed, Decode, Fine-tune, Examples, Reproducibility

facts.value: Zero-shot frozen embeddings for the headline comparison, with simple classifiers trained on top for annotation transfer. strengths.text: Every model was rerun by the authors on the same cells with released weights and default settings, and all embeddings were scored by one implementation on the absolute scale, so the figures within the report are not collected from different papers.
The differing conditions are declared rather than hidden: the tables mark batch-grouped inference and training with cell-type labels, and the text names which models those are.

The embeddings that were scored can be reproduced: the package carries its weights, and the README states the embeddings match the report bit for bit on a CUDA GPU with flash-attn, verified on all seven atlases.
A reference without pretraining is included and reported per atlas, so the reader can see where pretrained embeddings beat PCA of the counts and where they do not.

limitations.text: It is developer-run: the authors of the model under test chose the atlases, the metrics and the composite weights and ran every comparator themselves. There is no independent harness, and the benchmark scoring code is not among the published scripts.

The held-out claim is established for HyCell only: the seven atlases were removed from its pretraining corpus, but the report does not say whether the ten comparators were trained on cells of these atlases.

Models run under different conditions: Stack receives batch labels at inference, SCimilarity and scPRINT were trained with cell-type labels, and PCA is fitted to each atlas, so the single score column mixes settings. No uncertainty is printed for any value.

Only cell-level tasks are measured. Tasks defined per sample, such as predicting a donor's disease state, are not included, and the report notes that Stack's use of the other cells of a sample helps exactly those tasks.

run_guide.summary: Install the hycell package, embed an h5ad of raw counts, and use the embedding for clustering or annotation transfer as the example scripts do.
prerequisites: Python 3.10 or newer and torch 2.4 or newer; a CUDA GPU is recommended and CPU inference runs at about 13 cells per second with 16 threads in the authors' tests.
An h5ad file with raw integer counts and all measured genes, not a highly variable subset.
The code and weights are Apache-2.0; the weights were trained on CZ CELLxGENE Census data and the bundled test cells come from the scIB lung atlas, both CC BY 4.0.

steps.title: Install the package
steps.shell:
pip install "git+https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hyra-results.git#subdirectory=AI4Science/hycell"
pip install flash-attn --no-build-isolation
steps.explanation: Both lines are the README's. The second is optional and CUDA-only; it installs the attention kernel used in training, with which the README says the embeddings match the report bit for bit.

steps.title: Check the weights
steps.shell: hycell info --verify
steps.explanation: The weights ship inside the package; this command checks their sha256, as the README states.

steps.title: Embed the cells
steps.shell: hycell embed cells.h5ad -o cells_hycell.h5ad
steps.explanation: The README's command-line form, which writes the input with the embedding in obsm["X_hycell"]. The alternative form writes a numpy array plus a file of observation names.

steps.title: Run one of the example analyses
steps.shell: python docs/examples/decode_programs.py tests/data/lung_512.h5ad --groupby cell_type --a Macrophage --b "Type 2"
steps.explanation: The README's own example, run against the 512-cell scIB lung sample that ships with the package. It decodes gene programs for two cell groups and compares them with the fold change of the counts; the README reports that it lists SFTPC, SFTPB and SFTPA1 highest in type 2 pneumocytes. For annotation transfer between batches, the README names label_transfer.py in the same folder.

name: HyInv technical report inverse-folding comparison
description: Compares inverse-folding methods by the structural consistency, native recovery and diversity of the sequences they design for held-out protein backbones.

limitations: Author-assembled and author-run: the panels, the baseline settings and the scoring were all chosen by the team that released HyInv.
Baselines are single published settings, so comparisons are at comparable rather than equal sequence diversity.
ESMFold2 is the primary predictor and also the reinforcement-learning reward.
No chain list or split manifest is published, so the panels cannot be rebuilt.

split_manifest.note: No manifest is published for any panel.

attributes.scope_note: Five test panels (CATH4.3 test, CATH4.2 test, TS500, TS50, RecentPDB) with ESMFold2, RecentPDB also with Boltz2 and Protenix2, giving seven panel-predictor columns; a development panel (CATH4.3 validation) that fixed the checkpoint and sampler; and four single-chain design applications. Assembled and run by the model's own authors, so every evaluation in it is author-reported.
attributes.source_locator: Sections 5 and 6; Table 3; Appendices A, D and G
attributes.task: Protein inverse folding: design amino-acid sequences for a given backbone, scored by refolding the designs and comparing the predicted structure with the input backbone.

profile.summary: This is the inverse-folding comparison reported in the HyInv technical report, not a released suite. Ten published inverse-folding models and HyInv design sequences for the same held-out backbones from five panels (CATH4.3 test, CATH4.2 test, TS500, TS50 and RecentPDB), the designs are refolded, and the methods are compared by scTM, the TM-score between the predicted structure of a design and the input backbone, with native sequence recovery and sequence diversity reported beside it. It is useful to someone choosing a sequence-design model for screening libraries, with the caveat that the panels, the baseline settings and the scoring were all chosen and run by the team releasing HyInv.
profile.summary_source_locator: Report: Abstract; Section 5.1

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The task is protein inverse folding: given a backbone, produce amino-acid sequences that fold into it. The comparison asks how structurally consistent a method's designs are, at what sequence diversity. Screening needs many candidates rather than one, so the report states that a model is useful in proportion to the diversity it offers at a given structural quality, and compares methods at comparable diversity rather than at one temperature. Structural consistency is read from refolding: the designed sequence is folded by a structure predictor and the prediction is compared with the input backbone.
sections.source_locator: Report: Section 1

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Five test panels of single chains are used: CATH4.3 test (1,882 chains), CATH4.2 test (1,120), TS500 (500), TS50 (50) and RecentPDB, which is 121 chains from 111 recent PDB entries covering 26,766 residues at lengths 42 to 978. The panels hold standard chains with complete backbones, and RecentPDB was screened for homology to PDB and CATH entries before 2025. ESMFold2 folds every design on all five panels; RecentPDB is additionally folded by Boltz2 and Protenix2, neither of which is used in training. That gives seven panel and predictor columns. A sixth panel, CATH4.3 validation, is the development panel on which the checkpoint and the sampler setting were chosen before any test panel was generated. Four further application panels (de novo backbones, pocket-constrained libraries, loop and window redesign, and four named enzymes) have panel rules, thresholds and endpoints fixed before designs were generated. Not every backbone in them was chosen by rule: ten of the twelve pocket backbones were chosen by rule and two were single cases chosen earlier, the 8 loop and window backbones were chosen by rule, and the four named enzymes are a fixed list that the report says is homologous to the training data and chosen for display.
sections.source_locator: Report: Section 5.1; Appendix A; Appendix G, Table 10

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each method designs sequences for every backbone in a panel at its own published setting. The designs are folded and scored by scTM, the TM-score of the predicted structure of a design to the native backbone, computed on the C-alpha trace at valid sites, normalised by the native length and clipped at one; higher is better. A failed fold is a gap in the average rather than an imputed value. Panel values average the designs of a chain first and then the chains. Recovery is descriptive and has weight zero in the reward, and diversity is matched rather than ranked. The headline comparison is a paired difference: the macro-average of the per-chain scTM difference between HyInv and a baseline, with a 95 per cent percentile interval from 10,000 resamples with a fixed seed; a starred difference is one whose interval excludes zero, and intervals are not adjusted for multiple comparisons. For sampler and ablation comparisons the report instead reads scTM at a fixed diversity from a least-squares quadratic fit of scTM against diversity over a temperature grid, with no extrapolation.
sections.source_locator: Report: Appendix A; Appendix B

sections.title: What the comparison found
sections.body: HyInv has the highest scTM in all seven panel and predictor columns, with an average of 0.875 against 0.867 for ProteinZero V2 with ESM2 weights and 0.863 for ProteinMPNN. Of the 70 comparisons (ten baselines across the seven columns), all 70 point estimates favour HyInv and 61 have an interval that excludes zero. The report states which nine include zero. The parallel decoders PiFold, CMLM, LM-Design and DPLM-2 3B sample at much lower diversity than HyInv, so their differences are not at matched diversity.
sections.source_locator: Report: Section 5.2; Appendix D.2

sections.title: Application panels
sections.body: Beyond the five test panels, the report runs the same default setting on four single-chain design tasks. On 74 de novo backbones in 58 clusters at 30 per cent sequence identity, with 4 designs per backbone, the endpoint is the number of designs per backbone that are both foldable (ESMFold2 scTM at least 0.9) and novel (identity below 0.3 to the nearest UniRef50 sequence and to the nearest sequence of the pretraining library). On 12 ligand-pocket backbones, residues within 4 angstroms of the ligand keep their native identity, 384 designs are made per backbone and cell, and the endpoint is the number of different sequences after clustering at 50 per cent identity among the designs that pass an scTM of at least 0.90 and a site C-alpha RMSD of at most 1.0 angstroms. Loop and window redesign covers 8 backbones chosen by rule plus 4 named enzymes whose catalytic residues are fixed, with 128 designs per backbone and region. The report says the named enzymes are homologous to the training data and were chosen for display.
sections.source_locator: Report: Section 6; Appendix G

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: No scoring harness or panel manifest is published, so the panels themselves cannot be rebuilt from the release. What the repository does offer is the design step: the hyinv package installs with pip, and one command designs a given number of sequences for a PDB backbone, with options for fixed positions, the draft and rewrite temperatures, the device and the accelerated inference path. Refolding and the scTM calculation have to be supplied by the user.

facts.value: Five test panels of single chains: CATH4.3 test (1,882 chains), CATH4.2 test (1,120), TS500 (500), TS50 (50) and RecentPDB (121 chains from 111 recent PDB entries, 26,766 residues, lengths 42 to 978). CATH4.3 validation (1,529 chains in the store's dataset list) is the development panel. Four application panels add 74 de novo backbones, 12 ligand-pocket backbones, 8 loop and window backbones and 4 named enzymes.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Evaluation only: every panel is a test set and each test panel was evaluated once. Model selection used a separate development panel, CATH4.3 validation, on which the checkpoint and the sampler temperatures were chosen before the test panels were generated. The test panels are the published test splits of CATH4.3, CATH4.2, TS500 and TS50 plus the authors' own RecentPDB panel.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: scTM is the primary metric, higher is better: the TM-score of the predicted structure of a design to the native backbone on the C-alpha trace at valid sites, normalised by native length and clipped at one. Native sequence recovery (higher is more native-like, but descriptive only) and sequence diversity (mean pairwise normalised Hamming distance between a chain's designs, matched rather than ranked) are reported beside it. pLDDT, scRMSD (lower is better) and a C-alpha lDDT-style score are also reported. The application panels use novel-and-foldable yield per backbone, distinct passing designs per plate, site RMSD and region RMSD.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 5.1; Appendix B

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Ten released models at their published single-temperature settings: ProteinMPNN, ProteinMPNN with grouped decoding, ProteinMPNN low-noise grouped, ProteinZero V2 with ESM1 weights, ProteinZero V2 with ESM2 weights, PiFold, CMLM, LM-Design 650M, DPLM-2 3B and LigandMPNN. The native sequence refolded is shown as a reference line. ProteinMPNN is the only baseline with a temperature sweep.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 5.1; Appendix D.1; Appendix D.3

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Three controls, each partial. The RecentPDB panel was screened for homology to PDB and CATH entries before 2025. The reinforcement-learning pool of 50,000 backbones was filtered against the benchmark datasets with a homology mask. The application panels were screened with MMseqs2 against the pretraining library and the benchmark reference set, counting a hit at 30 per cent identity and 80 per cent coverage; the report states this is a coverage rule, so shorter similar fragments remain, and the four named enzymes are homologous to the training data by design. The baselines are released checkpoints whose own training data the report does not screen.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 1; Section 5.1; Appendix G, Homology of the panels

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Paired differences carry 95 per cent percentile intervals from 10,000 resamples of the resampling unit, with one resample shared across all compared rows and a fixed seed; the intervals are not adjusted for multiple comparisons, and the report flags that a few starred intervals have a lower end within 0.001 of zero. Two independent generate-and-fold runs on the development panel differed by -0.0008 and +0.0016, which the authors read as noise of about 0.0015 in one evaluation, and they say differences between checkpoints below about 0.003 are not resolvable. Scores at equal diversity carry intervals from 1,000 draws in which all curve points are recomputed from one cluster resample.
facts.source_locator: Report: Appendix A

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a protein backbone, given as a single chain, for which a method must design sequences; panel values are macro-averages over chains. In the application panels an example is a de novo backbone, a ligand-pocket backbone, or a backbone with a nominated loop or window.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 1; Appendix A

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Unreported. The panels are drawn from CATH and PDB chains and the four named enzymes are TEM-1 beta-lactamase, subtilisin, lysozyme and PETase, but the report gives no species composition for any panel.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 5.1; Appendix G

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: None. Every quantity in the comparison is computed from predicted structures and designed sequences, and the report states that none is an experimental measurement.
facts.source_locator: Report: Appendix B

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: A backbone structure. HyInv reads only the N, C-alpha, C and O backbone atoms of the input PDB, and LigandMPNN, which can read ligand atoms, is run on backbone coordinates only. In the constrained application panels a method is additionally given the positions whose native identity must be kept.
facts.source_locator: Report: Appendix D.1; Appendix G; README.md: HyInv

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: No adaptation to the panels. Every baseline is run from its released weights at the single setting at which it was published and is not tuned to the panels, and HyInv uses one setting throughout, chosen on the development panel. Some baseline cells were regenerated by the authors and used only where the procedure reproduced the released score on RecentPDB.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 5.1; Appendix D.1

strengths.text: The comparison is made at comparable sequence diversity rather than at one temperature, and the report quantifies how far from equal diversity the comparison is: the largest diversity offset, 0.016, is worth at most 0.0011 scTM at the slope of the development curve.
strengths.source_locator: Report: Appendix A, Scores at equal diversity

strengths.text: Model selection and the test evaluation are separated: the checkpoint and the sampler temperatures were fixed on a development panel before the test panels were generated, and each test panel was evaluated once.
Because the primary structure predictor is also the reinforcement-learning reward, the RecentPDB panel is additionally folded by two predictors that never enter training, Boltz2 and Protenix2.

Regenerated baseline cells are accepted only where the authors' procedure reproduced the released score on RecentPDB, and the per-baseline reproduction difference and fraction of identical sequences are printed.

limitations.text: Every number is author-reported: the team releasing HyInv chose the panels, ran all ten baselines at settings of their choosing, and defined the scoring. Only HyInv has a tuned setting and a temperature sweep on most panels.
Nothing here is an experimental measurement. Designs are judged by a structure predictor, and the primary predictor ESMFold2 is also the reward used to train HyInv.

The margins are small next to the stated run-to-run noise. The average margin over the strongest baseline is +0.008 scTM, while one evaluation carries noise of about 0.0015 and differences below about 0.003 are called unresolvable; 9 of the 70 baseline comparisons have an interval that includes zero.
limitations.source_locator: Report: Section 5.2; Appendix A; Appendix D.2

limitations.text: Two baselines are run outside their declared range or compared off matched diversity: ProteinZero V2 is declared for backbones of up to 100 residues but run on the full panels, and the parallel decoders sit at much lower diversity than HyInv.

steps.title: Install the package
steps.shell:
pip install -e .
pip install -e '.[fast]'
steps.explanation: The first line installs the reference implementation. The second is optional and adds the triton kernels used by the accelerated paths on CUDA GPUs.

steps.title: Design sequences for a backbone
steps.shell: python -m hyinv design --pdb structure.pdb --n 128 --seed 0 --out designs.fasta
steps.explanation: Writes 128 designed sequences for the backbone in structure.pdb to a FASTA file. The report's default setting is draft temperature 0.6 and rewrite temperature 0.34, which are the defaults of the options listed in the README.

steps.title: Keep chosen positions fixed
steps.shell: python -m hyinv design --pdb structure.pdb --chain A --fixed 12-20,45 --n 16
steps.explanation: The constrained application panels keep nominated residues at their native identity. This is the command form the README gives for that, with positions numbered by PDB residue number and qualified by chain for multi-chain inputs.

steps.title: Use the accelerated path
steps.shell: python -m hyinv design --pdb structure.pdb --n 128 --fast bf16 --out designs.fasta
steps.explanation: The bf16 setting is the fastest path but a numerically different one: the README states that sequences with the same seed are not identical to the default off path. The report's evaluated sequences all come from the reference sampler.

outputs: A FASTA file of designed sequences, one record per design, with chains separated by a forward slash for multi-chain inputs.
No score: the refolding and scTM calculation of the report are not part of the release.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
The commands reproduce the design step only. The panels, the refolding recipe and the scoring code of the comparison are not published, so the reported numbers cannot be reproduced from the release.
Outputs are identical only for the same seed, batch size, device type and PyTorch version, and the README states that CPU and GPU random streams differ.

name: HyPLM technical report protein language model evaluation
description: Compares protein language models on zero-shot fitness, masked-residue likelihood and frozen-representation probes for structure, function, localisation and fitness.

limitations: Developer-run: the authors chose the tasks, the adapters, the layer-selection rule and the statistics, and ran every baseline.
Every accuracy number is a BF16 run. The released default is the INT8 engine, for which no accuracy value is printed.
Per-task values are printed for 13 of the 29 models only.

ProteinGym scores depend on the assays included, the aggregation, the checkpoint and the scoring code; this suite's ProteinGym protocol is its own and is not the leaderboard's, though the authors report reproducing eight leaderboard checkpoints to within 0.0025.
attributes.scope_note: 32 tasks run on 29 models (HyPLM-Flash and 28 public checkpoints from 13 families), all in BF16 through the authors' own adapters. Assembled and run by the developer of HyPLM-Flash, so every evaluation in it is author-reported and none is independent of the developer.
attributes.source_locator: Section 4; Appendix A; Table 4
attributes.task: Protein representation learning: zero-shot variant scoring from the masked-language-model head, masked-residue likelihood, and linear probes on frozen representations.

profile.summary: This is the protein language model evaluation reported in the HyPLM technical report, not a released suite. HyPLM-Flash and 28 public checkpoints from 13 model families (29 models in all) are run through the same evaluation code in BF16 on 32 tasks: zero-shot variant scoring from the masked-language-model head on ProteinGym, masked-residue likelihood on two held-out panels, and linear probes on frozen representations for structure, function, localisation, interaction and fitness. It is useful to someone choosing a protein encoder for embeddings or variant scoring, with the caveat that the developer of one of the models chose the tasks, wrote the adapters and ran every baseline.
profile.summary_source_locator: Report: Section 4; Appendix A

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Three capabilities of a protein encoder, each read without fine-tuning the encoder. First, zero-shot variant effect: each substitution is scored by the masked-marginal log-likelihood ratio and the score is correlated with an experimental fitness measurement. Second, how well the model models protein sequence at all, as the negative log-likelihood of masked residues under identical masks. Third, what its frozen representations contain, probed by linear or bilinear heads for secondary structure, residue contacts, fold, enzyme and Gene Ontology annotation, subcellular localisation, metal-ion binding, human protein interaction, and fitness or property regression. Throughput on one GPU is measured beside the accuracy so that models can be placed on an accuracy against speed plot. That plot does not compare like with like on precision: HyPLM-Flash is timed on its INT8 engine and the baselines in their reference implementations, while all accuracy figures are BF16 runs.
sections.source_locator: Report: Sections 3 and 4.1 to 4.3; Figure 1 caption; Appendix A, Probes and Throughput

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The tasks are taken from existing benchmarks rather than built afresh: ProteinGym v1.3 for zero-shot substitutions, TAPE for secondary structure, ProteinNet contacts, remote homology, fluorescence and stability, CASP14 and CASP15 evaluation domains for contacts, the SaProt and DeepFRI splits for enzyme commission and Gene Ontology terms, DGEB for prokaryotic enzyme classification and archaeal retrieval, DeepLoc through PEER for localisation, PEER for human protein interaction, and FLIP and FLIP2 for AAV, GB1, Meltome, amylase and a cross-protein hydrolase split. Each row of the task table prints the number of proteins in the train, validation and test splits, and where a row groups several tasks the sizes are those of the first. Two panels are the authors' own: 479 proteins from their held-out UniRef split, and 887 recently released PDB chains, clustered at 50 per cent identity with MMseqs2 after removing exact matches to the training corpus.
sections.source_locator: Report: Table 4; Section 4.3

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Every model is run in BF16 through a thin adapter around its reference implementation, and inputs longer than a model's window are processed in windows with 50 per cent overlap whose residue representations are averaged. For the probes, sequence-level tasks use representations mean-pooled over residues without special tokens and per-residue tasks use the residue representations; for every task and model six layers at relative depths 0.25, 0.5, 0.625, 0.75, 0.875 and 1.0 are evaluated and the layer and the regularisation strength are selected on the validation split, or by 5-fold cross-validation on the training split where a task has none. Regression probes are closed-form ridge regressions, classification probes are L2-regularised logistic regressions fitted with L-BFGS, multi-label tasks fit one output per term and report Fmax, and the contact head is a symmetric bilinear form on 32-dimensional projections trained with AdamW on up to 8,000 ProteinNet proteins. A ProteinGym score is the sum over a variant's substitutions of the log probability of the mutant minus that of the wild type, with each position masked on its own, aggregated by the benchmark's official procedure. Confidence intervals come from 5,000 bootstrap replicates over assays, proteins, queries, sequences or pairs, with identical resamples for paired differences.
sections.source_locator: Report: Appendix A, Models, Probes, Zero-shot scores and likelihood, Statistics

sections.title: Reproduction checks and withheld results
sections.body: The authors state that their runs of eight published ESM-2 and ESM C checkpoints reproduce the ProteinGym leaderboard to within 0.0025. They withhold the zero-shot and likelihood results of xTrimoPGLM because their runs fall 0.07 to 0.09 below the leaderboard and its likelihood is implausibly high, which they attribute to an incompatibility between their adapter and that model's masked-language-model head; its embedding results are kept. Models without a suitable masked-language-model head (ProtT5, Ankh, Ankh3) are left out of the zero-shot and likelihood panels. ESM3-open and SaProt are evaluated from sequence alone although their published ProteinGym results also use structure inputs, and E1-600M is run on the query sequence alone although it is trained to use retrieved homologues. Three regression splits (GB1 two-vs-rest and three-vs-rest and the FLIP2 cross-protein hydrolase split) are reported but excluded from the summary statistics, because their validation data come from the training distribution while the test sets are strongly shifted and numerically equivalent runs of the same model differ by up to 0.2.
sections.source_locator: Report: Section 4.1; Appendix A, Statistics and Deviations

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: No evaluation harness, task packaging or scoring script is published, so the 32 tasks cannot be rerun from the release. The repository publishes the model and its inference engine: a download script for the weights, a pip install, an encode call that returns residue or mean-pooled representations from a chosen layer, and a logits call that masks a position so that a masked-marginal variant score can be computed. The README states that the INT8 default is within 0.01 of BF16 on zero-shot, structure, function-annotation and likelihood metrics, and recommends BF16 when training regressors on near-identical variants.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Installation; Usage; Precision

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: 32 tasks, drawn from published benchmarks except for two likelihood panels of the authors' own, the held-out UniRef split and the PDB time split. The task table lists ProteinGym v1.3 substitutions (217 assays), a held-out UniRef panel (479 proteins) and a PDB time split (887 entries); TAPE secondary structure (8,678 train, 2,170 validation, 513 test on CB513, with TS115 and CASP12 grouped in the same row), ProteinNet contacts (25,299 / 224 / 40), CASP14 and CASP15 contact domains (82 and 95), TAPE remote homology (12,312 / 736 / 718); EC in two splits (13,090 / 1,465 / 1,604 for the first), GO-MF, GO-BP and GO-CC (26,225 / 2,904 / 3,350 for the first), DGEB EC (512 train, 128 test), DGEB Arch retrieval (2,343 queries), DeepLoc through PEER (8,743 / 2,190 / 2,745), metal-ion binding (5,068 / 662 / 665), HumanPPI (26,319 / 234 / 180); and FLIP, FLIP2 and TAPE regression splits for AAV (28,626 / 3,181 / 50,776 for two-vs-many), GB1 (381 / 43 / 8,309), Meltome (5,149 / 643 / 1,366), amylase (2,574 / 644 / 488), a cross-protein hydrolase split (11,970 / 2,993 / 9,972), fluorescence and stability (21,446 / 5,362 / 27,217 for the first) and thermostability (5,056 / 639 / 1,336).
facts.source_locator: Report: Table 4

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Each probed task keeps the train, validation and test split of its source benchmark, with the sizes printed in the task table. The validation split selects the layer and the regularisation strength; where a task has no validation split (DGEB EC) selection is by 5-fold cross-validation on the training split. The zero-shot tasks have no training split and are scored on all 217 ProteinGym assays. The two likelihood panels are test-only: 479 held-out UniRef proteins and 887 recent PDB entries. Three FLIP and FLIP2 regression splits are deliberately shifted between validation and test and are excluded from the summary statistics for that reason.
facts.source_locator: Report: Table 4; Appendix A, Probes and Statistics

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: One primary metric per task, as the task table prints them. Spearman correlation for ProteinGym substitutions and for every fitness or property regression (higher is better); negative log-likelihood in nats, with perplexity beside it, for the two likelihood panels (lower is better); three-state accuracy for secondary structure, precision at L/5 over long-range pairs for contacts, fold accuracy for remote homology, Fmax for EC and the three Gene Ontology branches, macro F1 for DGEB EC, MAP@5 for DGEB Arch retrieval, and accuracy for localisation, metal-ion binding and HumanPPI (all higher is better). Contacts are residue pairs whose C-beta atoms, or C-alpha for ProteinNet, are closer than 8 angstroms, and long range means a sequence separation of at least 24. Embedding throughput in residues per second on one H20 is reported beside the accuracy. The speed figures are not a same-precision comparison: HyPLM-Flash is timed on its INT8 engine and the baselines in their reference implementations with the fastest attention kernel each supports, while every accuracy figure is a BF16 run.
facts.source_locator: Report: Table 4; Table 3; Appendix A, Probes; Figure 1 caption; Section 3; Appendix A, Throughput

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: 28 public checkpoints from 13 model families, from ESM-2 8M to ESM-2 15B, giving 29 models with HyPLM-Flash. The families named in the report are ESM-1b, ESM-2, ESM C, ESM3-open, E1, DPLM, SaProt, ProtBERT, ProtT5, Ankh, Ankh3, AMPLIFY and xTrimoPGLM. For the ProteinGym comparison the report also lists published leaderboard values for the top single-sequence entries, including the supervised predictors VespaG and VESPA.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 4; Appendix A, Models; Table 5

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: One task-level control and no control over the baselines' own training data. The PDB likelihood panel holds entries released later than the training data of every model evaluated, clustered at 50 per cent identity with MMseqs2 after exact matches to the authors' training corpus were removed, and the UniRef panel is held out of HyPLM-Flash training. For the probed tasks the report relies on the source benchmarks' own splits and describes no further identity cut-off or time split, and it does not screen any public checkpoint's training data against the task test sets.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 4.3; Table 4

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Paired bootstrap confidence intervals, 5,000 replicates, resampling the unit that matches the task: assays for ProteinGym with the official aggregation recomputed in each replicate, proteins for structure and likelihood, queries for retrieval, and sequences or pairs elsewhere; paired differences use identical resamples. The report prints 95 per cent intervals for the zero-shot differences between HyPLM-Flash and each comparable encoder. No seed replicates of the probe fitting are reported, but the report states that on the three excluded regression splits numerically equivalent runs of the same model differ by up to 0.2.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 4.1; Appendix A, Statistics

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A protein sequence in most tasks, with the unit of scoring varying by task: an assay of substitutions for ProteinGym (217 assays, scored one variant at a time and correlated within the assay), a protein for the likelihood panels and the sequence-level probes, a residue for secondary structure, a residue pair for contacts, a query for DGEB Arch retrieval, and a protein pair for HumanPPI.
facts.source_locator: Report: Table 4; Appendix A, Probes

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Unreported as a composition. The report names the source benchmarks rather than the species they cover; the only organism-linked labels it prints are the human cell Meltome split, the human protein interaction task, and DGEB's prokaryotic enzyme classification and archaeal retrieval tasks.
facts.source_locator: Report: Table 4

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Experimental measurements enter only through the source benchmarks. The zero-shot task correlates model scores with the 217 substitution assays of ProteinGym v1.3, and the regression probes are fitted to FLIP, FLIP2 and TAPE measurements of AAV and GB1 fitness, amylase and hydrolase activity, melting temperature, fluorescence and stability. The report does not describe any assay protocol itself, and the structure, annotation and likelihood tasks involve no assay.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 4.1; Table 4

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The amino-acid sequence alone, for every model. Models that can read more are deliberately restricted: E1-600M is run on the query sequence without retrieved homologues, and ESM3-open and SaProt are evaluated from sequence alone although their published ProteinGym results also use structure inputs. Representations may be taken from any of six layer depths, selected on validation data.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 4; Appendix A, Deviations

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot and frozen probes only; no encoder is fine-tuned. Zero-shot scores come from the masked-language-model head, and every supervised task fits a linear probe, or a bilinear contact head, on cached frozen representations, with the layer and the regularisation strength chosen on validation data. Features are cached in FP16, or FP32 for the Ankh models. Every accuracy number is from a BF16 run of the model.
facts.source_locator: Report: Section 4; Appendix A, Probes

strengths.text: Every model is run through one evaluation code path in the same precision, with the same probe family, the same six candidate layer depths and the same selection rule, so differences between models are not differences between published protocols.

The authors check their own pipeline against an external reference: runs of eight published ESM-2 and ESM C checkpoints reproduce the ProteinGym leaderboard to within 0.0025, and the one model they could not reproduce is named and its affected results withheld.
Differences carry paired bootstrap intervals over the natural resampling unit, and the report reads small zero-shot gaps as ties rather than wins.

The likelihood panel uses chains released later than the training data of every model evaluated, with exact matches to the authors' corpus removed, which is a time-based control rather than a random split.

limitations.text: The evaluation is run by the developer of one of the models under test: the authors chose the 32 tasks, wrote the adapters, selected the layers and ran every public checkpoint themselves.

The probed tasks inherit whatever leakage their source splits carry: apart from the two likelihood panels the report describes no identity cut-off or time split of its own, and it does not check any public checkpoint's training data against the test sets.

Models are compared outside the setting they were built for in at least three cases, which the report states but which still limits the comparison: E1-600M is trained with retrieved homologues and is run without them, and ESM3-open and SaProt can read structure but are run from sequence alone.

Three of the regression splits are unreliable by the authors' own account and are dropped from the summary statistics while still being printed in the tables, so a reader comparing per-task values must know which splits the averages exclude.

Neither the evaluation code nor the task packaging is released, and the report publishes per-task values for HyPLM-Flash and twelve other encoders only, so the 29-model comparison cannot be rerun or inspected task by task.

steps.title: Download the weights and install
steps.shell:
bash weights/download.sh
pip install -e .
steps.explanation: The script fetches, merges and verifies the two weight shards; the pip step installs the package and its dependencies. The README notes that a GITHUB_TOKEN is only needed if the API rate limit is reached.

steps.title: Extract frozen representations
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from hyplm import HyPLMEncoder

encoder = HyPLMEncoder.from_pretrained("weights")
sequences = ["MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ", "ACDEFGHIKLMNPQRSTVWY"]

residue = encoder.encode(sequences)
pooled = encoder.encode(sequences, pooling="mean")
layer16 = encoder.encode(sequences, layer=16)
PY
steps.explanation: The README's Python example, wrapped in a shell heredoc so it runs as one command. Mean-pooled vectors are what the report's sequence-level probes read, and the layer argument is how a particular depth is taken; the report selects among six relative depths on validation data.
steps.source_locator: README.md: Usage; Report: Appendix A, Probes

steps.title: Score one substitution zero-shot
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from hyplm import HyPLMEncoder

encoder = HyPLMEncoder.from_pretrained("weights")
sequence = "MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ"
logits = encoder.logits(sequence, masks=[2])[0]
log_probs = logits[2].log_softmax(-1)
tokens = encoder.tokenizer.tokens
score = log_probs[tokens.index("V")] - log_probs[tokens.index("T")]
print(score)
PY
steps.explanation: The README's masked-marginal example, wrapped in a shell heredoc. It gives the log probability of the mutant minus that of the wild type at a masked position, which is the per-substitution quantity the report sums for a ProteinGym variant.
steps.source_locator: README.md: Usage; Report: Appendix A, Zero-shot scores and likelihood

steps.title: Choose the precision for the task
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from hyplm import HyPLMEncoder

encoder = HyPLMEncoder.from_pretrained("weights", precision="bf16")
print(encoder.encode(["MKTAYIAKQRQISFVKSHFSRQ"], pooling="mean")[0].shape)
PY
steps.explanation: INT8 is the default. The README recommends bf16 when fitting regressors on near-identical variants, such as the AAV and GB1 splits of FLIP, because INT8 representations of variants of one protein differ by about 1 per cent. The keyword is the one named in the README's precision table.

name: CycPepNet
description: Open framework that compares molecular representations and machine-learning models for cyclic-peptide binding affinity, membrane permeability and half-life, covering 20 regression and classification tasks.

limitations: Prediction archives exist for only part of the historical run set; The NPMMPD input is a different snapshot from Figshare v1 and the matching version must be requested; The PEPlife2 original export query and selected fields must be recovered; The PepTherDia cyclic-selection predicate, scraper and page order have not been recovered; The Macrocycle-DB live export API is not a verified recipe and historical versions must be requested; Only the PepMSND data has a verified data licence

The script fetched each source and recorded its SHA-256.

attributes.source_locator: description: README first two paragraphs; the 12/8 split derives from benchmark.py supplementary markings; task: README for properties, thresholds, representations and tuning; benchmark.py for random and Butina split methods
attributes.task: Predict binding affinity (OPRM1 Ki, MC4R Ki, SSTR2 IC50), membrane permeability and half-life of cyclic peptides, as regression or as classification with fixed thresholds (Ki/IC50 ≤ 100 nM, log permeability ≥ −6, half-life ≥ 8 h). Random and Butina (Morgan fingerprint) splits are provided; hyperparameters are tuned on the validation split and models are scored on test.

profile.summary: CycPepNet compares molecular representations and machine learning models on cyclic peptides for three properties: binding affinity, membrane permeability and half-life. Each property is posed twice, as regression on the measured value and as classification against a stated threshold, giving 20 tasks. The framework covers those 20 tasks, 45 model configurations, two split methods and five seeds, and its analyses draw on a main pool of 22 configurations. The data come from six published cyclic peptide sources, which the framework does not redistribute: it ships an inventory with each input file's hash, a curator per source, the released split indices and the full archive of run records, so the published tables and figures can be reproduced without retraining. Its own result table shows the point: test root mean square errors on the small binding sets sit close to the mean baseline, while the larger permeability sets are predictable.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: top, Framework definition, Input data, Results and figures; results/learnability.csv

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How far machine learning can get on cyclic peptides, a class where the data are scarce and scattered. Three properties are covered: binding affinity, membrane permeability and half-life. Each is set up as a regression on the measured value and as a classification against a fixed cut, an inhibition constant or half maximal concentration at or below 100 nanomolar for binding, a log permeability at or above minus 6, and a half-life of 8 hours or more. Because the model and representation matrix is held fixed across tasks, the comparison is as much about which molecular representation helps as about which model wins, and the framework's own result table compares each selected model against a mean baseline on the same test split.
sections.source_locator: README.md: top, Framework definition; results/learnability.csv

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Six published sources supply the measurements: CycPeptMPDB and NPMMPD for permeability, Macrocycle-DB for binding affinity, and PEPlife2, PepMSND and PepTherDia for half-life. Nine exact provider files make up the snapshot and none of them is redistributed; an inventory records each one's size, hash, acquisition address and identity check, and most carry the status that redistribution terms are not established. Each source has its own curator script, and the permeability and half-life combinations are separate curation steps. One function, load_task_table, applies everything that defines a task: the filters, for example a single target and activity type within Macrocycle-DB, dropping missing values, deduplicating on SMILES by averaging replicate measurements and discarding any molecule whose replicates have a coefficient of variation above 1, the base-10 log transform of the target, and the classification threshold. The released splits are generated with an 80, 10, 10 ratio and a fixed seed, in two flavours: a Butina clustering split on Morgan fingerprints with a cutoff of 0.45, and a random split. The split size table shows how small the sets are: 28 test molecules for the binding task on one target, 19 for the combined half-life task, against 695 for CycPeptMPDB permeability.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Input data, Framework definition; cycpepnet/benchmark.py: load_task_table and generate_all_splits; results/splits_summary.csv; data/sources.csv

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model is trained on the train split, its hyper-parameters are chosen on the validation split, with Optuna over 50 trials for every non-baseline configuration, and it is scored on the test split. Selection is on the primary validation metric and reporting is on test, and the README states that nothing is reselected on a companion metric. The primary metric is the root mean square error for the regression tasks and balanced accuracy for the classification tasks, with Q squared F3 and the area under the ROC curve as companions and the coefficient of determination kept as descriptive. Each result is the mean over five seeds, with a seed standard deviation, a seed confidence interval and a separate test-set confidence interval, and the mean baseline's value on the same split. Root mean square error is never pooled across tasks because it carries each task's units; cross-task summaries use ranks, per-task min-max scores or dimensionless metrics, and the released tables include Friedman and Nemenyi ranks and adjusted p values for the confirmatory comparisons.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Framework definition, Results and figures, Getting started; results/learnability.csv

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Two routes. To check and reproduce the published analysis, install the package on Python 3.12 and run three commands: a verification pass that hashes the released artefacts and validates all 40 splits against the task tables they index, a reproduction pass that runs the analysis stages in order and stops at the first failure, and a comparison pass that checks the regenerated tables against the release to a tolerance of 1e-8. The README says these three need neither of the full environments and write 85 CSV and TeX outputs and 17 figures into a separate directory. To train models, install the locked Pixi environment, which is the one the published results came from, generate the fingerprint cache from the released tables, then call the runner with a task, a model, seeds and a split method. To rebuild the data from scratch, the provider files must be acquired first and verified by hash.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Installation, Reproduce the results, Getting started, Train models or rebuild datasets, Input data

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Six published sources behind nine provider files: CycPeptMPDB and NPMMPD for permeability, Macrocycle-DB for binding affinity, PEPlife2, PepMSND and PepTherDia for half-life. Ten distinct curated data splits, each used for a regression and a classification task, giving 20 tasks. Test set sizes from the released split table: 28 for Macrocycle-DB OPRM1, 49 for MC4R, 32 for SSTR2, 695 for CycPeptMPDB, 109 for NPMMPD, 288 for the CycPeptMPDB Townsend subset, 92 for the NPMMPD Rzepiela subset, 798 for the combined CycPeptMPDB and NPMMPD set, and 19 for the combined half-life set.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Input data, Framework definition; results/splits_summary.csv

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Two released split methods per task, both 80, 10, 10 train, validation and test with seed 42: a Butina clustering split on Morgan fingerprints at a Tanimoto cutoff of 0.45, and a random split. The split indices are released and refer to the task-filtered, deduplicated table, so substituting an input invalidates them. Forty splits in all are validated by the verification command.
facts.source_locator: cycpepnet/benchmark.py: generate_all_splits and generate_random_splits; README.md: Input data, Reproduce the results; results/splits_summary.csv

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Root mean square error, lower is better, as the primary metric for the regression tasks, with Q squared F3 as its companion, higher is better, and the coefficient of determination as a descriptive extra. Balanced accuracy, higher is better, as the primary metric for the classification tasks, with the area under the ROC curve as its companion. Selection uses the primary validation metric. Root mean square error is never pooled across tasks because it is in each task's own units; cross-task comparison uses ranks or dimensionless metrics.
facts.source_locator: results/learnability.csv; README.md: Results and figures

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: A mean predictor is the explicit baseline, and the released result table prints its value on the same test split beside each selected model, for example 1.7469 root mean square error against the selected model's 1.4303 on Macrocycle-DB OPRM1 regression, and 0.5 balanced accuracy for the classification tasks. The comparison set is the model and representation matrix itself: random forests and XGBoost on physicochemical descriptors and several fingerprint families, LSTM and transformer models on SMILES and fragSMILES, graph convolutional and message passing networks, two pretrained graph networks and two pretrained chemical language models, with the analyses drawing on a main pool of 22 configurations.
facts.source_locator: results/learnability.csv; README.md: Framework definition

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Three. A Butina clustering split on Morgan fingerprints at a 0.45 cutoff is released alongside the random split, so a method can be judged on structurally separated molecules. Duplicate structures are collapsed before splitting, by averaging replicate measurements and dropping molecules whose replicates disagree too much. Hyper-parameters are tuned on the validation split only, and the test split is used for reporting, with no reselection on a companion metric. The fingerprint and graph caches carry manifests that refuse a cache whose ordered SMILES or implementation hash do not match.
facts.source_locator: cycpepnet/benchmark.py: load_task_table and generate_all_splits; README.md: Framework definition, Curated tables

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Five training seeds per configuration, and the released table reports for each task the mean, the standard deviation across seeds, a confidence interval over seeds and a separate confidence interval over the test set, for example a seed interval of 1.3762 to 1.4826 against a test interval of 1.0557 to 1.8049 on the same 28-molecule task. The statistical tests table carries adjusted p values and the multiplicity families behind them, and a separate table records retired inferences and their replacements.
facts.source_locator: results/learnability.csv; README.md: top, Results and figures

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A cyclic peptide, given as a SMILES string, with one measured property value. Tasks are per molecule and per property, and duplicate structures are merged before splitting, so one row is one unique structure within a task.
facts.source_locator: cycpepnet/benchmark.py: load_task_table; README.md: Getting started

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Inapplicable in the usual sense: the examples are synthetic cyclic peptides, not sequences from a species. The binding affinity tasks name human targets, OPRM1, MC4R and SSTR2, in their filters and in the split table.
facts.source_locator: cycpepnet/benchmark.py: task filters; results/splits_summary.csv

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Three kinds of measurement, taken from the published sources: binding affinity as inhibition constants or half maximal inhibitory concentrations, membrane permeability as a log permeability, and half-life in hours. The target values are log transformed where the task says so, and the classification thresholds are applied on the transformed scale, 100 nanomolar for binding, minus 6 for log permeability and 8 hours for half-life.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Framework definition, Input data; cycpepnet/benchmark.py: task definitions

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The molecule, in whichever representation a model family uses. The released matrix covers physicochemical descriptors, several fingerprint families including ECFP, MAP4C, MXFP and HDF, SMILES and fragSMILES strings, and graph objects, and the two pretrained families read graphs and SMILES. No target structure or sequence is given to the model.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Framework definition

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Training per task, with pretrained models fine-tuned in the same loop. Every non-baseline configuration tunes its hyper-parameters with Optuna over 50 trials on the validation split, and the matrix includes two pretrained graph networks and two pretrained chemical language models alongside models trained from scratch. The README also shows how to drop in an external model: load the task table and the released split, train on train, choose on val and score test with the framework's own metric functions.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Framework definition, Getting started

strengths.text: The reproduction path is built in and checked. One command hashes the released artefacts and validates all 40 splits against the task tables, another regenerates the analysis, and a third compares the regenerated tables against the release to a tolerance of 1e-8, all without a GPU or retraining.
Both a structural and a random split are released for every task, with the clustering parameters in the code, so the gap between them can be read directly rather than argued about.

The reporting discipline is unusually explicit: selection on the primary validation metric with no reselection on a companion, no pooling of root mean square error across tasks, and both seed-level and test-level confidence intervals in the released table.

The data provenance is documented rather than assumed. An inventory records every input file with its hash, acquisition address and reviewed licence status, a separate evidence file holds the review, and the README states plainly that verification establishes identity, not redistribution rights.

limitations.text: The test sets are tiny for most tasks. The released split table gives 19 test molecules for the combined half-life task and 28, 32 and 49 for the three binding tasks, and the released result table shows test confidence intervals far wider than the seed intervals, for example 1.0557 to 1.8049 against 1.3762 to 1.4826.

The input data cannot simply be downloaded. Nine provider files are needed and none is redistributed; the inventory marks most as having redistribution terms not established, and the README records specific unresolved problems: the NPMMPD snapshot differs from the Figshare version, the PEPlife2 export query has to be recovered, and the PepTherDia selection predicate, scraper and page order have not been recovered.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: Input data, Acquiring each input; data/sources.csv

limitations.text: Only one of the six data sources has a verified licence. The README states that only the PepMSND Zenodo deposit carries a verified data licence, CC BY 4.0, that the curated tables are modified derivatives rather than provider archives, and that the MIT code licence does not cover the third-party data.

The archive is not complete to the prediction level, and some analyses have been superseded. Prediction files exist for only part of the historical run set and cannot be rebuilt from metrics, and a released table lists retired inferences with their replacements alongside a script that no workflow calls.

run_guide.summary: Verify the released artefacts, regenerate the published analysis and compare it against the release.
prerequisites: Python 3.12. For the three analysis commands the README says pip install -e . is enough and no GPU, pretrained weights or fingerprint caches are needed.

For training or curation, the Pixi environment with its exact lockfile, which is where the published results were produced; Conda is offered as an alternative without an exact lock, and Windows is covered by neither.
The code is MIT licensed and does not cover the third-party data. Training from the provider inputs requires acquiring those nine files under their own terms.

steps.title: Get the code
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/molML/CycPepNet.git
cd CycPepNet
git checkout --detach 1ed5e2b98d0239468b1998b64aa6c18148ede11a

steps.title: Install
steps.shell: pip install -e .

steps.title: Verify, reproduce and compare
steps.shell:
python -m cycpepnet.verify
python -m cycpepnet.reproduce
python -m cycpepnet.verify --compare outputs/reproduction/results
steps.explanation: The README's three reproduction commands, written without the pixi run prefix because it states these three work under a plain pip install. The first hashes the released artefacts and validates all 40 splits, the second runs the analysis stages in order and stops at the first failure, and the third compares the regenerated outputs against the release to a tolerance of 1e-8.

steps.shell:
pixi run python -m cycpepnet.prepare --dataset macrocycledb --stage representations \
  --from-release --representations morgan_fp
pixi run python -m cycpepnet.runner --tasks macrocycledb_mc4r_ki_reg --models mean \
  --seeds 0 --split-method butina_morgan --data-root outputs/processed
steps.explanation: The README's example: generate the fingerprint cache from the released tables, then run the runner for one task, one model, one seed and the Butina split. These commands need the full environment.

profile.summary: This benchmark pairs a deep mutational scan of the MET kinase domain with predictions from a large set of computational methods, so that the methods can be judged on whether they track a drug-dependent fitness landscape. The measurements cover 5,434 MET missense variants under twelve conditions, a DMSO vehicle control and eleven kinase inhibitors, which is 65,208 rows. Three published tables carry the same rows: mutational effects with predictions made in the 287-residue kinase domain context, the same with predictions made in the 1,390-residue full-length context, and protein-ligand affinity and binding free energy change. Counting the prediction columns across the three tables gives 57. Five further kinase scans, for CDK4, CDK6, EGFR, FGFR and SRC, are published beside them for the same comparison.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening and Repository layout; MET_muteff_kinase_domain.csv header and rows; PMC abstract

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a mutational-effect or affinity predictor responds to which drug is present. The scan gives, for each variant, a fitness score in each of twelve conditions, so a model that produces one number per variant regardless of the inhibitor can be seen to do so. The accompanying preprint's abstract states the question as how well these methods generalise beyond their training sets, and reports that current models produce largely ligand-invariant predictions despite experimentally distinct inhibitor-dependent landscapes, that ligand-aware geometric models such as LigandMPNN and LASErMPNN partially recover resistance-associated hotspots, and that affinity predictors underestimate mutation-induced changes in binding affinity. The repository supports a second question too, since the same variants are scored with predictions made in the kinase domain alone and in the full-length protein.
sections.source_locator: PMC abstract; README.md: Repository layout

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The experimental half is a deep mutational scan of the MET kinase domain read out under a vehicle control and eleven inhibitors, named in the README as A458, Cabo, Camp, Crizo, Gle, Glu, Mere, NVP, Savo, Tepo and Tiv. Each published table has one row per variant and condition: counting the main table in this pass gives 65,208 data rows, 5,434 distinct variants and twelve conditions, each condition carrying all 5,434 variants. Variants are numbered in kinase-domain coordinates from 1 to 287, with 1058 to be added for MET numbering, and every row is a missense variant. Alongside the measured score each row carries the same variant's score in DMSO, binary sensitised and resisted calls, and distances from the residue to the drug taken from a per-condition cofolded structure, with a flag for residues within 5 Angstrom of the drug. The structural side is published too: wild-type cofolds for the twelve conditions from three prediction methods. A clean folder holds the experiment on its own with no model predictions, including a 36-row table of kinase and inhibitor pairs with sequences, SMILES and the scanned position range. Five other kinase scans, CDK4, CDK6, EGFR, FGFR and SRC, are published as one CSV each and the README states they are not split.
sections.source_locator: README.md: opening, Repository layout, Annotation columns; MET_muteff_kinase_domain.csv; clean/kinase_drug_pairs.csv

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The repository is a paired dataset rather than a scoring harness: it publishes the measured target beside each method's prediction and leaves the comparison to the user. The README names the measured DMS score in a condition, the mean column, as the target, and the per-variant predictions sit in the same row, so a correlation or a ranking can be computed per condition or across conditions. Counting the non-annotation columns gives 23 prediction columns in the kinase-domain table, 18 in the full-length table and 16 in the affinity table, 57 in all, which is the figure the README's opening sentence gives as the number of computational methods. Two derived views are published rather than computed by the reader: a difference-score folder that takes the change in fitness score across inhibitor conditions, and a difference-tail folder for identifying candidate sensitising and resistance mutations. Three notebooks are published, for the difference scores, for statistical analysis of the fitness scores and for the figures. What is not in the files read here is a metric definition, a threshold, or a reference result: no aggregate score, no leaderboard and no fixed evaluation split.
sections.source_locator: README.md: opening, Repository layout, Annotation columns, scripts; the three CSV headers

strengths.text: The drug dimension is the point and it is complete: every one of the 5,434 variants appears in all twelve conditions, counted in this pass, so a ligand-invariant prediction can be detected directly.
Measurement and prediction sit in the same row, with the target column named in the README, so no join or reconstruction is needed to compare a method against the experiment.

The structural context is published rather than assumed: wild-type cofolds for each of the twelve conditions from three prediction methods, and per-condition residue-to-drug distances with a 5 Angstrom binding-region flag in the table itself.
strengths.source_locator: README.md: Repository layout and Annotation columns

strengths.text: The experiment is also published on its own, in a clean folder with no model predictions, including a combined table of every DMS measurement and a pair table with sequences and SMILES.

limitations.text: It is a dataset, not a scored benchmark. Nothing in the files read here defines a metric, a threshold, a split or a reference result, so two users can compare the same methods on these tables and report different numbers.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: Repository layout and Annotation columns

limitations.text: No licence is stated. The repository has no licence file and GitHub reports none, so the terms for reusing the tables are unclear.
limitations.source_locator: README.md, read in full: no licence section

limitations.text: The 57 figure counts prediction columns, not distinct methods: 23 in the kinase-domain table, 18 in the full-length table and 16 in the affinity table, and the same model families appear in both mutational-effect contexts.

One target protein carries the main comparison. MET is scanned under twelve conditions, while the five other kinases have one or a few inhibitors each and the README states they are not split, so conclusions rest largely on one kinase.

description: A mechanistic interpretability framework and benchmark of 8 spatial transcriptomics tasks that evaluates whether foundation model embeddings capture known spatial variation in gene expression, using Matryoshka sparse autoencoder features scored by correlation with a known spatial measure.

attributes.task: Evaluate whether embeddings from spatial transcriptomics foundation models, single-cell foundation models or gene expression capture a known measure of spatial variation. A Matryoshka sparse autoencoder with BatchTopK sparsity is trained on the embeddings Z. The score is the maximum |Spearman rho| between any SAE feature and the spatial measure tau, per spatial domain for global tasks and per sample for local tasks. Orthogonal matching pursuit runs when |rho| >= 0.3 to find a minimal reconstructing feature set.

profile.summary: SAFFRON is a framework and an 8-task benchmark for asking whether embeddings from spatial transcriptomics foundation models (or single-cell models, or plain gene expression) capture known spatial variation. A sparse autoencoder is trained on a model's embeddings and its features are scored by their Spearman correlation with a known spatial measure, in six tissue-gradient tasks and two Alzheimer's plaque microenvironment tasks. It is aimed at researchers comparing spatial foundation model embeddings.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction and Benchmark; dataset card: introduction

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether any interpretable feature of a representation tracks a known measure of spatial variation tau. Global tasks use a 1-D spatial axis in a tissue (tumour-stroma, renal radial, cortical depth, crypt-villus, crypt-surface). Local tasks use three measures around amyloid-beta plaques in Alzheimer's model mouse brains: a DAM score, microglial density and distance to plaque.
sections.source_locator: Dataset card: introduction and Tasks

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Eight AnnData files on Hugging Face, each a processed subset of a public dataset: six global tasks (human colorectal tumour, mouse kidney, two human cortex sections, mouse ileum, human colon) and two local tasks (STARmap PLUS and MERFISH Alzheimer's model mouse brain). Each file holds expression, coordinates, tau, spatial domains or scoring masks, and two baselines: 50-component PCA and an SAE trained directly on gene expression.
sections.source_locator: Dataset card: introduction, Tasks and File contents

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A user passes a cell-by-feature matrix H (normally SAFFRON SAE features of the model's embeddings) to benchmark.score. For global tasks, benchmark.py computes, within each spatial domain with at least 10 scored cells, the maximum |Spearman rho| between any feature and tau, and returns the mean over domains. For local tasks it returns per-unit |rho| values: for DAM score and microglial density the single best feature over all pooled evaluated cells is chosen and its |rho| reported per sample (at least 20 cells); for distance to plaque the maximum over features is taken within each unit. No aggregate across the eight tasks is defined.
sections.source_locator: saffron/benchmark.py: global_score, local_scores

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Clone the repository and install it with pip, load a task with benchmark.load (which downloads the file from Hugging Face), and score a feature matrix with benchmark.score. The README's example scores your model's SAE features and the stored PCA baseline.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Quick Start and Benchmark

strengths.text: Tasks cover several tissues, two species and five spatial technologies, at both tissue scale and plaque microenvironment scale.
The scoring code and the paper's baselines ship with the data, so a new model is scored with the same metric.

limitations.text: The score is the best correlation over many SAE features, so representations with more features have more chances to score well; the saved files describe no correction for this.
The data carry the licences of the original datasets, and the code repository has no licence that GitHub detects.
The paper is a bioRxiv preprint and was not read for this page, so the paper's results and data provenance are not described here.

run_guide.summary: Install SAFFRON, load one benchmark task and score the stored PCA baseline with the paper's metric.
prerequisites: Python 3.10 or later with pip; pip install -e . installs the dependencies in pyproject.toml, including torch, anndata and huggingface_hub.
Scoring your own model needs its cell-by-dimension embeddings for the task's cells.

steps.title: Get and install the code
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/chitra-lab/SAFFRON && cd SAFFRON
git checkout --detach c11c6d133b5e3932480211cc3698f0e808fd5125
pip install -e .
steps.explanation: Clone and install as the README's Quick Start says; the checkout line pins the reviewed commit.

steps.title: Load a task and score the PCA baseline
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from saffron import SAFFRON, benchmark
adata = benchmark.load("colorectal")
print(benchmark.score(adata, adata.obsm["X_pca"]))
PY
steps.explanation: Lines from the README's Benchmark example, wrapped in a shell heredoc, with print() added to show the result. To score a model, replace X_pca with SAFFRON SAE features of your embeddings: H = SAFFRON().fit(Z).sae_result_.Z.
