attributes.source_locator: description: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03806 abstract: BENchmark for DNA language models; predicts effects of DNA changes; whether predictions guide sequence design; eight tasks on five experimental datasets; task: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03806 abstract: eight tasks built on five experimental datasets; scope_note: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03806 abstract: tests how well models predict effects of DNA changes and whether predictions guide design
attributes.task: Eight tasks built on five experimental datasets

profile.summary: BEND 2.0 tests whether genomic models can predict the effects of DNA changes and use those predictions to choose sequences, across eight tasks built on five experimental datasets: a sequence prior, splicing effects, cell-type contrasts, tissue identification, genetic background interactions and three design tasks. Seven tasks score linear readouts fitted to a model's frozen embeddings; the prior task needs nucleotide probabilities. It is aimed at developers and users of DNA language models and sequence-to-function models, with a maintained leaderboard.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; docs/tasks.md

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Five capabilities needed for DNA design: recovering a hidden base from context (prior); predicting how a mutation changes splicing (opensplice); accounting for cell type and tissue (context, tissue_identification); accounting for genetic background (background); and selecting edits or sequences that give a requested response (repair_percentile, cell_selective, atlas_profile).
sections.source_locator: docs/tasks.md: task table

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Tasks draw on OpenSplice (590,104 interventions in 466 genes), the Siraj saturation mutagenesis data (context, background, repair and cell-selective tasks), the atlas of AI-designed enhancers (7,657 sequences), GTEx v10 median expression (5,782 held-out genes, 51 tissues) and 512 GRCh38 windows for the prior. Holdouts follow biology: whole genes for OpenSplice, whole elements with their backgrounds for Siraj, separate source and candidate sequence families for Atlas, and distinct 1-Mb blocks for the prior. Data download from a fixed Hugging Face revision with checksums.
sections.source_locator: docs/tasks.md: Plan a run, What stays fixed; docs/data.md

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: For embedding tasks BEND fits a readout to frozen representations and scores it on the task's holdout; for variant effects the paper's readout is ridge regression on the change in embedding between variant and reference, with standardisation estimated on training data only; native prediction heads are scored separately. Each task has its own metric and direction, and the documentation says to compare scores within a task. Spearman-based tasks average per-gene or per-element correlations so each group has equal weight, and uncertainty comes from bootstrapping whole genes, elements or loci. Experimental references (one set of measurements predicting another) are reported for comparison but are not ceilings. Leaderboard submissions are rescored by the maintainers.
sections.source_locator: docs/tasks.md: What stays fixed; Paper: Appendix, 'Uncertainty and scoring'; README.md

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Install the bend2 package with pip (Python 3.11 or later), try the included base-composition baseline on the Atlas task, then wrap your own encoder in a small my_model.py file that returns one embedding per sequence, run a task and view the results.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Evaluate your model

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: OpenSplice (590,104 interventions, 466 genes); Siraj saturation mutagenesis (170,292 context substitutions in 128 elements, 68,026 paired mutations, 331 repair targets, 127 cell-selective loci); Atlas of AI-designed enhancers (7,657 sequences, 16 requests); GTEx v10 (5,782 held-out genes, 51 tissues); 512 GRCh38 prior windows. The paper also tests transfer of OpenSplice-trained predictors to 4,618 COMPASS mutations in 88 genes.
facts.source_locator: docs/tasks.md: Plan a run

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Biological holdouts per task: five gene-held-out folds (OpenSplice); five element-held-out folds (Siraj context and background); separate source and candidate families (Atlas, 5,246 and 2,411); held-out genes (GTEx: 12,146 train, 1,350 validation, 5,782 test); distinct 1-Mb blocks (prior).
facts.source_locator: docs/tasks.md: What stays fixed

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Per task: conditional log loss in bits per base (lower better); macro-gene or macro-element Spearman (higher better); top-1 tissue accuracy (higher better); residual midrank percentile (lower better); cell-selective utility and gain over random selection in log2 (higher better). The leaderboard README also shows a combined score whose definition was not found in the saved files.
facts.source_locator: docs/tasks.md: task table; README.md: Benchmark results

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The README results table lists AlphaGenome, NTv3 (100M and 650M, pre- and post-trained), Enformer, Evo2 20B, GENERATORv2, CENO 1B and DNABERT-2, with native outputs and fitted readouts, plus an experimental reference row. A base-composition baseline runs on CPU.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Benchmark results

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Holdouts keep whole genes, elements or sequence families together; the prior windows avoid blocks used in earlier prior panels, though the documentation notes this does not mean they were unseen in pretraining. Submitters must declare known overlap of training data with benchmark sequences or labels.
facts.source_locator: docs/tasks.md; docs/data.md; docs/submitting.md

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: 95% bootstrap intervals that resample whole genes, elements or loci; Atlas reports two replicate values, which the documentation says are descriptive, not a confidence interval.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Appendix, 'Uncertainty and scoring'; docs/tasks.md

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: Varies by task: a DNA window (prior), a mutation or intervention (splicing, context, background), a gene (tissue identification), an element or locus design request (repair, cell-selective) and a sequence design request (Atlas).
facts.source_locator: docs/tasks.md

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human: GRCh38 windows, human cell lines HepG2 and K562 (Siraj), GTEx human tissues, and human cell types (Atlas).
facts.source_locator: docs/tasks.md; docs/data.md

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Exon inclusion measurements for mutations (OpenSplice), saturation mutagenesis reporter assays in HepG2 and K562 (Siraj, with ENCODE count data), reporter activity of designed enhancers in 12 cell types (Atlas) and bulk RNA-seq median expression (GTEx).
facts.source_locator: docs/data.md: Sources and terms

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: DNA sequence only. Seven tasks take one fixed-width embedding per sequence; prior takes four nucleotide probabilities. Tissue identification needs 131,072-base inputs. Native outputs may also be scored separately.
facts.source_locator: docs/tasks.md; README.md

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Frozen embeddings with linear readouts fitted by BEND; no fine-tuning of the model inside the benchmark. Native output heads are reported separately.
facts.source_locator: docs/tasks.md: What stays fixed

strengths.text: Holdouts follow biological units (genes, elements, sequence families, genomic blocks), and uncertainty is bootstrapped over the same units.
Design tasks score a model's choices against measured outcomes, not only prediction accuracy.
A pip package, fixed data revision with checksums, and a leaderboard where maintainers rescore submissions.

limitations.text: Four of the eight tasks use the Siraj data, which is CC BY-NC 4.0: no commercial use.
Scores use linear readouts on frozen embeddings, so they measure what a linear probe can extract, not a fine-tuned model; native heads are scored separately.
Pretraining overlap with benchmark sequences is self-declared; for the prior task the documentation says the windows may have been seen in pretraining.
Human data only, and tasks have different units, so the documentation advises comparing within a task; the README's combined score is not defined in the saved files.

run_guide.summary: Install BEND 2.0, run the CPU composition baseline on the Atlas task, then run your own encoder on it.
prerequisites: Python 3.11 or later.
Your model's framework and weights, installed separately.
Larger tasks download data from Hugging Face (93 MB for Siraj, 425 MB for OpenSplice, 835 MB reference genome for tissue identification).

steps.title: Install
steps.shell: python -m pip install bend2
steps.explanation: Install the package in your model's environment.

steps.title: Run the included baseline
steps.shell: bend2 run composition --tasks atlas_profile --output results/composition
steps.explanation: Runs the base-composition baseline on CPU without model weights; Atlas data are included with the package.
steps.source_locator: README.md: Try an included example first

steps.title: Connect your encoder
steps.shell:
cat > my_model.py <<'PY'
import numpy as np
from bend2 import Model


def embed(sequences: list[str]) -> np.ndarray:
    return your_encoder(sequences)  # [batch, features]


model = Model("My model", embed=embed, revision="checkpoint-v1")
PY
steps.explanation: The README's my_model.py, written with a heredoc. Replace your_encoder with your model's inference and use your real checkpoint revision.

steps.title: Run a task and view results
steps.shell:
bend2 run my_model.py --tasks atlas_profile --output results/my-model
bend2 show results/my-model
steps.explanation: Runs the Atlas design task with your encoder and prints the saved scores.

outputs: A result directory with scores and predictions as JSON and Parquet files, readable with bend2 show or the Run class.

profile.summary: LncBench is a collection of 15 RNA task datasets released with the LncRFM long non-coding RNA language model, each a Parquet file with sequence, label and split columns and its own training entry point in the LncRFM repository; two sets are test only. It is useful to developers of RNA language models who want ready-split datasets; there is no paper in the saved sources and no leaderboard.
profile.summary_source_locator: Zenodo description; README.md: Downstream learning

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How well an RNA sequence model, fine-tuned or with a trained head, predicts per-task labels on 15 datasets named lnc_binary, RNAErnie-lncRNA, iLoc-lncRNA D1 and D2, lncATLAS-Localization, lncATLAS-RCI, Disease, Expression, POSTAR3-UPF1, mRNA-DMS, mRNA-Structure, 5UTR-MRL, RiNALMo-Splice, RNAChallenge and lncRNA-Structure. The README describes only some labels: Expression has five ordered categories, splice labels carry a donor or acceptor site and a value, DMS labels are per-base values and structure labels are base-pair index lists. The saved sources do not otherwise describe what each task measures.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Downstream learning; Zenodo file list

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Each of the 15 files carries its own train, validation and test assignment in a split column, which the loader preserves. RNAChallenge and lncRNA-Structure hold test data only and are used with a trained task head. The Zenodo record says CC BY 4.0 covers the authors' own contributions and upstream data keep their original terms. The saved sources do not say where each dataset comes from or how its split was drawn.
sections.source_locator: Zenodo description; README.md: Downstream learning; lncbench_data.py

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each task has its own training script. The scripts select the best epoch on a validation metric (F1, micro-F1, ROC AUC, Pearson correlation or Pearson r squared, depending on the task) and then report final test metrics. No aggregate score across tasks and no leaderboard are described. The README lists comparison models (RNA-FM, structRFM, RNAErnie, SpliceBERT, UTR-LM, RiNALMo micro, LncRNA-BERT) without results.
sections.source_locator: LncDowntask scripts; README.md: Comparison methods

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Create the conda environment and install LncRFM, download the pretrained weights and the LncBench files from Zenodo, then run a task's training script with --data_file pointing at its Parquet file. The README's example trains a frozen-encoder adapter on iLoc-lncRNA_D1.

run_guide.summary: Install LncRFM and train and evaluate a frozen-encoder adapter on one LncBench task.
prerequisites: Conda, Python 3.10, PyTorch with CUDA 11.8 and a matching CUDA toolkit to build the state-space kernels.

steps.title: Get the code
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/chuyhu/LncRFM
cd LncRFM
git checkout --detach 429d79fb99dfecc180cbe8e41a554af0bb3bdaf1
steps.explanation: The README gives no clone command; this clones the repository named in the record and pins the reviewed commit.

steps.title: Install
steps.shell:
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate lncrfm
pip install --no-build-isolation causal-conv1d==1.4.0 mamba-ssm==2.2.2
pip install -e .
steps.explanation: As in the README's Installation section.

steps.title: Train and evaluate on iLoc-lncRNA_D1
steps.shell:
python LncDowntask/finetune_iloclnc_reference.py \
  --model_backend lncrfm \
  --finetune_scheme adapter --freeze_encoder --no_eval_test_each_epoch \
  --from_pretrained checkpoints/lncrfm_pretrained \
  --data_file LncBench/iLoc-lncRNA_D1.parquet --output_dir outputs/iloc
steps.explanation: The README's downstream example. Other tasks use the entry point listed for them in the README's table.

outputs: The script prints the best validation micro-F1 and the final test metrics, and saves the best checkpoint under the output directory.

name: ELIXIR - Protein-Protein Interface Benchmark - OpenEBench Experiment
description: A benchmark that asks methods to classify a protein homodimer interface as physiological or crystallographic, scoring each entry so that higher means more likely physiological.

limitations: Leave-one-out evaluation in the random-forest consensus reference method does not remove homologous entries from the training set, so its AUROC should be read as an upper estimate with respect to the other methods.
Methods scored different numbers of entries (1,123 to 1,671), and methods scoring fewer than 1,671 entries are evaluated on their own subset, so values are not strictly comparable across rows.
16 labels differ from the original 2023 publication.
Reference scores are those submitted to the original benchmark repository.
Released under CC BY-NC 4.0.

attributes.task: Discriminate physiological from crystallographic (non-physiological) protein homodimer interfaces. Input: a CSV with columns entry_id and score, higher score = more likely physiological.

profile.summary: This benchmark asks a method to look at a protein homodimer interface and say whether it is physiological or a crystallographic contact, scoring each entry so that a higher score means more likely physiological. The entries are 1,671 curated homodimer interfaces, 840 physiological and 831 non-physiological, taken from the community-wide study of Schweke and colleagues published in 2023. This package is not the original study: it turns that benchmark into an OpenEBench experiment, with gold-standard labels, four homology-aware five-fold cross-validation splits, the scores of 14 reference methods, validation and scoring scripts, and a static page that scores a submitted CSV in the browser and ranks it against those methods. Anyone with an interface classifier can run it against a published leaderboard without reimplementing the comparison.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: Original work and Benchmark task; Zenodo record description

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a scoring function can tell a biologically real homodimer interface from one that only exists because of crystal packing. A submission is a ranking of the benchmark entries, higher meaning more likely physiological, so the main metrics are threshold-free, and threshold-based metrics are reported alongside. The package's own contribution is comparability: it fixes the labels, the folds and the metric code, so a new method's numbers can be put beside the 14 reference methods rather than computed under its own conventions.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Benchmark task, How to submit your own predictions; Zenodo record description

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The entries come from the original community study's curated annotation: 1,677 entries less the six flagged for deletion, leaving 1,671, of which 840 are physiological and 831 are not. The Zenodo record states that these labels are the curated annotation and that they differ for 16 entries from the original 2023 publication, which reported 836 physiological and 841 non-physiological interfaces. The reference scores are the ones the 13 research groups submitted to the original benchmark repository, plus a random-forest consensus whose scores are the leave-one-out probabilities provided there. The splits are the package's own work and are documented as such: they are not the folds of the original study. Four strategies are offered, all built so that homologous interfaces stay in one fold, because 1000 of the 1671 entries, 60 per cent, share a CATH superfamily with at least one other entry and a random split would put near-identical interfaces on both sides. Strategy 1 groups by CATH superfamily with a UniProt gene fallback, 853 groups. Strategy 2 clusters chain sequences with MMseqs2 at 25 per cent identity and 50 per cent one-sided coverage, 1076 clusters. Strategy 2b is a BLASTClust clustering at the same nominal parameters, 1045 clusters, which the document calls the most defensible sequence-identity split. Strategy 3, the recommended default and the one the published leaderboard uses, takes the connected components of the union of Strategies 1 and 2b, 688 components with a largest component of 132 entries. All four are verified to have no group spanning more than one fold.
sections.source_locator: Zenodo record description; README.md: Example of results; CV_SPLITTING_STRATEGIES.md

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is a CSV with one row per entry and a score where higher means more likely physiological. It is then validated and scored. The validation step checks the submitted identifiers against the public reference list and reports how many are missing or unexpected; read in the code, it requires the columns entry_id and raw_score and marks a submission as an error when coverage is not above 0.5. The scoring step computes AUROC, through the Mann-Whitney rank formulation, and AUCPR as average precision, plus accuracy at a threshold, balanced accuracy, F1 and the Matthews correlation coefficient. The threshold matters and the code is explicit about it: a published decision threshold is used when one is passed, and otherwise the script derives the optimal threshold by Youden's J from the same scored population and flags the value as data-driven rather than published. For the cross-validated leaderboard the README states that the thresholds for balanced accuracy, F1 and MCC are learned on the training folds only, and results are reported as a mean and standard deviation over the five folds. A consolidation step turns the per-participant assessments into one leaderboard. The numbers are also reproducible in two ways: the README reports that its demo submission's AUROC computed with the bundle's cross-validation script agrees with the figure the in-browser page produces.

sections.title: Reading the reference table
sections.body: The README's table of the 14 reference methods carries two caveats that change how it should be read, and both are the package's own. First, the top row is not like the others: the random-forest consensus is a trained classifier rather than a single fixed score, its scores are leave-one-out probabilities taken unchanged from the original benchmark repository, and because leave-one-out does not remove homologous entries from the training set its AUROC should be read as an upper estimate relative to the other methods. Second, the methods did not all score the same entries. The n column ranges from 1,123 to 1,671, a method with fewer entries is evaluated on its own subset, and the README points at QSQE, whose AUCPR exceeds its AUROC, as an example of what that does to a value. Beside the current results the repository also keeps analyses computed before a correction, in a superseded folder, for transparency.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Example of results, Random-forest consensus note, What is in this repository

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Two ways. The quick way is the interactive page, which scores a submitted CSV in the browser, lets the user pick a cross-validation strategy with Strategy 3 as the recommended default, and ranks the result against the 14 reference methods; the README states no file is uploaded anywhere. The local way is the bundle's pipeline script, which is the plain-Python equivalent of the Nextflow description: for every participant directory it runs the validation script against the public reference dataset, then the metrics script against the gold-standard directory, and finally the consolidation script, which writes a data model export and a leaderboard image. One detail to watch, read from the splitting document rather than the README: the cross-validation scripts read cv_fold_assignment.csv, which is Strategy 1, kept for backward compatibility, so using the recommended Strategy 3 locally means pointing the gold-standard directory at a copy of the Strategy 3 fold file under that name.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One set of 1,671 curated homodimer interface entries, 840 physiological and 831 non-physiological. It is the 1,677 entries of the benchmark authors' curated annotation without the six flagged for deletion. The package also ships the gold-standard labels, four fold assignment files, the 14 reference methods' score sets, a demo prediction file of 1,610 entries and a prediction template.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Benchmark task, Example of a new submission, What is in this repository; Zenodo record description

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Four homology-aware five-fold cross-validation splits, defined by this package rather than taken from the original study. Strategy 1 groups by CATH superfamily with a UniProt gene fallback, 853 groups, largest 42 entries. Strategy 2 is an MMseqs2 clustering at 25 per cent identity and 50 per cent one-sided coverage, 1076 clusters, largest 25. Strategy 2b is the BLASTClust clustering at matched nominal parameters, 1045 clusters; the document's prose says the largest holds 27 entries while its own summary table row for 2b says 26, and the document does not resolve the difference. Strategy 3, the recommendation and the basis of the published table, is the connected components of the union of 1 and 2b, 688 components, largest 132. All four are verified to place every group inside a single fold. The scripts, however, read the Strategy 1 file by default.
facts.source_locator: CV_SPLITTING_STRATEGIES.md; README.md: Example of results

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: AUROC and AUCPR, both threshold-free and higher is better, with AUROC the ranking metric of the published leaderboard. Beside them the scoring script computes accuracy at a threshold, balanced accuracy, F1 and the Matthews correlation coefficient, also higher is better. The threshold is a published one if supplied, otherwise Youden's J computed on the same scored population and flagged as data-driven; in the cross-validated table the thresholds are learned on the training folds only. Values are reported as a mean and standard deviation across the five folds.
facts.source_locator: workflow/compute_metrics.py docstring; README.md: Example of results

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Fourteen reference methods, 13 research groups' submitted scores plus a random-forest consensus on the top 221 features. In the README's Strategy 3 table they are, in AUROC order, the random forest consensus, DeepRank-GNN, Rosetta InterfaceAnalyzer, IES normalised, DLScore-BC, QSQE, Voronota, NIPacking, ISPRED4, MaSIF, GOAP, CP/COCOMAPS, shape_hydro_tails and ProbaConsensus with the ScanNet F_Network, counted from the rows of that table.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Example of results; Zenodo record description

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Homology-aware folds, and this is the package's main addition. The splitting document states that 1000 of the 1671 entries, 60 per cent, share a CATH superfamily with at least one other entry, so a random five-fold split would put near-identical or homologous interfaces in both the training and held-out folds and inflate any cross-validated estimate. Every strategy therefore keeps a homology group inside one fold, and all four are verified to have no group spanning folds. The documented exception is the random-forest consensus row, whose leave-one-out probabilities come from the original repository and do not remove homologues from the training set, which is why the package says its AUROC is an upper estimate.
facts.source_locator: CV_SPLITTING_STRATEGIES.md: why a plain random split is unsafe; README.md: Random-forest consensus note

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: A standard deviation across the five cross-validation folds, printed beside every value in the reference table and in the demo submission's result. No bootstrap or confidence interval is reported, and no repeated resampling of the folds themselves.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Example of results and Example of a new submission

facts.value: One protein homodimer interface, identified by an entry_id, with a binary gold-standard label, physiological or non-physiological.

facts.value: Not stated. The entries are protein homodimer structures from the original community-wide study, identified by entry identifier, and no species information appears in the files read here.

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Not restricted by the package. A submission is only a table of entry identifiers and scores, so any input a method uses is permitted; the reference methods range from interface energy functions and geometric descriptors to graph neural networks. The original benchmark's structures are distributed by the community repository the package derives from, and this package ships the labels and folds rather than the structures.
facts.source_locator: README.md: How to submit, Original work; workflow/validate.py; Zenodo record related identifiers

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Either, and the package distinguishes them. Thirteen of the reference methods are single fixed scores used as submitted, while the random-forest consensus is a trained classifier whose leave-one-out probabilities are used unchanged and are not retrained within the folds. A new submission is a score file, so a method may be trained however its authors wish; what the folds control is the threshold fitting, which in the published table happens on training folds only.

strengths.text: The splits are designed against the leakage this dataset actually has, with the figure stated: 60 per cent of entries share a CATH superfamily with another entry, so homologous interfaces are kept in one fold, and no group spans folds in any of the four strategies.

The package says what it did and did not inherit: the folds are its own proposal and explicitly not the folds of the original study, and the reference scores are the ones the groups submitted to the original repository.

The two caveats a reader needs are printed next to the table rather than buried: that the consensus row is a trained classifier whose AUROC is an upper estimate, and that methods scored between 1,123 and 1,671 entries so rows are not strictly comparable.

Submission is cheap and checkable: a two-column CSV scored in the browser with no upload, and the same numbers reproducible locally with the bundle's scripts, which the README demonstrates by matching its demo result to the in-browser value.
strengths.source_locator: README.md: Interactive page and Example of a new submission; workflow/run_pipeline.sh

limitations.text: Rows of the leaderboard are not strictly comparable. Methods scored different numbers of entries, from 1,123 to 1,671, and a method with fewer is evaluated on its own subset, which the README illustrates with QSQE's AUCPR exceeding its AUROC on 1,123 entries.

The top row has an advantage the others do not. The random-forest consensus is a trained classifier whose leave-one-out probabilities come from the original repository, and leave-one-out does not remove homologous entries from its training set, so the package itself says its AUROC is an upper estimate relative to the other methods.

The labels are a curated annotation that differs from the published study. The Zenodo record states that this annotation differs for 16 entries from Schweke et al. 2023, which reported 836 physiological and 841 non-physiological interfaces against the 840 and 831 used here, and that six entries flagged for deletion were removed.
The licence is non-commercial. The package is released under CC BY-NC 4.0, both in its licence file and in the Zenodo record, although the source benchmark it derives from is CC BY 4.0.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: Licence and citation; LICENSE; Zenodo record metadata

steps.title: Put the predictions where the pipeline looks for them

mkdir -p datasets/participant/my_method
cp my_predictions.csv datasets/participant/my_method/predictions.csv

steps.explanation: This is the bundle's own local pipeline, described in the script as the plain-Python equivalent of the Nextflow skeleton. It runs validate.py against the public reference directory, then compute_metrics.py against the metrics reference directory, for each participant, and finally consolidate.py for the leaderboard. An output directory can be passed as the first argument; it defaults to a directory beside the repository root.

profile.summary: CellBench is an evaluation of single-cell foundation models used as frozen feature extractors, that is with their weights unchanged and only a light head fitted on top. The authors compare 13 such models with classical methods fitted on the training data itself, across 12 human and mouse cohorts and four genetic perturbation screens. Their reported conclusions are that different models preserve different biological information, that classical baselines stay competitive, that human-pretrained representations transfer to supervised mouse analyses but under a shared decoder none beats simply predicting no change for unseen perturbation targets, and that neither model size nor reported pretraining data volume predicts performance. This page is written from the abstract and metadata alone, because the preprint's full text is on bioRxiv, which this run was not allowed to request.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC record: title and abstract, Summary and In Brief sections

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: What a single-cell foundation model's embedding keeps, and whether it is worth using instead of a method fitted on the data at hand. The authors frame the open question as which biological information the embeddings preserve and when the models beat dataset-fitted methods. Two kinds of task are distinguished in the abstract: representing observed cellular states, which the authors treat as the observational side, and predicting how cells respond to genetic interventions, which they report as a different matter where success on the first does not carry over. A third question is evidential rather than biological: whether a model's apparent advantage survives the removal of cohorts that overlap its own pretraining records.
sections.source_locator: Europe PMC record: abstract, Summary, The Bigger Picture and Highlights sections

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The abstract gives the shape of the data and nothing more: 12 human and mouse cohorts, covering tissues and species, and four genetic perturbation screens. The comparison set is 13 frozen foundation models against classical baselines that are fitted on the training data. The perturbation side is said to include unseen perturbation targets. Nothing in the material that could be fetched names the cohorts, the cell counts, the gene sets, the screens or the splits, so none of those is stated here.
sections.source_locator: Europe PMC record: abstract, Summary and In Brief sections

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Three things can be said from the abstract. First, the backbones are frozen, so what is evaluated is the representation rather than a fine-tuned model, and the comparison is against methods fitted on the training data. Second, the perturbation task is scored on genome-wide absolute error against an explicit reference of predicting no change, and the authors report that under a shared decoder no model improves on that reference for unseen targets. Third, a sensitivity analysis removes cohorts whose sample or donor identifiers match a model's pretraining records, and the authors report that this reduces the annotation advantages while leaving the model rankings largely unchanged. The metrics for the other tasks, the aggregation across cohorts, the number of seeds and the exact splits are not in the material that could be fetched.
sections.source_locator: Europe PMC record: abstract, Summary, Highlights and In Brief sections

sections.body: Each checkpoint's frozen embeddings feed elastic-net Cox models for survival and logistic regression for classification, with regularisation chosen by cross-validation on training data. Four feature representations (raw, standardised, PCA 32, PCA 64) are tried per checkpoint and the one with the highest average score is reported. A gene-expression baseline uses the same tasks, splits and heads on log gene expression.

name: BioML-bench
description: Benchmark of autonomous LLM agents on end-to-end biomedical machine learning: an agent reads a task description, builds and runs its own pipeline and submits test-set predictions, which are graded by the task's original metric and placed on that task's public human leaderboard.

attributes.version: v0.1-alpha; 24-task set listed in experiments/biomlbench_v0.1a.txt at commit 673f3d8 and Table 3 of bioRxiv v3
attributes.task: End-to-end biomedical ML by autonomous agents, scored against public human leaderboards
attributes.scope_note: Four domains: drug discovery (9 tasks), protein engineering (6), single-cell omics (5) and biomedical imaging (4). Only the three molecular and omics domains are recorded; the imaging domain and the all-task Table 2 aggregate (which includes imaging) are out of scope.
attributes.source_locator: Sections 3.1-3.4; Table 1; Table 3; repository README
limitations: Scores are leaderboard percentiles: they depend on who submitted to each public leaderboard and when, not only on the task metric.

profile.summary: BioML-bench measures what an autonomous agent can do with a biomedical machine learning task from end to end. The agent reads a task description, works with the data, writes and runs its own pipeline and produces a submission file; the submission is then scored by that task's own metric and placed against that task's leaderboard, giving a percentile, a medal band and a comparison with human baseline scores. The v0.1-alpha task list holds 24 tasks drawn from four sources: nine from Polaris Hub, six ProteinGym deep mutational scanning tasks, five Open Problems single-cell tasks and four Kaggle competitions. It is built on the MLE-bench scaffold and is agent-agnostic: anything that can read a description and write a submission can be evaluated.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: Description and Key Features; experiments/biomlbench_v0.1a.txt (24 rows counted)

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether an agent can carry a biomedical prediction problem through every step on its own: understanding the task from prose, looking at the data, choosing a method, implementing it, running it and submitting test-set predictions in the required format. The score is not just the task metric but where that metric places the agent among the people who have already attempted the same task, which is why the grader reports a leaderboard percentile, medal bands and a separate comparison with human baseline scores. Because the task set spans drug properties, protein fitness, single-cell omics and medical imaging, it also measures how far one agent generalises across biomedical domains.
sections.source_locator: README: Description and Key Features; grade.py, grade_submission

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The tasks are repackaged from existing public sources rather than created. The v0.1-alpha list names 24 tasks, counted here from the file: nine with the polarishub prefix (an EGFR potency set, three ADME-Fang endpoints and five Therapeutics Data Commons sets covering CYP2D6 substrate, lipophilicity, Caco-2 permeability, hERG and blood-brain barrier penetration), six with the proteingym-dms prefix (including the SARS-CoV-2 spike binding scan and four Tsuboyama 2023 stability scans, two of them indel sets), five with the manual prefix for Open Problems single-cell tasks (modality prediction, single-cell perturbations, cell-cell communication, spatially variable genes and label projection), and four Kaggle competitions covering pulmonary fibrosis progression, histopathologic cancer detection, brain tumour radiogenomic classification and gastrointestinal tract image segmentation. Each task in the repository carries its own preparation script, configuration and grader, and the data-source layer has separate implementations for Kaggle, Polaris, ProteinGym and manually prepared data.
sections.source_locator: experiments/biomlbench_v0.1a.txt; README: Key Features; repository layout

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Grading reads a submission for a task, computes the task's own metric with that task's grader, then ranks the score against the task leaderboard. Reading grade_helpers.py, rank_score returns the gold, silver and bronze medal flags with their thresholds, whether the score is above the median, the leaderboard percentile from 0 to 100 where higher is better, and the leaderboard size; the direction of the metric is read from the leaderboard rather than assumed. Human comparison is separate: calculate_human_performance_metrics takes the median human score for beats_human and computes a human percentile as the share of humans the agent matches or exceeds, respecting the metric's direction. Aggregation across tasks counts medals and tasks that beat humans and reports the average, best and worst leaderboard percentile over the tasks that produced one.
sections.source_locator: grade.py, grade_submission, aggregate_reports and calculate_human_performance_metrics; grade_helpers.py, rank_score

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Three commands, after installing the package with uv and pulling the prebuilt agent images. prepare downloads and prepares one task's data, run-agent runs a named agent container on a task, and grade scores the resulting submission file and writes a report. The repository ships prebuilt agent images; the only agent the saved sources name is a dummy agent for checking the pipeline, and the readme notes that running a real agent needs an API key file at the repository root. Python 3.11 or later, Docker and uv are the stated prerequisites.
sections.source_locator: README: Quick Start, Prerequisites, Installation, Basic Usage

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: 24 tasks in the v0.1-alpha list, counted from the file by source prefix: 9 polarishub tasks (polaris-pkis2-egfr-wt-c-1, three adme-fang endpoints, and tdcommons sets for CYP2D6 substrate, lipophilicity, Caco-2, hERG and blood-brain barrier), 6 proteingym-dms tasks (SPIKE_SARS2_Starr_2020_binding, SBI_STAAM_Tsuboyama_2023_2JVG, PSAE_PICP2_Tsuboyama_2023_1PSE, CBX4_HUMAN_Tsuboyama_2023_2K28, Q8EG35_SHEON_Campbell_2022_indels and CSN4_MOUSE_Tsuboyama_2023_1UFM_indels), 5 manual Open Problems single-cell tasks, and 4 kaggle competitions. Per-task dataset sizes are not stated in the saved sources; each task's data is downloaded by its own preparation script at run time.
facts.source_locator: experiments/biomlbench_v0.1a.txt, all 24 rows counted

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Each task keeps the train and test split of its original source, prepared by that task's own preparation script, and the agent sees only the training side while the grader holds the test labels. The saved sources do not state the split rule for any individual task. There is no benchmark-level split: all 24 tasks are evaluation tasks.
facts.source_locator: README: Basic Usage; grade.py, grade_submission

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Each task is scored by its own metric, whose direction is read from that task's leaderboard rather than fixed. On top of that the grader reports a leaderboard percentile from 0 to 100, higher being better, the leaderboard size, gold, silver and bronze medal flags with their thresholds, whether the score is above the median, and two human comparisons: a boolean for beating the median human and a human percentile from 0 to 100. Aggregation over tasks gives medal counts, a count of tasks beating humans, and the average, best and worst leaderboard percentile.
facts.source_locator: grade_helpers.py, rank_score docstring; grade.py, aggregate_reports and calculate_human_performance_metrics

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Two kinds. The human leaderboard of each task is the reference the score is ranked against, with built-in human baseline scores for a separate median comparison. For agents, the repository ships prebuilt agent images, pulled with scripts/pull_prebuilt_images.sh; the only agent named in the saved sources is the dummy agent, which exists to check the pipeline rather than to compete. The saved sources do not say which agents or models produced the published results.
facts.source_locator: README: Key Features, Quick Start, Basic Usage; grade.py

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None described in the saved sources, and the design makes leakage likely to matter. Every task is a repackaging of a public competition or public data set, so the data, the published solutions and in several cases the leaderboard itself predate the agents' training cut-offs; the repository holds no identity filter, time split or contamination check, and the readme and grading code do not mention one. The ProteinGym and Open Problems tasks come with their own source splits, which are the only separation in place.
facts.source_locator: README: Description; experiments/biomlbench_v0.1a.txt

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Unreported in the saved sources. The grading code produces one report per submission with no replicate handling, and nothing in the repository defines a number of runs per agent and task, a seed policy or an interval on the aggregate percentiles; the aggregate function simply averages the per-task percentiles. How many runs stand behind a published figure is not stated in anything fetched here.
facts.source_locator: grade.py, aggregate_reports

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a whole task: a description, a data set and a submission format, which the agent must turn into test-set predictions in one autonomous run. Below that level the entity differs per task, from a small molecule to a protein variant to a cell to a medical image, but the benchmark's unit of scoring is the task, and a run is graded from a single submission file.
facts.source_locator: README: Description, Basic Usage; grade.py

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Mixed, and not stated as a composition. The task identifiers name human proteins and cell data, a mouse protein (CSN4_MOUSE), a bacterial protein (Q8EG35_SHEON, from Shewanella oneidensis) and the SARS-CoV-2 spike receptor binding domain, while the Kaggle and Polaris tasks concern human patients and small molecules. No source fetched here gives a species breakdown.
facts.source_locator: experiments/biomlbench_v0.1a.txt

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Whatever each source data set measured, inherited rather than described. The ProteinGym tasks are deep mutational scans, including a binding scan of the SARS-CoV-2 spike and stability scans from Tsuboyama 2023. The Polaris tasks are small-molecule property measurements (potency, metabolic clearance, plasma protein binding, solubility, permeability, hERG inhibition, blood-brain barrier penetration). The single-cell tasks come from Open Problems and the imaging tasks from clinical data. No assay protocol is described in the saved sources.
facts.source_locator: experiments/biomlbench_v0.1a.txt

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The task description in prose plus the prepared task data, inside a container with biomedical libraries already installed, including RDKit and BioPython. The agent writes and runs its own code, so within the container it may use anything available there; what it must produce is a submission file or folder. The saved sources do not state whether network access or external model calls beyond the agent's own API keys are restricted during a run.
facts.source_locator: README: Key Features, Prerequisites

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: The agent trains whatever it decides to train, from scratch, inside the run: there is no fixed model, no frozen representation and no prescribed method. That is the point of the benchmark, which the readme describes as implementing complete solutions from scratch. Nothing in the benchmark is fine-tuned by the maintainers.
facts.source_locator: README: Description

strengths.text: The score is anchored to people rather than to other agents: each submission is ranked against that task's existing leaderboard and separately against human baseline scores, with the metric direction read from the leaderboard rather than assumed.
strengths.source_locator: grade.py, grade_submission and calculate_human_performance_metrics; grade_helpers.py, rank_score

strengths.text: It is agent-agnostic and executable end to end: a submission is just a file or folder, the task set is a plain list of identifiers, and prepare, run-agent and grade are three commands. Everything is MIT licensed.
strengths.source_locator: README: Key Features, Basic Usage; LICENSE; experiments/biomlbench_v0.1a.txt

strengths.text: The task set is genuinely multi-domain rather than one field repeated: the 24 identifiers cover small-molecule properties, protein mutational scans, single-cell omics and medical imaging, each with its own data-source implementation in the repository.
A dummy agent ships with the benchmark, so the pipeline can be checked without spending model calls, and prebuilt agent images are provided to avoid build differences between users.

limitations.text: A percentile is a statement about a particular leaderboard, not only about the agent: it depends on who submitted to that competition and when, and the grader reports the leaderboard size precisely because the denominator varies between tasks.

Contamination is not addressed anywhere in the saved sources. All 24 tasks are public competitions or public data sets with published solutions, and no identity filter, time split or contamination check exists in the repository.
This is a pre-release. The readme labels the version v0.1-alpha and says to expect bugs and incomplete features, which is a caution worth carrying into any comparison based on it.

Nothing in the repository pins how many runs an agent gets, so the published aggregates cannot be read as having a known variance: the grading code averages per-task percentiles with no replicate or interval handling.

Running it costs money and depends on outside services: real agents need API keys for commercial model providers, and each task's data is fetched from its original host (Kaggle, Polaris Hub, ProteinGym or a manual source) at preparation time.

run_guide.summary: Install the benchmark, prepare one task's data, run an agent container on it and grade the submission against that task's leaderboard.
prerequisites: Python 3.11 or later, Docker for the agent containers, and the uv package manager.
For a real agent, an API key file at the repository root with the relevant provider keys.

cd biomlbench

uv sync
source .venv/bin/activate

steps.title: Prepare a task, run an agent and grade it
steps.shell:
biomlbench prepare -t polarishub/tdcommons-caco2-wang
biomlbench run-agent --agent dummy --task-id polarishub/tdcommons-caco2-wang

name: Harmonised single-cell and spatial foundation model benchmark (Chen et al. 2026)
description: Harmonised evaluation of six single-cell and spatial foundation models (Nicheformer, CellPLM, scGPT-spatial, GenePT-w, scELMo, Novae) on zero-shot and continually pretrained clustering, supervised cell type annotation, marker-gene concordance and perturbation prediction.

attributes.task: Clustering, cell type annotation and perturbation prediction from foundation model embeddings
attributes.scope_note: No non-foundation-model baseline (for example PCA or scVI) is reported in the result tables.
attributes.source_locator: Abstract; Methods 'Downstream evaluation tasks'; Tables 1-5

profile.summary: One paper's harmonised benchmark of six single-cell and spatial foundation models (Nicheformer, CellPLM, scGPT-spatial, GenePT, scELMo, Novae) across scRNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics and Perturb-seq data. Five tasks are scored under shared metrics: zero-shot clustering, clustering after continual pretraining, supervised cell type annotation, marker-gene concordance and perturbation prediction. It is for researchers choosing which foundation model, if any, to use for a given modality and task.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods 'Downstream evaluation tasks'

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The benchmark asks when a foundation model's representation actually helps biological inference, and whether the answer holds across modalities. Clustering tasks ask whether an embedding separates reference cell types or spatial domains; the supervised task asks whether fine-tuning or adapting a model on labels gives accurate annotation; the marker-gene task asks whether clusters found in the embedding recover the same differentially expressed genes as the reference labels; the perturbation task asks whether a representation supports predicting post-perturbation expression for perturbations not seen in training. The authors report that model rankings shifted with modality, preprocessing, tokenisation, biological prior, domain shift and metric choice, and that no model dominated.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Introduction; Methods 'DEG Analysis' and 'Perturbation Prediction'

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Three scRNA-seq datasets are used: ATAA (ascending aortic tissue from 11 individuals, 11 major cell types), BMMC (the NeurIPS 2021 challenge CITE-seq subset, bone marrow mononuclear cells from 12 healthy donors, 45 annotated cell types) and HS (human splenic dendritic cells, seven subtypes). Four spatial datasets are used: HBCA1 (10x Visium human breast cancer, 20 domain labels), MHPC (mouse hippocampus, Slide-seqV2, 14 domain labels), MOSTA (mouse organogenesis Stereo-seq, section E9.5 E1S1, 12 anatomical regions) and SEAAD (middle temporal gyrus MERFISH, 27 aged donors, a 140-gene panel, 24 annotated cell types). All spatial datasets except SEAAD came from the BenchmarkST data resource. Three Perturb-seq datasets in K562 cells are used: Adamson (87 single-gene perturbations), Norman (131 two-gene and 105 single-gene perturbations) and Replogle (genome-wide CRISPR interference). Reference labels are the original studies' annotations. Each model is run with its own recommended preprocessing, so the harmonisation is in the tasks, splits and metrics rather than in one shared input pipeline.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Datasets'; Methods 'Zero-shot cell type clustering'

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Clustering: embeddings are clustered with Leiden, sweeping the resolution until the number of clusters matches the number of reference labels, and scored with adjusted Rand index (ARI), normalised mutual information (NMI) and silhouette score; k-means results are reported in the supplement for models that originally used it. Continual pretraining repeats this after two epochs of self-supervised adaptation on the target dataset, with other hyperparameters at each model's defaults. Supervised annotation uses a stratified 8:2 train and test split, 7:1:2 where a validation set is needed, and is scored with accuracy, precision, recall, macro F1, macro PR-AUC and macro ROC-AUC. Marker-gene concordance takes the top 20 differentially expressed genes per Leiden cluster and per reference cell type with Wilcoxon rank-sum tests in Scanpy, and compares the sets with pairwise Jaccard indices. Perturbation prediction follows a scGPT-style GEARS framework with the standard simulation split, and is scored with mean squared error and Pearson correlation over all genes and over the top 20 differentially expressed genes per condition, plus the same measures on the change from control. The paper fixes random seeds at 42; the GenePT-w folder's README also lists pytorch_lightning.seed_everything(202310).
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Zero-shot cell type clustering', 'Continually-pretrained cell type clustering', 'Cell type annotation', 'DEG Analysis', 'Perturbation Prediction'

sections.title: Task coverage differs by model
sections.body: Not every model runs every task. Novae is evaluated on spatial transcriptomics only. Perturbation prediction is restricted to CellPLM, scGPT-spatial, GenePT-w and scELMo, because Nicheformer and Novae provide no comparable workflow for the GEARS setting. Supervised annotation is restricted to datasets with cell-level labels: the three scRNA-seq datasets and the single-cell-resolution SEAAD MERFISH atlas, and for SEAAD a section-wise split is used to avoid leakage between train and test. Two tasks had to be implemented by the authors where the original model did not support them: Nicheformer's cell type annotation, Novae's annotation through a frozen encoder plus a small classifier, and CellPLM's continual pretraining, because its repository provided no such pipeline.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Zero-shot cell type clustering', 'Cell type annotation', 'Continually-pretrained cell type clustering', 'Perturbation Prediction'

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The code is public under the MIT licence and organised by model, one directory each for CellPLM, Nicheformer, scGPT-spatial, GenePT, scELMo and Novae, with each directory holding the model's codebase plus the notebooks or scripts that run the shared tasks. The GenePT folder's README lists three notebooks, one per task, the Python packages they need, and the gene embedding pickle they read from a local data folder. The repository documents no installation or command-line entry point, so running a task means opening the relevant notebook and supplying the dataset.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Overview and License; GenePT/README.md: Contents, Requirements, Data Layout

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Ten datasets. scRNA-seq: ATAA (11 individuals, 11 major cell types), BMMC (12 healthy donors, 45 annotated cell types), HS (seven dendritic-cell subtypes). Spatial: HBCA1 (20 domains), MHPC (14 domain labels), MOSTA E9.5 E1S1 (12 anatomical regions), SEAAD (27 aged donors, 140-gene panel, 24 annotated cell types). Perturb-seq in K562: Adamson (87 single-gene perturbations), Norman (131 two-gene and 105 single-gene perturbations), Replogle (genome-wide CRISPR interference). Cell counts are not printed in the text.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Datasets'

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: By task. Clustering tasks have no split: the whole dataset is embedded and clustered. Supervised annotation uses a stratified 8:2 train and test split, with the training part cut 7:1 into train and validation where a model needs one (7:1:2 overall), except SEAAD, which is split section-wise with two sections held out as validation. Perturbation prediction uses the GEARS standard simulation split with seed 42, so test perturbation conditions are unseen in training.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Cell type annotation' and 'Perturbation Prediction'

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Clustering: ARI, NMI and silhouette score, higher is better. Supervised annotation: accuracy, precision, recall, macro F1, macro PR-AUC and macro ROC-AUC, higher is better. Marker-gene concordance: Jaccard index between top-20 gene sets, higher is better. Perturbation prediction: Pearson correlation (higher is better) and mean squared error (lower is better), over all genes and over the top 20 differentially expressed genes, and the same on the change from control.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Zero-shot cell type clustering', 'Cell type annotation', 'DEG Analysis', 'Perturbation Prediction'

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The six foundation models are compared with each other; ground-truth annotations and ground-truth-label marker genes are the references. Ground-truth UMAPs were made with Scanpy on 2,000 highly variable genes and 40 principal components, but the result tables report no non-foundation-model baseline such as PCA or scVI.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Ground truth visualisation'; Methods 'Downstream evaluation tasks'

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Per task, and partial. Perturbation prediction uses the GEARS simulation split so that test conditions are unseen. SEAAD annotation is split by tissue section to avoid leakage between train and test. Overlap between the evaluation datasets and each model's pretraining corpus is not controlled or reported; the authors say current foundation models remain vulnerable to domain shift.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Perturbation Prediction' and 'Cell type annotation'; Introduction

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: None reported: no replicates, repeated splits or confidence intervals are described. The paper states a random seed of 42 for splits and stochastic steps; the GenePT-w folder's README also lists pytorch_lightning.seed_everything(202310).
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Zero-shot cell type clustering' and 'Cell type annotation'; GenePT/README.md: Requirements

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A cell for clustering and annotation (a spot or cell with tissue coordinates for the spatial datasets), and a held-out perturbation condition for perturbation prediction, scored over a shared gene set.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Zero-shot cell type clustering' and 'Perturbation Prediction'

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human and mouse. Human: ATAA aortic tissue, BMMC bone marrow, HS spleen, HBCA1 breast cancer, SEAAD brain, and the K562 Perturb-seq screens. Mouse: MHPC hippocampus and MOSTA embryo.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Datasets'

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: scRNA-seq and CITE-seq; spatial transcriptomics by 10x Visium, Slide-seqV2, Stereo-seq and MERFISH; Perturb-seq genetic screens including CRISPR interference. Labels are the original studies' expert or marker-based annotations.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Datasets'

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Each model's own documented inputs, prepared by its own recommended preprocessing: raw counts for Nicheformer, library-size normalised and log1p counts for CellPLM, vocabulary-aligned binned expression for scGPT-spatial, normalised counts combined with text-derived gene embeddings for GenePT-w and scELMo, and spatial coordinates with neighbourhood graphs for Novae. Genes outside a checkpoint's vocabulary are discarded.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Zero-shot cell type clustering', per-model paragraphs

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Three settings are scored: zero-shot (frozen pretrained embeddings), continual pretraining (two epochs of self-supervised adaptation on the target dataset), and supervised annotation with each model's default or recommended set-up: most models are fine-tuned, GenePT-w uses a k=7 nearest-neighbour vote on its embeddings, and Novae trains a small classifier on a frozen encoder.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Downstream evaluation tasks', 'Continually-pretrained cell type clustering', 'Cell type annotation'; GenePT/README.md: cell_type_annotation.ipynb

strengths.text: Tasks, splits, clustering procedure, metrics and seeds are the same across models, and where the Leiden resolution could bias the comparison it is swept to match the number of reference labels.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Zero-shot cell type clustering' and 'Continually-pretrained cell type clustering'

strengths.text: Perturbation metrics are computed on one shared gene set per dataset, the intersection of the dataset's genes with every evaluated model's vocabulary, so differences are not driven by unequal gene coverage.

The per-model implementation details are written out, including checkpoints, batch sizes, learning rates, masking ratios and where the authors had to implement a task the original model did not provide.
The code that runs the tasks is public under the MIT licence, organised per model.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Data and Tool Availability; LICENSE; README.md: Overview

limitations.text: No non-foundation-model baseline is reported in the result tables: the models are compared with each other and with ground-truth labels, so a reader cannot see whether a simple method such as highly variable genes or PCA would match them. Highly variable genes are used only for the ground-truth UMAPs.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Ground truth visualisation'; Methods 'Downstream evaluation tasks'

limitations.text: Overlap between the evaluation datasets and the models' pretraining corpora is not checked, so a model may be scored on cells it was pretrained on.

No replicates or intervals are reported; the paper fixes its seeds at 42 and the GenePT-w README also lists a seed of 202310. The authors' own finding is that rankings shift with preprocessing and metric choice, so small differences between models should not be read as decisive.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods 'Zero-shot cell type clustering'

limitations.text: Coverage is uneven and partly author-implemented: Novae is spatial only, perturbation prediction covers four of the six models, and the Nicheformer and Novae annotation tasks and the CellPLM continual pretraining pipeline were written by the authors because the original models did not provide them.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Cell type annotation', 'Continually-pretrained cell type clustering', 'Perturbation Prediction'

name: SCMBench
description: Benchmark of 19 domain-specific models and four single-cell foundation models (scGPT, UCE, Geneformer, scFoundation) for paired and unpaired single-cell multi-omics (RNA and ATAC) integration, scored on integration accuracy, biomarker detection, trajectory conservation and batch correction.

attributes.task: Single-cell multi-omics data integration
attributes.scope_note: Foundation models receive scATAC-seq as MAESTRO gene activity scores, a non-standard input for RNA-pretrained models (Methods).
attributes.source_locator: Abstract; Fig. 1; Methods; Supplementary Data 1-2

profile.summary: SCMBench compares 23 methods for integrating single-cell multi-omics data, 19 domain-specific models and four foundation models (scGPT, UCE, Geneformer, scFoundation), on three paired and two unpaired RNA and ATAC datasets from four organs and two species, plus a triple-omics dataset and simulated data with increasing batch effects. Thirteen metrics cover integration accuracy, biological conservation (biomarker detection, differentially accessible regions, enriched motifs, trajectory conservation) and batch correction. It is for researchers choosing an integration tool, and for model developers who want to know where foundation models stand on this task.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results 'SCMBench provides a comprehensive benchmarking pipeline'; Figure 1 caption; README.md: Downstream tasks

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The benchmark asks whether an integration method puts cells from different omics into one latent space that keeps the biology. Three groups of questions are asked: can cell types be told apart in the joint embedding (integration accuracy), does the embedding preserve informative features and dynamics (biomarker genes, differentially accessible chromatin regions, enriched motifs, developmental trajectories), and does it remove batch effects without over-correcting. Both paired data, where the two omics are measured in the same cells, and unpaired data, where they come from different cells, are covered, and the authors state that unpaired alignment is the harder case.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results 'SCMBench provides a comprehensive benchmarking pipeline'; Figure 1 caption

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Three paired datasets (PBMC-10k from 10x Multiome, 9631 cells; Chen-2019 SHARE-seq mouse cortex, 9190 cells; Ma-2020 SHARE-seq mouse skin, 32231 cells) and two unpaired datasets (Muto-2021 human kidney, 19985 RNA and 24205 ATAC cells; Yao-2021 mouse MOp, 69727 RNA and 54844 ATAC cells) are used, with a triple-omics mouse cortex dataset adding DNA methylation and a Chen-Traj subset of 1469 cells for trajectory work. Datasets were picked for species, organ, sample size, batch effects and sequencing technique. Ma-2020 and Muto-2021 carry batch effects and are partitioned by batch, then sampled to 2500 cells per batch for the batch-effect experiments, with the originals kept for the imbalanced case. Features are filtered with Scanpy's seurat_v3 flavour to 80,000 peaks and 8000 genes. Simulated paired data come from scMultiSim: 10,000 cells, 3000 genes and peaks, three batches, with batch effect size varied across 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 and 3. Because pretrained foundation models cannot take ATAC peaks, chromatin accessibility is turned into a gene-centric activity matrix with MAESTRO's ATACCalculateGenescore, weighting peaks by distance to transcription start sites; Seurat4's GeneActivity and BABEL translation are evaluated as alternatives.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results and Methods 'Datasets and preprocessing', 'Real data preprocessing', 'Simulated data generation'; Supplementary Data 1 Dataset sheet

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each method produces latent embeddings and cell-type inferences, which are then scored. Integration accuracy uses four metrics, mean average precision (MAP), normalised mutual information, average silhouette width and the adjusted Rand index, with the overall score the mean of the four; all metrics are higher is better. Biological conservation is scored by consistency rather than by a single truth: cell types are annotated from each method's embedding with a k-nearest-neighbour classifier, the top 100 differentially expressed genes per cell type are taken with Scanpy's rank_genes_groups t-test, and the Jaccard similarity index of marker sets is averaged across cell types and method pairs to give that method's biomarker score. The same construction is applied to the top 100 differentially accessible regions and to motifs enriched in them with GimmeMotifs. For PBMC-10k there is also a recall against curated CellMarker 2.0 markers. Trajectory conservation uses a TC score against the original data's lineage. Batch correction uses iLISI, kBET, graph connectivity and batch-ASW. Datasets with batch information are split into smaller ones before computing integration metrics, and the overall box plots are across datasets, n = 5 for paired and n = 6 for unpaired.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Figure 2 caption, Methods 'Evaluation metrics' and 'Biomarkers Detection Consistency'; README.md: Downstream tasks

sections.title: How foundation models are handled
sections.body: Only scGPT came with an implementation for paired multi-omics integration, with both fine-tuning and zero-shot modes; UCE, Geneformer and scFoundation were modified by the authors to produce embeddings for each omics separately in a zero-shot way. Several adaptation strategies are then benchmarked as if they were separate methods: an adapter that feeds foundation model embeddings into scVI's framework (FM-scVI), fine-tuning at different transformer depths, parameter-efficient tuning, and training from scratch with only the pretrained gene token embeddings. The authors report that pretrained weights did not help substantially against training from scratch on this task, that scGPT's blood-specific model generally beat its whole-human model, and that foundation models generally underperform the domain-specific models, with UCE the only one able to handle the mouse Yao-2021 data. Foundation models are left out of the triple-omics comparison because continuous methylation beta values do not match the sparse counts they were trained on.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results 'SCMBench provides a comprehensive benchmarking pipeline', 'Benchmarking data integration on both paired and unpaired datasets', and the adaptation section

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository holds the benchmark package, the data preprocessing instructions, the per-method wrappers and the evaluation pipelines. Methods are grouped into four environments by language and version, each created by its own installation script, because the tools conflict. Data are preprocessed to one h5ad format with the same keys. A method is then run as a script taking the RNA and ATAC h5ad files and writing per-omics embedding CSVs plus a run-info file; Python methods and R methods have the same argument shape. Downstream evaluation is documented separately in the evaluation folder.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Directory structure, Installation, Quick start, Data preprocessing, Downstream tasks

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Six real datasets plus simulations. Paired: PBMC-10k (9631 cells), Chen-2019 (9190), Ma-2020 (32231). Unpaired: Muto-2021 (19985 RNA, 24205 ATAC cells), Yao-2021 (69727 RNA, 54844 ATAC cells). Triple-omics mouse cortex (2317 ATAC, 3377 methylation, 55803 RNA cells) and a Chen-Traj trajectory subset of 1469 cells. Simulated: 10,000 cells, 3000 genes and peaks, three batches at six batch-effect sizes.
facts.source_locator: Supplementary Data 1 Dataset sheet; Paper: Methods 'Simulated data generation'

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No train and test split: integration is unsupervised and every method is run on the whole dataset, then its embedding is scored. Instead the data are partitioned by batch where batches exist: Ma-2020 and Muto-2021 are split by batch and sampled to 2500 cells per batch for the batch-effect experiments, and datasets with batch information are split into smaller ones before the integration metrics are computed. For unpaired results the authors report a single batch (Muto-2021-Batch1) to remove batch effects from the accuracy comparison.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Real data preprocessing'; Figure 2 caption; Results on unpaired datasets

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Thirteen metrics, all higher is better. Integration accuracy: MAP, NMI, ASW, ARI, with the overall score their mean. Biological conservation: Jaccard similarity index for biomarker detection, for differentially accessible regions and for enriched motifs, a recall against CellMarker 2.0 markers for PBMC-10k, and a trajectory conservation (TC) score. Batch correction: iLISI, kBET, graph connectivity and batch-ASW.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Downstream tasks; Paper: Results and Methods 'Evaluation metrics'

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The 19 domain-specific models are the reference points for the four foundation models: statistical methods PCA, MOFA, bindSC, LIGER, online-iNMF, scMoMaT, MMD-MA, Pamona, UnionCom, Harmony, Seurat4 and Seurat5, and deep learning methods scMDC, scJoint, GLUE, Cobolt, scVI, TotalVI and DeepMAPS. Seventeen of the methods can be applied to unpaired data, and seven handle the triple-omics case.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results 'SCMBench provides a comprehensive benchmarking pipeline' and the unpaired and triple-omics results; Supplementary Data 1 Method sheet

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None described for pretraining overlap: the paper does not report whether the benchmark datasets appear in the foundation models' pretraining corpora. The controls it does apply are about batch effects rather than leakage: partitioning and subsampling batched datasets, reporting one batch for unpaired accuracy, and adding simulated data at six batch-effect sizes.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Real data preprocessing' and 'Simulated data generation'; Results on batch correction

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Spread across datasets rather than repeated runs: the overall scores are box plots with median and quartiles over individual dataset scores, n = 5 for paired and n = 6 for unpaired. The authors also report critical difference diagrams and significance reports, and state that the top methods are not significantly separated, for example that GLUE ranks first but does not significantly outperform scJoint, and that scJoint's lead on the unpaired data is not statistically significant.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Figure 2 caption; Results on paired and unpaired integration

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A cell, embedded in a joint latent space; for paired data the same cell carries both omics, for unpaired data the two omics come from different cells that must be aligned.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results 'Benchmarking data integration on both paired and unpaired datasets'; Figure 1 caption

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human and mouse: PBMC-10k and Muto-2021 are Homo sapiens, Chen-2019, Ma-2020, Yao-2021, the triple-omics set and Chen-Traj are Mus musculus. The authors note that most foundation models, trained mainly on human data, scale poorly to mouse, and that UCE was the only one that could handle the mouse Yao-2021 data.
facts.source_locator: Supplementary Data 1 Dataset sheet; Paper: Results on unpaired datasets and the adaptation section

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Single-cell transcriptomics and chromatin accessibility, by 10x Multiome, SHARE-seq, snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq and 10x v3, plus snmC-seq DNA methylation and Drop-seq RNA in the triple-omics set. Labels are the datasets' own cell-type annotations; marker references come from CellMarker 2.0.
facts.source_locator: Supplementary Data 1 Dataset sheet; Paper: Methods 'Biomarker Detection with Prior Knowledge'

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Paired or unpaired RNA and ATAC matrices in one h5ad format with the same keys, filtered to 80,000 peaks and 8000 genes. Foundation models cannot take ATAC peaks because of their token limits, so they receive a gene-centric activity matrix computed by MAESTRO's ATACCalculateGenescore; Seurat4 GeneActivity and BABEL translation are tested as alternatives and neither uniformly wins.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results on activity matrices, Methods 'Real data preprocessing'; README.md: Data preprocessing

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: All of them, and the comparison of settings is part of the benchmark. Domain-specific models are fitted to each dataset. Foundation models are run zero-shot, fine-tuned (scGPT at different transformer depths), parameter-efficiently tuned, trained from scratch with only pretrained gene token embeddings, and combined with scVI as an adapter (FM-scVI); each adaptation is benchmarked as a standalone method.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results 'SCMBench provides a comprehensive benchmarking pipeline' and the adaptation section; Figure 2 caption

strengths.text: Significance is reported, not just ranking: critical difference diagrams show overlapping groups, and the authors say in the text where a lead is not statistically significant.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results on paired and unpaired integration

strengths.text: The foundation model setting is not taken for granted: three models were adapted to the task, several adaptation strategies are benchmarked as separate methods, and the alternatives to the MAESTRO activity matrix are tested rather than assumed.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results on activity matrices and on adaptation

strengths.text: The spread of conditions is wide: paired, unpaired and triple-omics real data from two species and four organs, with simulated data at six batch-effect sizes and a computational efficiency comparison of time and memory.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Figure 1 caption, Figure 2 caption, Results on triple-omics

strengths.text: Code and environments are public under the MIT licence, with one installation script per method group and an archived release on Zenodo.
strengths.source_locator: README.md: Installation; LICENSE; Zenodo record 19050984; Paper: Code availability

limitations.text: The biomarker, differentially accessible region and motif scores measure agreement between methods, not correctness: each method's score is the average Jaccard similarity of its marker sets with the other methods'. Only the PBMC-10k recall against CellMarker 2.0 compares with outside knowledge, and the authors note it cannot credit novel or unannotated markers.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods 'Biomarkers Detection Consistency' and 'Biomarker Detection with Prior Knowledge'

limitations.text: The foundation models are not fed their native input: chromatin accessibility reaches them as a gene activity matrix because of token limits, which the authors call a reasonable strategy with several feasible alternatives rather than a settled choice.

Coverage is uneven: 17 of 23 methods run on unpaired data, seven on triple-omics, foundation models are excluded from the triple-omics comparison, and Yao-2021 has no activity matrix because the computation ran out of memory, so not every method has a score on every dataset.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results on unpaired and triple-omics; Supplementary Data 1 Dataset sheet

limitations.text: Data are not redistributed and are subsampled: every dataset is fetched from its original repository, and the batched datasets are cut to 2500 cells per batch so that a wide range of methods could run, so the published scores are not on the full data.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Data availability; Methods 'Real data preprocessing'
