name: Differential expression classification benchmark for perturbation models (Sun et al. 2026)
description: Three-class (non-DE, up, down) differential expression prediction for unseen genetic perturbations within a cell line and for seen perturbations in a held-out cell line, on K562, RPE1, HepG2 and Jurkat essential-gene Perturb-seq screens.

attributes.task: Prediction of differential expression status after genetic perturbation
attributes.scope_note: DE labels from Wilcoxon rank-sum tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction per perturbation (adjusted p < 0.01) on observed and predicted expression alike.
attributes.source_locator: Sections 1, 3.1-3.3; Tables 1-5

profile.summary: One paper's benchmark of whether perturbation models get differential expression right, rather than mean expression. Each gene under each held-out perturbation is classified as up-regulated, down-regulated or not differentially expressed, and five deep learning models are compared with three simple classifiers on essential-gene Perturb-seq screens in K562, RPE1, Jurkat and HepG2, under two regimes: unseen perturbations within a cell line, and perturbations seen elsewhere in a held-out cell line. It is for anyone choosing a perturbation model for the downstream task that actually gets used, deciding which genes responded.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Section 1; Section 3.1

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The task is three-class classification: for a gene and a perturbation, predict non-DE, up-regulated or down-regulated. The authors argue this is the decision that matters downstream, because an effect's significance has to be judged against the variability in the data, and that existing benchmarks measure continuous expression accuracy instead, or at best a top-k DE gene overlap score that ignores class-wise performance. Their headline finding is that simple baselines are competitive with and often beat deep learning models on this task, by being more precise while the deep models favour recall, and that better continuous-expression scores do not imply better DE prediction.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Section 1; Section 3.1

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Four essential-gene Perturb-seq screens are used: K562, RPE1, Jurkat and HepG2. Raw UMI counts are normalised by total counts per cell, scaled to 10,000 and log(1+x) transformed. DE labels come from Wilcoxon rank-sum tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction per perturbation, with a pair counted as DE when the adjusted p-value is below 0.01 and the sign of the log fold change deciding up or down; the same procedure produces the labels from observed expression and the predictions from each deep model's predicted expression. The classes are very unbalanced: per the paper's Table 5, non-DE is 96.61% for K562, 95.96% for RPE1, 97.61% for HepG2 and 98.35% for Jurkat, over 17.61 to 23.03 million pairs per dataset, with 2,057 to 2,393 perturbations and 8,561 to 9,623 genes. Every cell line is scored twice: on the full data, and on the PerturbQA-downsampled subset where non-DE pairs were cut and DE pairs restricted to the most significant, using that paper's own train and test split.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.2 and Table 5

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Both tasks score the same held-out 40% of perturbations. For unseen perturbations, a cell line's perturbations are split 60% train and 40% test, and every method trains on that same split and reports on that same test set. For cellular context, a cell line is held out, models train on perturbation and gene pairs from the other cell lines over the 6,641 genes common to all four, and performance is reported on the held-out cell line's 40% test set; STATE is the exception, trained with the held-out line's 60% training set as its official codebase does, which the authors say makes it few-shot rather than zero-shot. The metrics are per-class F1 for up, down and non-DE, macro F1 averaging the three equally, and balanced accuracy averaging per-class recall; alongside these the paper reports continuous metrics (DE overlap at 50, MAE, MSE, global Pearson, Pearson delta, per-gene Pearson) to show that they disagree with the DE metrics. A sparsity calibration step sets predicted expression at or below a gene-specific quantile threshold to zero, with the scaling factor r = 1.

sections.title: How the split is actually made
sections.body: The repository's own code differs in wording from the paper, and the difference matters. The split script takes each perturbation's dominant DE class, merges rare strata into the most common one, and makes a stratified 80/20 split of perturbations with test_size 0.20 and random_state 305, writing a split_80 column. A second step turns 25% of the training perturbations into a calibration set. The preprocessing README then states that the calibration perturbations are merged into the test set for final reporting, which gives the 60/40 train and test split the paper describes. A second 60/40 split, in which the original evaluation perturbations all move to training, exists for robustness.
sections.source_locator: preprocessing/train_test_split.py; preprocessing/README.md steps 2 to 4

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository reproduces the analyses. One conda environment is created from the repository root, with VAE and scVI listing extra requirements in their own folders. The raw h5ad files for the four screens, the processed train and test splits with DE labels, the PerturbQA downsampled data and the embeddings used in the study are all downloadable from addresses the README gives. Each method has its own folder with its own README holding the commands, and there are separate folders for the metrics and for the post-prediction calibration. The preprocessing folder holds the DE calling and split scripts that every model shares.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Environment, Repository layout, Data access; preprocessing/README.md

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Four essential-gene Perturb-seq screens: K562 (17.61M perturbation-gene pairs, 2,057 perturbations, 8,561 genes), RPE1 (20.93M, 2,393, 8,748), HepG2 (23.03M, 2,393, 9,623) and Jurkat (21.25M, 2,393, 8,881). Each is also scored as the PerturbQA-downsampled subset. The cross-cell-line task uses the 6,641 genes common to all four.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 5; Sections 3.1 and 3.2

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: By perturbation, 60% train and 40% test, the same split for every method. The code makes it as a stratified 80/20 split on each perturbation's dominant DE class with random_state 305, then turns a quarter of the training perturbations into a calibration set which is merged back into the test set for reporting. Per-dataset train and test pair counts are in Table 5, for example 10.56M train and 7.05M test pairs for K562. For the cross-cell-line task the training data are the other cell lines, with the held-out line's 40% test set scored; STATE additionally trains on the held-out line's 60% training set. The downsampled arm uses PerturbQA's own split.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1, Table 5; preprocessing/train_test_split.py; preprocessing/README.md

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Macro F1 (the mean of the up, down and non-DE F1 scores), balanced accuracy (the mean of per-class recall) and per-class F1, all higher is better. Reported alongside them: DE overlap at 50, global and delta and per-gene Pearson correlations (higher is better) and mean absolute error and mean squared error on pseudobulk expression (lower is better).
facts.source_locator: Paper: Sections 3.5.1 and 3.5.2

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Three non-deep-learning methods: a perturbation majority vote that predicts each gene's most common class across training perturbations and ignores perturbation identity, a weighted k-nearest-neighbour classifier on GenePT perturbation embeddings, and a regularised logistic regression on those embeddings. The deep models compared are scVI (sampling and mean), Scouter and a VAE adapted from scGen for the within-cell-line task, with STATE and TranScouter added across cell lines.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 1; Sections 3.3.1 and 3.3.2

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The split is by perturbation, so a test perturbation is unseen in training, and the cross-cell-line task holds out a whole cell line. The authors flag the one breach themselves: STATE is given the held-out cell line's training perturbations, following its official codebase, which makes its cross-cell-line result few-shot rather than zero-shot and not directly comparable with the others. No sequence or gene-level identity control is described.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Not reported as intervals in the text read: the code's split uses one fixed seed (random_state 305) and the paper reports single values per model, dataset and metric, with a second 60/40 split available in the repository for robustness rather than as error bars.
facts.source_locator: preprocessing/train_test_split.py; preprocessing/README.md step 4

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A perturbation and gene pair, labelled non-DE, up or down; the counts run to tens of millions of pairs per cell line.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1; Table 5

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human: the four screens are human cell lines (K562, RPE1, Jurkat, HepG2), which the paper calls four human cell-line datasets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.2; Section 4

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Perturb-seq: CRISPR-based genetic perturbation paired with single-cell RNA sequencing, here the essential-gene screens. Labels are not measured directly but computed from the counts by Wilcoxon rank-sum tests against non-targeting cells with Benjamini-Hochberg correction and no log2 fold-change cutoff.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 1 and Section 3.2; preprocessing/README.md step 1

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Normalised expression of the training perturbations, plus a representation of the perturbation. The simple baselines use GenePT large-language-model embeddings of the perturbed gene; the majority vote uses no perturbation information at all; the deep models take the expression data in their own formats. For the cross-cell-line task the input gene space is restricted to the 6,641 genes common to the four cell lines.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 1; Sections 3.1 and 3.3.2

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Training on the benchmark's own training split: every method, baseline or deep model, is fitted on the same 60% of perturbations and scored on the same 40%. A post-prediction sparsity calibration is evaluated as a separate condition, and STATE's cross-cell-line runs are few-shot because they see the held-out line's training perturbations.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Sections 3.1 and 3.4

strengths.text: The DE labels and the split are computed once and shared: every method is trained on the same 60% of perturbations and reported on the same 40% test set, with the preprocessing code published.
Class-wise results are kept rather than collapsed: per-class F1 for up, down and non-DE alongside macro F1 and balanced accuracy, which matters when non-DE is 96 to 98% of pairs.

Both the full data and the downsampled subset are scored, and the authors report that model performance and ranking on the subsampled data can differ drastically from the full dataset, which is the setting a user faces.
Continuous expression metrics are reported next to the DE metrics, which is how the authors show that the two disagree and that a model can look better on one and worse on the other.

limitations.text: One model is not on the same footing: STATE is trained with the held-out cell line's training perturbations, so its cross-cell-line numbers are few-shot rather than zero-shot, as the authors state.

The labels are themselves a statistical call, not a measurement: DE status comes from Wilcoxon tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction at adjusted p below 0.01 and no fold-change cutoff, applied to observed and predicted expression alike, so the benchmark inherits whatever that test does on sparse counts.

Scope is narrow and fixed: four human essential-gene screens, single-gene genetic perturbations, no uncertainty intervals, and one split seed in the published code, so small differences between models should not be read as decisive.

It is a preprint not certified by peer review, and the data are not redistributed by the benchmark: the h5ad files, the processed splits and the embeddings are served from shared drive links the README gives, and the code repository states no licence.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: page header; README.md: Data access

name: Static GRN reconstruction from single-cell foundation models (Ye et al. 2026)
description: Zero-shot GRN reconstruction from six single-cell foundation models with three extraction strategies (token-embedding cosine, hidden-state cosine, attention) against GENIE3, DeepSEM and GRNBoost, on six BEELINE scRNA-seq datasets and four reference network types.

attributes.task: Gene regulatory network inference from single-cell expression
attributes.scope_note: Uses BEELINE datasets and preprocessing with TF-prioritised gene sets (TFs+500, TFs+1000); edges restricted to TF-target candidates and ranked by absolute weight.
attributes.source_locator: Sections 2.1-2.2; Appendix A-B; Tables 4-7

profile.summary: A single paper's benchmark of how well six single-cell foundation models recover gene regulatory networks without any training, compared with three classical network inference methods. Networks are built from six BEELINE single-cell RNA-seq datasets from mouse and human and checked against four kinds of reference network. A second task, dynamic transition probing, asks whether a model can move early-cell expression profiles towards later states. It is for researchers choosing a foundation model, or a way of reading one, for network inference.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Section 2.1

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The benchmark asks which part of a single-cell foundation model carries gene regulatory information and how that compares with conventional inference. Three readings of each model are compared: cosine similarity of the pretrained gene token embeddings (costok), cosine similarity of final-layer hidden states (coshid), and last-layer attention scores (attn). The inferred networks are scored at the edge level, the transcription factor (TF) level and the topology level. A second task, dynamic transition probing, tests whether a model's learned gene relationships can drive early-cell expression towards the observed late-cell state without temporal supervision.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 1, 2.1 to 2.3

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Six BEELINE datasets are used: mouse dendritic cells (mDC), three mouse haematopoietic stem-cell lineages (mHSC-E, mHSC-GM, mHSC-L), human mature hepatocytes (hHep) and human embryonic stem cells (hESC). Raw data were preprocessed with the BEELINE protocol. Genes whose expression varies with pseudotime were selected with a generalised additive model and Bonferroni correction (corrected P < 0.01). Two TF-prioritised gene sets were then built: TFs+500 and TFs+1000 keep all significant TFs plus the top 500 or 1000 most dynamically variable non-TF genes. Main results use TFs+500. Reference networks are cell-type-specific ChIP-seq, non-specific ChIP-seq, STRING functional interactions and OmniPath. Table 2 gives the TF and gene counts and network density for each dataset, gene set and reference.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 2.1; Appendix A.1, Table 2

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Every method outputs ranked gene pairs. Scoring is restricted to TF-target candidates: the source gene must be a reference TF and the target must be in the reference gene set. Edges are ranked by absolute weight, and the top K edges, with K equal to the number of reference edges, give the early precision. The early precision ratio (EPR) divides this by the edge density of the candidate space, and the AUPRC ratio divides the average precision by the same density, so values above 1 beat random ranking. Main-text results average over the six datasets and three references (STRING, non-specific ChIP-seq and OmniPath); cell-type-specific ChIP-seq is reported in the appendix only, because every method was near random on it. TF-level F1 and five graph metrics, compared with STRING through a normalised closeness score, are secondary analyses. For dynamic transition probing, early and late cells are the lowest and highest 20% pseudotime quantiles, and the score is directional accuracy on the 30% of genes with the largest observed change; mDC is left out of the aggregate comparison.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 2.2, 3.1, 3.4; Appendices B.2, B.3, C, D.1

sections.title: Dynamic transition probing
sections.body: Continuous-value models (scGPT, scFoundation, scPRINT) start from the mean expression vector of early cells and pass the state repeatedly through the model, with an exponential moving average (alpha = 0.9). Rank-driven models (Geneformer, LangCell, scCello) start from ranked gene tokens and accept random token swaps that raise the masked-token likelihood, 8 proposals per iteration. The model never receives time labels, pseudotime or late-cell profiles. A gene counts as correct when the sign of the predicted change matches the observed early-to-late change. As a control, the scGPT analysis was repeated with randomly initialised weights.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.4; Appendices C.1 and C.2

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Six BEELINE single-cell RNA-seq datasets: mDC, mHSC-E, mHSC-GM, mHSC-L, hHep and hESC, each in two TF-prioritised gene sets (TFs+500 and TFs+1000) and against four references. Sizes vary by reference; for example, against STRING under TFs+500, hESC has 343 TFs and 517 genes and mHSC-L has 39 TFs and 74 genes (Table 2). The number of cells per dataset is not given in the paper.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 2.1; Appendix A.1, Table 2

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: None for the static task: foundation models are used zero-shot with no training split, and the classical baselines are fitted on each test expression matrix. For dynamic probing, early cells are the lowest 20% and late cells the highest 20% of pseudotime.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1; Appendix C.1

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Early precision ratio (EPR) and AUPRC ratio for edges, both ratios over a random predictor, higher is better, values above 1 beat random. Secondary: TF-level F1 (higher is better) and a closeness score to STRING for five graph metrics. Dynamic probing: directional accuracy on the top 30% most-changed genes, higher is better.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1 caption; Appendices B.3 and D

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: GENIE3, DeepSEM and GRNBoost, which infer networks directly from the expression matrix. For dynamic probing, scGPT with randomly initialised weights is the control.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 2.1; Section 3.4

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Not reported. The paper does not say whether the BEELINE datasets or the reference networks overlap with the foundation models' pretraining data.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Sections 2 and 4; Appendix A

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Mean and standard deviation across the six datasets are reported in the main table. No seeds, replicates or confidence intervals are reported.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1 caption

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A ranked TF-target gene pair (edge) for the static task; a gene's direction of expression change for dynamic probing.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Sections 2.1 and 2.3

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Mouse (mDC and the three mHSC lineages) and human (hHep and hESC).
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 2.1

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Single-cell RNA-seq expression for inputs. Reference edges come from cell-type-specific and non-specific ChIP-seq, STRING functional interactions and OmniPath pathway or signalling interactions.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 2.1

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The single-cell expression matrix and, for foundation models, their own token embeddings, hidden states or attention. In dynamic probing the model sees only the early-cell state, with no time labels, pseudotime or late-cell profiles.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 2.1; Appendix C.1

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot only: foundation models are not fine-tuned, prompted or adapted. The classical baselines are trained on each dataset.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 4

strengths.text: All methods share one preprocessing, one candidate gene set, one graph-construction rule and one set of references and metrics, so the three ways of reading a model are compared on equal terms.

Four reference types with different evidence (ChIP-seq of two kinds, STRING, OmniPath) are scored separately, and the complete per-dataset tables for both gene sets are printed in the appendix, including the near-random cell-type-specific ChIP-seq results.
The dynamic probing task includes a randomly initialised scGPT control, which the authors use to show that the signal depends on pretraining rather than the iteration itself.

limitations.text: The authors state that reference networks are incomplete and biased towards well-studied genes, and every method was near random against cell-type-specific ChIP-seq, so that reference is left out of the main comparison.
Only zero-shot use is tested, and the extraction strategies are deliberately simple; the authors say fine-tuning or head-selective attention might recover more signal.
The paper names no code, data release or leaderboard, and reports no seeds or confidence intervals, so the results cannot be rerun from public files. It is a preprint not certified by peer review.

The Table 1 caption lists the references as STRING, Cell-type-specific ChIP-seq and OmniPath, while the text says the main comparison uses non-specific ChIP-seq. Readers should check which ChIP-seq column they are reading.

name: DNALONGBENCH
description: Five long-range DNA prediction tasks with inputs up to about 1 Mb: enhancer-target gene, eQTL, 3D contact map, regulatory sequence activity and transcription initiation signal prediction.

attributes.task: Long-range DNA sequence prediction
attributes.scope_note: Each task compares a task-specific expert model, a CNN, and fine-tuned HyenaDNA (medium-450k), Caduceus-Ph and Caduceus-PS.
attributes.source_locator: Abstract; Table 2; Tables 3-7

profile.summary: DNALONGBENCH is five DNA prediction tasks that need long input sequences, up to about 1 million base pairs: enhancer-target gene pairs, eQTLs, 3D chromatin contact maps, regulatory sequence activity and base-pair transcription initiation signals. Each task compares a task-specific expert model, a CNN and fine-tuned DNA foundation models (HyenaDNA, Caduceus-Ph, Caduceus-PS). It is for developers testing whether long-context DNA models capture long-range dependencies.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a model can use long DNA context for problems where distant sequence matters: linking enhancers to target genes, flagging eQTLs, predicting chromatin contacts, predicting thousands of epigenomic tracks, and predicting transcription initiation at base-pair resolution.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, Proposed dataset

sections.title: Enhancer-target gene and eQTL tasks
sections.body: Enhancer-target gene pairs are CRISPRi-validated enhancer-promoter interactions in K562 cells from three studies, kept within 450 kb of the TSS; 2,602 samples, scored by AUROC. The eQTL task adapts Enformer's SuSiE fine-mapped eQTL set for the top nine tissues, keeps candidates within 450 kb of the TSS, masks other variants in each interval, and splits 8:1:1 by stratified random sampling; 31,282 samples, scored by AUROC.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods; README.md: Data Download table

sections.title: Contact map, regulatory activity and transcription initiation tasks
sections.body: Contact maps use Akita's processed data for five cell lines plus four more from the 4DN portal, 1 Mbp inputs at 2 kb bins, split by random virtual contigs 8:1:1 into 7008, 419 and 413 sequences, scored by SCC and PCC. Regulatory activity uses Enformer's 5313 human and 1643 mouse tracks, with 1937 human and 2017 mouse test sequences, scored by PCC averaged over test samples. Transcription initiation uses Puffin's data for five assays on both strands, evaluated on test chromosomes 8 and 9 by PCC.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Each task reuses processed data from earlier studies (CRISPRi screens, Akita, Enformer, Puffin) and provides inputs as BED coordinates so flanking context can be changed. The datasets are deposited on Harvard Dataverse.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results; Data availability

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Models are trained or fine-tuned on each task's training split and scored on its test set with the task's metric: AUROC for the two classification tasks, SCC and PCC for contact maps, PCC for the two regression tasks. Foundation models feed sequence features to linear heads; for eQTL, reference and alternate representations are combined before a classifier. The paper reports that expert models scored highest on every task.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Representative models; Methods; Discussion

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Create the conda environment, clone the repository and install the package, download a task's data from Dataverse, then run the CNN baseline's train.py for that task; the script trains, saves the best validation checkpoint to best_model.pt, and prints the test metric for the final-epoch model, not the saved checkpoint.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Experiments; experiments/CNN/README.md; train.py

strengths.text: Covers several long-range genomic problems with different output types: classification, binned 1D and 2D regression, and base-pair regression.
Inputs are given as BED coordinates, so the flanking context can be changed without reprocessing.
Data are on Harvard Dataverse under CC0 1.0 and the code is BSD-3-Clause, with a Zenodo archive of the published version.
strengths.source_locator: Dataverse records; Paper: Code availability; LICENSE

limitations.text: Transformer foundation models such as DNABERT-2 and Nucleotide Transformer were not evaluated because of their compute cost on long inputs.
Expert models were each designed and trained for their task, and ABC uses extra experimental inputs, so expert and sequence-only scores are not like-for-like.
Several splits are random (contact map contigs, eQTL pairs), and no uncertainty estimates are reported in the text read.
Most task data are reprocessed from earlier studies (Akita, Enformer, Puffin) rather than newly generated.

The CNN baseline's train.py saves the best validation checkpoint to best_model.pt but never reloads it: the test metric it prints comes from the model after the last epoch, not from the best validation epoch.

steps.title: Train and test the CNN on enhancer-target gene prediction
steps.shell:
cd experiments/CNN
python train.py \
    --task_name enhancer_target_gene_prediction \
    --root ./data \
    --save_dir ./results/ETGP \
    --subset None \
    --batch_size 2

It trains for --num_epochs epochs (default 5), saves the weights of the best validation epoch to best_model.pt, and then scores the test set with the model as it is after the final epoch; the script never reloads best_model.pt.

outputs: Per-epoch validation scores, then a line of the form 'Test <metric>: <score>' printed by train.py for the test set; --save_dir names ./results/ETGP.

name: GenBench
description: Benchmark suite of short- and long-range genomic tasks for fine-tuned genomic foundation models.

attributes.task: Genomic sequence classification and regression
attributes.scope_note: Tables 3-8 and 10.
attributes.source_locator: Tables 2-10

profile.summary: GenBench is a benchmark suite and codebase for genomic foundation models. It gathers forty-three datasets covering coding regions, non-coding regions and genome architecture, split into short-range tasks (inputs under 1,000 bases) and long-range tasks, and runs ten models through the same fine-tuning framework. Tasks include sequence classification, token classification and regression, scored by accuracy, AUC-ROC, Pearson or Spearman correlation and mean squared error depending on the task.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Sections 3.1 to 3.4; README.md: Introduction

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The suite is organised around three parts of the genome: the coding region, the non-coding region and genome architecture. Short-range tasks, with inputs under one thousand bases, cover enhancers, promoters, transcription factor binding, splice sites, epigenetic marks, open chromatin, species discrimination and SARS-CoV-2 variant classification. Long-range tasks cover splice site annotation, species classification, promoter prediction, bulk RNA expression across 218 tissue types and genomic structure prediction. The paper's stated aim is to see whether attention-based and convolution-based models differ in where they do well.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 1, 3.2 and 3.3

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The datasets are taken from earlier published collections rather than created: the Genomic Benchmarks tasks (mouse enhancers, coding versus intergenomic, human versus worm, enhancers, regulatory regions, non-TATA promoters, open chromatin), the GUE tasks (promoters, transcription factor binding, splice sites, yeast epigenetic marks, SARS-CoV-2 variants), the GENA-LM long-range tasks (splice sites, promoters, Drosophila enhancer activity), genomic structure prediction from Orca and species classification from HyenaDNA. Table 2 lists each task's type, training and test size and input length, from 30 bases for transcription factor prediction up to 256 Mb for genomic structure. For practicality the authors limited genomic structure prediction to 6,000 bases and capped long sequence tasks at 30 kb in their own experiments.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 3.3 and 4, Table 2; README.md: supported datasets

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Models are fine-tuned within the suite's own framework, which loads pretrained weights from Hugging Face, so every model goes through the same pipeline. Metrics are chosen per task: cross-entropy as the error for classification and mean squared error for regression; top-1 accuracy and AUC-ROC for classification; Spearman and Pearson correlation for regression. Parameter count and floating point operations are also reported as computational measures. The published tables report top-1 accuracy for the short-range tasks, AUC-ROC for long-range splice site prediction, Pearson for Drosophila enhancer activity and genomic structure, and Spearman with MSE for bulk RNA expression.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 3.4, 3.5 and 4, Tables 3 to 8

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The codebase is organised into a core layer, an algorithm layer and a user interface layer, with configuration files per experiment. Create the conda environment from the shipped file, install the package, then run train.py with an experiment configuration, a dataset name and the path to a pretrained model. Each supported dataset has its own download link and configuration directory in the README.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Installation, Getting Started; Paper: Section 3.5

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Forty-three datasets, grouped in Table 2 into twenty-one benchmark tasks: eight Genomic Benchmarks tasks at 500 bases, eight GUE and DeepSTARR short-range tasks from 30 to 256 bases, and five long-range tasks (splice site prediction at 15 kb, species classification at 80 Mb, promoters prediction at 8 kb, genomic structure at 256 Mb and bulk RNA expression at 196 kb). Test sizes run from 3 examples for genomic structure to 57K for human Ensembl regulatory regions.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Abstract and Table 2

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Fixed training and test sizes per task, inherited from the source benchmarks and printed in Table 2; the paper does not describe how those splits were drawn.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 2

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Per task: top-1 accuracy and AUC-ROC for classification (higher is better), Pearson and Spearman correlation for regression (higher is better), and cross-entropy or mean squared error as the error metric (lower is better). Parameter count and FLOPs are reported alongside.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.4

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Ten models: four attention-based (DNABERT, Nucleotide Transformer, DNABERT-2, GENA-LM) and six convolution-based or task-specific (HyenaDNA, Caduceus, a CNN, SpliceAI, DeepSTARR, Orca). The last four are trained from scratch with one-hot encoding as expert comparisons.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1 and Section 3.1

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None described. The paper does not state any identity cut-off, time split or held-out family, and does not check overlap between task data and model pretraining data.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Sections 3.2 and 3.3

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Unextracted: the checklist states error bars were reported with respect to the random seed, but the result tables read print single values without intervals.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Checklist; Tables 3 to 8

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A DNA sequence, with a class label for classification tasks or a continuous target for regression; splice site prediction and genomic structure prediction are scored per token or per position.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 2.1 and Table 2 caption

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human, mouse, Drosophila, yeast, worm and SARS-CoV-2, as the task names indicate.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 2

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Varies by source dataset and is not described per task. The paper states that bulk RNA sequencing measures average gene expression across a group of cells in a tissue, and that Drosophila enhancer activity is two measured scores, housekeeping and developmental.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.3

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: DNA sequence only, as A, G, C, T or N, tokenised by each model's own tokeniser (k-mer, byte pair encoding, character or one-hot).
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 2.1 and Table 1

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Fine-tuning: pretrained weights are loaded and the model is trained on each downstream task within the suite's framework. The expert baselines are trained from scratch.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 2.1 and Table 1

strengths.text: Covers both short and long inputs, with tasks up to the hundreds of kilobases, which the authors say earlier benchmarks either avoided or reduced to classification.
All ten models run through one modular codebase with per-experiment configuration files, released under Apache 2.0.
Task types go beyond classification to token-level classification and regression, including two-value regression for Drosophila enhancer activity and 218-dimensional bulk RNA output.

limitations.text: The authors state GenBench covers only downstream task prediction, with no comparison of pretraining choices, and that they did not test whole-chromosome performance because of compute limits.

Sequence lengths were cut for practicality: genomic structure prediction was limited to 6,000 bases and long sequence tasks were capped at 30 kb, so the stated input lengths in Table 2 are not what was run.
No leakage control is described, so a model pretrained on the human genome may have seen the test sequences as unlabelled data.
Some test sets are very small: three examples for genomic structure prediction, 242 for mouse enhancers and 500 for species classification.

name: GENEB leaderboard
description: Frozen-embedding probing benchmark of genomic foundation models over 100 tasks in 13 categories, with full-data, 10-shot and 1-shot regimes.

attributes.task: Genomic sequence classification from frozen embeddings
attributes.scope_note: MCC aggregates only: micro average over all 100 tasks, macro average (unweighted mean of the 13 category MCCs), and per category.
attributes.source_locator: leaderboard/README.md (Evaluation table: logistic-regression probe on frozen embeddings, max_iter=1000; Macro = mean of the 13 category scores); leaderboard.json

profile.summary: GENEB compares 40 genomic foundation models on 100 DNA sequence classification tasks in 13 functional categories, such as promoters, enhancers, histone marks, DNA methylation and splice sites. Every model is scored the same way: a logistic-regression probe trained on frozen sequence embeddings, in full-data, 10-shot and 1-shot regimes, with MCC as the main metric. It is meant for choosing a DNA model for a particular kind of task rather than for a single overall ranking.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening paragraphs and Benchmark table; Paper: Abstract

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: GENEB tests how much task-relevant information a pretrained DNA model's frozen embeddings carry. Tasks are binary or multi-class sequence classification problems in 13 categories: histone modifications (30 tasks), promoters (22), enhancers (8), DNA methylation (8), splice sites (7), lncRNA (6), mouse enhancers (5), TF binding (5), species classification (3), regulatory elements (2), virus or phage (2), coding versus non-coding (1) and chromatin accessibility (1). The authors argue that rankings change across categories and data regimes, so results are reported per task and per category as well as overall.
sections.source_locator: benchmark_spec.json: categories; README.md: opening note

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The tasks are taken from nine earlier benchmark collections: the original and revised Nucleotide Transformer tasks, GUE, Genomic Benchmarks, the Plant Genomic Benchmark, iPro-WAEL, deep4mc, iDNA-ABF and iDHS-EL. Each task is one CSV with a sequence, a label and a train or test split. The released train and test partitions of the source benchmarks are used as published, without relabelling or resplitting. Tasks with more than 10^5 sequences are subsampled. The task data are pinned to one Hugging Face dataset revision in benchmark_spec.json.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Appendix B; README.md: Evaluation protocol; benchmark_spec.json: dataset

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is an embedding extractor that turns each DNA sequence into one fixed-length vector. The harness fits a logistic-regression probe (max_iter=1000) on the training embeddings and scores the test set, in three regimes: all training data, 10 examples per class and 1 example per class. Results are averaged over five fixed seeds (13, 17, 42, 123, 997). MCC is the primary metric; accuracy and macro-F1 are also reported. The leaderboard gives a micro average over all 100 tasks and a macro average, the unweighted mean of the 13 category scores. Encoders must not be fine-tuned on task labels. Evaluation is run by the contributor; continuous integration checks the submission file but does not recompute embeddings, and community entries are marked self-reported.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 3 Probing setup; README.md: Evaluation protocol, Leaderboard; run_GENEB.py: few_shot_idx; CONTRIBUTING.md: What CI verifies

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Download the pinned task data with the repository's sync tool, write an extractor class for your model under harness/extractors/, run harness/run_GENEB.py (the README suggests --limit 5 for a smoke test) and validate the submission file it writes. The README commands use placeholder names for the extractor and model.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Evaluate your model; CONTRIBUTING.md: Quick start

strengths.text: Every model is run on the full task suite under one probe protocol, which the authors say allows matched comparisons across architecture, tokenisation and pretraining data.
Results are reported per task and per category, and in three data regimes, not only as one aggregate.
The task data revision is pinned in the benchmark definition, and the harness, submissions and leaderboard build are public.

limitations.text: Results are self-reported: maintainers do not re-run submissions, and CI only checks the file format and ranges.
Splits are inherited from the source benchmarks and no check for overlap with pretraining data is made, so some models may have seen test sequences during pretraining.

limitations.text: Few tasks need long-range context beyond 10 kb, and 12 of the 13 categories are eukaryotic; the authors also say some constituent tasks may be noisy or weakly defined.
The Apache-2.0 licence covers the code only; the task data keep the terms of their upstream sources, which the files read do not list.

name: GFMBench-API
description: Python interface that wraps existing genomic tasks (GUE, VariantBenchmarks, LRB, BEND, TraitGym, SongLab ClinVar, BRCA1, VEP-eval, LOL-EVE) and a new ClinVar indel task behind one evaluation API.

attributes.task: Supervised classification and zero-shot variant effect prediction on DNA sequence
attributes.scope_note: Tasks are re-implementations of existing benchmarks with some changes, for example fixed test folds instead of cross-validation for VariantBenchmarks.
attributes.source_locator: Technical Methods; Appendix task descriptions; Tables 1-5

profile.summary: GFMBench-API is a Python interface that puts many existing genomic benchmarks behind one evaluation API. A model implements a small set of inference methods, and the library then runs it on 22 tasks covering supervised sequence and variant classification and zero-shot variant effect prediction, writing one CSV of task and metric rows. It is for comparing genomic foundation models without rewriting a pipeline per benchmark.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening, Supported Benchmarks & Tasks, Benchmark Output

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two families of task. Supervised classification and variant prediction: promoter, splice site and transcription factor binding from GUE; coding, non-coding, expression, common versus rare, methylation QTL and splicing QTL variant classification from VariantBenchmarks; causal eQTL, enhancer and histone mark tasks from the Long Range Benchmark. Zero-shot variant effect prediction: ClinVar SNVs by embedding distance and by likelihood, ClinVar insertions and deletions, BEND expression and disease effects, BRCA1 functional impact, TraitGym complex and Mendelian variants, LRB pathogenic OMIM variants and LOL-EVE causal eQTL indels.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Supported Benchmarks & Tasks

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The tasks wrap data from existing benchmarks rather than new data collection. All task data sit under one root directory, one subdirectory per task named after the task class, holding train.csv, dev.csv and test.csv; missing files are downloaded automatically on first use. Classification data carry a sequence and a label; variant effect data carry a reference sequence, an alternative sequence and a label. Sequences use A, T, C, G, N and P for padding at chromosome boundaries, and are upper-cased. The NOTICE states that the downloaded third-party data include datasets with non-commercial terms.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Data Preparation; NOTICE

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model supplies inference methods by duck typing: sequence to label probabilities, variant and reference pairs to label probabilities, sequence to regression outputs, sequence to per-nucleotide probabilities and embeddings, a position mapping helper, and masked-position token probabilities. Any method a model does not implement can return None and the metrics that need it are skipped. Supervised classification tasks compute accuracy, MCC, AUROC and AUPRC. Zero-shot SNV tasks add cosine similarity AUROC and AUPRC between variant and reference embeddings at the variant position, and AUROC and AUPRC on the masked-token log-likelihood ratio. Tasks expose eval_test_set, eval_validation_set and eval_cross_validation_fold, and results go to a CSV with one row per task and metric and one column per model name, with NO_RESULTS where a result is missing.
sections.source_locator: README.md: How Model & Task Interfaces Work, Benchmark Output; base task classes

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Install your model's own dependencies first, then the library's basic_requirements.txt on top, and run usage_examples/run_benchmark.py with a model key. Flags select linear probing, the number of fine-tuning epochs, the output CSV path and the inference cache size. A sanity check mode runs on 100-sample subsets. If a model's dependencies clash with the benchmark stack, the model can run in a separate Python environment and process behind a thin adapter.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Quick Start, Example: Running Benchmarks

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: 22 tasks wrapping data from GUE, VariantBenchmarks, the Long Range Benchmark, BEND, TraitGym, the SongLab ClinVar set, BRCA1, VEP-eval, LOL-EVE and a ClinVar indel task. The README gives no example counts per task.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Supported Benchmarks & Tasks

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Fixed files per task: train.csv, dev.csv and test.csv in the task's data directory. Supervised tasks return train, validation and test datasets; zero-shot tasks return a test dataset only. A cross-validation fold method also exists.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Task Data Structure; Adding Tasks

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Supervised classification: accuracy, MCC, AUROC and AUPRC, macro-averaged over labels for multi-label tasks. Zero-shot SNV tasks add embedding cosine similarity AUROC and AUPRC and masked log-likelihood ratio AUROC and AUPRC. The README says regression tasks exist but the files read do not list their metrics. Higher is better for all the metrics listed.
facts.source_locator: base_gfm_supervised_classification_task.py: metrics list; base_gfm_zeroshot_snv_task.py: _get_additional_metrics; README.md

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: No baseline scores are published. The README uses DNABERT2 as the default model key, ships a mock model and an isolated mock model, and has a tutorial for NTv3 8M; other models are added through MODEL_REGISTRY.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None described: splits are inherited from the wrapped benchmarks and the README does not mention identity cut-offs, time splits or held-out families.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Data Preparation

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: No replicates, seeds or intervals are required. The README notes that num_workers greater than 0 can make results non-deterministic on several tasks and recommends keeping num_workers at 0 for reproducibility.

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A DNA sequence with a label for classification tasks, or a variant and reference sequence pair with a label for variant effect tasks; the LRB enhancer and histone mark tasks score genomic bins.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Dataset Format; Supported Benchmarks & Tasks

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Unextracted: the task descriptions in the README name human datasets such as ClinVar, BRCA1 and TraitGym but do not state the species for every task.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Supported Benchmarks & Tasks

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Mostly not stated: of the wrapped benchmarks, only the GUE transcription factor task's source is named (ChIP-seq). The other tasks' underlying measurements are not described in the files read.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Supported Benchmarks & Tasks

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: DNA sequence, as A, T, C, G, N and P characters, case-insensitive; variant tasks also pass the reference sequence and the variant position. Some tasks pass conditional input metadata, for example tissue context for the LRB causal eQTL task.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Sequence Symbol Conventions; Adding Tasks

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot, linear probing (backbone frozen, projection layer trained) and full fine-tuning are all supported. Full fine-tuning must run in the same process as the model; linear probing can keep the backbone in a separate environment.

strengths.text: One interface covers many existing benchmarks: a model implements a handful of inference methods and can be run on all 22 tasks.
Model dependencies are kept separate from the benchmark stack, and a model whose packages clash can run in its own environment and process behind an adapter.
NVIDIA-authored code is Apache-2.0, and third-party attributions and data addresses are listed in a notices file.

limitations.text: The tasks wrap data from other benchmarks, such as GUE and BEND; the files read do not say whether scores here match those benchmarks' published protocols.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: opening and Supported Benchmarks & Tasks

limitations.text: Some of the data it downloads carry non-commercial licence terms, which the user must review themselves.
No leakage controls are described, and no uncertainty estimate is required; reproducibility depends on keeping num_workers at 0.
There is no leaderboard or shared results file: each user writes their own CSV, and the paths and task list in the example script must be edited by hand.

name: GUANinE v1.1
description: Genome Understanding and ANnotation in silico Evaluation, version 1.1: functional genomics, conservation, gene-expression and variant tasks on hg38.

attributes.task: Regulatory sequence, conservation, expression and variant-effect prediction
attributes.scope_note: Tasks in this batch: dnase-propensity, ccre-propensity, cons30, cons100, gpra-c, gpra-d (Table 2), cadd-snv (Table 3), clinvar-snv (Table 4).
attributes.source_locator: Abstract; Table 1; Tables 2-4

profile.summary: GUANinE v1.1 is a set of large genomic prediction tasks on the human reference genome hg38 and synthetic yeast promoters: chromatin accessibility and regulatory element propensity, sequence conservation, promoter expression, and two variant tasks for deleteriousness (cadd-snv) and pathogenicity (clinvar-snv). Pretrained models are compared with frozen features and a linear probe, scored by Spearman's rho. It suits people comparing supervised sequence-to-function models with genomic language models.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract and Introduction; v1.0 paper Table 1

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Six tasks from v1.0 cover three domains with two tasks each: regulatory element annotation (dnase-propensity, ccre-propensity), sequence conservation (cons30, cons100) and expression of synthetic yeast promoters (gpra-c, gpra-d). Version 1.1 adds cadd-snv, which separates proxy-benign from proxy-deleterious variants, and clinvar-snv, which separates benign from pathogenic noncoding ClinVar variants. The authors say clinvar-snv is a splicing-rich subset of ClinVar, not a test of general pathogenicity.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Newly constructed tasks; Table 1 footnote

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: dnase-propensity labels 511 bp hg38 sequences with an ordinal score from 0 (inaccessible) to 4 (almost always accessible), aggregated from over 700 ENCODE SCREEN v2 DHS tracks; ccre-propensity relabels the positive DHSs by four epigenetic marks. cons30 and cons100 label 512 bp segments by binned mean phyloP30 or phyloP100 (0 to 24). gpra-c and gpra-d are 80 bp random yeast promoters labelled by binned fluorescence (0 to 17). cadd-snv uses gnomAD v3 singletons as proxy deleterious and simulated or frequent variants as proxy benign. clinvar-snv has no training set and just under 12 000 variants. Regulatory and variant tasks use chromosome 21 as development and chromosome 22 as test; conservation and yeast tasks use random splits.
sections.source_locator: v1.0 paper: Section 2 and Table 1; v1.1 paper: Table 1 and Newly constructed tasks; docs/tasks/dnase_propensity.rst

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Models are frozen; features are extracted and a linear probe (ridge or logistic regression) is fitted, with the regularisation chosen on the development set before test inference. clinvar-snv has no training set, so models that cannot score zero-shot are calibrated on the development set. Scores are Spearman's rho, reported multiplied by 100 in the documentation example. Most test labels are private; the README says test predictions are submitted through a Google form until an automatic evaluation server launches.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation methods; docs/scoring.rst; README.md: Submissions

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Install Git LFS and the optional Python tools, clone a task dataset from Hugging Face, download hg38.2bit, extract sequences around each region centre, and score development-set predictions with scipy's spearmanr. Test-set scoring needs a submission to the maintainers.
sections.source_locator: docs/installation.rst; README.md: Download a task, Load a task; docs/scoring.rst

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Eight tasks in the store's scope: dnase-propensity, ccre-propensity, cons30, cons100, gpra-c, gpra-d (test sets printed as 44 k, 101 k, 55 k, 51 k, 230 k and 170 k), cadd-snv (test 1.04 M) and clinvar-snv (test 12.0 K). The docs also list a cadd-indel task.
facts.source_locator: v1.0 paper Table 1; v1.1 paper Table 1; HF listing

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Chromosome 21 development and chromosome 22 test for dnase-propensity, ccre-propensity, cadd-snv and clinvar-snv; random splits for cons30, cons100, gpra-c and gpra-d. clinvar-snv has no training set.
facts.source_locator: v1.0 paper Table 1; v1.1 paper Table 1

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Spearman's rho for every task; higher is better.
facts.source_locator: docs/scoring.rst; v1.0 paper Section 2

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Non-neural GC-content and k-mer models, a supervised T5 baseline, and for the variant tasks VEP build 115 and CADD v1.7, among dozens of evaluated models.
facts.source_locator: v1.0 paper Section 3.1; v1.1 paper Newly evaluated models

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Held-out chromosomes for the regulatory and variant tasks and private test labels. The v1.0 authors warn that DeepSEA, Beluga and Basenji2 trained on chromosome 22, so their propensity scores may be exaggerated; v1.1 reports little divergence between ChromBPNet folds that did and did not see chromosomes 21 and 22. Conservation and yeast tasks are split at random.
facts.source_locator: v1.0 paper footnote 3 and Table 1; v1.1 paper Results; docs/scoring.rst

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: No confidence intervals are described in the sources read. The scoring guide recommends averaging 30 to 50 jittered scores to handle ties.
facts.source_locator: docs/scoring.rst

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A DNA sequence region (511 or 512 bp human, 80 bp yeast promoter) for six tasks; a single-nucleotide variant for cadd-snv and clinvar-snv.
facts.source_locator: v1.0 paper Section 2; v1.1 paper Table 1

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human (hg38) for six tasks; yeast for gpra-c and gpra-d.
facts.source_locator: v1.0 paper Table 1

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: DNase-seq and histone mark or CTCF peak calls from ENCODE SCREEN v2, phyloP conservation scores, a dual-reporter fluorescence assay in yeast, gnomAD v3 population data and ClinVar classifications.
facts.source_locator: v1.0 paper Section 2; v1.1 paper Table 1 footnote

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: DNA sequence. The README recommends extracting longer context from hg38 using the BED coordinates for large-context models.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Load a task

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Frozen features with a linear probe, using a 1% few-shot training split where recommended; zero-shot scoring is allowed where a model supports it, and full supervised training is possible on the large training sets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation methods; docs/tasks/dnase_propensity.rst; v1.0 paper Introduction

strengths.text: Test sets are large (about 12 thousand to about a million examples per task), which the authors say allows well-powered model ranking.
Frozen-feature linear probing removes fine-tuning hyperparameters as a confounder, in the authors' view.
Private test labels for most tasks are meant to prevent accidental overfitting to the test set.
Covers both functional annotation and evolutionary conservation, plus two variant tasks.

limitations.text: Conservation and yeast promoter tasks use random splits, so nearby or related sequences can fall in both training and test sets.
No public leaderboard or automatic scoring: test predictions go to the maintainers through a Google form.
Supervised models trained on ENCODE tracks, including chromosome 22, may score inflated on the propensity tasks.
Licence terms vary by task: cadd-snv and cadd-indel derive from a modified MIT licence and commercial users may need a licence to release models built on them.

run_guide.summary: Download one GUANinE task, install the tools and extract sequences from hg38 for a model of your own; scoring is described in prose because the guide's code is a template.
prerequisites: Git and Git LFS.
Python with twobitreader, scipy and pandas (optional but recommended in the docs).
The hg38.2bit reference genome from UCSC.
A model of your own that turns a sequence into a prediction; GUANinE does not supply one for this step.

steps.title: Install tools
steps.shell:
git lfs install
pip install twobitreader scipy pandas
steps.explanation: Sets up Git LFS and the optional i/o packages the docs recommend.

steps.title: Download a task
steps.shell:
git clone https://huggingface.co/datasets/guanine/dnase_propensity
ls dnase_propensity
steps.explanation: Clones the dnase_propensity task; the README says the folder holds 1per, bed, dev, test and train.

steps.title: Get the reference genome
steps.shell: wget -nc https://hgdownload.soe.ucsc.edu/goldenPath/hg38/bigZips/hg38.2bit
steps.explanation: Needed to extract sequence around each BED region.

steps.title: Extract a sequence
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
import pandas as pd
import twobitreader

train_bed = pd.read_csv('dnase_propensity/bed/train/train.bed', sep='\t')

width  = 2000
chr    = train_bed.iloc[0]['#chr']
center = train_bed.iloc[0]['center']
start  = center - width//2
end    = center + width//2

hg38   = twobitreader.TwoBitFile('hg38.2bit')
sequence = hg38[chr][start:end]
print(chr, center, train_bed.iloc[0]['y'], sequence)
PY
steps.explanation: The README's Python example, wrapped in a shell heredoc. It prints the chromosome, centre, label and 2,000 bp of sequence for the first training example.

outputs: The chromosome, centre, label and 2,000 bp sequence of the first training example, printed by the README's example. Development-set scoring then follows docs/scoring.rst with the user's own model and scipy's spearmanr (rho multiplied by 100 in its example).

name: Nucleotide Transformer benchmark (18 tasks)
description: Eighteen human genomic classification tasks (ten histone marks, enhancers, enhancer types, three promoter sets and three splice-site sets) scored by MCC with tenfold cross-validation.

attributes.task: Genomic sequence classification
attributes.scope_note: Probing (Supplementary Table 6) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (Supplementary Table 7) of NT models, with DNABERT-2, HyenaDNA, Enformer, BPNet and randomly initialised controls.
attributes.source_locator: Supplementary Table 5; Supplementary Tables 6, 7 and 9

profile.summary: The Nucleotide Transformer benchmark is a set of 18 human genomic classification tasks: ten histone marks in K562, three promoter tasks, two enhancer tasks and three splice site tasks. Each is a small balanced dataset of short sequences with a fixed chromosome-based test split, scored by Matthews correlation coefficient under tenfold cross-validation. The paper uses it to compare DNA language models after probing or fine-tuning, and the data are published on Hugging Face with an interactive leaderboard.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Methods, Nucleotide Transformer downstream tasks; Supplementary Table 5; Hugging Face dataset record

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a model's representation of a short DNA sequence carries the signal for a specific regulatory or structural feature. The ten epigenetic tasks ask whether a 1 kb sequence overlaps a histone mark peak in K562. The promoter tasks ask whether a 300 bp sequence contains a promoter, a TATA-box promoter or a promoter without a TATA box. The enhancer tasks ask whether a 400 bp sequence contains an enhancer, and in the multi-label version whether it is tissue-specific or tissue-invariant. The splice tasks ask whether a 600 bp sequence has an acceptor or donor site in the centre.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Nucleotide Transformer downstream tasks

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Histone marks come from ten ENCODE ChIP-seq narrowPeak files for K562, each identifier listed in the Methods. Promoters come from the Eukaryotic Promoter Database (29,598 regions, 3,065 of them TATA-box). Enhancers come from ENCODE SCREEN, with distal and proximal combined and tissue specificity from the Meuleman DHS index. Splice sites come from GENCODE V44, excluding level-3 automated annotations, extracted with the HISAT2 script. Sequences containing N are removed, each dataset is balanced by subsampling negatives to the number of positives, and the sets are then capped at 30,000 training and 3,000 validation and test examples so a new model can be benchmarked quickly. Supplementary Table 5 lists the resulting sizes per task, from 5,062 training sequences for Promoter non-TATA to 30,000 for most tasks.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods; Supplementary Table 5

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The split is by chromosome: chromosomes 20 and 21 are the test set and the rest is training. Evaluation uses tenfold cross-validation on the training set, training ten times with a different tenth held out for validation and checkpoint selection, and evaluating every run on the same held-out test set; the median across the ten folds is the reported performance. The metric is binary or multi-class MCC. For a single number per model, the authors take the median MCC within each of the three task categories (chromatin profiles, regulatory elements and splicing) and then the mean of those three.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset splits and performance evaluation

sections.title: Probing and fine-tuning
sections.body: The paper reports two ways of using a pretrained model. Probing stores embeddings from ten layers of the model and trains a downstream logistic regression or MLP on them, with a hyperparameter search of 100 trials guided by a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator and the same tenfold scheme; the authors say this produced 760,000 downstream models. Fine-tuning is parameter-efficient on the transformer part. A logistic regression on the tokenised sequence, before the transformer layers, is the raw baseline.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Probing

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The task data are published as a Hugging Face dataset, the revised version released after peer review, which the dataset card recommends using in place of the older one. The paper gives no command line pipeline for a third party to score a model, and results are collected in an interactive leaderboard on Hugging Face Spaces.
sections.source_locator: Hugging Face dataset record: description; Paper: Data availability

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: 18 tasks. Ten histone marks (H2AFZ, H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K36me3, H3K4me1, H3K4me2, H3K4me3, H3K9ac, H3K9me3, H4K20me1) at 1 kb; Promoter all, TATA and non-TATA at 300 bp; Splice site all, donor and acceptor at 600 bp; Enhancer and Enhancer types at 400 bp. Training sets run from 5,062 to 30,000 sequences and test sets from 212 to 3,000, as Supplementary Table 5 prints them.
facts.source_locator: Supplementary Table 5

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Test is chromosomes 20 and 21; everything else is training, and the training set is further split tenfold for validation and checkpoint selection. Each dataset is class-balanced by subsampling negatives.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset splits and performance evaluation

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Matthews correlation coefficient, binary or multi-class depending on the task, higher is better; the median over the ten folds is reported per task.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods; Supplementary Table 5

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: A logistic regression on the tokenised sequence as a raw probe, BPNet at three sizes, and three published pretrained models: DNABERT-2, HyenaDNA at 1 kb and 32 kb context, and Enformer's torso. DNABERT-1 was excluded because its maximum input is 512 bp.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Comparison with published pre-trained genomics models; Supplementary tables

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The chromosome split is the only control: there is no sequence identity filter and no removal of homologous regions. The authors warn that Enformer was pretrained with different data splits, so its benchmark performance may be inflated by leakage.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Comparison with published pre-trained genomics models

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Tenfold cross-validation per model and task, reported as the median; the supplementary tables print a value with a spread for each model and task.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods; Supplementary tables

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A short DNA sequence of fixed length (300, 400, 600 or 1,000 bp) with a binary or multi-class label.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods; Supplementary Table 5

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human only; Supplementary Table 5 lists Human for all 18 tasks.
facts.source_locator: Supplementary Table 5

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Histone ChIP-seq in K562 for the epigenetic tasks; the other labels are annotations, from the Eukaryotic Promoter Database, ENCODE SCREEN with the Meuleman DHS index, and GENCODE V44 transcript annotation.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Nucleotide Transformer downstream tasks

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: DNA sequence only, of the task's fixed length.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Nucleotide Transformer downstream tasks

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Both probing (frozen embeddings with a trained logistic regression or MLP head, with a hyperparameter search) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning of the transformer; HyenaDNA was fully fine-tuned because the parameter-efficient method did not fit its architecture.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Probing; Comparison with published pre-trained genomics models

strengths.text: Small, balanced and capped datasets, so a new model can be evaluated on all 18 tasks quickly.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset splits and performance evaluation

strengths.text: Tenfold cross-validation with a fixed held-out test set and a median across folds, rather than a single training run.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset splits and performance evaluation

strengths.text: The data are published on Hugging Face in a revised post-review version, with an interactive leaderboard for cross-model comparison.
strengths.source_locator: Hugging Face dataset record; Paper: Data availability

limitations.text: Short sequences and a chromosome split only; the paper describes no sequence identity or homology filtering and does not say whether the test chromosomes were in each model's pretraining data.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset splits and performance evaluation

limitations.text: Two of the comparison models are not on equal footing: Enformer was trained supervised with different splits, which the authors say may inflate its score, and HyenaDNA was fully fine-tuned while the others were not.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Comparison with published pre-trained genomics models

limitations.text: Some test sets are small (212 sequences for Promoter non-TATA, 776 for H3K4me3), so differences on those tasks rest on few examples.
There is no released evaluation harness: the data and a leaderboard are public, but the paper describes no command line pipeline for a third party to score a model the same way.

name: TraitGym
description: Causal versus matched non-causal noncoding variants for 113 Mendelian and 83 complex traits, scored by AUPRC computed per chromosome and averaged with sample-size weights.

attributes.task: Causal regulatory variant prediction
attributes.scope_note: Datasets mendelian_traits_matched_9 and complex_traits_matched_9 (nine matched controls per causal variant), subset 'all'. Zero-shot scores and chromosome-held-out logistic regression (linear probing).
attributes.source_locator: README 'Resources' and 'Running'; dataset paths in this batch

profile.summary: TraitGym tests whether a model can pick out causal non-coding single-nucleotide variants in the human genome. It has two datasets: causal variants for 113 Mendelian traits and strong causal candidates for 83 complex traits, each paired with matched control variants. It is for people comparing DNA language models, sequence-to-function models and conservation or integrative scores on regulatory variant interpretation.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The task is binary classification: is a variant putatively causal for any trait or not. Only non-coding single-nucleotide variants are included, because the authors see interpretation of non-coding variants as a key use for DNA sequence models. A model sees the reference and alternate alleles and the surrounding DNA sequence.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 4, Benchmark datasets and Task definition

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Mendelian positives are causal non-coding variants for 113 Mendelian diseases from OMIM, with variants above 0.1% minor allele frequency in gnomAD removed; common gnomAD variants are the controls. Complex-trait positives come from statistical fine-mapping of UK Biobank association studies: variants with posterior inclusion probability above 0.9 in any trait. Each positive is matched to 9 controls on chromosome, consequence and distance to the transcription start site; complex-trait controls are also matched on minor allele frequency and LD score. Table 1 gives 338 causal variants among 3,380 for Mendelian traits and 1,140 among 11,400 for complex traits. Larger versions with millions of controls per positive are also provided.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 4 and Table 1

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Models are scored zero-shot, or by ridge logistic regression on extracted features (linear probing). Linear probing uses one fold per chromosome: each chromosome is tested with a model trained on the others, and the regularisation is tuned by cross-validation on the training chromosomes. The metric is AUPRC per chromosome, averaged across chromosomes with weights by sample size, with a bootstrap standard error. With 9 controls per positive, a random score has AUPRC 0.1. The README names AUPRC_by_chrom_weighted_average as the main metric.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 4 and 5; README.md: Resources

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The README says to clone the repository, create the conda environment from workflow/envs/general.yaml, optionally download the precomputed datasets and predictions (6.7G) from Hugging Face into results/dataset, and ask Snakemake for a result path. Your own features go in a parquet file under results/dataset/{dataset}/features/, and Snakemake then computes zero-shot or logistic regression metrics for them. A Colab notebook, TraitGym.ipynb, is also offered.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Quick start, Installation, Running

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Two: Mendelian traits (338 putatively causal variants, 3,380 in total, 113 traits) and complex traits (1,140 putatively causal variants, 11,400 in total, 83 traits), per Table 1. Expanded versions with millions of negatives also exist.

facts.value: Zero-shot scores and linear probing (ridge logistic regression on extracted features, trained on other chromosomes).

strengths.text: Controls are matched to each positive on chromosome, consequence and TSS distance, and for complex traits also on MAF and LD score, so simple confounders are less likely to drive scores.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Section 4, Matching positives and negatives

strengths.text: Small enough to run large models: the authors chose 9 controls per positive for that reason, and the README offers a Colab notebook that runs in about 5 minutes.
The authors state it is the only benchmark of causal non-coding variant prediction covering both Mendelian and complex human traits.
Data, features, predictions and per-model metrics are published on Hugging Face under an MIT licence, with code under MIT.
strengths.source_locator: HF card data; LICENSE; README.md: Resources

limitations.text: The authors say it has limited ability to resolve subtle differences in performance; some differences only show on the expanded datasets.
Datasets are small for supervised probes: the authors note overfitting, and several linear probes score worse than zero-shot on Mendelian traits.
Disease variants are few in the complex-trait set: 53 of the 1,140 putative causal variants affect a disease trait.
Human only and single-nucleotide variants only.
