name: PLABench
description: Leakage-controlled, target-centric benchmark of protein-ligand binding affinity prediction: Davis and KIBA under warm, cold-target and cold-drug splits, CASP16 ligand series L1000 and L3000, and a ChEMBL35 test set filtered against the training data of the evaluated models.

attributes.task: Protein-ligand binding affinity prediction and target-centric ligand ranking
attributes.scope_note: Tables 2-4 extracted. Figure-only analyses (input pose accuracy ladder, interaction counts, per-target Kendall tau) not extracted.
attributes.source_locator: Abstract; Figure 1; Tables 1-4

profile.summary: PLABench scores protein-ligand binding affinity prediction with the training leakage taken out. It runs nine sequence-based and structure-based models over the same targets with the same metrics, and varies the input structure so that pose quality can be told apart from model quality. Its arms are Davis and KIBA under warm-start, cold-target and cold-drug five-fold cross-validation, two CASP16 ligand series, and a ChEMBL35 test set with every ligand within ECFP4 Tanimoto 0.85 of any ligand in fourteen audited training corpora removed. It is for anyone comparing affinity predictors who needs to know how much of a reported score comes from overlap with training data.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening paragraphs; Results; ChEMBL35

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The benchmark measures how well a model predicts binding affinity when the easy routes are closed. Three things are varied deliberately: the split, so that a target or a drug unseen in training can be scored separately; the training overlap, so that scores on ligands similar to training compounds can be separated from scores on the rest; and the input structure, through a four-rung pose ladder, so that a structure-based model's errors can be attributed to the pose it was given rather than to the model. Protein-family breakdowns show where each model is accurate.
sections.source_locator: README.md: opening paragraphs, Results, Per-family accuracy; results/README.md: casp16/ and leakage

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Davis and KIBA use the folds MixingDTA defined, five folds in three regimes, with train, validation and test for the warm-start arm and both cold-start arms. The test folds ship as CSV and everything else in the pickle format MixingDTA released, with a script to export the rest as CSV. CASP16 uses two ligand series, with 140 compounds in total for stage 1, converted to pKd from the Prediction Center's target files, and a size-weighted average across them. ChEMBL35 is cut from the Shimizu et al. release; the published arm removes every test ligand within ECFP4 Tanimoto 0.85 of any ligand in fourteen audited training corpora and then drops targets left with fewer than ten ligands, leaving 4,862 ligands over 71 targets, against an unfiltered arm of 7,650 ligands over 84 targets. Standardised affinity tables for CASF-2013, CASF-2016 and two CSAR-HiQ sets are included, and the structures the benchmark scored are AlphaFold3 predictions for ChEMBL35 and CASP16 and Boltz-2 predictions for CASP16, CASF and CSAR-HiQ. The data are on Zenodo in four archives, 1.4 GB to download and 5.8 GB unpacked, with a per-path record of origin and licence in data/SOURCES.tsv. Corpora the authors may not redistribute (PDBbind v2020, CSAR-HiQ structures, the CASF core sets, the CASP16 stage-2 complexes) are linked rather than shipped: 46 of the 68 dataset configs run from the deposit as it stands.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Results, Data, Davis and KIBA cross-validation, License; Zenodo record 22716174

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Every arm except the Davis and KIBA cross-validation runs through one Hydra entry point, python run_benchmark.py with a model and a dataset config; there is one config per model and 68 dataset configs, one per combination of input source, benchmark and evaluation mode. Predictions land under outputs/<model>/<dataset>/latest/ and are scored in a separate analysis environment by scripts/collect_results.py, which writes results/benchmark_summary.csv (one row per model and dataset), results/per_target_evaluation.csv and results/benchmark_failures.csv, after which scripts/weighted_summary.py aggregates the first two into target-count-weighted summaries. The reported metrics are RMSE, Pearson, Spearman and the concordance index for Davis and KIBA; Kendall tau for the CASP16 ranking arms; and MSE, RMSE, Pearson, Spearman, Kendall, Rm2 and the concordance index for ChEMBL35. The Davis and KIBA rows come instead from the dedicated cross-validation collector, which averages the five folds. Runs that produce no usable prediction are recorded with a reason rather than dropped.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Running a benchmark, Results, Davis and KIBA cross-validation; results/README.md: top-level tables

sections.title: The leakage audit
sections.body: The audit is published as files, not just as a statement. For each of fourteen training corpora there is one table giving every benchmark ligand's highest ECFP4 Tanimoto against that corpus and whether its InChIKey skeleton appears there, after desalting and neutralisation; the filter cuts on the row-wise maximum across the fourteen. A per-corpus summary separates the ligands a corpus reaches on its own from the rows attributed to it as the closest analogue, so the first column does not sum to the number of removed rows. Further tables cover how the drop rate moves with the threshold, how much of the overlap is target-conditioned, which ligands match a training compound exactly, and how much protein sequence the benchmark shares with the corpora. The README reports that SAIR, built from ChEMBL 35, reaches Tanimoto 0.85 against 32.7% of the unfiltered benchmark, 2,413 of the 2,735 rows the similarity cut removes. CASP16 gets the same audit plus a stricter version that requires protein, ligand and affinity label to match before calling a row leaked.
sections.source_locator: results/README.md: leakage; README.md: ChEMBL35

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Clone with submodules, because the nine model sources are git submodules under forks/, each pinned to a plabench branch holding the exact upstream commit that was benchmarked plus the patches needed to run it. Each model needs its own conda environment, exported under environments/, since their dependencies conflict, and the analysis scripts get a tenth. Weights that PLABench trained are fetched by scripts/download_checkpoints.sh, which has the address and SHA256 baked in; third-party weights are never re-uploaded and are fetched and verified by scripts/download_third_party.sh. Benchmark inputs and structures come from the Zenodo data deposit. A run is then one Hydra command with a model and a dataset, scored afterwards in the analysis environment.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Install, Checkpoints, Data, Running a benchmark, Environments

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Davis and KIBA (five folds in warm-start, cold-drug and cold-target regimes); two CASP16 stage-1 ligand series, 140 compounds in total; ChEMBL35, 4,862 ligands over 71 targets after the leakage filter and 7,650 ligands over 84 targets unfiltered; plus standardised affinity tables for CASF-2013, CASF-2016 and the CSAR-HiQ 36 and 51 sets. 68 dataset configs cover the reported combinations.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Results, ChEMBL35, Data, Running a benchmark

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Davis and KIBA: five-fold cross-validation in three regimes, warm start, cold drug and cold target, on the folds MixingDTA defined, with train, validation and test for each. ChEMBL35: a test set with a similarity filter rather than a random split, removing ligands within ECFP4 Tanimoto 0.85 of any ligand in fourteen audited training corpora and then targets left with fewer than ten ligands. CASP16: the organisers' stage-1 targets, scored against labels in the data deposit. PDBbind is used as a training corpus, with a 4,465 and 497 refined partition carried as identifiers only.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Results, Davis and KIBA cross-validation, ChEMBL35, Data

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Davis and KIBA: RMSE (lower is better), Pearson, Spearman and the concordance index (higher is better). CASP16 stage 1: Kendall tau (higher is better), with a size-weighted average over the 140 compounds. ChEMBL35: MSE and RMSE (lower is better), Pearson, Spearman, Kendall, Rm2 and the concordance index (higher is better). Aggregates are target-count-weighted.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Results tables; results/README.md: top-level tables

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Nine models, all rerun by the benchmark: Boltz2, FLOWR.ROOT, FlowDock, Graph_RG, LCDD-team (BA-Pred), MFE, DeepDTA, LLF and MixingDTA, each pinned to a named upstream commit, plus a Boltz2 and FLOWR.ROOT ensemble row in the ChEMBL35 tables. The CASP16 tables also compare three teams' own CASP16 entries with their PLABench arms.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Running a benchmark, Model forks; results/README.md: chembl35/ and casp16/

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The point of the benchmark. Cold-target and cold-drug splits for Davis and KIBA; a similarity filter against fourteen audited training corpora for ChEMBL35, cutting on the row-wise maximum ECFP4 Tanimoto at 0.85 after desalting and neutralisation, with the per-corpus audit, the threshold sensitivity and the exact-match tables all published; and the same audit for CASP16 plus a stricter rule requiring protein, ligand and affinity label to match. Both the filtered and unfiltered ChEMBL35 arms are reported so the effect of the filter is visible.
facts.source_locator: README.md: ChEMBL35; results/README.md: chembl35/ and leakage

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Five-fold cross-validation with per-fold metrics for the Davis and KIBA arms, written to analysis/davis_kiba_cv_metrics.csv, with the headline rows being fold averages. No confidence intervals, repeated seeds or error bars are described for the other arms in the files read.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Davis and KIBA cross-validation

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A protein-ligand pair with a measured affinity, scored per target and then aggregated; for CASP16 the unit is a compound in a ligand series ranked against the others.
facts.source_locator: README.md: opening paragraphs, Results; results/README.md: top-level tables

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Not stated in the files read. The targets are proteins from public affinity collections (Davis, KIBA, ChEMBL 35, CASF, CSAR-HiQ, CASP16) and are grouped by protein family rather than by species.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Results, Per-family accuracy, Data

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Measured binding affinities from public collections, standardised to one scale: Davis and KIBA affinities on the MixingDTA folds, pKd labels converted here for the CASP16 stage-1 targets, ChEMBL 35 activity data cut from the Shimizu et al. release, and standardised PDB code, SMILES and pKd tables for CASF and CSAR-HiQ.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Data, License

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Both sequence-only and structure-based models are supported, and the input structure is treated as a variable: the deposit carries AlphaFold3 structures for ChEMBL35 and CASP16, Boltz-2 structures for CASP16, CASF and CSAR-HiQ, and a template-guided CASP16 rung, so the same model can be scored on different pose sources. MFE reads one directory per complex with protein.pdb and ligand.mol2.
facts.source_locator: README.md: opening paragraphs, Data

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Both. Three sequence models (DeepDTA, LLF, MixingDTA) are retrained on the Davis and KIBA folds and on PDBbind, and MFE's weights were also trained by PLABench; these weights ship in the deposit. The other structure-based models, and MixingDTA's Davis and KIBA warm-start weights, come from released third-party weights. An ensemble of two models is also scored.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Results, Checkpoints; results/README.md: chembl35/

strengths.text: The leakage audit is reproducible from published files: one table per training corpus with every benchmark ligand's highest similarity, the row-wise cut that defines the filtered set, and the threshold sensitivity beside it.

Every model is rerun by the benchmark rather than quoted, in its own conda environment, from a fork pinned to the upstream commit that was benchmarked, with the external tool versions and the per-model runtime stack written out.
strengths.source_locator: README.md: Install, Versions and commit hashes

strengths.text: Failed runs are kept: a table records runs that produced no usable prediction, with the reason, instead of leaving them out of the summary.

The licence position is set out per path: a per-path record of origin and terms for the 25 sources the benchmark reads, with corpora that forbid redistribution linked rather than shipped and identifier-only partitions provided instead.

limitations.text: Not everything runs from the deposit: 46 of the 68 dataset configs work as shipped, and the other 22 wait on the CASF core sets, the CSAR-HiQ structures or the CASP16 stage-2 complexes, each of which needs a registration or a separate download.

The data are not open for every use: the AlphaFold3 structures are under the AlphaFold3 Output Terms of Use, non-commercially, and must not be used to train structure-prediction models; the filtered ChEMBL35 arm carries ChEMBL's CC BY-SA 3.0, with share-alike propagating; and the third-party checkpoints each keep their own terms.

It is heavy to reproduce: nine conflicting conda environments plus an analysis environment, model weights fetched per model, and 1.4 GB of archives expanding to 5.8 GB, with five models launched as subprocesses whose interpreters must be set through environment variables.

The dataset config names are easy to misread: the README warns that the ordering of tokens in a name encodes the input source, benchmark and mode, and tells the reader to consult the configs documentation before choosing one. There is also no public leaderboard: the numbers are the repository's own tables.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: Running a benchmark; results/README.md: top-level tables

gaps: The paper's full text was not read: the only open copy is the bioRxiv PDF, and bioRxiv was not to be requested in this run, so the splits, metrics and leakage rules recorded here come from the repository and the data deposit rather than from the manuscript.

name: Universal antibody-antigen affinity evaluation on AlphaBind (MochiBind study)
description: Evaluation framework for antibody-antigen binding affinity on four AlphaBind antigen systems with each antigen held out in turn; pairwise accuracy and retrieval metrics.

attributes.task: Antibody-antigen relative binding affinity prediction
attributes.scope_note: Pairwise accuracy (Table 2) only; retrieval metrics are in figures.
attributes.source_locator: Introduction; Figure 1; STAR Methods; Table 2

profile.summary: This is the evaluation framework published with MochiBind, a study of whether antibody-antigen affinity predictors generalise to antigens they have never seen. The data are the four antigen systems of the AlphaBind dataset, PP489, PEM, VHH72 and TRA, each a large pool of antibody variants with measured affinities. The task is posed pairwise: given two antibodies against the same antigen, say which binds more strongly. Antigens are rotated so that each in turn is the held-out test antigen while two train and one validates, which means the test antigen is absent from training entirely. Scoring is pairwise accuracy over 200,000 sampled test pairs per antigen, plus retrieval accuracy and precision at K after a global ranking is derived with TrueSkill. Anyone comparing sequence-based and structure-based affinity predictors for candidate ranking can use it as a cross-antigen generalisation test.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Introduction; STAR Methods, Cross-antigen evaluation setup; Table 2

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a predictor can rank antibodies against an antigen it was never trained on. The authors' stated reason for building the framework is that studies in this area differ in dataset curation, splitting and metrics, so models cannot be compared, and that most published models are evaluated in-sample. Two things are measured. Pairwise accuracy asks whether the stronger of two antibodies is identified correctly. Retrieval accuracy and precision at K ask whether the strong binders can be pulled out of a large pool, which is what an in silico screening campaign actually needs. The authors argue that ranking and retrieval are more robust than absolute regression when affinity measurements are noisy.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results, Retrieval performance and Pairwise accuracy

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The data come from the AlphaBind dataset, which holds four antigen systems: AAB-PP489, a humanoid scFv against human TIGIT; Pembrolizumab-scFv against PD-1; VHH72, a camelid single-chain antibody against the SARS-CoV-1 RBD with cross-reactivity to SARS-CoV-2; and Trastuzumab-scFv against human HER2. The paper states that each system contains approximately 30,000 antibody variants generated and validated with AlphaSeq. For this benchmark the pools are cut down by stratified sampling to keep the affinity distribution: 5,000 antibodies are drawn from the fine-tuning set and 5,000 from the evaluation set for PP489, PEM and VHH72, giving 10,000 variants each, while 5,000 are drawn for TRA. The four antigens have almost no sequence similarity to one another: Needleman-Wunsch global alignment with BLOSUM62 gives off-diagonal normalised scores between minus 0.053 and 0.034. Pairs are then sampled, 200,000 per antigen, and the training pairs are restricted to those whose relative affinity difference exceeds 10 per cent while the test pairs carry no such threshold. The published sampling script differs from the paper here: as shipped it samples up to 500,000 pairs per antigen with the threshold set to 0 and writes sampled_pairs_500k_0th.pkl, so the released sampler is not the configuration the paper describes, and the 10 per cent value survives in it only as a function default. The script also adds a condition the paper does not mention: a pair is only eligible if both antibody sequences have the same length.
sections.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Data source and preprocessing and Pairwise data generation; Introduction; data/sample_alphabind_pairs.py

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model is given two antibodies against the same antigen and must say which binds more strongly. The split is a rotation over antigens: in each configuration two antigens supply 400,000 training pairs, one supplies 200,000 validation pairs used to pick the checkpoint, and the fourth supplies 200,000 test pairs with no affinity-difference threshold, and the rotation is repeated so that every antigen is the test antigen once. Pairwise accuracy is the share of test pairs ordered correctly, and Table 2 reports it per held-out antigen for each method. Significance against each baseline is tested with a one-sided McNemar chi-squared test on the 200,000 test pairs, with all p values below 0.0001. For retrieval, pairwise predictions are turned into a global ranking with the TrueSkill algorithm, then retrieval accuracy and retrieval precision at K are computed; in the precision figure an antibody with log Kd below 2, Kd in nanomolar, counts as a good binder. Complex-wise baselines are handled on their own terms: Boltz-2 and GeoDock supply structure-derived confidence scores used as proxies rather than trained affinity predictions, and Graphinity is reported after fine-tuning on the training split because the published model, trained on single-point mutations, did not perform well on this data.
sections.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Cross-antigen evaluation setup and Pairwise setup; Results; Table 2 and Figure 2 captions

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The code is published as a reproducibility release. The repository holds MochiBind checkpoints for each of the four antigen systems, the sampled AlphaBind CSV files and the preprocessed pair pickles, the model and training code, and notebooks for pairwise accuracy and for the Graphinity, GeoDock and Boltz-2 retrieval comparisons. The README gives a conda environment and a requirements install, an embedding generation step and a training entry point at model_src/main_mean.py, and notes that full training expects precomputed ESM mean embeddings in a data_processed_esm_mean directory. The release terms matter: the repository is CC BY-NC 4.0 and the README states it is a non-commercial research release, published for academic reproducibility, with pull requests not accepted so that the code stays as it was used in the paper. The underlying AlphaBind data are MIT licensed, which the README states and links.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Release statement, Repository structure, Directory description, Installation and First Run, License

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One dataset, AlphaBind, with four antigen systems: PP489, PEM, VHH72 and TRA. The paper states each system holds approximately 30,000 antibody variants measured with AlphaSeq. The benchmark uses stratified subsamples of those pools: 10,000 variants each for PP489, PEM and VHH72, made of 5,000 from the fine-tuning set and 5,000 from the evaluation set, and 5,000 for TRA. From those pools 200,000 pairs are sampled per antigen.
facts.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Data source and preprocessing and Pairwise data generation

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: A cross-antigen rotation with no antigen overlap. In each configuration two antigens give 400,000 training pairs, one gives 200,000 validation pairs for checkpoint selection, and one gives 200,000 test pairs; the rotation repeats so each of the four antigens is the held-out test antigen once. Training and validation pairs are restricted to relative affinity differences above 10 per cent; test pairs have no threshold, so they include near-ties.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Retrieval performance; STAR Methods, Pairwise data generation and Cross-antigen evaluation setup

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Pairwise accuracy is the headline for the comparison in Table 2: the percentage of test pairs in which the stronger binder is identified correctly, higher is better, with significance against each baseline from a one-sided McNemar chi-squared test. Two retrieval metrics complement it, both higher is better: retrieval accuracy, the share of the K highest-ranked candidates that are among the true top binders, and retrieval precision, the share of good binders captured among the recommendations relative to the good binders available. The authors argue for ranking and retrieval over absolute regression metrics such as mean absolute error or correlation.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Retrieval performance and Pairwise accuracy; Introduction

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Three: Graphinity, an equivariant graph neural network on structural inputs, reported after fine-tuning on the training split because the released model, trained on single-point mutations, did not perform well here; and two structure-derived proxy scorers, Boltz-2, used through its ipLDDT score, and GeoDock. MochiBind, the authors' own sequence-only pairwise model built on ESM-2 embeddings, is the method under test.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results; Table 2; STAR Methods, Key resources table

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The split itself is the control, and it is the point of the benchmark: the training, validation and test sets cover distinct antigen systems with no overlap, so the test antigen is unseen. Two further things support it. The four antigens have near-zero global sequence similarity to one another, measured by Needleman-Wunsch alignment with BLOSUM62 and normalised, between minus 0.053 and 0.034. And within an antigen the variants come from one seed framework with varied multi-point mutations, which the authors say forces models to learn binding determinants rather than memorising identities. Nothing is said about overlap between the AlphaBind antibodies and the training data of the pretrained ESM-2 model or of the structure-based baselines.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results, Retrieval performance

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Significance testing rather than replicates. Each baseline is compared with MochiBind by a one-sided McNemar chi-squared test on the 200,000 test pairs, with all p values below 0.0001 and the chi-squared statistics in Table S1. The paper reports no repeated training runs, seeds or confidence intervals on the accuracies. A sensitivity analysis is given instead: accuracy is stratified by the relative affinity gap within a pair, and it rises as the gap widens, with a large share of test pairs falling in the 0 to 10 per cent band that training excludes.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Pairwise accuracy; Figure 5 caption

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A pair of antibody variants against the same antigen, with the measured affinities of both. For the complex-wise baselines the scored unit is one antibody-antigen complex, which is then used to order the pair, and for retrieval the unit is one antibody in a ranked pool.
facts.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Pairwise setup

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human targets with antibodies of mixed origin. The four antigen systems are human TIGIT, human PD-1, human HER2 and the receptor binding domain of SARS-CoV-1 with cross-reactivity to SARS-CoV-2. The antibody frameworks include a humanoid scFv, two humanised mouse antibodies formatted as scFv, and a camelid single-chain antibody.
facts.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Data source and preprocessing

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: AlphaSeq affinity measurements. The paper states that each antigen system's approximately 30,000 variants were generated and validated using AlphaSeq, and the labels are measured binding affinities reported as log Kd. The authors treat those labels as noisy, which is their stated reason for a pairwise rather than a regression formulation.
facts.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Data source and preprocessing; Results

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Either sequence or structure, which is the comparison the benchmark exists to make. MochiBind reads the antibody and antigen sequences only, through a pretrained protein language model; Graphinity reads structural graphs; Boltz-2 and GeoDock take complexes and return interface confidence scores. The published sampling code adds one restriction on the pairs themselves: both antibody sequences in a pair must be of the same length.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; STAR Methods, Pairwise setup; data/sample_alphabind_pairs.py

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Supervised training on the two training antigens for the pairwise models, and zero-shot use for the proxy scorers. MochiBind is trained on the 400,000 training pairs with the validation antigen used to select a checkpoint. Graphinity is fine-tuned on the same training split, and the paper reports its accuracy before and after fine-tuning in a supplementary table. Boltz-2 and GeoDock are used as published, supplying structure-derived confidence scores with no affinity training.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Retrieval performance; STAR Methods, Cross-antigen evaluation setup

strengths.text: The split answers the question the paper poses: every antigen is held out in turn and the test antigen appears in neither training nor validation, so the reported accuracy is a cross-antigen number rather than an in-sample one.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Cross-antigen evaluation setup

strengths.text: Training and test pairs are filtered differently on purpose. Training keeps only pairs whose affinities differ by more than 10 per cent, while test pairs are unfiltered, so the evaluation includes the near-ties that a real screen has to cope with.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Pairwise data generation

strengths.text: Differences between methods are tested rather than asserted, with a one-sided McNemar chi-squared test on the 200,000 test pairs for each baseline comparison and the statistics reported in a supplementary table.

Per-antigen heterogeneity is reported instead of being averaged away: the affinity distributions differ markedly between antigens, and the authors show that retrieval precision depends on that composition.

limitations.text: Four antigens is a narrow base for a generalisation claim. Each rotation has two training antigens, one validation antigen and one test antigen, so a reported accuracy rests on a single held-out system and the authors themselves name dataset scarcity as the limiting factor.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: STAR Methods, Cross-antigen evaluation setup; Limitations of the study

limitations.text: The benchmark was built and run by the authors of the method it favours, MochiBind, and the structure-based comparators are not matched to it: Boltz-2 and GeoDock supply confidence scores that were never trained to predict affinity, and Graphinity had to be fine-tuned before it performed.

Pairs are not drawn from the whole pool. The published sampling script only forms a pair when both antibody sequences have the same length, which is a restriction the paper does not state, so the test pairs do not cover insertion or deletion variants.

The code release is non-commercial and frozen. The repository is CC BY-NC 4.0, the README describes it as a non-commercial research release for academic reproducibility, and pull requests are not accepted so that the code stays exactly as used in the paper.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: Release statement, License, Pull requests; LICENSE

description: Drug-target affinity regression on Davis and KIBA with the predefined DeepDTA training and test folds (5:1).

attributes.version: DeepDTA folds (Ozturk et al. 2018), as used in Marijan and Tanasijevic 2026
attributes.task: Drug-target binding affinity regression
attributes.scope_note: Holdout test fold results from Tables 2 and 3; cold-start results are figures only.

profile.summary: This benchmark asks a model to predict the binding affinity of a drug-target pair as a number, on the two kinase affinity data sets used by the DeepDTA paper: Davis, with dissociation constants for 442 proteins and 68 ligands, and KIBA, with combined kinase inhibitor bioactivities for 229 proteins and 2111 drugs. The DeepDTA authors split each data set into six equal parts, held one part out as an independent test set, and used the remaining five parts for five-fold cross validation, and they publish those fold files so that later methods can train and test on the same pairs. It is used by people comparing drug-target affinity regression methods, including methods that read only the protein sequence and the compound SMILES string.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Materials and Methods (Data sets), Experiment Setup; data/README.md: Train and test folds

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The task is regression: given a drug and a protein target, predict how strongly they bind. The authors argue this is more informative than the binary interaction prediction that earlier work used, because binding strength is continuous and because a binary data set has to invent negative examples. Both data sets are kinase data, so the question is how well a method ranks and estimates affinities across a protein family and a library of inhibitors. The paper's own interest is whether sequence alone is enough: it compares models that read raw protein sequences and SMILES strings against models given precomputed Smith-Waterman protein similarity and PubChem compound similarity.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Materials and Methods (Data sets); Results

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Davis holds selectivity assays of kinases and their inhibitors with dissociation constants, as interactions of 442 proteins and 68 ligands, 30056 interactions in the form used here. The authors convert the Kd values to a log scale, pKd. They note that the peak at pKd 5 covers more than half of Davis, 20931 of 30056 values, and that these are pairs with very weak affinity or not seen in the primary screen. KIBA combines kinase inhibitor bioactivities from Ki, Kd and IC50 measurements into a single KIBA score; it originally covered 467 targets and 52498 drugs and was filtered by earlier work to drugs and targets with at least 10 interactions, leaving 229 proteins and 2111 drugs and 118254 interactions. Compound SMILES strings come from PubChem and protein sequences from UniProt. Each data set is stored as an affinity matrix with the pairs that have a measurement, and the published fold files hold positions in that matrix: one test fold shared by all five training sets, and five training folds. The data folder also ships drug-drug similarities from PubChem structure clustering and target-target Smith-Waterman similarities, which were used to reproduce the comparison methods.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A method predicts an affinity value for every pair in the test fold. The headline metric is the Concordance Index, which asks whether two randomly chosen pairs are predicted in the same order as their measured affinities, so higher is better. Mean squared error is also reported, where lower is better. The authors fix hyper-parameters by five-fold cross validation on the five training folds, then train the chosen configuration five times, each time on four of the five training folds combined (the cross validation training set, leaving out that round's validation fold), score each of those five models on the same held-out test fold, and report the average with the standard deviation in parentheses. Significance between methods is tested with a paired t test at a 95% confidence interval. The comparison is made fair by giving the baselines the same train and test folds. The repository's own script follows this: it reads the test set and the outer training sets, uses get_cindex as the performance measure, trains with a mean squared error loss, and prints the per-fold test Concordance Index and mean squared error along with their average and standard deviation.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation Metrics, Experiment Setup, Results (Tables 3 and 4); run_experiments.py: nfold_1_2_3_setting_sample, run_regression

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Clone the repository, install the Python, Keras and TensorFlow versions the README lists, place the data folder under the source directory, and run run_experiments.py with the window sizes, batch size, epoch count, sequence and SMILES length limits and the dataset path for the data set you want. The README's example uses the KIBA data path and problem type 1. The script loads the affinity matrix, finds the positions that have a measurement, reads the published test and training folds, searches the given filter combinations by cross validation, retrains on each of the five four-fold training sets and logs the test Concordance Index and mean squared error.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Two kinase affinity data sets as used by DeepDTA. Davis, with Kd values, 442 proteins, 68 compounds and 30056 interactions. KIBA, with KIBA scores, 229 proteins, 2111 compounds and 118254 interactions, after earlier work filtered the original 467 targets and 52498 drugs to those with at least 10 interactions.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: A random one in six holdout, the same for both data sets. The pairs are divided at random into six equal parts, one part is the independent test set, and the other five parts are the training folds used for five-fold cross validation to choose hyper-parameters. The published fold files give the test fold and the five training folds, and the test fold is the same for all five training sets. Counting the entries of the saved fold files gives 5010 test pairs for Davis and 19709 for KIBA.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Concordance Index, higher is better, on both data sets, with mean squared error as a second metric, lower is better. The repository script uses get_cindex as the performance measure and trains with a mean squared error loss.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: KronRLS and SimBoost, both given Smith-Waterman protein similarity and PubChem compound similarity. On Davis the paper reports CI 0.871 for KronRLS and 0.872 for SimBoost; on KIBA, 0.782 and 0.836. DeepDTA variants that replace one or both similarity inputs with a convolutional block are also reported, the combined model reaching CI 0.878 on Davis and 0.863 on KIBA.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None beyond the random split: the pairs are divided at random, so the same drug and the same protein appear in both training and test folds. The authors do not apply a sequence identity cut-off; they report similarity statistics for the data sets instead, that Smith-Waterman similarity between proteins is at most 60 per cent for 99 per cent of KIBA protein pairs and for 92 per cent of Davis protein pairs, and call both data sets non-redundant.

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Five training runs, each on four of the five training folds combined, all scored on the same test fold, reported as an average with the standard deviation in parentheses. Differences between methods are tested with a paired t test at a 95 per cent confidence interval. The repository script computes the average, the mean loss and the standard deviation across the folds.

facts.value: A drug-target pair with a measured affinity. In the published files, one example is a position in the affinity matrix for which a value exists, identified by a drug index and a protein index.

facts.value: Not reported. The saved files say the proteins are kinases and that their sequences came from UniProt, but they do not name the species the data cover.

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Dissociation constants from kinase selectivity assays for Davis, converted to pKd. For KIBA, a score combining kinase inhibitor bioactivities reported as Ki, Kd and IC50 from different sources, then preprocessed by earlier work by negating the scores and shifting them.

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Sequence level inputs are enough: the protein amino acid sequence and the compound SMILES string, with no structures or external features. The data folder also ships precomputed drug-drug PubChem similarities and target-target Smith-Waterman similarities, and the paper reports methods that use those instead.

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Training on the benchmark's own training folds. Hyper-parameters are chosen by five-fold cross validation within the training parts, then a model is trained from those parameters five times, each time on four of the five training folds combined, and scored on the held-out test fold. The saved files describe no zero-shot or probing setting.

strengths.text: The folds are published, so a later method can train and test on exactly the same drug-target pairs. The DeepDTA authors state they gave their baselines the same train and test folds for the comparison.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Experiment Setup; data/README.md: Train and test folds

strengths.text: Affinity is scored as a continuous value, which avoids the invented negative examples that the authors describe as a problem for binary interaction data sets.
Results are reported as an average over five training runs with a standard deviation, and method differences are tested with a paired t test rather than read off a single run.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Experiment Setup, Evaluation Metrics, Tables 3 and 4

strengths.text: Only sequence level inputs are needed, so the benchmark is open to methods that cannot use a protein-ligand complex structure. The authors note that structure based scoring is limited to the complexes in the PDB.

limitations.text: The split is random over pairs, so a drug or a protein in the test fold can also appear in training. The benchmark as published does not hold out unseen drugs or unseen targets, and the authors name prediction for novel targets and novel pairs as future work.

Davis is dominated by one value. The authors report that the peak at pKd 5 is more than half the data set, 20931 of 30056 pairs, and that these are weak or unobserved pairs, so both the metrics and the apparent differences between methods are driven by a large block of near-identical labels.

Both data sets are kinases and their inhibitors, so a score here says nothing about other protein families. The labels are also not one assay: KIBA scores merge Ki, Kd and IC50 measurements from different sources.

There is no leaderboard and no licence. The saved repository files state no licence for the code or the data, and the only published result is the paper's own tables, so a new score has to be produced by rerunning the comparison methods or taken from those tables. The code also pins old versions, Python 3.4 or later with Keras 2 and TensorFlow 1.

name: Protein embeddings for GNN PPI prediction (OGBl-ppa and HuRI)
description: Comparison of sequence, structure and function protein embeddings as node features for graph neural network PPI link prediction on OGBl-ppa and HuRI, with a protein-only MLP ablation.

attributes.task: Protein-protein interaction link prediction
attributes.scope_note: Tables 5 (Hits@100) and 6 (Accuracy). Supplementary leaderboard values (Table S2) not extracted.
attributes.source_locator: Experimental design; Tables 4-6

profile.summary: This is one review paper's own comparison, not a released suite. It asks how much a graph neural network for protein interaction prediction gains from protein-level node features, and which kind of protein information helps most. Nine protein embedding methods, three each from sequence, structure and function, are used in two ways on two link prediction benchmarks (OGBl-ppa and HuRI): on their own in a protein-only multilayer perceptron, and as node features for six graph neural network configurations, against the same networks with randomly initialised node features. It is useful to someone deciding whether to attach protein language model, inverse folding or knowledge graph embeddings to a PPI link predictor.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Experimental design

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Link prediction on a protein interaction network: given the known edges of an interactome, score candidate protein pairs. The comparison is set up around three questions. Whether adding biologically informative node features to a graph neural network improves it over random features. Which source of node features, sequence, structure or function, works best. And whether combining network topology with protein representations beats using protein representations alone. The third question is answered by an ablation in which the task is reformulated as binary classification over concatenated protein embeddings with a multilayer perceptron and no network at all.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Comparative analysis, research questions; Experimental design

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Two existing benchmarks are reused, chosen to differ in species coverage and in how negatives are made: OGBl-ppa, a multi-species benchmark with randomly sampled negatives under a closed-world assumption, and HuRI, a human dataset with experimentally validated true negatives. The paper reports graph sizes of 576 289 nodes and 30 326 273 edges for the OGBl-ppa interaction graph and 8248 nodes and 51 813 edges for HuRI. Protein identifiers were mapped to UniProt, sequences taken from UniRef50 and then mapped to PDB identifiers through CATH for structures. The function embeddings come from a biomedical knowledge graph built by linking the proteins of the interaction graph to the Gene Ontology classes that describe them, using a STRING release matched to the one OGB uses and a 2020-06-01 Gene Ontology Annotation release, converted to a directed labelled RDF graph; the paper reports 620 555 nodes and 5 989 238 edges for the OGBl-ppa knowledge graph and 52 513 nodes and 321 259 edges for the HuRI one.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Data; Table 4

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each benchmark keeps its own task and evaluation protocol; the paper reproduces the OGBl-ppa leaderboard hyperparameters so that its numbers are comparable with that leaderboard. Two metrics are reported for every cell, Hits@100 and accuracy, both higher is better. On the OGB side, Hits@100 means ranking each positive validation or test edge against 3,000,000 randomly sampled negative edges and counting the fraction ranked in the top 100. Every embedding and network combination is compared against the same network with randomly initialised node features, which is the control that answers the first question. A majority-vote ensemble over the different representations is reported as an eleventh column. The results tables mark the best score per method and per table, bold the cells where a biological embedding beats random features, and give a maximum standard deviation for the table rather than per cell: 0.0711 for OGBl-ppa and 0.0928 for HuRI.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Experimental design; Tables 5 and 6 footnote; OGB page: ogbl-ppa prediction task

sections.title: What the comparison found
sections.body: Function-derived embeddings were strongest. The paper reports gains over the random-feature baselines such as ESM-2 with GraphSAGE on OGBl-ppa and NGNN combined with SEAL on HuRI for sequence features; structural embeddings improved on the baselines in both tasks, with the largest gain for NGNN with a GraphSAGE branch; and knowledge graph embeddings gave the largest improvements overall. Functional representations beat sequence and structure consistently, while no consistent difference appeared between sequence and structure. The majority-vote ensemble often beat individual sequence or structure embeddings but usually lost to the functional ones. The protein-only multilayer perceptron ablation reaches performance close to the simpler graph baselines with knowledge graph features alone, which the authors read as evidence that network structure and protein features are complementary.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results and discussion

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Two link prediction benchmarks and the knowledge graphs built over them. OGBl-ppa: interaction graph of 576 289 nodes and 30 326 273 edges, with a knowledge graph of 620 555 nodes and 5 989 238 edges. HuRI: interaction graph of 8248 nodes and 51 813 edges, with a knowledge graph of 52 513 nodes and 321 259 edges. A Gene Ontology graph of 44 266 nodes and 71 515 edges is listed beside them. The paper gives no test-set size for either task.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 4

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Each benchmark's own split is used and the paper does not restate it. For OGBl-ppa the OGB documentation describes a biological throughput split: training edges are associations measured by high-throughput technology or obtained computationally, while validation and test edges are associations that can only be measured by low-throughput laboratory experiments. The negatives differ between the two tasks, which the paper treats as the important difference: OGBl-ppa samples negatives at random under a closed-world assumption, HuRI carries experimentally validated true negatives. No split rule is given for HuRI.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Data; Results and discussion; OGB page: ogbl-ppa dataset splitting

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Hits@100 (Table 5) and accuracy (Table 6), both higher is better, reported for every combination of node feature source and model on both datasets. Hits@100 is the OGB ranking metric: the fraction of positive test edges ranked in the top 100 against 3,000,000 randomly sampled negative edges. No other metric is reported in the two result tables.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Tables 5 and 6 captions; OGB page: ogbl-ppa prediction task

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The same graph neural networks with randomly initialised node features are the reference point, run with the leaderboard hyperparameters for OGBl-ppa. The models are GCN, GraphSAGE, NGNN with a GCN or a GraphSAGE branch, each of those two combined with SEAL, and a multilayer perceptron; a majority-vote ensemble over the representations is reported as well. The protein-only multilayer perceptron with random embeddings is the baseline for the ablation.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Experimental design; Tables 5 and 6

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None of the study's own. The comparison relies on the two benchmarks' own splits, and the authors name homology-based partitioning as future work rather than something they did. Two further sources of leakage are acknowledged but not controlled: the protein embedding models are pretrained on public sequence, structure and annotation data that overlap these proteins, and the functional embeddings come from a Gene Ontology knowledge graph whose annotation coverage favours well-studied proteins. The paper quantifies the coverage: in OGBl-ppa 10.6 per cent (61 352) of proteins are not annotated, of which 7.8 per cent are also test proteins, while HuRI proteins are fully annotated.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results and discussion; Conclusions

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: A single maximum standard deviation per dataset, given in the footnote of both result tables: 0.0711 for OGBl-ppa and 0.0928 for HuRI. No per-cell standard deviation, no confidence interval and no statistical test between cells is reported, and the number of repeated runs behind those figures is not stated.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Tables 5 and 6 footnote

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a candidate edge between two proteins: a protein pair that the model must score as interacting or not. The nodes carrying the features are individual proteins, each represented by a 1024-dimensional sequence or structure embedding or a 128-dimensional function embedding.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Comparative analysis; Experimental design

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Multi-species for OGBl-ppa and human only for HuRI. The paper's degree figure covers 55 species in OGBl-ppa across eight kingdoms (Pseudomonadati, Bacillati, Fungi, Metazoa, Viridiplantae, Discoba, Amoebozoa and Alveolata), while the OGB documentation describes the dataset's nodes as proteins from 58 different species. HuRI is described as a human-specific dataset.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Figure 5 caption; Data; OGB page: ogbl-ppa graph

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: The labels are experimental interaction evidence carried by the two source benchmarks, not measurements made for this study. For OGBl-ppa the edges are biologically meaningful protein associations from STRING, including physical interactions, co-expression, homology and genomic neighbourhood, and the split separates high-throughput from low-throughput evidence. HuRI supplies experimentally validated true negatives as well as positives. The paper describes no assay protocol itself.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Data; Results and discussion; OGB page: ogbl-ppa graph and splitting

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The interaction network plus one protein-level representation per node. Three sources are allowed, one at a time: sequence, from the protein language models ESM-2, ProtTrans and ProGen2 over UniRef50 sequences; structure, from the inverse folding models ESM-IF1, PiFold and ProstT5 over PDB structures reached through CATH; and function, from the knowledge graph embedding methods TransE, ComplEx and RDF2Vec over a Gene Ontology and STRING knowledge graph. The random-feature baselines read the topology alone, and the ablation reads the embeddings alone.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Experimental design; Data

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: The protein embeddings are precomputed once from released models and injected as fixed node features; the graph neural networks are trained on each task, reproducing the OGBl-ppa leaderboard hyperparameters. No protein embedding model is fine-tuned on the interaction task. The ablation trains only a multilayer perceptron on concatenated embeddings.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Experimental design

strengths.text: The three sources of protein information are compared under one framework with three representative methods each, and every combination is run against the same network with random node features, so the gain attributable to the features can be read directly.

The two datasets were chosen to differ in a way that matters for interpretation: one is multi-species with randomly sampled negatives, the other single-species with experimentally validated negatives, and the authors use that contrast to explain part of the performance gap.
The confound behind the winning feature type is reported rather than hidden: the authors measure annotation coverage in OGBl-ppa and note that annotation bias favours well-studied proteins.
A protein-only ablation with no network is run alongside the hybrid models, which separates the contribution of the embeddings from the contribution of the topology.

limitations.text: Uncertainty is reported as one maximum standard deviation per dataset with no per-cell figure, and no test is applied between cells. Several of the differences the paper discusses are smaller than those maxima (0.0711 for OGBl-ppa and 0.0928 for HuRI), so individual rankings cannot be separated from run-to-run variation.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Tables 5 and 6 footnote; Results and discussion

limitations.text: There is no control for homology or for pretraining overlap. The embedding models are pretrained on the same public sequence, structure and annotation resources the test proteins come from, and the authors themselves list homology-based partitioning as work still to be done.

The winning feature type depends on annotation availability rather than on the protein itself, which limits how far the conclusion carries: the functional embeddings read Gene Ontology annotations, and the authors say the advantage comes with greater dependence on annotation availability and quality and that broader evaluation on weakly annotated benchmarks is needed.

The text and the tables do not agree on one method. The results text reports a gain for GraphSAGE with DistMult on HuRI, but the knowledge graph columns of Tables 5 and 6 are TransE, ComplEx and RDF2Vec, with no DistMult column.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results and discussion; Tables 5 and 6 column headers

limitations.text: Nothing executable is published with the paper. The code and the dataset sources are listed in supplementary tables rather than in the article, so the comparison cannot be rerun from the text, and the article itself is under a non-commercial licence.

name: ViroBench
description: Benchmark of nucleotide foundation models on viral genomics: taxonomy and host classification under genus-disjoint and temporal splits, plus genome modelling and CDS generation.

attributes.task: Viral taxonomy and host classification; viral genome modelling and CDS generation
attributes.scope_note: This batch covers the classification axis only (Table 25 and two Table 4 rows): 12 protocols, ALL, DNA and RNA virus sets x taxonomy and host x genus-disjoint and temporal splits. Generation results (Tables 5, 6, 27, 28) are not extracted.
attributes.source_locator: Abstract; Section 3; Table 1; Table 25

profile.summary: ViroBench tests nucleotide foundation models on viral sequences from NCBI. Its classification half asks a model to predict a virus's taxonomy (Kingdom to Family) and its host category, under two hard splits: one that holds out whole genera and one that splits by deposit date. Models are compared with a frozen backbone and a small trained head, scored by macro-F1, precision, recall and AUPRC. It is for anyone judging how a DNA or RNA model generalises to viruses it has not seen.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Section 3; README.md: Benchmark Suite

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two classification tasks. Taxonomy classification predicts five hierarchical labels from Kingdom to Family, testing whether a model's representation reflects viral evolutionary structure. Host prediction assigns a sequence to one of eight coarse host categories, testing whether the representation carries ecological signal. Each task is run on the whole viral corpus (ALL) and separately on the DNA and RNA subsets, under both splits, giving 12 classification scenarios. The paper also defines six generation scenarios on a second axis, which this page does not cover.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.2.1; README.md: Benchmark Suite

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The authors retrieved 273,974 virus-associated TaxIDs from NCBI RefSeq and GenBank and recorded taxonomy, the earliest discovery date and host for each. Raw host metadata, over 8,000 inconsistent strings, was standardised into eight coarse categories using the Qwen3-235B language model. Entries with incomplete taxonomy or missing timestamps were removed, only verified high-quality assemblies were kept, and species-level redundancy was resolved, leaving 58,314 samples. Two split protocols are defined over the same data: a genus-disjoint split with no genus shared between train, validation and test, and a temporal split by deposit date with stated cutoffs per panel (for example 2017.10 and 2020.02 for the ALL set). Both use an 8:1:1 train, validation and test ratio.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1, Table 1

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The backbone is frozen: sequence embeddings are precomputed with each model's own pooling strategy and a lightweight multi-task classification head is trained on them. Long sequences are handled by windowing, with 8, 4 or 2 windows sampled per sequence during training; at validation and test time all windows are scored and aggregated into one sequence-level prediction. Learning rates from 10^-2 to 10^-4 and the different window configurations are tried, and results are reported as the mean with standard deviation across those settings. Metrics are AUPRC, recall, precision and macro-F1, chosen for the class imbalance. A CNN trained from scratch is the non-pretrained reference.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 4.1, Appendix frozen-backbone protocol; README.md: Unified Evaluation Protocol

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Clone the repository, put the classification splits under data/all_viral/cls_data/, and run script/run_all.py with a model name and a dataset name of the form {DNA|RNA|ALL}-{taxon|host}-{genus|times}. The dataset itself is downloaded from the Hugging Face repository. The README says model-specific setup must follow each model's own documentation.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One curated corpus of 58,314 viral samples from NCBI RefSeq and GenBank, used as ALL, DNA and RNA panels. Table 1 gives the label counts per panel, for example 29 / 55 / 214 / 390 / 319 labels at Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order and Family for ALL viruses.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1, Table 1

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Two protocols over the same data, both 8:1:1 train, validation and test. Genus-disjoint: no genus appears in more than one partition. Temporal: split by deposit date, with per-panel cutoffs (ALL 2017.10 and 2020.02; DNA 2022.07 and 2023.08; RNA 2017.03 and 2017.11).
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Macro-F1 is the headline classification metric (Table 25); AUPRC, recall and precision are also reported. Higher is better.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: 66 nucleotide foundation models plus 4 conventional baselines, 70 methods in total; the paper names BLAST, Kraken2, a BiLSTM and a CNN trained from scratch among the conventional ones. The README says 67 baselines.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 4.1.1, Table 3; README.md: Baselines

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The genus-disjoint split removes genus overlap between partitions, which the authors describe as mandating phylogenetic extrapolation; the temporal split holds out later deposits. Overlap between test sequences and a model's own pretraining data is not controlled.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.2.1; README.md: Highlights

facts.value: Viruses, split into DNA, RNA and unknown nucleic-acid types; host labels cover eight coarse categories such as bacterial, plant and human.

facts.value: Inapplicable: labels are database annotations (NCBI taxonomy, deposit dates and host metadata standardised by a language model), not experimental measurements.

strengths.text: Both splits are harder than a random split: one removes whole genera, the other holds out later deposits, so memorised near-duplicates do not inflate scores.
All models go through the same frozen-backbone protocol with a standard head, which the authors say reduces bias from different tokenisers and architectures.
Results are reported with standard deviations over learning rates and window settings rather than a single tuned number.

limitations.text: Host prediction is a single label over coarse categories, using the primary-host annotation; the authors say a multi-label version is future work.
The temporal split uses NCBI deposit dates, which the authors say reflect sequencing intensity rather than when a virus actually emerged.
Host labels were standardised from over 8,000 inconsistent strings by a language model (Qwen3-235B), so label quality depends on that step.
The repository carries no licence file, and the model counts differ between the paper (66 models, 70 methods) and the README (67 baselines).

name: PepSpecBench
description: Benchmark for peptide MS/MS fragment intensity prediction with harmonised PROSPECT and MassIVE-KB subsets, backbone-disjoint splits, a shared canonical fragment-ion evaluation space and a cross-species out-of-distribution suite.

attributes.task: Peptide tandem mass spectrum (fragment intensity) prediction
attributes.scope_note: Peptide length 6-40, precursor charge 1-6, PTMs UNIMOD 1, 4 and 35. In-domain: PROSPECT-Mini and MassIVE-KB-Mini, 500k/50k/50k spectra each. OOD: seven 20k-spectrum subsets over five species from ProteomeXchange (MaxQuant 1% FDR); zero-shot transfer.
attributes.source_locator: Sections 3.1-3.3; Appendix C
limitations: Preprint; six models all retrained by the benchmark authors.

profile.summary: PepSpecBench is a benchmark for predicting peptide tandem mass spectra: given a modified peptide sequence, a precursor charge and a normalised collision energy, a model must predict the fragment-ion intensity pattern. It harmonises two public spectral libraries, PROSPECT and MassIVE-KB, into matched 500k/50k/50k train, validation and test subsets under one scope (peptide length 6 to 40, charge 1 to 6, three PTMs), splits them so that no peptide backbone appears in two partitions, and projects every model's output into one 234-dimensional canonical ion space so that architectures with different native outputs can be compared. It adds a seven-subset cross-species suite of 20k spectra each, evaluated zero-shot, and metadata perturbation probes. Six models were retrained by the authors on these splits.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Sections 3.1 to 3.3

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How well a model reproduces the measured fragment-intensity pattern of a peptide's MS/MS spectrum, and how far that ability survives three stresses. First, fair comparison: all models are scored in one canonical ion space rather than in their own output formats. Second, leakage: whether apparent accuracy depends on seeing the same peptide backbone in training, tested by comparing three split rules under one model and one data source. Third, robustness: whether a model trained on human libraries transfers zero-shot to other species and to a cancer cell line, and whether it uses collision energy and precursor charge in a physically sensible way, probed by perturbing that metadata.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Sections 4.1 to 4.3; Section 5

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Two in-domain sources are combined under one scope: PROSPECT, a curated spectral library with broad PTM coverage and several collision energies per peptide, and MassIVE-KB, a larger community-curated human library. Both are filtered to peptides of length 6 to 40, charge 1 to 6 and the UNIMOD 1, 4 and 35 modifications, and reconstructed into 500k train, 50k validation and 50k test spectra each; the appendix names these PROSPECT-Mini and MassIVE-KB-Mini. Because MassIVE-KB mixes heterogeneous sources, a single default normalised collision energy of 25 is applied to all its spectra. The cross-species suite is seven subsets drawn from ProteomeXchange studies, each truncated to 20k spectra after the same filtering, covering human reference and HeLa, yeast, two E. coli subsets, C. elegans and A. thaliana, identified with MaxQuant at 1 per cent false discovery rate.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1, Table 1; Appendix A, Composition and Collection

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is an intensity prediction for an input triplet of modified sequence, precursor charge and normalised collision energy. Because the six baselines have different native output spaces, each has a projection into one shared canonical ion space that enumerates every combination of cleavage position, b or y ion type and fragment charge up to a maximum; with a reference length of 40 and maximum fragment charge 3 this space has 234 dimensions. Prediction and ground truth are both projected, a validity mask is built, and three metrics are computed over the masked positions: spectral angle (SA), where lower is better and the range is 0 to 1, spectral angle similarity (1 minus SA), and Pearson correlation. Results are aggregated as medians with bootstrap confidence intervals. All six baselines were retrained by the authors on the benchmark splits.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 3.1 to 3.3

sections.title: The split rule and what it is worth
sections.body: A partition is backbone-disjoint when the sets of unmodified amino-acid sequences in any two partitions are mutually exclusive, which blocks both exact sequence reuse and the same backbone appearing with different modifications. PROSPECT is split by deterministic hashing of the backbone; for MassIVE-KB the official disjoint splits are kept, filtered within each partition, and checked for zero backbone overlap. The benefit is measured rather than asserted: with Prosit and PROSPECT held fixed, a naive random split lowers median SA from 0.1376 to 0.1254 and raises Pearson correlation from 0.8921 to 0.9099, while a modified-sequence split stays close to backbone-disjoint (SA 0.1392, correlation 0.8895). The authors read this as exact backbone reuse being the dominant leakage path, and state in their limitations that backbone disjointness does not remove higher-order sequence homology.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1, Backbone-Disjoint Split; Section 4.2, Table 3; Section 5

sections.title: What the comparison found
sections.body: The in-domain ranking depends on the source: Prosit Transformer has the best median SA on MassIVE-KB (0.0977 against 0.0995 for Prosit), while Prosit leads on PROSPECT (0.1376 against 0.1419), which the authors attribute to MassIVE-KB holding longer peptides and higher charges. Mid-tier models are less stable: UniSpec beats PredFull on PROSPECT but collapses on MassIVE-KB to SA 0.3369 with near-zero correlation, while PredFull holds at SA 0.1673. The in-domain ranking does not survive transfer: under MassIVE-KB training, PredFull beats both Prosit models on all five out-of-distribution testbeds, and the appendix shows the Prosit models reaching negative median correlation on several subsets. Under PROSPECT training the picture splits again, with Prosit best on C. elegans and A. thaliana and PredFull on E. coli and yeast. The authors note that one apparent out-of-distribution advantage is a Simpson's paradox caused by covariate shift.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 4.1 and 4.3; Tables 2 and 4

sections.title: How to get the data
sections.body: The dataset is published on Hugging Face under the MIT licence, with a dataset DOI. Its configurations mirror the benchmark components: massive_kb and prospect, each in a native representation with the original mass-to-charge and intensity arrays and in the canonical 234-dimensional representation, each with train, validation and test splits; an ood configuration in both representations with a test split only; and a small sample configuration. No evaluation code, model code or leaderboard address is given in the paper.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Data Availability; Hugging Face dataset record

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Two in-domain components of 500k train, 50k validation and 50k test spectra each: PROSPECT-Mini, from ProteomeTools, balanced 50 per cent unmodified and 50 per cent modified in every split, and MassIVE-KB-Mini, from the MassIVE-KB v1 human subset at its natural modification rate (unmodified 75.40, 72.83 and 72.09 per cent in train, validation and test). Plus PepSpecBench-OOD, seven subsets of 20k spectra each: human reference, human HeLa, yeast, E. coli reference, E. coli enriched, C. elegans and A. thaliana. All components share the same length, charge and PTM scope.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Appendix A, Composition and Distribution

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Backbone-disjoint train, validation and test splits for both in-domain sources: the unmodified amino-acid backbone sets of any two partitions are mutually exclusive, so neither an exact sequence nor another modified form of it can cross the boundary. PROSPECT is partitioned by deterministic hashing of the backbone; MassIVE-KB keeps its official disjoint splits, scope-filtered within each partition and verified to have zero backbone overlap. The seven cross-species subsets are test-only and used zero-shot. Two weaker rules, a naive random split and a modified-sequence split, are run as a controlled ablation for comparison.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1, Backbone-Disjoint Split; Section 4.2

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Three metrics over the masked positions of the canonical space, the same for every task. Spectral angle (SA) is the primary one: the angular distance between the normalised predicted and observed intensity vectors, in the range 0 to 1, and lower is better. Spectral angle similarity is 1 minus SA, so higher is better. Pearson correlation measures whether relative intensity rankings are preserved, higher being better. All values are reported as medians with bootstrap confidence intervals.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.3; Tables 2 and 4

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Six models, all retrained by the authors on the benchmark splits. Sequence-centric, predicting b and y ion intensities by cleavage position and fragment charge: Prosit (GRU encoder-decoder, about 2.5M parameters), Prosit Transformer (about 86M) and AlphaPeptDeep (modular Transformer, about 1.8M). Full-spectrum or dictionary models projected into the canonical space: PredFull (residual CNN with squeeze-excitation, about 8.2M) and UniSpec (attention-based dictionary model, about 12M). FastSpel, a linear model of about 50K parameters, serves as a lower-bound reference.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.2

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The backbone-disjoint split is the benchmark's central control: no unmodified peptide backbone may appear in two partitions, which blocks exact reuse and PTM-variant overlap. Its effect is quantified by the split ablation, and residual similarity is measured in the appendix as the minimum Levenshtein edit distance from each test backbone to the nearest training backbone. The authors state the limit plainly: backbone disjointness does not eliminate higher-order sequence homology, and their own biases note says the backbone split does not eliminate homology-level leakage. Cross-species evaluation is an additional, stronger control, since those subsets come from different organisms and are used zero-shot.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1; Section 4.2; Appendix A, Biases; Appendix B.1; Section 5

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Metric values are medians with bootstrap confidence intervals, reported in the appendix for the in-domain results; the main tables print the medians only. No training replicate or seed variation is reported: each baseline is retrained once per source under the benchmark split.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.3; Tables 2 and 4; Section 4.3

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a single tandem mass spectrum, scored as the intensity vector of its fragment ions. The input is a triplet of modified peptide sequence, precursor charge state and normalised collision energy, and the target is the measured fragment-intensity pattern projected into the 234-dimensional canonical ion space.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human for both in-domain sources, and five species across the cross-species suite: human (a reference proteome subset and a HeLa cancer cell subset), yeast, E. coli (two subsets), C. elegans and A. thaliana. The authors describe the training data as human-centric.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Appendix A, Composition and Biases

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Tandem mass spectrometry. The in-domain labels come from two public spectral libraries, PROSPECT (built on ProteomeTools, with several collision energy settings per peptide) and MassIVE-KB v1, a community-curated library of human measurements. The cross-species spectra come from ProteomeXchange studies and were identified with MaxQuant at a 1 per cent false discovery rate. The authors note that the instrumentation is dominated by the Q Exactive family.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.1; Appendix A, Collection and Biases

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Three things and no more: the modified peptide sequence, the precursor charge state and the normalised collision energy. No structure, alignment or spectrum is given at prediction time. The benchmark restricts the scope to peptide length 6 to 40, charge 1 to 6 and the UNIMOD 1, 4 and 35 modifications, and a model's output may be in its own native format as long as a projection into the canonical space is defined.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Sections 3.1 and 3.2

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Training from scratch on the benchmark's own training split: all six baselines are retrained on the benchmark data under the backbone-disjoint splits, separately for each in-domain source, with per-model adaptations and hyperparameters documented in the appendix. The cross-species evaluation is strictly zero-shot, with no fine-tuning or adaptation on the out-of-distribution subsets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Sections 3.1 and 3.2

strengths.text: The shared 234-dimensional canonical ion space lets models with different native outputs, from sequence-indexed ion ladders to binned full spectra and fragment dictionaries, be scored on the same footing, and every metric is computed only in that space.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Section 3.2, Shared Canonical Evaluation Space

strengths.text: The value of the strict split is measured rather than asserted: with the model and data source held fixed, a naive random split is shown to flatter the model by 0.012 median SA, while a modified-sequence split is shown to make little difference.

Out-of-distribution transfer is tested separately for models trained on each in-domain source, which separates architectural robustness from training-source bias and shows that the in-domain ranking does not predict the transfer ranking.

The data are released on Hugging Face under the MIT licence, in both a native representation with the original mass-to-charge and intensity arrays and the canonical representation used for scoring, with a dataset DOI.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Data Availability; Hugging Face dataset record

limitations.text: Every number is produced by the benchmark's authors, who retrained all six baselines themselves rather than using published checkpoints, so the comparison depends on their training recipes and per-model adaptations.

The leakage control stops at exact backbones. The authors state that backbone-disjoint splitting does not eliminate higher-order sequence homology and list that as a remaining bias, so residual similarity between training and test peptides remains.

The scope is deliberately narrow and partly homogenised: three modifications only, one peptide length and charge window, instrumentation dominated by one family, and a single default collision energy of 25 imposed on all MassIVE-KB spectra, which removes real variation from that source.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Sections 3.1 and 5; Appendix A, Biases

limitations.text: No evaluation code, projection implementation or leaderboard is published with the paper: only the dataset is released, so a third party cannot reproduce the canonical projections or the reported medians without reimplementing them from the appendix.

Comparisons across the out-of-distribution subsets need care: the authors show that one apparent transfer advantage is a Simpson's paradox created by covariate shift in collision energy and modification state, and that they cannot causally attribute the source effect because the two sources differ in distribution.
