profile.summary: PRIME is an evaluation framework for protein language models on a single viral protein: the SARS-CoV-2 spike receptor binding domain. Frozen embeddings from five protein language models, with and without domain-specific fine-tuning on 347,432 outbreak RBD sequences, feed a small multi-task network that predicts two deep mutational scanning phenotypes, ACE2 binding affinity and protein expression. The point of the framework is the split: because viral sequences are near-identical, a random split lets mutations at the same residue appear in training and test, so PRIME holds out whole residue positions instead and shows that the random-split numbers are inflated. It is useful to anyone reading reported fitness-prediction accuracy on viral proteins.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Background; Methods, Data collection and curation; Position-stratified validation protocol

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two things. First, how well a protein language model's representation of an RBD sequence predicts a measured phenotype: ACE2 binding affinity and expression level from yeast display deep mutational scanning. Second, and the reason the framework exists, how much of that apparent accuracy comes from homology leakage. The same embeddings and the same regression head are evaluated under two split rules, a random split and a position-stratified split that holds out all mutations at a residue position together, and the gap between them is the measurement. The framework also tracks whether domain-specific fine-tuning on outbreak sequences recovers predictive signal, and whether the embeddings separate known viral lineages.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Background; Results, Scaling and fine-tuning overcome the generalization gap

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Three datasets. The outbreak dataset is 347,432 unique SARS-CoV-2 RBD sequences (spike residues 319 to 541) curated from GISAID and the Sequence Read Archive as of 3 February 2023, with duplicates and ambiguous sequences removed; it is used for fine-tuning and for lineage analysis, and is dominated by Omicron (52.70 per cent) and Delta (35.71 per cent). The DMS dataset supplies the labels: 116,257 unique RBD sequences with measured ACE2 binding affinity and 105,525 with quantified expression, from a published yeast display experiment. The betaCov dataset is 75 RBD sequences from diverse Sarbecovirus members, used for cross-species analysis rather than for the regression benchmark.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data collection and curation; Results, Benchmark data collection

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Frozen embeddings, taken from the last hidden layer or mean-pooled over residues, are fed to a fully connected network of five layers whose hidden size follows the embedding size, with ReLU activations, no dropout and mean squared error loss, predicting binding and expression jointly. Evaluation is 5-fold cross-validation over residue positions: positions are randomly partitioned into five subsets and a sequence joins the training or test side according to whether its mutated positions fall exclusively in that subset. Within each fold the network is reinitialised, trained for 1000 epochs at a learning rate of 1e-5, and scored on the fold's test set; the coefficient of determination and RMSE are computed per fold and averaged. The stratified evaluation was repeated under three fold-assignment seeds (0, 1 and 2) to check that results do not depend on the fold construction.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Position-stratified validation protocol and Input features

sections.title: What the comparison found
sections.body: The random split flatters every model. For ESM-C 600M with mean embeddings, a random split gives a coefficient of determination of 0.7711 for binding affinity, while the same base model under the position-stratified split has no predictive signal at all and a negative value of -0.1050. Fine-tuning on the outbreak dataset restores part of it: for the same model the stratified binding figure rises to 0.1823 plus or minus 0.2149 with mean embeddings and 0.2087 plus or minus 0.1451 with sequence-level CLS embeddings. Table 1 reports both splits, both phenotypes, both embedding methods and the fine-tuned and non-fine-tuned conditions for all five models; many of the stratified values are negative. Separately, fine-tuning raised masked language modelling accuracy on RBD sequences from 5.06 per cent to 96.33 per cent for ESM-2 8M, while a BERT model trained from scratch on RBD sequences alone reached 94.09 per cent but failed on rare residues.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Scaling and fine-tuning overcome the generalization gap; Table 1

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository installs as a Python package into a conda environment, with two requirement sets because the authors moved to newer GPUs during revision. Masked language modelling is run by calling the relevant lightning script, and the transfer-learning models take flags for the target phenotype, the learning rate, the number of epochs and the path to a pretrained masked language model checkpoint; the readme ships SLURM examples because the work was done in a SLURM environment. The split comparison lives in its own directory: reading split_comparison.py, it wraps the multi-task fully connected head from the package, sets torch and numpy seeds, trains with Adam under a summed binding and expression mean squared error loss, and uses scikit-learn's KFold and train_test_split to build the two partitions. Its docstring warns that this random split is not the one used originally, so its values do not match the published random-split numbers.
sections.source_locator: README: Installation, Usage; split_comparison.py

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Three. The DMS dataset carries the benchmark labels: 116,257 unique RBD sequences with measured ACE2 binding affinity and 105,525 with quantified expression, from a published yeast display experiment. The outbreak dataset is 347,432 unique SARS-CoV-2 RBD sequences (spike residues 319 to 541) from GISAID and the Sequence Read Archive as of 3 February 2023, used for fine-tuning and lineage analysis; 99.75 per cent of its sequences are 223 amino acids long. The betaCov dataset is 75 Sarbecovirus RBD sequences used for cross-species analysis.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data collection and curation; Results, Benchmark data collection

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Two regimes over the same DMS data, both as 5-fold cross-validation rather than a fixed test set. The position-stratified split partitions residue positions into five subsets and assigns a sequence to training or test according to whether its mutated positions fall exclusively in that subset, so all mutations at a position are held out together. The random split is the comparison condition, in which mutations at the same site can appear on both sides. No per-fold test size is reported. Fold assignment was repeated under three seeds.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Position-stratified validation protocol

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: The coefficient of determination (higher is better, and negative values mean worse than predicting the mean) and RMSE (lower is better), computed per fold and averaged across folds, for each of the two phenotypes. The masked language modelling experiments report residue prediction accuracy instead, and the lineage analysis reports the Adjusted Rand Index against established lineage assignments.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Input features; Table 1; Results

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Five protein language models across two families, each with and without domain-specific fine-tuning, and each with CLS and mean embeddings: ESM-2 at 8M (6 layers), 150M (30 layers) and 650M (33 layers), and ESM-C at 300M and 600M. A BERT model trained from scratch on RBD sequences with a 320-dimensional embedding space (BERT-RBD) serves as a domain-specific control. The fine-tuned ESM-2 8M model is called ESM-RBD. The repository also lists other transfer-learning heads (BLSTM and GCN, single-task and multi-task) that the benchmark tables do not use.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model architecture and scale; README: Models

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The position-stratified split is the control, and it is the point of the paper: all mutations at a given residue position are held out together, so a model cannot see another mutation at the same site during training. The paper is explicit that this measures generalisation to unseen positions rather than to unseen mutants. No sequence identity cut-off, clustering step or time split is applied, and the pretrained models' own training corpora are not screened against the DMS sequences. The 347,432-sequence outbreak set used for fine-tuning is drawn from the same protein as the test data by design.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Background; Methods, Leakage control

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Values are means across the five cross-validation folds with a standard deviation, which Table 1 prints for every cell. The spreads are large next to the differences being discussed: the fine-tuned ESM-C 600M stratified binding figure is 0.1823 plus or minus 0.2149. Fold-construction sensitivity was checked by repeating the stratified evaluation under three independent seeds, and the paper reports that the mutation count distributions stay consistent across seeds and folds. No bootstrap interval or statistical test between models is reported.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Cross-validation and Input features; Results; Table 1

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a mutated SARS-CoV-2 RBD sequence, 223 amino acids long for almost all of the outbreak data, with two continuous phenotype labels. The unit that the stratified split holds out is not the sequence but the residue position, so a fold is defined by positions and the sequences follow from them.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data collection and curation and Position-stratified validation protocol

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: One virus for the benchmark itself: SARS-CoV-2, the receptor binding domain of its spike protein. The cross-species betaCov analysis adds Sarbecovirus members including SARS-CoV-1, MERS-CoV, a pangolin virus and bat coronaviruses, whose RBDs target several mammalian hosts (bat, pangolin, civet, camel and human). The phenotype measurements come from yeast display, so yeast is the measurement host.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data collection and curation; Results, Benchmark data collection

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Deep mutational scanning by yeast display, from a published study: ACE2 binding affinity for 116,257 sequences and protein expression level for 105,525. No assay was run for this work; the outbreak and betaCov sequences carry no phenotype measurement at all.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, DMS dataset

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The amino acid sequence of the RBD alone. The model sees it as a frozen embedding, either the last hidden layer or a mean over residues, and nothing else: no structure, no alignment and no metadata enters the regression head.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Input features

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Two settings per model, reported side by side. Without fine-tuning, the released checkpoint's embeddings are frozen and only the regression head is trained, which makes it a linear-probe-style evaluation. With fine-tuning, the model is first adapted to RBD sequences by masked language modelling on the outbreak dataset (15 per cent of residues masked, AdamW, learning rate 1e-5, 100 epochs for ESM-RBD 8M and 15 epochs for the scaling tests, effective batch size 512 across eight A100 GPUs), and its embeddings are then frozen for the same head. BERT-RBD is trained from scratch as a control.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Domain-specific fine-tuning and Input features

strengths.text: The leakage effect is isolated properly: the same frozen embeddings and the same regression head are run under both split rules, so the difference between them cannot be attributed to a different model or a different training recipe.

The split rule is the right shape for a viral protein: holding out whole residue positions blocks the specific shortcut that near-identical viral sequences create, where another mutation at the same site is already in training.

Sensitivity to the fold construction is tested rather than assumed: the stratified evaluation is repeated under three independent fold-assignment seeds and the mutation count distributions are shown to stay consistent.
The code is published, including the split comparison as its own directory, and the licence file grants permissive reuse in the wording of the MIT licence.
strengths.source_locator: README: Random vs Position-Stratified Split; LICENSE.md

limitations.text: One protein and two phenotypes. Everything here is the SARS-CoV-2 spike receptor binding domain scored for ACE2 binding and expression, so the numbers say nothing directly about other proteins or other fitness measures.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data collection and curation

limitations.text: Author-reported: the PRIME authors ran every model and also contribute the fine-tuned ESM-RBD models, which are the rows that recover predictive signal under the strict split.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results, Scaling and fine-tuning overcome the generalization gap

limitations.text: The surviving signal is weak and the spread is wide. The best stratified binding figure quoted in the text is 0.2087 plus or minus 0.1451, and many Table 1 cells are negative, meaning worse than predicting the mean.

The published split comparison does not reproduce the paper's own random-split numbers. The script's docstring states that its random split differs from the one used originally and that the values do not match, so the two sets of random-split figures are not interchangeable.

The underlying sequence data cannot simply be downloaded: the outbreak sequences are identified by a GISAID data set identifier, which requires GISAID access rather than an open file, so a third party cannot rebuild the fine-tuning corpus from the repository alone.

steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/lanl/prime
cd prime
git checkout --detach d940c51aa0f475b8945789e89761fab0687d5b74

conda create -n blackwell_prime python=3.13.12 -y
conda activate blackwell_prime

steps.shell:
cd src/pnlp/ESM_MLM
python lightning-esm.py --esm2_model esm2_8m

The readme states that the model flag defaults to the smallest available model and that batch size may need adjusting for larger ones; for ESM-C the script is lightning-esmc.py. python lightning-esm_mlm_fcn_be.py \

name: Ludaic and Elofsson 2026 RNA structure benchmark
description: Independent benchmark of ten deep learning methods on non-redundant monomeric RNAs and RNA-RNA and RNA-protein complexes released after the methods' training cut-offs, split into easy and hard sets by structural similarity to the PDB training data.

Easy/hard split for monomers: maximum RNA-align TM-score to the PDB training data at a 0.5 cut-off; for complexes: an RNA or protein chain with TM-score >= 0.7 to a pre-cut-off complex is easy.

profile.summary: An independent test of 10 deep learning RNA 3D structure predictors on RNA structures released after the methods' training cut-offs. It covers 79 monomeric RNAs and 158 RNA-RNA and RNA-protein complexes, split into easy and hard sets by structural similarity to the training data. It is for structural biologists choosing an RNA structure predictor and wanting to know how far accuracy holds on new folds.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Materials and methods, Benchmark dataset

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether gains reported by RNA structure predictors carry over to RNA structures they could not have seen in training. Ten methods are tested on monomeric RNA; four of them (AF3, Boltz-1, HF3 and RF2NA) are also tested on RNA-RNA and RNA-protein complexes.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Model generation

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: PDB entries released after 30 September 2021 (complexes) and 13 April 2022 (monomers) were downloaded in January 2026, plus RNA-containing CASP16 targets. Sequences were clustered with CD-HIT-EST at 80% identity, both within the set and against PDB RNA deposited before the cut-off. Structures with pairwise TM-score above 0.7 within the set were removed. Complexes with more than four subunits, on which Boltz-1 ran out of memory, were dropped, leaving 158 complexes; the monomer set has 79 structures. Three long monomers (8BU8, 8TVZ, R1248) that DRfold and DeepFoldRNA did not produce were also left out of the main comparison; the text read does not say whether the 79 counts them. Monomers are easy or hard by a 0.5 TM-score cut-off to the PDB training data; a complex is easy if any protein or RNA chain has TM-score of at least 0.7 to a pre-cut-off complex.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Benchmark dataset and Model generation; Results

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Every method was run with default settings and the same MSAs, generating five models per target; the top-ranked model is scored. Monomers are scored by TM-score (RNA-align), INF, lDDT and GDT-TS; complexes by US-align TM-score, DockQ, F1, fnat, iRMSD and LRMSD. Predictions are trimmed to the residues resolved in the reference. Success rates use CASP16 thresholds, and differences between methods are tested with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

profile.summary: The RNAGym fitness leaderboard ranks sequence models by how well their scores agree with measured deep mutational scanning fitness on non-coding RNA assays. In version 0.1.1 the metric is the signed Spearman correlation between a model's score and the measured DMS fitness, averaged within each of three ncRNA categories (ribozyme, tRNA, aptamer) and then averaged over the three categories with equal weight. It is for someone choosing an RNA or genomic language model to score ncRNA variants without task-specific training.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a model's scores rank RNA variants in the same order as a wet-lab fitness measurement. The leaderboard keeps only assays whose readout reports the function of the RNA molecule itself: ribozyme cleavage, tRNA function and aptamer binding. Version 0.1.1 dropped the 37 mRNA-coding assays, because their readout is protein function, and the two mRNA-splicing assays, because their readout is a regulatory phenotype in human cells. Scores on the excluded assays are kept separately for reference.
sections.source_locator: leaderboard/fitness/README.md: Why we now exclude the mRNA assays

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The assays come from published deep mutational scanning experiments, one row each in the repository's reference sheet with an RNA type, the wild-type construct sequence, a description of the assay and, where one exists, a PDB structure and an Rfam family. The v0.1.1 leaderboard uses the three ncRNA categories: 26 ribozyme assays, 3 tRNA assays and 2 aptamer assays. Processed assay data, raw assay data, alignments, 3D structures, cross-validation splits for supervised use and the baselines' own predictions are distributed as separate downloads, and the data are also published as a Hugging Face dataset under CC BY 4.0.
sections.source_locator: leaderboard/fitness/README.md: Notes. fitness/reference_sheet_final.csv: header and rows. README.md: Resources. Hugging Face API record: cardData.license

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model supplies one score per variant. Within an assay the score is correlated with the measured DMS fitness by Spearman correlation, keeping the sign, so a negative entry means the model ranks fit variants as unfit. Assay values are averaged within each category, and the headline number is the unweighted average of the three category means. All masked language models on the v0.1.1 board are scored the same way: the masked-marginal log-likelihood ratio, masking each mutated position one at a time in the variant's own sequence and summing over the variant's mutated positions. The leaderboard page says this convention matters because 99.4% of the ncRNA variants carry more than one mutation, and that RiNALMo and RNA-FM were rescored to reach it.
sections.source_locator: leaderboard/fitness/README.md: Metric; Leaderboard; Scoring convention

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: Twelve models are listed. Evo 2 (40B) is first with a macro value of 0.2120, then RNA-ERNIE at 0.1937 and Evo 2 (7B) at 0.1904; GenSLM is last at -0.0338. The tRNA column holds the largest values for most models, for example 0.4310 for Evo 2 (40B) against 0.1081 on ribozymes. The page also reports all five released AIDO.RNA checkpoints on the same 31 assays, where the macro value rises with size at every step, from 0.0801 at 1M parameters to 0.1824 at 1.6B.
sections.source_locator: leaderboard/fitness/README.md: Leaderboard; AIDO.RNA across model sizes. leaderboard_signed_3ncRNA.csv

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Create the conda environment from the repository's rnagym_env.yml, download the processed assay data and the baselines' predictions from the project's download host, and aggregate with the script in fitness/. Note that the script at the pinned commit is the earlier one: it computes the absolute Spearman correlation for eight named models and writes results by RNA type, by mutation depth and by both. The leaderboard page says the v0.1.1 scoring scripts, and the performance_fitness.py that reproduces the signed ncRNA aggregate, are on the v0.2 branch.

strengths.text: One scoring convention is applied to all masked language models on the board, and two earlier entries were rescored to reach it, so the ranking is not a mixture of conventions. The page explains why this matters: almost all ncRNA variants are multi-mutants.

The page states what changed in v0.1.1 and why, including the earlier RiNALMo and RNA-FM scoring faults it corrects, and it keeps the superseded mRNA numbers in a separate file with a warning that they predate the rescoring.
strengths.source_locator: leaderboard/fitness/README.md: Scoring convention; Why we now exclude the mRNA assays

strengths.text: The underlying per-category values are published as CSV files beside the tables, and the assay data, raw data, alignments, structures and baseline predictions are all downloadable, with the data also on Hugging Face under CC BY 4.0.
strengths.source_locator: leaderboard/fitness/README.md: Leaderboard. README.md: Resources. Hugging Face API record

limitations.text: The macro mean gives a third of the weight each to sets of 3 tRNA assays and 2 aptamer assays, and the page itself says this gives them outsized, higher-variance weight and that rank differences below about 0.01 are not separations. Most of the leaderboard's spread sits in the tRNA column.
No uncertainty is published with the ranking: the table and its CSV hold one number per model and category, with no interval, seed or replicate.

The code needed to reproduce the v0.1.1 numbers is not at the version the leaderboard is pinned to. The leaderboard page points to a v0.2 branch for the scoring scripts and for the aggregate command, and the fitness/performance_fitness.py file at this commit computes the absolute Spearman correlation over five RNA types for eight models, not the signed ncRNA macro mean.
limitations.source_locator: leaderboard/fitness/README.md: Scoring scripts. fitness/performance_fitness.py: calculate_metrics and main

limitations.text: The leaderboard covers only non-coding RNA function. Readouts that depend on protein function or on splicing were removed from the headline metric in this version, so a model's position here says nothing about those tasks.

run_guide.summary: Get the repository at the pinned commit, build its conda environment, download the processed assay data and the baseline predictions, and run the repository's fitness aggregation script.
prerequisites: conda, to create the environment from the repository's rnagym_env.yml.
Python 3.8 or later, as the repository's badge states.
About 73MB for the processed assay data and 438MB for the model predictions, unzipped, as the README's table gives them.
The code is MIT licensed; the data on Hugging Face are CC BY 4.0.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/MarksLab-DasLab/RNAGym
cd RNAGym
git checkout --detach 2828cf99316d75daaa8d832a2573cbb25bbd35fe
steps.explanation: The repository address is the one the README's own links use. The clone and checkout lines were added here to pin the version the rest of these steps were read from.

steps.title: Create the environment
steps.shell:
conda env create -f rnagym_env.yml
conda activate rnagym
steps.explanation: The two commands the README gives for the RNAGym environment.

steps.title: Download the fitness data and the baseline predictions
steps.shell:
mkdir -p fitness/processed_DMS_files fitness/model_predictions fitness/model_checkpoints
curl -o fitness_processed_assays.zip https://marks.hms.harvard.edu/rnagym/fitness_prediction/fitness_processed_assays.zip
unzip fitness_processed_assays.zip && rm fitness_processed_assays.zip
curl -o model_predictions.zip https://marks.hms.harvard.edu/rnagym/fitness_prediction/model_predictions.zip
unzip model_predictions.zip && rm model_predictions.zip
steps.explanation: The README gives the folder layout it recommends for the fitness task and one worked curl and unzip pair; the two addresses here are the processed assay data and the model predictions rows of its download table, substituted into that pattern.

steps.title: Aggregate per-assay performance
steps.shell:
python fitness/performance_fitness.py \
  --reference_file fitness/reference_sheet_final.csv \
  --combined_dir <folder holding one <DMS_ID>.csv per assay> \
  --performance_dir performance
steps.explanation: The flags are the four the script's argument parser defines. The script reads the reference sheet, then for each DMS_ID looks for <combined_dir>/<DMS_ID>.csv and correlates the DMS_score column with each model's score column. At this commit it reports the absolute Spearman correlation, AUC and MCC for eight named models and writes results by RNA type, by mutation depth and by both. It does not produce the signed ncRNA macro mean the v0.1.1 leaderboard publishes; the leaderboard page points to the v0.2 branch for that.

name: Zero-shot RNA language model benchmark (Wang et al. 2026)
description: Standardised zero-shot evaluation of 21 RNA language models, with DNA language models as reference controls, on attention-based secondary structure prediction, embedding-based RNA classification and likelihood-based mutational fitness prediction.

attributes.task: Zero-shot RNA secondary structure, RNA classification and ncRNA fitness prediction
attributes.scope_note: No fine-tuning. Secondary structure on TS (70 PDB structures) and TS-Hard (15) with a head-layer and threshold chosen on VL1 (40); classification of homologous versus non-homologous sequence pairs on RfamSample (561 Rfam families) and ArchiveII-Nr (1273 RNAs) from FFT or CLS embeddings; fitness on 31 RNAGym ncRNA deep mutational scanning assays (wild-type length <= 440 nt) with WT-LLR or PLL-D scores.
attributes.source_locator: Main text Methods 'RNA secondary structure', 'RNA classification', 'RNA DMS assays'; Supplementary Tables 4-11
limitations: RNA-MSM is from the corresponding authors' group (Zhang et al.); the TS and VL1 sets come from the same group's earlier work (ref. 29).
Models are included per task only where their attention, embeddings or logits were available (Supplementary Table 3).

profile.summary: This paper evaluates 21 RNA language models, with DNA language models as reference controls, on three zero-shot tasks: secondary structure prediction from attention maps, RNA family and type classification from embedding similarity, and mutational fitness prediction from sequence likelihoods. No model is fine-tuned. It helps researchers judge what structural, functional and evolutionary information a pretrained RNA model carries before choosing one.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Each task reads a different part of the model. Secondary structure prediction reads attention weights, RNA classification reads embeddings, and fitness prediction reads token-level logits. Together they test whether a model has learned base pairing, functional similarity between RNAs, and the effect of mutations, without any task training.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Key Points; Data and methods

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Secondary structure labels are base pairs from experimentally resolved 3D structures: a validation set VL1 (40 PDBs) and a test set TS (70 PDBs) curated in earlier work, with sequence identity below 80% and TM-score below 0.45 between them, and a TS-Hard subset (15 PDBs) with no shared Rfam family. RfamSample takes 10 sequences from each Rfam 14.0 family with more than 10 members, giving 561 families. ArchiveII-Nr is ArchiveII reduced with MMseqs2 at 80% identity to 1273 RNAs. Fitness uses 31 ncRNA deep mutational scanning assays from RNAGym with wild-type length up to 440 nucleotides. Models were included if released before 1 August 2025 with open weights; each task uses the models whose attention, embeddings or logits were available.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Data and methods, Datasets

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Structure: attention maps from every head and layer are symmetrised, corrected with average product correction and passed through a sigmoid; one head-layer and threshold are chosen on VL1 by F1 and applied unchanged to TS and TS-Hard, scored by MCC and F1. Classification: embeddings are reduced to fixed length with a Fourier transform (FFT) or taken from the CLS token, and cosine similarities of homologous and non-homologous pairs are compared by MCC, AUC and the overlap ratio (OR), reported as 1 - OR so that higher is better; 100,000 homologous and 100,000 non-homologous pairs are sampled from RfamSample. Fitness: variants are scored by wild-type conditioned log-likelihood ratio (WT-LLR) or pseudo-log-likelihood difference (PLL-D) and compared with assay values by MCC, AUC and absolute Spearman correlation. Metrics are averaged over repeated random samplings where applicable.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Zero-shot evaluation; Statistical analysis; Results

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Download bib.zip from the Zenodo record, then in each task folder run the shell scripts and combine results with metric.py. The authors note that each language model needs its own Python environment and model path, set by the user, and that the scripts are an example for reference.
sections.source_locator: ReadMe.md

strengths.text: One protocol per task, applied to 21 RNA models and DNA controls, with code and data released on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0.
The structure test includes a homology-excluded TS-Hard set; the authors report a Spearman correlation of 0.99 between median MCC rankings on TS and TS-Hard.
Tests three separate model outputs (attention, embeddings, logits), so a model's strengths can be compared across them.

limitations.text: Test sets are small: TS-Hard has 15 structures, and the authors refer to its limited size.
Models are included in a task only where their attention, embeddings or logits are available, so the model set differs between tasks.
The run scripts need per-model environments and model paths set by the user; the authors call them an example for reference.
The data availability statement links to Zenodo record 14430869 but prints record 18218776; the two are different versions of the deposit.

name: AlphaFold and ESMFold benchmark on PDB structures released 2022 to 2024
description: Independent benchmark of AlphaFold2, AlphaFold3 and ESMFold on non-redundant PDB entries released between 2022 and 2024 whose sequences have no close homologue among pre-2022 structures.

attributes.task: Predict monomeric and dimeric protein structures from sequence
attributes.scope_note: Targets are PDB entries from 2022 to 2024 with sequence identity below 40% or query coverage below 70% against structures released up to 31 December 2021; CD-HIT at 90% identity removed redundancy and chains shorter than 20 or longer than 2700 residues were excluded.
attributes.source_locator: Materials and methods, 'Collection of benchmarking datasets and structure selection criteria'; Tables 1 and 2
limitations: Classification thresholds are the authors' own (RMSD and LDDT for monomers, DockQ for dimers).

profile.summary: This is one paper's own benchmark, not a released suite. It scores AlphaFold2, AlphaFold3 and ESMFold on experimental structures deposited in the Protein Data Bank between 2022 and 2024 whose sequences have no close homologue among structures released up to the end of 2021, giving 1666 monomeric and 994 dimeric targets. Monomer predictions are classified from RMSD and LDDT against the experimental structure, dimer predictions from DockQ at the interface. It is useful to someone asking how these three predictors behave on recent targets without usable templates, and the per-structure results are published through the authors' ProModEv portal and a Zenodo deposit.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How accurately three structure predictors reproduce an experimental structure from sequence, on targets chosen to be hard for template-based modelling. For monomers the question is global and local agreement with the crystallographic, cryo-electron microscopy or NMR structure. For dimers it is whether the predicted interface matches the experimental one, which is a harder question than getting each chain right. The paper also asks whether the predictors know when they are wrong, by comparing the predicted confidence pLDDT with the measured accuracy class, and whether remaining template similarity explains the failures, by stratifying each class by a template quality score.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, quality assessment sections; Results

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: All 39,298 protein structures released between 1 January 2022 and 31 December 2024 were downloaded from the PDB and their sequences compared by BLAST with every PDB sequence released up to 31 December 2021, at an e-value cut-off of 0.001. The authors state that these dates were chosen so that the targets are outside the training data of all three predictors. Sequences below 40 per cent identity were kept whatever the coverage, and sequences below 70 per cent query coverage were kept whatever the identity. Entries were then classified as monomer, dimer or higher-order oligomer using PDBe biological assembly annotations plus manual curation, and only monomers and dimers were kept, giving 2799 monomers and 2179 dimers; for dimers an entry was kept even if only one chain lacked a homologous structure. CD-HIT at 90 per cent identity removed redundancy, with the two chains of a dimer concatenated before clustering, and chains shorter than 20 or longer than 2700 residues were dropped. The final set is 1666 monomers and 994 dimers.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Collection of benchmarking datasets and structure selection criteria

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Five structures per sequence were generated with AlphaFold2 v2.2.3 and with the AlphaFold3 server, and one with ESMFold v1.0.3 at default parameters. For monomers the top-ranked AlphaFold model (ranked_0) and the single ESMFold model were aligned with the experimental structure and scored by RMSD and LDDT, with TM-score reported as a further similarity measure. From the two primary metrics each prediction falls into one of three classes: accurate (RMSD at most 3.0 angstroms and LDDT at least 0.7), correct with domain movement (RMSD above 3.0 angstroms but LDDT at least 0.7), and incorrect (RMSD above 3.0 angstroms and LDDT below 0.7). For dimers, ligands were stripped from the experimental files, residue numbering was fixed with the DockQ package's fix_numbering.pl script, DockQ was computed for all five AlphaFold predictions and the best-scoring model kept, and the result was classified by the CAPRI bands: incorrect below 0.23, acceptable 0.23 to 0.49, medium 0.49 to 0.80, high quality 0.80 and above. pLDDT was recorded for every prediction, monomer and dimer, as a per-residue confidence measure on a 0 to 100 scale. Statistics are Spearman correlations and t-tests between metrics.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Tertiary structure predictions; Residue alignment and quality assessment; Quality assessment of predicted dimer structures; Statistical analysis

sections.title: What the comparison found
sections.body: The headline numbers are that AlphaFold2 and AlphaFold3 correctly predicted 88 per cent of the monomers and 77 per cent of the dimers, while ESMFold reached 76 per cent of the monomers and 41 per cent of the dimers; restricted to X-ray and cryo-electron microscopy structures, accuracy rose to 95 per cent for AlphaFold and 83 per cent for ESMFold on monomers, because most failures involved NMR structures. Confidence tracks accuracy poorly at the failure end: of the 200 incorrect AlphaFold2 monomer predictions, 150 (75 per cent) still had pLDDT at least 70, and of the 191 incorrect AlphaFold3 predictions, 158 (83 per cent) did. Residual template similarity is low across the set: of the 1666 monomers, 652 (39 per cent) have no homologous structure at all (template quality 0), 936 (56 per cent) have template quality between 1 and 40, and 78 (5 per cent) above 40, and the incorrect class is enriched in targets with no homologue.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, monomer sections

sections.title: Where the results live
sections.body: The per-structure benchmarking values are not printed in the article. They are served by ProModEv, a web portal the authors built for the purpose, with sortable tables and in-browser structure comparison, and they are also deposited on Zenodo. The Zenodo record holds nine archives: the experimental monomer and dimer structures (RCSB_Monomers, RCSB_Dimers), the AlphaFold2, AlphaFold3 and ESMFold predictions for both, and a pLDDT graph archive. The record is dated 1 January 2026 and carries a CC BY 4.0 licence.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Development of ProModEv; Data availability; Zenodo record 17749805

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Two sets drawn from the same pool: 1666 monomeric and 994 dimeric PDB structures released between 1 January 2022 and 31 December 2024. They come from 39,298 structures released in that window, reduced to 2799 monomers and 2179 dimers by the homology and assembly filters and then to the final counts by CD-HIT clustering at 90 per cent identity and the length limits. Among the monomers, the paper prints 1314 (79 per cent) solved by X-ray diffraction, 160 (9.6 per cent) by electron microscopy and 190 (11.4 per cent) by NMR; these sum to 1664, not 1666, so the paper's method breakdown leaves two monomers unaccounted for; the 994 dimers are 795 (80 per cent) homodimers and 199 (20 per cent) heterodimers, with 760 (76.5 per cent) by X-ray diffraction, 219 (22 per cent) by electron microscopy and 15 (1.5 per cent) by NMR.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, dataset collection; Results, Sequence selection and model generation

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No train or validation split: this is an evaluation-only set and all 1666 monomers and 994 dimers are scored. The separation is temporal and by homology rather than by split: targets were released after the training cut-off of all three predictors and were filtered against every PDB sequence released up to 31 December 2021.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, dataset collection

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Monomers: RMSD (lower is better) and LDDT on a 0 to 1 scale (higher is better) are the two primary metrics, combined into three accuracy classes, with TM-score reported beside them as a topological similarity measure. Dimers: DockQ (higher is better), which combines interface RMSD, ligand RMSD and the fraction of native contacts, classified by the CAPRI bands. pLDDT on a 0 to 100 scale (higher is better) is recorded for every prediction as the predictor's own confidence, not as an accuracy measure.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, quality assessment sections

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Three predictors, compared with each other rather than against a baseline method: AlphaFold2 v2.2.3 run locally, AlphaFold3 through its web server, and ESMFold v1.0.3 run locally at default parameters. There is no template-based or physics-based reference method, and no null model.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Tertiary structure predictions

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Two controls, both stated. A time cut-off: only structures released from 1 January 2022 are used, which the authors say puts them outside the training data of all three predictors. A homology filter: every sequence was BLASTed against all PDB sequences released up to 31 December 2021 at e-value 0.001 and kept only if identity was below 40 per cent or query coverage below 70 per cent; for dimers an entry was kept if one chain met the rule. Residual similarity is then quantified rather than assumed, through a template quality score that is the product of identity and coverage, and reported per accuracy class. The authors note that for dimers an entry could enter with one homologous chain.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, dataset collection; Results, template quality analysis

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: No replicate or interval is reported for any accuracy figure. Sampling variation is handled by selection rather than by averaging: five models per sequence are generated for AlphaFold2 and AlphaFold3 and the best one is taken (the top-ranked model for monomers, the highest-DockQ model for dimers), while ESMFold produces a single model. The statistics reported are Spearman correlations and t-tests between metrics, not confidence intervals on the class counts.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, quality assessment and Statistical analysis

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a PDB entry whose biological assembly is a monomer or a dimer, predicted from its amino acid sequence and compared with the deposited experimental structure. For dimers the unit of scoring is the interface between the two chains.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, dataset collection and dimer assessment

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Unreported. The targets are whatever PDB entries pass the release-date, assembly and homology filters; the paper reports their experimental method, oligomeric state and length but gives no species composition.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Sequence selection and model generation

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Experimental structure determination is the reference. The paper gives the monomer targets as solved by X-ray diffraction (1314), electron microscopy (160) and NMR (190), which sum to 1664 of the 1666 monomers; the dimer targets by X-ray diffraction (760), electron microscopy (219) and NMR (15). No binding, activity or other functional assay is involved.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Sequence selection and model generation

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The amino acid sequence, as retrieved from the PDB entry. Each predictor then uses whatever it normally uses internally: AlphaFold2 and AlphaFold3 build multiple sequence alignments, which the paper notes affects their dimer run time, while ESMFold reads sequence alone. Ligands are not supplied to any predictor, and were removed from the experimental files before interface scoring for that reason.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Tertiary structure predictions; dimer assessment

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot inference from released tools. Nothing is trained or fine-tuned: AlphaFold2 v2.2.3 and ESMFold v1.0.3 were installed from their own repositories and run, ESMFold at default parameters, and AlphaFold3 was used through its public web server.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Tertiary structure predictions

strengths.text: The target selection is independent of the predictors and documented step by step, from 39,298 released structures down to 1666 monomers and 994 dimers, with the date cut-off, the BLAST thresholds, the assembly classification, the CD-HIT clustering and the length limits all stated.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, dataset collection

strengths.text: Residual template similarity is measured rather than assumed: a template quality score is computed for every target and the accuracy classes are broken down by it, so a reader can see that 39 per cent of monomers have no homologue at all.
Predicted confidence is reported against measured accuracy, which exposes how often a confident prediction is wrong on these targets.

The per-structure results are published rather than summarised only: an interactive portal serves them, and the predicted and experimental structures are deposited on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0 as nine archives.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Development of ProModEv; Data availability; Zenodo record 17749805

limitations.text: The accuracy classes rest on thresholds the authors chose themselves (RMSD 3.0 angstroms and LDDT 0.7 for monomers), so the headline percentages move if a reader prefers other cut-offs. The DockQ bands, by contrast, follow the CAPRI standard.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, quality assessment sections

limitations.text: The three predictors are not run under equal conditions. AlphaFold2 and AlphaFold3 get five models per target and the best is selected, while ESMFold produces one, and AlphaFold3 was run through a web server rather than locally, so its exact version and settings are outside the authors' control.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, Tertiary structure predictions; dimer assessment

limitations.text: The homology filter is weaker for dimers than for monomers, because a dimeric entry was kept even when only one of its two chains lacked a homologous structure, so some dimer targets contain a chain with a close template.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Materials and methods, dataset collection

limitations.text: No uncertainty is attached to the reported percentages, and the comparison between predictors is made on class counts with no interval or test between them.

No evaluation code is released. The portal and the Zenodo deposit hold the structures and the per-structure scores, but the custom shell and Python scripts behind them are not published, and the article itself is under a non-commercial licence.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Statistical analysis; Data availability; licence statement

profile.summary: LiPP, the Lipid-Protein Poses benchmark, asks a docking or cofolding tool to place a lipid in its binding site on a protein and scores the pose against the crystal structure. The set holds 331 nonredundant buried, or nonannular, lipid-protein complexes filtered out of BioDolphin version 1.1, all X-ray structures better than 2 Angstrom, covering the eight LIPID MAPS lipid classes and a range of protein functions. Within it, the 36 complexes released after 1 October 2021 form a test set that postdates the training or calibration cutoff of every tool the paper evaluates. Success is a lipid pose whose symmetry-corrected all-atom RMSD is below a cutoff, with a stricter criterion that also requires the pose to pass the PoseBusters physical checks. It is the set to use when choosing a tool for lipid-protein modelling, where small-molecule benchmarks do not apply.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, LiPP Benchmark Set; Materials and Methods, Curation and Comparison of Modeled and Native Structures

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a tool can reproduce the pose of a lipid bound inside a protein pocket. The authors restrict the question to nonannular interactions, meaning lipids held in buried or partly buried pockets as biological ligands, and leave out annular lipids that form a nonspecific shell around a membrane protein. Their reason for building the set is that lipid-protein modelling has no benchmark of its own: the available sets, such as the PoseBusters Benchmark and PDBbind, cover drug-like small molecules, and PDBbind's drug-likeness filter excludes many lipids because of their long aliphatic chains. A second question runs through the evaluation: whether the poses a tool produces are physically plausible at all, which is scored separately from how close they are to the crystal pose.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Materials and Methods, Physically Plausibility; Table 1 footnote

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The starting pool is BioDolphin version 1.1, 127,359 PDB entries each holding one lipid-protein pair. The filters follow the PoseBusters Benchmark recipe: keep X-ray structures better than 2 Angstrom; drop entries with unknown atom types or nonstandard residues, lipids that fail RDKit sanitisation, incomplete entries, and lipids covalently bonded to the protein; drop complexes whose PDB ligand report shows stereochemical errors or atomic clashes; require the minimum lipid to protein distance to lie between 0.2 and 5 Angstrom; and drop entries where the lipid sits within 5 Angstrom of a protein symmetry mate. Redundancy is removed by clustering proteins at 90 per cent sequence identity with DIAMOND and keeping one randomly chosen pair per protein cluster and lipid Chemical Component Dictionary code. The remaining entries were curated by hand against the PDB structures and their papers. What is left is 331 pairs, with 235 unique lipids, lipid molecular weights from 88 to 1,229 Da and protein lengths from 107 to 856 residues. The split is by release date: 36 structures released after 1 October 2021 form the test set and the other 295 the precutoff set. Similarity between the two is assessed with ProteinCartography structure clustering and RDKit atom-pair Tanimoto similarity for the lipids.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Curation of the LiPP Benchmark Set and Curation of the LiPP Test Set; Results, LiPP Benchmark Set; repository test_set.csv

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is a modelled complex per benchmark entry, and the five tools evaluated are given different inputs by design. The cofolding tools AlphaFold 3, Chai-1 and RoseTTAFold AA get a protein sequence and a lipid identifier, a SMILES string or a CCD code. The docking tools AutoDock Vina and DiffDock-L get the experimental coordinates of protein and lipid and have to place the lipid; Vina is given pocket positions inferred from the experimental complex while DiffDock-L is run without pocket information. All tools are run with default parameters and no post-prediction refinement, and one top pose per complex is kept, chosen by that tool's own score. Cofolded complexes are superimposed on the experimental structure through the protein coordinates before measurement, which is unnecessary for the docking tools because they were given the experimental protein. The lipid pose error is the symmetry-corrected RMSD computed with spyRMSD. Success is the percentage of complexes under a cutoff, reported from 2 to 3 Angstrom, and the stricter criterion also requires the model to pass every PoseBusters category, which the paper calls PB-valid. Success rates are reported with 95 per cent confidence intervals from the exact binomial distribution, and are broken down by lipid molecular weight and lipid class. A separate analysis asks how well each tool's own confidence score predicts its error, using ipTM for AlphaFold 3 and Chai-1, inter-PAE for RoseTTAFold AA, the confidence score for DiffDock-L and the affinity score for AutoDock Vina.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Molecular Docking and Structure Prediction Protocols, Physically Plausibility, Comparison of Modeled and Native Structures, Evaluation of Scoring Power; Table 2 footnote

sections.title: The PoseBusters comparison columns
sections.body: Tables 2 and 3 put two further columns beside the LiPP results: PoseBusters v1 with 428 complexes and PoseBusters v2 with 308. These are protein and small-molecule sets, not lipid data, and the paper states that the values in those columns were taken from the literature rather than measured here. Several cells are empty because a tool has not been evaluated on PoseBusters, and the AlphaFold 3 column carries a footnote that the published rates used a 2019-09-30 training cutoff. They are context for reading the lipid numbers, not part of the LiPP set.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Tables 2 and 3 and their footnotes

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The sets and the reproduction code are in the mcshanlab/LiPP_Benchmark repository. The data folder holds the general set, the test set and a small example set as CSV tables of BioDolphin identifiers with metadata, plus PDB files for each complex and for the protein and lipid split apart. To reproduce the published benchmark a user installs whichever of the five tools they want to test, along with OpenStructure and ProteinCartography, records the paths in config.yaml, and downloads the BioDolphin version 1.1 table into the data folder. Each tool has its own folder under scripts/run_tools with a README: for AlphaFold 3 it is three conda environments, a preprocessing script, a run.sh meant to be submitted to a cluster scheduler, a PyMOL superposition step, an OpenStructure scoring step and a summarising script. The analysis folder holds the evaluation, whose compare.py reads one concatenated table of lipid and protein errors for all methods and produces the success rates and figures.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Dataset availability and Guidance for reproducing the publications; config.yaml; scripts/run_tools/AF3/README.md; scripts/analyze/Evaluation/README.md

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Four tables appear in the benchmark's results. The LiPP benchmark set: 331 nonredundant nonannular lipid-protein crystal structures better than 2 Angstrom, with 235 unique lipids, lipid weights from 88 to 1,229 Da and protein lengths from 107 to 856 residues. The LiPP test set: the 36 of those released after 1 October 2021. The precutoff set: the other 295. Beside them, two small-molecule comparison columns taken from the literature, PoseBusters v1 with 428 complexes and PoseBusters v2 with 308. The repository's general_set.csv has 331 data rows and test_set.csv has 36, counted in this pass.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, LiPP Benchmark Set; Tables 2 and 3; repository CSV files

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: A time split, and no training split. The benchmark is evaluation only: the 331 complexes are divided by PDB release date into the 36-complex test set released after 1 October 2021 and the 295-complex precutoff set, because 1 October 2021 is the day after the latest training or calibration cutoff among the five tools evaluated. The paper reports results on the full 331 and on the 36 separately.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Curation of the LiPP Test Set, Precutoff Set

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Success rate, higher is better, under two criteria. The first is the percentage of complexes whose lipid pose has a symmetry-corrected all-atom RMSD below a cutoff, reported from 2 to 3 Angstrom, with 2 Angstrom used in Table 2. The second, in Table 3, additionally requires the model to pass every PoseBusters category, that is to be PB-valid. Success is also broken down by lipid class and molecular weight. Separately, each tool's own confidence score is compared against its RMSD to judge scoring power, and protein structure error is reported as TM-score and RMSD from OpenStructure.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Comparison of Modeled and Native Structures, Evaluation of Scoring Power, Protein Structure Errors; Table 3 title

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Five tools, run by the authors: three cofolding tools, AlphaFold 3 version 3.0.0, Chai-1 version 0.2.0 and RoseTTAFold All-Atom at commit 6c85140; one deep learning docking tool, DiffDock-L version 1.1.3; and one physics-based docking tool, AutoDock Vina version 1.2.3. The paper reports AlphaFold 3 as the best on the full set at 76.1 per cent under the 2 Angstrom criterion, falling to 47.2 per cent on the test set.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Materials and Methods, Molecular Docking and Structure Prediction Protocols; Table 2

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Two. A redundancy filter at the set level: proteins are clustered at 90 per cent sequence identity with DIAMOND and only one pair is kept per cluster and lipid code, so near-identical complexes do not inflate the set. And a time split for training overlap: the 36-complex test set contains only structures released after the latest training or calibration cutoff of the five tools, which the paper lists per tool in Table 1. The authors also compare the test set and the precutoff set for protein structure and lipid chemical similarity rather than assuming the two are alike.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Curation of the LiPP Benchmark Set, Curation of the LiPP Test Set, Protein Similarity, Lipid Similarity

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: 95 per cent confidence intervals on every success rate, calculated from the exact binomial distribution and printed in brackets beside each value. Sampling inside the tools is fixed rather than repeated: AlphaFold 3 used a single random seed with five diffusion samples, Chai-1 a single seed with five samples, RoseTTAFold AA one structure per sample, DiffDock-L ten poses and AutoDock Vina nine poses with no fixed random seed. One top pose per complex is carried into the scoring.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 2 footnote; Materials and Methods, per-tool protocols

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One experimental lipid-protein complex structure, that is one lipid bound in one protein pocket, identified by a BioDolphin identifier. A model's lipid pose in that complex is what gets scored.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Curation; README.md: PDB Structures of the LiPP dataset

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Not stated as such. The entries are PDB crystal structures selected for resolution and quality, and the paper characterises them by protein functional class, including enzymes, immunological receptors, membrane proteins, signalling receptors and lipid transport proteins, rather than by species.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, LiPP Benchmark Set

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: X-ray crystallography. Every entry is an X-ray structure at better than 2 Angstrom resolution, and the lipid pose in that structure is the ground truth; entries whose PDB ligand report showed stereochemical errors or atomic clashes were removed. No binding measurement is used as a label.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Curation of the LiPP Benchmark Set

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: It depends on the tool class, and the paper is explicit that the two classes are not given the same information. Cofolding tools receive the protein sequence and a lipid SMILES string or CCD code only. Docking tools receive the experimental protein and lipid coordinates; AutoDock Vina is additionally given a pocket inferred from the experimental complex, DiffDock-L is not. RoseTTAFold AA additionally used multiple sequence alignments of up to 1024 sequences and up to four structural templates under its default configuration.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Molecular Docking and Structure Prediction Protocols; RoseTTAFold AA

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Out of the box, with no fine-tuning. Every tool was run at its released version with default parameters and settings, and no refinement was applied to its output. The authors note that a curated lipid-protein set could be used for fine-tuning docking force fields or cofolding weights, but that is proposed as future use and not done here.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Molecular Docking and Structure Prediction Protocols; Introduction

strengths.text: The time split is tied to documented training cutoffs: Table 1 lists the training or calibration cutoff of each of the five tools, and the test set contains only structures released after the latest of them.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Materials and Methods, Curation of the LiPP Test Set

strengths.text: Physical plausibility is scored separately from pose accuracy. A pose only counts under the stricter criterion if it passes every PoseBusters category, which stops a numerically close but chemically impossible pose from counting as a success.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Physically Plausibility and Comparison of Modeled and Native Structures

strengths.text: The sets, the per-tool run scripts and the analysis code are published in one repository, with the exact tool versions, commits and default settings written down in the paper.
Every success rate carries a 95 per cent confidence interval, which matters on the 36-complex test set where the intervals are wide.

limitations.text: The unseen-data subset is small. Thirty-six complexes give confidence intervals tens of points wide, so test-set rankings between tools of similar strength are not settled by it.

The two tool classes are not given the same inputs, so the comparison across them is not apples to apples. Docking tools start from the experimental protein and lipid coordinates and AutoDock Vina is also handed a pocket inferred from the experimental complex, while cofolding tools get only a sequence and a lipid identifier. The authors state the two represent distinct modelling regimes rather than directly equivalent methods.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Materials and Methods, Molecular Docking and Structure Prediction Protocols

limitations.text: Coverage is deliberately narrow. The set keeps only buried, nonannular lipids in high-resolution X-ray structures, so annular lipids are excluded by design and large or flexible classes, glycerophospholipids and sphingolipids among them, are underrepresented because quality filtering removes them. The authors say LiPP prioritises structural quality over full coverage and that results should be read in that light.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results, LiPP Benchmark Set

limitations.text: Reproducing the benchmark needs the BioDolphin version 1.1 table downloaded from a separate project site, the five prediction tools installed locally, AlphaFold 3 parameters obtained from Google DeepMind for non-commercial use, and a cluster scheduler for the per-tool run scripts. No licence is stated for the LiPP repository in the metadata read here.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, AlphaFold 3; README.md: Prerequisites; scripts/run_tools/AF3/README.md
