name: Scaffold-Lab unconditional generation
description: Unified evaluation of protein backbone generation methods: 100 backbones per length group are refolded with ProteinMPNN and ESMFold and scored for designability, novelty, diversity and runtime.

attributes.task: Generate protein backbones unconditionally and evaluate them in a shared refolding pipeline
attributes.scope_note: Per group, 100 backbones with 10 ProteinMPNN sequences each are refolded; a backbone is designable if the refolded structure shares a TM-score above 0.5 with it. Short covers lengths 50 and 100, medium 200 to 500 and long 600 to 1000.
attributes.source_locator: Table 2 (length grouping), Table 3, and the Metrics section (designability, novelty, diversity, efficiency, ranking)
limitations: Methods are evaluated only at the lengths the authors could run them at, so the groups hold different method sets.

profile.summary: Scaffold-Lab evaluates protein backbone generation methods in one pipeline. For the unconditional task a method generates 100 backbones at each evaluated length, ProteinMPNN designs 10 sequences for each backbone, ESMFold refolds them, and the backbones are scored for designability (a self-consistency TM-score above 0.5), novelty (the highest TM-score to any PDB structure), diversity (unique Foldseek clusters over total backbones) and efficiency (average seconds per backbone), with the four combined into a ranking by TOPSIS. Lengths are grouped short (50 and 100), medium (200 to 500) and long (600 to 1000), and each group holds only the methods that could be run at those lengths. It is useful to someone choosing a backbone generator and wanting the designability, diversity and runtime trade-off on one page.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Figure 1 caption; Evaluation metrics; Tables 2 and 3

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Four things about a set of generated backbones, plus a description of their physical plausibility. Designability asks whether any sequence folds into the backbone, read from refolding. Novelty asks how far the backbone is from everything already in the PDB. Diversity asks how varied a method's own output is, which matters because a generator that always produces the same fold gives few candidates to choose from. Efficiency is the runtime per backbone. Structural properties (secondary structure content, radius of gyration and MolProbity validity) are described rather than ranked. The first four are combined into a single ranking, because the authors treat the choice of method as a multi-criteria decision rather than a single score.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation metrics, Designability to Ranking

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: There is no fixed target set: the data are generated by the methods under test. For each method and each evaluated length, 100 backbones are generated, and the lengths are grouped: short covers 50 and 100, medium covers 200, 300, 400 and 500, and long covers 600, 800 and 1000. Which methods appear in a group depends on what could be run there, so the short group holds Genie, FrameFlow, FrameDiff, Chroma and RFdiffusion, the medium group FrameDiff, Chroma and RFdiffusion, and the long group only Chroma and RFdiffusion. Seven methods are evaluated across the two tasks, with release dates from January to November 2023. The reference for novelty is the whole PDB, searched with Foldseek.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Tables 1 and 2; Figure 1 caption; Evaluation metrics, Novelty

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Every method goes through the same refolding pipeline: ProteinMPNN designs 10 sequences per backbone, ESMFold predicts each sequence's structure, and the prediction is compared with the generated backbone. A backbone counts as designable when the self-consistency TM-score exceeds 0.5, which the authors prefer to the self-consistency RMSD below 2 angstroms used elsewhere because RMSD becomes less discriminative as proteins get longer; the RMSD criterion is kept for the motif-scaffolding task, where designs are typically under 150 residues. Rather than taking the single best sequence, the headline figure uses a top N strategy with N equal to 3: the mean score of the three best sequences must pass the threshold, on the argument that a backbone accommodating several sequences is more robust. The best-sequence success rate is reported alongside, and success is also plotted against a sweep of thresholds with the area under that curve reported, to avoid depending on one subjective cut-off. Novelty is the highest TM-score to any PDB structure, with a penalty added for backbones that are novel but undesignable. Diversity is unique Foldseek clusters at a TM-score threshold of 0.5 divided by the number of backbones in the group. Efficiency is the mean time per backbone over 100 backbones under identical hardware. The four are combined by TOPSIS, with the relative closeness value reported per length and averaged per group to give a rank.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Material and methods; Evaluation metrics

sections.title: What the ranking found
sections.body: Table 3 reports the four metrics and the TOPSIS closeness per length, with a mean closeness and a rank per group. In the short group FrameFlow ranks first (mean closeness 0.517), ahead of Genie (0.464), Chroma (0.403), FrameDiff (0.365) and RFdiffusion (0.238), although RFdiffusion has the highest designability at length 100 (0.956) and the lowest diversity at length 50 (0.12). In the medium group RFdiffusion ranks first (0.531) ahead of FrameDiff (0.399) and Chroma (0.296). The values show the trade-off the ranking is built to expose: designability falls with length for Chroma and FrameDiff while their diversity rises, and efficiency ranges from 0.11 seconds per backbone for FrameFlow at length 50 to several seconds for Genie and Chroma.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Table 3

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The framework installs from its conda environment file and as a package, and needs a Foldseek PDB database built locally for the novelty and diversity steps. One command runs the unconditional evaluation on whatever backbones are pointed at. Reading config/unconditional.yaml, the defaults are the demo backbone directory, a local ProteinMPNN installation, an output directory, 10 sequences per backbone with a ProteinMPNN batch size of 10, ESMFold as the prediction method, a Foldseek cluster TM-score threshold of 0.5, a seed of 33 and a required Foldseek database path with no default. AlphaFold2 can be used instead of ESMFold through LocalColabFold, configured in the same file. Configuration is through Hydra, so any of these can be overridden on the command line.
sections.source_locator: README: Installation, Usage; config/unconditional.yaml

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: No fixed target set: the evaluated data are generated by the methods under test, 100 backbones per method per evaluated length, each with 10 ProteinMPNN sequences. Nine lengths are evaluated in three groups (50 and 100; 200, 300, 400 and 500; 600, 800 and 1000). The external reference data are the whole PDB, used through Foldseek for the novelty metric. The motif-scaffolding task, outside this record's scope, uses 24 benchmark cases with 100 backbones each.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Figure 1 caption; Table 2; Evaluation metrics, Novelty

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Inapplicable: there is no training, validation or test division, because the benchmark scores freshly generated samples rather than held-out data. The only partition is by sequence length into the short, medium and long groups, and each group holds only the methods that could be run at those lengths, so the method sets differ between groups.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 2; Material and methods

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Four ranked metrics plus descriptive ones. Designability: the fraction of backbones whose mean self-consistency TM-score over the three best sequences exceeds 0.5, higher is better; the best-sequence rate and the area under a threshold sweep are reported beside it. Novelty: pdb-TM, the highest TM-score to any PDB structure, lower is better (more novel), with a penalty term added when the backbone is undesignable. Diversity: unique Foldseek clusters at a TM-score threshold of 0.5 divided by the number of backbones, higher is better. Efficiency: mean seconds per backbone over 100 backbones, lower is better. The TOPSIS closeness value aggregates the four, higher is better. Secondary structure content, radius of gyration and MolProbity validity are reported without ranking. The motif-scaffolding task uses self-consistency RMSD below 2.0 angstroms instead.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation metrics; Table 3 header

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Seven backbone generation methods across the two tasks, with their release dates and categories given: Genie (2023-01, diffusion), FrameDiff (2023-03, diffusion), RFdiffusion (2023-04, diffusion), TDS (2023-06, diffusion), GPDL (2023-10, ESM-based), FrameFlow (2023-10, flow-based) and Chroma (2023-11, diffusion). Of these, Genie and FrameDiff are evaluated on unconditional generation only, TDS and GPDL on the conditional task only, and RFdiffusion, FrameFlow and Chroma on both. The pipeline's own fixed components, ProteinMPNN and ESMFold, were themselves checked against alternatives (ESM-IF1 for sequence design, AlphaFold2 and OmegaFold for prediction).
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Material and methods

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None, and the concept barely applies in the usual sense: the backbones are generated rather than held out, so there is no test set to leak. What the benchmark does instead is measure the related quantity directly, as novelty: every generated backbone is searched against the whole PDB with Foldseek and its highest TM-score reported, so a method that reproduces known folds is visible. The authors add a penalty so that a backbone cannot score as novel while being undesignable. There is no control over what the generators themselves were trained on.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation metrics, Novelty

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Distributions rather than intervals. Each cell rests on 100 backbones and 10 sequences per backbone, and the paper reports the full distributions of self-consistency TM-score and pdb-TM as box plots with medians, plus an area under the threshold sweep so that a result does not hang on one cut-off. T-tests are used where two readings of the same group are compared, for example novelty with and without the designability penalty. No confidence interval is attached to the designability, diversity, efficiency or TOPSIS values in Table 3, and no repeated generation runs are reported.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Figure 2 caption; Table 3

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a generated protein backbone, a single chain of a chosen length, carrying the 10 sequences designed for it and their predicted structures. Aggregation is per method and length group.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Material and methods; Figure 1 caption

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Inapplicable: the backbones are generated de novo and belong to no organism. The only natural data involved is the PDB, used as the reference set for the novelty search, and no species composition is given for it.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation metrics, Novelty

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: None. Every metric is computed in silico from generated and predicted structures. The authors state that these are proxies for high-throughput in vitro experiments rather than measurements, and no wet-lab result is part of the benchmark.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation metrics

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: For the generator, a target length and nothing else: unconditional generation is sampling a backbone of the requested size. For the scoring pipeline, the generated backbone coordinates, from which ProteinMPNN designs sequences; the configuration exposes a CA_only option, which is off by default. The motif-scaffolding task additionally supplies a motif placement specification.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Figure 1 caption; config/unconditional.yaml

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Released checkpoints run at their own settings, with nothing trained or fine-tuned by the benchmark. The fixed parts of the pipeline, ProteinMPNN for sequence design and ESMFold for refolding, are the same for every method, which is the point of the framework; the paper justifies each choice against an alternative.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Material and methods

strengths.text: Every method is scored through one refolding pipeline with the same sequence designer, the same structure predictor and the same hardware, so differences are not differences between each paper's own protocol.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Material and methods; Evaluation metrics, Efficiency

strengths.text: The designability criterion is examined rather than inherited: the authors explain why they use a TM-score threshold instead of RMSD at long lengths, report both the top-three and best-sequence rates, and publish the area under a sweep of thresholds so a reader is not tied to one cut-off.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation metrics, Designability; Figure 2 caption

strengths.text: Novelty cannot be gamed by producing unfoldable structures, because the novelty score carries an explicit penalty when the backbone's own designability falls below the threshold.
The framework is published and runnable: MIT licensed, installable from an environment file, with one command per task, a Hydra configuration for the parameters and a Colab notebook for a quick run.
strengths.source_locator: README: Installation, Usage; LICENSE; Paper: Data Availability

limitations.text: The length groups do not hold the same methods, because each method was only run at the lengths it could handle: five methods in the short group, three in the medium, two in the long. A group ranking therefore cannot be read across groups.

Nothing here is measured in a laboratory. Designability means that a structure predictor reproduces the backbone from a designed sequence, which the authors describe as a proxy for in vitro experiments.

The headline ranking depends on choices the authors made and not only on the measurements: the top-three rather than best-sequence rule, the 0.5 TM-score thresholds for designability and for clustering, the novelty penalty weight set to 1, and the TOPSIS aggregation with its weighting.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Evaluation metrics, Designability, Novelty, Diversity and Ranking

limitations.text: The scores depend on two fixed tools whose own behaviour shapes the result. ProteinMPNN is the only sequence designer and ESMFold the only refolding predictor in the reported runs, and the paper's justification for each rests on supplementary comparisons on a subset.

No repeated generation runs and no interval are reported for the ranked metrics, so a reader cannot tell how much of a small gap between two methods is sampling noise. Table 3 prints mean values without preprocessing.

diagram.title: Scaffold-Lab unconditional evaluation workflow
steps: method generates 100 backbones at one length
ProteinMPNN designs 10 sequences per backbone
ESMFold predicts each sequence's structure
self-consistency TM-score over the top 3 sequences gives designability
Foldseek gives pdb-TM for novelty and clusters for diversity
TOPSIS combines designability, novelty, diversity and runtime into a rank
diagram.caption: The generator is the only thing that changes between columns: the sequence designer, the structure predictor, the thresholds and the hardware are fixed.
diagram.source_locator: Paper: Figure 1 caption; Evaluation metrics

gaps: Only part of Table 3 is recorded here: the full grid of four metrics by method and length, and the long group's values, were not transcribed.

The distributions in Figure 2, the structural property analysis and the motif-scaffolding results are described in the text but their values sit in figures and supplementary files that were not retrieved.
The mathematical detail of the TOPSIS weighting is in the supplementary materials, which were not retrieved, so the weights behind the published ranking are not recorded.
The dataset and grouping details the paper defers to its supplementary materials were not retrieved.
No information is given about repeated generation runs, so the stability of the ranking is unknown.

profile.summary: A retrospective comparison from the RhoFold+ paper on the six natural RNA targets of CASP15. For each of ten methods or CASP15 groups it reports per-target r.m.s.d. and the sum of Z-scores for GDT-TS and TM score, taking the best of five models. sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How close predicted 3D structures of single-chain natural RNAs come to the CASP15 reference structures, per target and summed in CASP15's Z-score style. Designed targets and RNA-protein complexes were left out as outside RhoFold+'s domain.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The targets are R1107, R1108, R1116, R1117, R1149 and R1156. The comparison set holds CASP15 groups (server and expert, including AIchemy_RNA, the authors' preliminary RhoFold entry) and published methods. Five models per method were collected: RhoFold+ was run five times with different sampled MSAs, AlphaFold3 once (five models), and other methods' models were taken from the CASP15 website. Two methods lack reported values for R1107 and R1108, giving eight N/A entries.

profile.summary: This is the cell type annotation comparison reported with scFoundation, not a standalone benchmark. Two published single-cell data sets are used, Zheng68K, a peripheral blood mononuclear cell set, and Segerstolpe, a pancreatic set, and seven methods are scored by macro-averaged F1 for assigning a cell type label to each cell. The saved sources print one number per method and data set: scFoundation 0.736 and 0.914, CellTypist 0.725 and 0.812, SingleCellNet 0.598 and 0.806, ACTINN 0.649 and 0.722, scBERT 0.670 and 0.670, Scanpy 0.547 and 0.540, scANVI 0.395 and 0.521. It is useful as a reference point for annotation methods on two well-known data sets, but the splits and the fitting details are not in the files that are open.
profile.summary_source_locator: Supplementary Table 4 and the macro F1 definition in the supplementary notes; README.md: Cell type annotation

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a method can put the right cell type label on each cell of a published data set. Two data sets are used, Zheng68K from blood and Segerstolpe from pancreas, and the comparison puts a foundation model's embedding against dedicated annotation tools and against plain pipelines. Because the score is a macro average over cell types, a method is judged on the rare types as much as the common ones: the per-cell-type table for Zheng68K shows where that bites, with CellTypist scoring an F1 of 0 on CD4-positive T helper 2 cells and scFoundation 0.17, against 0.85 and 0.86 on CD14-positive monocytes.
sections.source_locator: Supplementary Tables 4 and 5; README.md: Cell type annotation

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The two data sets are taken as published, Zheng68K of blood cells and Segerstolpe of pancreatic cells, and the repository describes the task as cell type annotation on pancreatic and blood data. The repository ships the precomputed scFoundation embeddings for this task as a zip file and points to Figshare for the raw gene expression data, saying the embeddings can also be regenerated through the model's API or local code. How the cells were divided into training and test parts, how many cells were used, and which labels were kept are not stated in any of the saved files: the main text of the paper is behind a paywall and was not read. Supplementary Table 5 lists per-cell-type results for 11 Zheng68K cell types, counting its rows, which is the only label list in the saved files.
sections.source_locator: Supplementary Table 5; README.md: data table; annotation/README.md

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The reported metric is the macro F1 score, defined in the supplementary notes as the average of the per-cell-type F1 scores, where each type's F1 is computed from its true positives, false positives and false negatives. Higher is better. Supplementary Table 4 gives one number per method and data set, with no interval, no seed count and no statistical test. A second table reports the same Zheng68K annotation task for three model sizes, 0.705 for the 3M model, 0.714 for the 10M and 0.736 for the 100M, and states that the experimental setting is the same as the cell type annotation downstream task. Supplementary Table 5 breaks Zheng68K down by cell type with precision, recall and F1 for CellTypist and scFoundation.
sections.source_locator: Supplementary notes, Macro F1 score; Supplementary Tables 2, 4 and 5

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository has a folder for this task. Clone it, unzip the bundled annotation data into a data folder, and open the plotting notebook, which the folder README says holds the results. The raw expression data are on Figshare and the embeddings can be regenerated from the model, through its API or the local model code in the repository. The saved files give no training command, no split file and no scoring script for this task.

strengths.text: The comparison set is wide for a paper table: six other methods on the same two data sets, including dedicated annotation tools, a transformer model and plain pipelines, with every number printed rather than shown only in a figure.
The metric is defined in full in the supplementary notes, as the mean of per-cell-type F1 scores, so the aggregation is unambiguous and rare cell types are not drowned out.
Results are also broken out per cell type for Zheng68K, with precision and recall for CellTypist and scFoundation, which shows which classes drive the macro average.
The task has its own folder in the repository under an Apache-2.0 code licence, with the embeddings used for the figures bundled in and the raw data addressed on Figshare.
strengths.source_locator: README.md: Cell type annotation and Code License; annotation/README.md; LICENSE

limitations.text: The protocol is not in the open files. No split, no cell counts, no fitting procedure and no leakage control for this task appear in the supplementary information or the repository folder, so a new score cannot be made comparable to these numbers from what is public.

Single numbers with no uncertainty. Each method and data set has one macro F1 in Supplementary Table 4, with no repeats or intervals, so small differences, for example 0.736 against 0.725 on Zheng68K, cannot be read as separating two methods.

All the numbers were produced by the authors of the model being promoted, on two data sets of their choosing, and the model licence is separate from the code licence: the repository states that any use of the model weights is subject to a Model License rather than Apache-2.0.

Two data sets, one blood and one pancreas, and the macro average is sensitive to a few hard classes: on Zheng68K CellTypist scores an F1 of 0 on CD4-positive T helper 2 cells and scFoundation 0.17, so the headline figure moves with the fate of individual small populations.

name: MSAlign molecular retrieval evaluations
description: Spectrum-to-molecule retrieval comparisons on NPLIB1, Spectraverse and two MassSpecGym splits, reported in MSAlign Table 3. Formula availability and candidate pools remain separate.

run_documentation.source_locator: Section 5.1; Table 3
run_documentation.summary: The paper describes its common evaluation implementation and candidate pools. Rewire has not executed this benchmark and has no verified pinned runner recipe; original split and evaluator revisions remain unextracted.

profile.summary: This is the retrieval evaluation reported in the MSAlign paper, not a separate suite. Given a tandem mass spectrum and a candidate set of 256 molecules pulled from PubChem by mass, a method must rank the true structure first; recall at 1, 5 and 20 is reported. The current version of the paper scores Spectraverse and MassSpecGym under two splits, a chemical-formula split the authors recommend and MassSpecGym's harder MCES split, and reports methods that need the target formula separately from those that do not. It is for developers of spectrum-to-structure methods who need results that are comparable across models and splits.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper v3: Abstract; Section 5.1; Table 3

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The task is molecule retrieval from a tandem mass spectrum: the method scores each molecule in a candidate set against the spectrum, and is judged on whether the true structure appears at the top of the ranking. The paper frames this as the tractable version of metabolite identification, and treats the choice of data split as part of what is being measured, because splits trade leakage against distribution shift. A second contribution is therefore a measure of how far a split moves the test distribution from the training distribution.
sections.source_locator: Paper v3: Abstract; Sections 2 and 4

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The current version uses two open benchmarks: MassSpecGym, 231,104 curated and standardised spectrum and molecule pairs, and Spectraverse, 488,797 pairs with broader coverage of adducts and ionisation modes, more than half of its spectra from adducts other than [M+H]+. The paper warns that pair counts overstate chemical diversity because the same molecule recurs under different ionisation conditions, and gives unique molecule counts in an appendix table. The first version of the paper also used NPLIB1, the smallest benchmark at 10,633 spectrum and molecule pairs. Candidate sets follow MassSpecGym's standardised protocol: molecules are drawn from PubChem's 118M compounds whose mass matches the target within 10 ppm, prioritising databases of decreasing metabolite relevance, and the pool is cut to 256 candidates per spectrum, which the paper says are typically structurally close to the target.
sections.source_locator: Paper v3: Section 5.1 'Supervised Datasets' and 'Candidates Sets'; Paper v1: Section 5.1

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Recall at 1, 5 and 20 over the 256-candidate pool is the reported metric, higher is better. Methods that assume the target's molecular formula is known are reported in a separate block, because in practice the formula has to be estimated; MSAlign is also run in that setting by filtering candidates to those matching the ground-truth formula, which cuts the pool to about 100. The main split is by chemical formula, so that train, validation and test molecules have distinct formulas, with results averaged over three random seeds of the splitting algorithm; MassSpecGym's official MCES split is reported as well, averaged over its two variants obtained by swapping validation and test, because generating new MCES splits is expensive and the validation set is used for calibration and checkpoint selection. The repository states the ranking rules: candidate 0 is the target, padded candidates score minus infinity, a negative tied with the target ranks ahead of it, fusion weights are calibrated on validation data and metrics come from test data, and results across splits are macro-averaged.
sections.source_locator: Paper v3: Table 3 and Section 5.1 'Data Splitting and seeds'; Section 5.2; README.md: Evaluation rules

sections.title: The split-shift measure
sections.body: Rather than argue about splits, the paper measures them. Each spectrum and molecule pair is encoded as the concatenation of an L2-normalised spectrum embedding and an L2-normalised molecule embedding, and the sliced Wasserstein distance between the training and test distributions is computed with the POT library using 100 random projections, then divided by the value from a random split so that a random split scores 1. On MassSpecGym the MCES and Murcko splits induce the largest shift and the formula and 2D InChIKey splits sit in between; the authors recommend the formula split because it is strictly more challenging than InChIKey, two molecules with the same InChIKey necessarily having the same formula, and still reflects deployment. The repository exposes this as its own command.
sections.source_locator: Paper v3: Section 4, Table 2; README.md: Measure train-test distribution shift

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository reproduces both the MSAlign models and the baselines. Datasets are downloaded and prepared per split and seed, or the prepared archives are downloaded from Zenodo with a checksum check. The four frozen input representations (DreaMS spectra, MolDeBERTa molecules, Morgan fingerprints, with spectrum bins computed on demand) are precomputed on a GPU, MolDeBERTa being a gated Hugging Face model that needs its terms accepted and a token set. One command then trains a model on one split, another evaluates the selected checkpoint once on the test candidates, and a third calibrates and evaluates the score fusion. A separate playground environment scores a spectrum against candidate SMILES from a pretrained checkpoint without any training data.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Applying pretrained MSAlign to my data; Reproducing the training experiments, steps 1 to 6

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: In the current version, two: MassSpecGym (231,104 spectrum and molecule pairs) and Spectraverse (488,797 pairs). The first version also used NPLIB1 (10,633 pairs). Unique molecule counts, rather than pair counts, are given in an appendix table that was not read here.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Section 5.1 'Supervised Datasets'; Paper v1: Section 5.1

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Two kinds. The main split is by chemical formula, so train, validation and test molecules have distinct formulas, averaged over three random seeds of the splitting algorithm; the repository prepares five seeds, formula_seed0 to formula_seed4. The second is MassSpecGym's official MCES split, which requires molecules in different folds to have an edit distance of at least 10, averaged over its two validation and test swapped variants. The paper's shift measure also covers random, InChIKey, Murcko scaffold and Murcko histogram splits.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Sections 4 and 5.1; Table 2; README.md: step 1 and MassSpecGym MCES splits

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Recall at 1, 5 and 20 (R@1, R@5, R@20) over the candidate pool, higher is better, reported as percentages with a standard deviation over the splits. Ties count against the method: a negative tied with the target ranks ahead of it. The split-shift analysis reports a normalised sliced Wasserstein distance, where 1 is a random split and larger means more shift.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Table 3 and Table 2 captions; README.md: step 4 and Evaluation rules

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: In the current version, DeepSet, JESTR, Emb-Cos and the two MSAlign variants in the no-formula block, and MIST, MVP and FLARE in the block that needs the target formula, with MSAlign plus candidate filtering alongside them. The first version also reported FFN and SAIL. The repository's model zoo holds reproductions of DeepSets, EmbCos, JESTR, FLARE and MVP.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Table 3; Paper v1: Table 3; README.md: Repository layout

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The split itself, and it is measured rather than asserted. Molecules in train, validation and test have distinct chemical formulas in the main setting, which the paper argues is strictly stronger than an InChIKey split, and the induced distribution shift is quantified by the normalised sliced Wasserstein distance. The paper's point is that stricter splits such as MCES prevent leakage at the cost of a large shift, with MCES test sets forming a distinct cluster away from the training data.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Section 4; Section 5.1

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Standard deviation over three random seeds of the formula split for the main arms, and over the two swapped variants for the MCES split. The split-shift table reports mean and standard deviation over five splits, except MCES which has two.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Table 3 and Table 2 captions; Section 5.1

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A tandem mass spectrum paired with its true molecule, scored against a candidate set of 256 molecules drawn by mass; candidate 0 is the target.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Section 5.1 'Candidates Sets'; README.md: Evaluation rules

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Inapplicable: the examples are mass spectra of small molecules and their candidate structures, not sequences or cells from a species. The datasets are described by their coverage of adducts and ionisation modes rather than by organism.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Section 5.1 'Supervised Datasets'

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) spectra, with candidate structures taken from PubChem. Spectraverse covers more than 50% of spectra from adducts other than [M+H]+.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Sections 2 and 5.1

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The spectrum and the candidate molecules. Whether the target's molecular formula may be used divides the table into two blocks: the paper reports formula-using methods separately because in practice the formula is unknown and must be estimated, and MSAlign's filtered variant uses the ground-truth formula to cut the pool to about 100 candidates. The frozen representations used by MSAlign are DreaMS for spectra and MolDeBERTa or Morgan fingerprints for molecules, with binned spectra as the simple alternative.
facts.source_locator: Paper v3: Table 3 caption, Section 3, Section 5.3; Paper v1: Section 5.2

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Training on the benchmark's own training split: every model, MSAlign and the baselines, is trained on the training fold of each split, with the validation fold used for checkpoint selection and for calibrating the score fusion, and the test fold evaluated once. Pretrained foundation models (DreaMS, MolDeBERTa) are used as frozen encoders inside this training.
facts.source_locator: README.md: steps 3, 4 and 6, Evaluation rules; Paper v3: Section 3

strengths.text: The split is treated as a measurable choice rather than a convention: a normalised sliced Wasserstein distance quantifies the shift each splitting rule induces, and the paper states which rule it adopts and why.
Methods that need the target's molecular formula are kept in a separate block, so a reader does not compare an oracle-assisted method with one that works from the spectrum alone.
Every number has a spread: standard deviation over three formula-split seeds, or over the two swapped MCES variants, with the reason for the latter stated.

The code is public under the MIT licence with reproductions of the baselines, the prepared data and checkpoints on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0, and the ranking rules written out, including how ties are handled.
strengths.source_locator: README.md: Evaluation rules and Repository layout; LICENSE; Zenodo record 23372807

limitations.text: This is one paper's evaluation, not a maintained suite: there is no leaderboard, and the arms changed between versions. The first version reported four dataset arms including NPLIB1 and the baselines FFN and SAIL; the current version reports three arms without NPLIB1 and a different baseline set, so figures from the two versions are not interchangeable.
limitations.source_locator: Paper v1: Table 3 and Section 5.1; Paper v3: Table 3 and Section 5.1

limitations.text: Scores are tied to the candidate set: the paper states that its NPLIB1 results use the 256-candidate pool it built and cannot be compared with retrieval performance on different candidate sets, and the formula-filtered variant scores on a pool of about 100.

The baselines are the authors' own reruns and some fall below their published numbers: the paper notes JESTR performing slightly below its original report, echoing issues raised in public implementations, and a similar trend for FLARE, while simpler baselines improved when trained for more epochs.

Reproducing it is gated and heavy: a CUDA GPU, several uv environments including a separate one for the graph baselines on a DGL wheel limited to Linux, Python 3.11 and CUDA 12.1, and a Hugging Face token for the gated MolDeBERTa model whose terms must be accepted.

name: GeneRNIB
description: A living benchmark for gene regulatory network inference that scores a submitted ranked TF-gene network with an official pipeline of pathway, TF-binding, regression and virtual-cell metrics on held-out data.

review.method_note: Independent review pass. Both pinned artifacts were re-downloaded and their SHA-256 checked against the source records, the mutable abstract page included, and both matched. A pdftotext -layout run (poppler 26.08.0) on the refetched PDF is byte for byte the contents of the archived gzipped text layer, so the archive is provably derived from the pinned bytes. npm run batch -- check-values reproduced the extractor's figures exactly (64 in_cell, 11 in_row, 6 locator_not_parsed, no wrong_column and no overclaimed_in_row) and wrote the same value-check.tsv. All 81 results were then re-read by review/recheck_tables.py, written for this pass and using neither extract/parse_tables.py nor extract/check_tables.py: it takes each table's column spans from the character offsets of that table's own printed header line, assigns every numeric token on a body line to the column whose header centre is nearest, and matches cells to records through each result's source_locator text rather than its ID, checking printed_value, numeric_value, the printed spread and the system the result's evaluation names. Two negative controls confirmed it fails on a swapped pair of values and on a cell shifted into the neighbouring column. A manual check of 16 cells covered column assignment in all three tables, including Table 2's unlabelled PerturbPFN score line, Table 1's third label and value pair on each of its three rows, and Table 3's middle columns. The printed overall score was re-derived as the equal-weight mean of each row's three normalised columns. The 54 descriptive records were read against Sections 2 to 5, Appendices A to E and Tables 4 to 8 of the pinned PDF.

profile.summary: geneRNIB is an open, continuously updated benchmark for gene regulatory network inference, run as an Open Problems task. A method reads an expression matrix, optionally with chromatin accessibility, and returns a weighted directed network of transcription factor to gene links, capped at 50,000 links by default. The benchmark then scores that network with a fixed pipeline against data the method never saw: held-out perturbation or later-timepoint expression, external transcription factor binding references, gene set collections and a virtual-cell prediction task. Eleven data sets are available, including the 300BCG cohort of blood cells, and the documentation publishes a leaderboard in which scores are normalised per data set, ranked by percentile and averaged so that transcriptomics and multiomics count equally. It is for anyone choosing or publishing a network inference method.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: top, GRN Inference, GRN Evaluation, Component type sections; leaderboard page: Overall score normalization; PerturbPFN: Section 4.3

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether an inferred regulatory network is any use, judged without a ground-truth human network. Instead of comparing to one reference graph, the pipeline asks several different questions of the same submitted network: do the pathways enriched among a transcription factor's predicted targets match the pathways active in held-out expression data, does the network agree with experimental transcription factor binding references, do regulators chosen from the network predict held-out target gene expression, and can a model constrained by the network predict perturbed expression. The PerturbPFN authors describe this as evaluating both the predictive and the biological utility of the inferred network, and note that it therefore tests whether a learned causal structure transfers to regulatory relationships rather than reproducing a curated graph.
sections.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.3 and Appendix E.3; README.md: Component type metrics

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Each data set is split into an inference part, which a method may read, and an evaluation part, which it may not. The repository ships eleven data sets: op, parsebioscience, 300BCG, replogle, xaira_HEK293T, xaira_HCT116, nakatake, norman, MSCIC, soundlife and soundlife_vaccine, and the config file records for each what cells it holds, what kind of perturbation it used, whether inference data are single cell or bulk, the measurement time and the modality. The perturbation types span drugs, chemicals, cytokines, CRISPR knockout, CRISPRa and overexpression, and cells span blood cells and lines such as K562, HEK293T and HCT116. Standard file formats are defined for the expression data, the optional accessibility data, the network prediction and the score, all as AnnData objects. Alongside the data sits a prior folder with supporting files such as the list of known transcription factors and consensus files the metrics use to standardise comparisons. For the 300BCG data set the config records blood cells, chemical perturbation and measurement at time zero and at three months; the PerturbPFN authors describe the official split as inference from baseline profiles of 38 donors, with the three-month profiles and the external references kept for evaluation, and the inference matrix as 380 log-normalised profiles.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Available datasets, File format sections; config.py: DATASET_INFO; datasets documentation page; PerturbPFN: Section 4.3 and Appendix E.1

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is an AnnData file whose prediction slot holds source, target and weight triples, with a default cap of 50,000 links. The scoring entry point is the all_metrics component: it reads the data set identifier from the evaluation data and runs the list of metrics registered for that data set, so the metric set is not the same for every data set. The code implements regression, Wasserstein distance, structural equation modelling, transcription factor recovery, transcription factor binding, replicate consistency, virtual cell and gene set recovery metrics. For the 300BCG data set the registered list at the commit read here is regression, virtual cell, replicate consistency, transcription factor binding and gene set recovery, with the structural equation metric excluded because that data set has a single perturbation condition. Thresholds in the same file record when a metric counts as meaningful, for example 0.001 for the regression metrics and 0.5 for the Wasserstein ones. The output is a score file listing metric identifiers and values. For the leaderboard, only metrics that pass the applicability criteria for a data set are used, raw scores are clipped at zero and min-max normalised per metric within each data set, methods are then ranked by percentile across all applicable data set and metric pairs, and the overall score is the mean of the per-modality median percentile ranks so that transcriptomics and multiomics weigh equally. Higher is better for all metrics. A method that is not part of geneRNIB must first update the consensus prior with its own network before evaluation.
sections.source_locator: README.md: GRN Evaluation, File format score; all_metrics/helper.py; config.py: DATASETS_METRICS and METRIC_THRESHOLDS; leaderboard page: Overall score normalization

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Clone the repository with its submodules, then either install Docker, Java and Viash, or create the conda environment for the baseline methods and the evaluation. Download the benchmark data from the public S3 bucket, 24 GB for the core data or a 380 MB test subset to check the setup. Infer a network for one data set with one of the methods in src/methods, writing an AnnData prediction file. Then run the evaluation, either the Docker script or the local all_metrics script, naming the prediction, the data set and where to write the score. The README says the Docker route writes the scores into output/score_uns.yaml. Whole-pipeline scripts exist for running every method and every metric.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Installation, Download resources, GRN Inference, GRN Evaluation, Run the entire pipeline

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Eleven data sets named in the README: op, parsebioscience, 300BCG, replogle, xaira_HEK293T, xaira_HCT116, nakatake, norman, MSCIC, soundlife and soundlife_vaccine. The config file describes each by cells, perturbation type, inference data type, measurement time and modality, for example 300BCG as blood cells with chemical perturbation measured at time zero and three months, replogle as K562 knockouts at 7 days, nakatake as overexpression in a pluripotent stem cell line. The core download is 24 GB with a 380 MB test subset. No saved file states the number of samples per data set in text: the documentation's table of sample counts is an image.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Available datasets, Download resources; config.py: DATASET_INFO; datasets documentation page

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Inference data against evaluation data, per data set. A method sees only the inference matrix, and the evaluation part, which may be held-out perturbation data, single-cell data or differential expression data, is used only for scoring. For 300BCG the PerturbPFN authors describe the official split as baseline profiles from 38 donors for inference, with the three-month profiles and the external reference networks reserved for evaluation.
facts.source_locator: README.md: File format sections; datasets documentation page; PerturbPFN: Section 4.3, Appendix E.1

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: A per-data-set set of metrics, all oriented so that higher is better. The code implements regression precision and recall, Wasserstein precision and recall, virtual cell, structural equation modelling, transcription factor recovery precision and recall, replicate consistency, transcription factor binding F1 and gene set recovery F1. For 300BCG the registered set at the commit read here is regression, virtual cell, replicate consistency, transcription factor binding and gene set recovery. The leaderboard turns these into percentile ranks after per-data-set min-max normalisation, then averages the per-modality medians.
facts.source_locator: config.py: METRICS and DATASETS_METRICS; all_metrics/helper.py; leaderboard page

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The method list in the config file holds positive_control, pearson_corr, grnboost, ppcor, portia, scenic, geneformer, scgpt, scenicplus, celloracle, figr, granie, scglue, scprint and negative_control. For the 300BCG table in the PerturbPFN paper the comparison was Pearson correlation, PPCOR, GRNBoost2, PORTIA and SCENIC, with Pearson correlation scoring GS-F1 0.4693, TFB-F1 0.1102, R-Precision 0.6154, R-Recall 0.2742 and VC 0.1882, and PerturbPFN 0.6410, 0.1146, 0.2250, 0.1977 and 0.0731. Those baseline numbers were taken from the official geneRNIB score archive for the same data set and link budget.
facts.source_locator: config.py: METHODS; PerturbPFN: Table 3 and Appendix E.3

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The evaluation data and the external reference networks are withheld from inference: a method is given the inference matrix and the transcription factor list only. The PerturbPFN authors state that none of the evaluation resources were accessed during inference, and that the baselines were scored on the same held-out data, references and metric code. One control is explicitly needed from the user: a model that is not part of geneRNIB has to update the consensus prior with its own network first, so that the consensus the metrics use is not built only from the existing methods.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Appendix E.1 and E.3; README.md: GRN Evaluation

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: A seed is part of the method interface, defaulting to 32, and one of the registered metrics is replicate consistency, which the pipeline computes for several data sets including 300BCG. The sources read here do not describe repeated runs, confidence intervals or standard errors for the leaderboard scores, and the PerturbPFN table of 300BCG scores prints single values.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Component type method; config.py: DATASETS_METRICS; PerturbPFN: Table 3

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A whole network. One submission is a ranked, weighted, directed set of transcription factor to gene links for one data set, written as source, target and weight triples, capped at 50,000 links by default. Within the metrics the unit of comparison becomes an edge, a transcription factor, a gene set or a held-out expression profile, depending on the metric.
facts.source_locator: README.md: File format GRN prediction, Component type method; PerturbPFN: Section 4.3

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Not stated for the data sets in the files read. The config file records the cell types PBMC, K562, HEK293T, HCT116 and SEES3 (PSC), a pluripotent stem cell line, and the file format carries an optional organism field per data set, but no saved file gives the organism of any data set.
facts.source_locator: config.py: DATASET_INFO; README.md: File format gene expression data

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Transcriptomics, with multiomics for some data sets. The config file records single-cell or bulk RNA for inference, with chromatin accessibility as an optional second modality for the multiomics data sets, and perturbation types that include drugs, chemicals, cytokines, CRISPR knockout, CRISPRa and overexpression. The evaluation also uses external transcription factor binding references: the PerturbPFN authors name UniBind, ChIP-Atlas and ReMap as the references the official scorer used.
facts.source_locator: config.py: DATASET_INFO; README.md: File format chromatin accessibility data; PerturbPFN: Appendix E.3

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The inference expression matrix, the list of candidate transcription factors, and for multiomics data sets an optional chromatin accessibility matrix. The method interface exposes the RNA file, the optional ATAC file, the transcription factor list, the link budget, the layer, the seed and the data set identifier. Evaluation data and reference networks are not inputs.
facts.source_locator: README.md: Component type method, GRN Inference; PerturbPFN: Appendix E.1

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Open. The benchmark asks only for a network inferred from the inference data, so a method may be fitted on that data, as the correlation and tree-based baselines are, or applied as a pretrained model without gradient updates, as PerturbPFN was. Pretrained single-cell models including Geneformer, scGPT and scPRINT are in the method list.
facts.source_locator: config.py: METHODS; PerturbPFN: Appendix E.1

strengths.text: It does not rest on one reference network. Because no complete human regulatory network exists, the pipeline scores a submission against several independent kinds of evidence, including held-out expression, binding references and gene set activity, and the leaderboard only counts metrics that pass applicability criteria for that data set.

Everything needed to reproduce a score is public and MIT licensed: the code, the file formats, the metric implementations, and the benchmark data in a no-sign-request S3 bucket, with a small test subset for checking a setup first.

The submission format is fixed and the link budget is fixed, so networks of very different density are compared at the same size: a prediction is source, target and weight triples with a default cap of 50,000 links.
strengths.source_locator: README.md: File format GRN prediction, Component type method

strengths.text: The aggregation is written down rather than left implicit: clip at zero, min-max normalise per data set and metric, rank by percentile, then average the per-modality medians so that the more numerous transcriptomics data sets do not outweigh the multiomics ones.

limitations.text: It is a living benchmark, so a score is only meaningful with the revision attached. The metric set per data set is read from a config file at run time, and that file records changes, for example that the structural equation metric is excluded for 300BCG because it has a single perturbation condition and for nakatake because only five control samples remain. A number from an earlier run may not come from the same metric set.

The leaderboard score is a relative one. Raw scores are min-max normalised across the methods present and then turned into percentile ranks, so adding or removing methods changes the numbers, and the published overall score cannot be read as an absolute measure of a network's quality.

Running it is heavy. The core data download is 24 GB, the Singularity images for the advanced inference methods are 48 GB, and the README says the pipeline had to be split into separate inference and evaluation steps because the task is resource-intensive.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: Installation, Download resources, Run the entire pipeline

limitations.text: Evaluating a method from outside the benchmark changes the shared resources: the README requires such a model to update the consensus prior before scoring, which means the prior the metrics use is not fixed across submissions.

name: Sci-Plex highest-dosage holdout benchmark (GIM protocol)
description: Twelve cell line and drug protocols from Sci-Plex in which a model predicts the single-cell expression distribution at a drug's highest dose from controls, the drug's lower doses and the other drugs' doses.

limitations: Dose extrapolation, not unseen-drug prediction: lower doses of the held-out drug are in the context (Appendix D.2).

Table 2 prints only min-max normalised scores; each normalised value depends on which seven rows are compared, so the numbers are not comparable with any other study or comparison set (Appendix D.3). Raw MD, Pearson r and W2 appear only as box plots in Figure 2 with no printed values.
Four HDAC inhibitors in three cell lines and 50 marker genes per protocol; a small slice of Sci-Plex.

profile.summary: This is a dose extrapolation test on the Sci-Plex chemical transcriptomics data. For each of twelve cell line and drug pairs, three cancer cell lines crossed with four HDAC inhibitors, the cells treated at the drug's highest dose are held out, and a model must predict the single-cell expression distribution at that dose from control cells, the lower doses of the same drug and all doses of the other drugs in the same cell line. Expression is reduced to 50 marker genes chosen from the training conditions only. The protocol and the preprocessing come from the Generative Intervention Models paper and its codebase; the record holds the version reported by the PerturbPFN paper, which scores predictions by mean distance, gene-wise Pearson correlation and a 2-Wasserstein distance between the predicted and observed cell distributions.
profile.summary_source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.2 and Appendix D.1 to D.3; GIM: Appendix D.2

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The question is whether a model can predict what a drug does to cells at a dose it has not seen, without being told the drug's target. Each test case gives the model the control cells, the same drug at lower doses and the other drugs at all doses, then asks for the distribution of expression vectors at the highest dose. The PerturbPFN authors describe this as dose extrapolation under unknown perturbation targets, and point out that the held-out drug is not wholly unseen because its lower doses are in the context. Because the prediction is a distribution over cells rather than a mean, the scoring can catch a model that gets the direction of the response right but the magnitude wrong.
sections.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.2, Appendix D.2 and D.3

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The data are the Sci-Plex single-cell drug perturbation data of Srivatsan et al., restricted by the GIM authors to four drugs of the epigenetic regulation pathway in three human cancer cell lines, A549, K562 and MCF7, which gives twelve cell line and drug settings. The GIM preprocessing script lists the four drugs as dacinostat, givinostat, belinostat and quisinostat 2HCl and the doses as 0, 10, 100, 1000 and 10000, with 10000 as the held-out dose. Cells are normalised to the median count of the unperturbed cells, cells with fewer than 200 counts and genes expressed in fewer than 20 cells are dropped, counts are log transformed, then the top 1000 highly variable genes are taken and reduced to 50 marker genes. The script computes both of those steps on the training data only, scoring every gene against control for each drug with a Wilcoxon test ranked by absolute score, then keeping the 50 genes with the largest sum of absolute scores across the drugs, using the training cells only, so the gene set is specific to each held-out protocol. A code comment says it selects the genes most often among the top 50 marker genes, but the code sums the absolute scores and does not use that count. Perturbation features are one-hot drug and dose codes plus a rescaled dose value, and control cells form the observational regime. The GIM paper states that holding out the highest dose leaves 16 perturbations for training in each setting.
sections.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Appendix D.1 and D.2; GIM: Appendix D.2; preprocess_sciplex_data.py

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A method predicts a set of cells for the held-out condition. Three metrics are computed per protocol. Mean distance is the Euclidean distance between the predicted and true mean response, lower is better. Pearson correlation measures gene-wise agreement between those mean responses, higher is better. The 2-Wasserstein distance compares the whole predicted and observed cell distributions, approximated by a debiased entropic Sinkhorn cost with squared Euclidean ground cost, epsilon 0.1, at most 200 iterations and tolerance 10 to the minus 6, computed on equally sized deterministically sampled cell sets, lower is better. For the table, each metric is oriented so that higher is better and min-max normalised across the models being compared within each protocol, then averaged over the twelve protocols, and the three columns are averaged for the overall rank. The PerturbPFN authors say plainly that these normalised scores depend on which models are in the comparison, and give the raw per-protocol distributions only as box plots in a figure. All methods are evaluated on the same held-out cells with the same metric code, and metrics for the baselines were recomputed with that code where prediction arrays were available.
sections.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.2 (Metrics), Appendix D.3 and D.4, Table 2

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The protocol lives in the GIM repository. Create its conda environment, install the package and the bundled cdt source, download the raw Sci-Plex files into data/sciplex/raw, then run the preprocessing script once per cell line, which produces the twelve data sets with their train and test splits. The repository's shell scripts then run GIM and the baselines on the single-cell data, and a notebook makes the figures. The PerturbPFN paper publishes no code of its own, so its own model cannot be run from the sources read here.
sections.source_locator: GIM README.md: Getting Started, Sciplex-3 Data

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: The Sci-Plex single-cell drug perturbation data of Srivatsan et al., reduced to three cell lines, A549, K562 and MCF7, and four epigenetic pathway drugs, belinostat, dacinostat, givinostat and quisinostat 2HCl, giving twelve cell line and drug protocols. Doses in the preprocessing script are 0, 10, 100, 1000 and 10000. Each protocol uses 50 marker genes chosen from its own training conditions. No saved file gives the number of cells in any protocol.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Appendix D.1; preprocess_sciplex_data.py

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: One held-out condition per protocol: the highest dose of one drug in one cell line. The context, that is the training data, holds the control cells, the lower doses of that drug and all doses of the other drugs in the same cell line. The GIM paper states this leaves 16 perturbations for training in each of the twelve settings. The held-out dose in the code is 10000, which the GIM paper writes as 10 micromolar.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Appendix D.2; GIM: Appendix D.2; preprocess_sciplex_data.py

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Three per protocol: mean distance between predicted and true mean response, lower is better; gene-wise Pearson correlation of those mean responses, higher is better; and a 2-Wasserstein distance between the predicted and observed cell distributions, approximated by a debiased Sinkhorn estimator, lower is better. For the ranking in Table 2 each metric is min-max normalised within a protocol so that higher is better, averaged over the twelve protocols, and the three columns are averaged.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.2 (Metrics), Appendix D.3

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Six reference points in Table 2: GIM, CondOT, a multilayer perceptron, a random-forest X-Learner, a Naive baseline that reuses the nearest observed lower dose of the held-out drug, and an Observational baseline that predicts the control distribution. On the normalised average score the random-forest X-Learner ranks first at 0.8870, PerturbPFN second at 0.8394, CondOT third, the multilayer perceptron fourth, GIM fifth at 0.6151, Naive sixth and Observational last at 0.0233. GIM is fit separately per protocol with 100,000 optimisation steps, and the table also reports runtime per protocol.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.2 (Baselines), Table 2, Appendix D.4

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Two. The held-out condition is removed from the context, and the gene selection is computed on the training conditions only, both the highly variable gene step and the marker gene ranking, as the preprocessing code shows. There is no control against the model having seen Sci-Plex elsewhere, and the lower doses of the held-out drug remain in the context by design.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Appendix D.1 and D.2; preprocess_sciplex_data.py

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: None for the scores. Table 2 prints a standard deviation for runtimes only, and no seeds, repeated runs or intervals for the normalised metric columns. The Wasserstein estimate is made deterministic by sampling equally sized cell sets in a fixed way.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Table 2 caption, Appendix D.3

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A held-out experimental condition, one cell line and drug pair at the highest dose. The prediction is a set of single-cell expression vectors over the protocol's 50 marker genes, and the comparison is between that predicted cell distribution and the observed one.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.2, Appendix D.1 and D.2

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human. The three cell lines are the human cancer lines A549, K562 and MCF7.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Appendix D.1; GIM: Section 5.1

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Single-cell RNA sequencing of drug-treated cells, from the Sci-Plex chemical transcriptomics experiment of Srivatsan et al., in which cells were treated with small molecules at several doses and profiled at single-cell resolution. The labels are the measured expression counts themselves after normalisation and log transformation.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Appendix D.1 and reference list; GIM: Appendix D.2

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The context cells and the perturbation descriptors. A model reads control cells, the lower doses of the held-out drug and the other drugs' doses in that cell line, with one-hot drug and dose codes plus a rescaled dose value as the perturbation features. Drug targets and mechanisms are not provided.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.2, Appendix D.1 and D.2

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Either is allowed, and both are in the comparison. GIM is fitted from scratch for each held-out protocol by instance-specific optimisation, while PerturbPFN is applied in context with no parameter updates at test time. The protocol itself only requires that the held-out condition is not in the context.
facts.source_locator: PerturbPFN: Section 4.2, Appendix D.4

strengths.text: The whole cell distribution is scored, not only the mean. The PerturbPFN authors argue this matters because a model can correlate well with the true mean response while getting the size of the response wrong, and the Wasserstein column does separate the methods: GIM scores 0.2934 there against 0.8611 on correlation.

The gene selection is computed from the training conditions only, in both the highly variable gene step and the marker ranking, so the 50 genes a method is scored on are not chosen with knowledge of the held-out dose.

The comparison is run on the same held-out cells with one metric implementation, and the baselines' metrics were recomputed with that same code where the predictions were available, rather than copied from their papers.
The protocol is reproducible from a public codebase: the GIM repository ships the preprocessing script that builds the twelve train and test splits and the scripts that run the baselines on them.

limitations.text: The published scores are not comparable with any other study. Table 2 prints only min-max normalised values, and the authors state that these depend on which models are in the comparison. The raw mean distance, correlation and Wasserstein values appear only as box plots in a figure, with no numbers printed.

It is a narrow slice of Sci-Plex: four HDAC pathway drugs in three cell lines, twelve test conditions in all, and only 50 genes per condition. A result here says little about other compound classes or about genome-wide responses.
It is dose extrapolation, not unseen drug prediction. The lower doses of the held-out drug stay in the context, which the authors say themselves.

No uncertainty is reported for the scores, and the numbers come from one group running every method. Table 2 gives a standard deviation for runtimes only, and no seeds or repeats for the metric columns.

name: POISK co-folding binder-versus-decoy benchmark
description: Scores structure prediction models as zero-shot binder classifiers on 22,494 antibody-antigen complexes drawn from patent filings, by how their interface confidence ranks patent-supported binders against putative non-binders for the same antigen.

limitations: The negatives are putative. 7,647 of the 11,247 are nearest-CDR matches from the Observed Antibody Space and 3,600 are germline-reverted with randomised CDR-H3 at 85% or more total identity; the paper states they have not been experimentally validated for lack of binding.
Binder labels come from an LLM extraction of patent text, audited by the same model and then on a 40-record manual sample.

Excluding antibodies within 95% identity of SAbDab reduces but does not establish absence from any model's training data; the Discussion says incomplete training-data disclosure prevents fully excluding overlap.
Discrimination does not establish where the antibody binds: the best engine contacts an annotated epitope residue in 62.8% of the 1,232 annotated records.
Neither the benchmark code nor a split manifest is offered for download; only the dataset, the folding artifacts and the ipSAE tool URL are.
Author-reported throughout, retrospective, and not reproduced by Rewire.

profile.summary: This record is one paper's evaluation built on the POISK dataset, a collection of antibody sequences and binding metadata extracted from patent filings by a large language model pipeline. The evaluation treats structure prediction models as zero-shot binder classifiers: for each antibody and antigen pair the model folds the complex and its interface confidence scores, ipTM and ipSAE, are used to rank patent-supported binders against putative non-binders for the same antigen. The released folding metrics cover six co-folding models with 22,494 rows each. The paper itself is a bioRxiv preprint that this pass could not fetch, so this page is written from the Zenodo release and is deliberately thin on results.
profile.summary_source_locator: Zenodo record 21775623: Overview and Relationship to the folding predictions

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a co-folding model's confidence in the interface it builds can tell a real antibody-antigen pair from a plausible but non-binding one, without any training for that task. The quantity used is not a predicted affinity but a structural confidence score, ipTM or an ipSAE-style score, so the output is a ranking rather than a measurement. The release warns that a score must be read with the chain pair it was computed on: each ipSAE-style score ships beside a column naming that pair, and a value whose pair is not antibody against antigen is not a binding metric.
sections.source_locator: Zenodo record: Overview; Relationship to the folding predictions

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The underlying data are extracted from patent text rather than curated from a database. The release is a flat CSV of 93,193 rows and 47 columns, one row per unique record, carrying variable region sequences for the heavy and light chains, the target sequence with its provenance (what the release holds, what the patent's GenBank deposit holds and what the named UniProt entry holds), target metadata including gene symbols, UniProt identifiers and source organisms, experimental binding affinities with assay methods such as surface plasmon resonance and biolayer interferometry, and epitope information including linear ranges and structural contact residues. Extraction was done by a pipeline driven by large language models, with both prompts published verbatim: an extractor prompt run once per patent and an auditor prompt run once per record to re-locate its support in the patent.
sections.source_locator: Zenodo record: Dataset Structure and Documentation; Methodology

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The released folding metrics are the evaluation's raw material: one CSV per model for six models, 22,494 rows each, sharing 28 columns whose order differs between files, so a user must align on names rather than position. The metrics include ipTM and ipSAE, and each ipSAE-style score carries the chain pair it was computed on, including a variant that treats the antibody as a single chain. The archives also hold the predicted structures and the predicted aligned error arrays for each model. A caveat the release states plainly is that these predictions were run against dataset version 1.0.1, not against the version 1.1 release they sit beside, so a pairing of metrics to records has to account for the version change, which the release describes as correcting errors found in 1.0.1.
sections.source_locator: Zenodo record: Relationship to the folding predictions; Overview; file list

sections.title: What the release says about its own reliability
sections.body: The release is explicit that the labels come from a generative pipeline and may be wrong. It warns that large language model extraction is subject to hallucinations, naming the misassociation of affinity values with antibody variants and errors in residue indexing as the discrepancies to expect. Against that it ships an audit layer with three columns: a verdict in three tiers, where CONFIRMED means every field was explicitly supported by the patent text, PLAUSIBLE means nothing contradicted the record but support was partial, indirect or inferred, and REVIEW means the record appeared incorrect or could not be established and a human should look, which the release says is not an assertion that the row is false; a flags column naming fields with potential mismatches; and a reasoning column explaining how the value was reached. Users are told to verify critical sequences or affinity data against the original patent before any experimental work.
sections.source_locator: Zenodo record: Quality Control and Algorithmic Audit; Usage and Limitations

limitations.text: The labels are machine-extracted from legal text and the release says so: large language model extraction is subject to hallucinations, with affinity values potentially attached to the wrong antibody variant and residue indexing potentially wrong, and users are told to check critical values against the original patent before any experimental work.

limitations.text: The folding metrics do not match the release they ship with: they were run against version 1.0.1, while version 1.1 exists specifically because errors were found in 1.0.1. Any join between a metric row and a dataset row has to account for that.

limitations.text: Nothing in the released scores is a binding measurement. They are structural confidence values, and the release warns that one computed on the wrong chain pair is not a binding metric at all, so a careless ranking can be meaningless rather than merely noisy.
limitations.source_locator: Zenodo record: Relationship to the folding predictions

limitations.text: No benchmark code, pair list or split manifest is in the release: it holds the dataset table, the folding outputs and the two prompts, so the binder-against-decoy comparison cannot be reconstructed from the saved record alone.

The paper behind the evaluation could not be read in this pass, because its only open copy is a bioRxiv preprint that this run is not permitted to request. Every claim about the pair construction, the negatives, the epitope analysis and the per-model results therefore stays off this page.
