profile.summary: This is Rewire's own study, not a third-party suite. One Evo 2 7B container image, pinned by digest, scored the 3,893 BRCA1 single nucleotide variants of the Findlay et al. saturation genome editing table on three cloud GPUs, and the resulting zero-shot loss-of-function scores were compared with CADD, mammalian phyloP and a consequence rule on the same variants. Alongside the AUROCs it records what each run cost, how much GPU memory it used, how fast it scored, and whether different hardware gives the same per-variant numbers. It answers an operational question rather than a biological one: can this model be run reproducibly on commercial clouds, and does the hardware change the answer.
profile.summary_source_locator: protocol.md: Research question, Data, Workloads. README.md: Status and Main findings. results.json: platforms and brca1_evo2_vs_baselines

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Three things at once. First, whether a pinned Evo 2 7B workload runs at all on each platform, gated by a correctness test that reproduces Arc's expected forward-pass loss of 0.3476563 within 0.001. Second, how well the model's zero-shot score separates loss-of-function from functional BRCA1 variants, overall and split into coding and noncoding, against three baselines that need no GPU. Third, the operational facts a clinical informatician would ask for: GPU memory, wall time, throughput, cost, and whether two machines give the same per-variant score. The authors state the point of the study is an executable recipe rather than another benchmark.
sections.source_locator: protocol.md: Purpose and contribution, Workloads, Metrics and uncertainty

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Everything is pinned and public. The container is built from NVIDIA's PyTorch 25.04 image with evo2 0.6.0 and vtx 1.1.0 and referenced by digest; the weights are Hugging Face revisions with SHA-256 checks before loading, which the authors require because Arc's loader uses pickle; the inputs come from a pinned Arc commit and are hash-checked rather than redistributed. The variant set is the Findlay et al. 2018 BRCA1 saturation genome editing table: 3,893 single nucleotide variants labelled FUNC (2,821), INT (249) or LOF (823), with consequence, a CADD score and mammalian phyloP in the same table. W1 scores each variant in an 8,192 base pair window centred on it, as the Arc notebook does, taking the variant's mean log-likelihood minus the reference's. Labels are LOF against FUNC plus INT.
sections.source_locator: protocol.md: Software and model pins, Data, Workloads. README.md: Controls that matter in a clinical setting

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: AUROC of the negated score, with 95% intervals from 2,000 bootstrap resamples at seed 7, resampling positions and keeping the three variants at a position together. Each baseline is compared with Evo 2 by a paired bootstrap difference in AUROC with its own interval, and no significance threshold is applied. Cross-platform agreement is measured against a reference platform as the maximum and median absolute difference in per-variant scores, the Spearman correlation, and how many variants move more than 1% of the list in rank; W4 repeats the first 200 variants in a second process on the same machine to separate run-to-run from cross-hardware variation. Each platform runs once from a clean committed revision with the same image digest, outputs are committed as evidence, and failed attempts are kept. results.json holds only scientific outputs; timings and costs live in operations.json and are not compared.
sections.source_locator: protocol.md: Metrics and uncertainty, Analysis plan and stopping conditions, Reproduction and tolerances

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: Evo 2 7B reached AUROC 0.875 (95% CI 0.859 to 0.891) over all 3,893 variants, 0.840 on coding and 0.953 on noncoding. Against the baselines in the same table, the paired differences favour Evo 2 overall (CADD 0.804, phyloP 0.781, consequence rule 0.769), but on coding variants the difference against CADD is -0.0008 with an interval from -0.026 to 0.023, so no advantage is detected there, while on noncoding the advantage holds against all three. The two H100 platforms, on different clouds, produced identical scores (maximum absolute difference 0.0, Spearman 1.0), while the L40S differed (maximum 1.3e-3, median 1.2e-4, Spearman 0.983) and its AUROC came out at 0.877 instead of 0.875. Each platform repeated its own scores exactly. Throughput was 2.93 sequences per second on the Google Cloud H100 and 2.91 on the Runpod H100, against 0.61 on the L40S, with peak W1 GPU memory of about 16.8 GiB and costs of USD 4.78, 2.82 and 2.96 for the run.
sections.source_locator: results.json: brca1_evo2_vs_baselines, platforms, agreement_with_reference, same_platform_repeat. operations.json: per-platform throughput, memory and cost. README.md: Main findings

sections.title: The amendment 7 follow-up
sections.body: A later analysis, planned in advance and run without a GPU, asks whether the noncoding advantage holds against current predictors rather than the CADD v1.3 column shipped with the Findlay table. It adds CADD v1.7 for GRCh37, SpliceAI as annotated in that CADD release, and REVEL for missense variants, scored on the same variants and labels with the same grouped bootstrap, and fixes in advance what counts as an advantage holding: the 95% interval of the paired difference above zero. The repository reports the answer as no: against CADD v1.3 the noncoding advantage holds, against CADD v1.7 and SpliceAI it is not detected, and on coding and missense variants CADD v1.7 and REVEL lead. The amendment also states in advance that CADD v1.7 uses SpliceAI as a feature so the two are not independent, and that REVEL may be optimistic on BRCA1 because its training data may include these variants.
sections.source_locator: amendment-007.md: Question, Inputs, Analysis, Caveats stated in advance. README.md: Main findings

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository is the deliverable: a make target runs the offline input fetch, hash checks and tests, and one orchestration command launches a platform, runs the pinned image and assembles results. Each launcher creates a machine with a one-off SSH key and a three-hour limit, copies the committed code and inputs, runs the image, copies results back and deletes the machine whatever happens. Credentials are kept outside the repository and the provider quotas needed are listed. Note what this costs: scoring ran at USD 0.45 to 0.80 per 1,000 variants at October 2026 list prices, and at least 100 GB of disk is needed because the image is about 25 GB unpacked and the two 7B checkpoints are 13.8 GB and 13.0 GB.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Before you start, Run it, Choosing hardware

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One variant set plus two small auxiliary sets. BRCA1: the Findlay et al. 2018 saturation genome editing table, 3,893 single nucleotide variants labelled FUNC 2,821, INT 249 and LOF 823, with consequence, CADD score and mammalian phyloP in the same file. Also chromosome 17 of GRCh37 as the sequence context, 122 labelled exon and non-exon positions from Arc's exon classifier notebook, Arc's four forward-pass test sequences, and synthetic DNA generated from seed 20261007 for the memory probe.
facts.source_locator: protocol.md: Data

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: There is none: the model is used zero-shot, so every one of the 3,893 variants is scored and included in the AUROC. The only partitions are for reporting: coding (missense, nonsense, synonymous) against noncoding (all other consequences), and in the bootstrap, resampling by genomic position so that the three variants at a position stay together.
facts.source_locator: protocol.md: Workloads, Metrics and uncertainty

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: AUROC of the negated Evo 2 score for LOF against FUNC plus INT, higher better, with 95% bootstrap intervals and paired differences against each baseline. The exon workload reports AUROC on 122 positions. The operational measures are sequences per second and peak GPU memory, plus wall times and cost in US dollars; agreement is reported as maximum and median absolute score difference, Spearman correlation and rank movement.
facts.source_locator: protocol.md: Workloads, Metrics and uncertainty. results.json. operations.json

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Three that need no GPU, all taken from the same Findlay table: the CADD score, mammalian phyloP (treated as higher means more conserved means predicted loss of function), and a consequence rule ordering nonsense and canonical splice above splice region above missense above other. The amendment 7 follow-up adds CADD v1.7, SpliceAI and REVEL on the same variants. No other foundation model is run.
facts.source_locator: protocol.md: Workloads. amendment-007.md: Question and Inputs

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Little is possible and the study says so. Evo 2 7B is used zero-shot on a published variant table, and nothing is stated about whether BRCA1 or these variants appear in the model's pretraining data. Where a control was impossible the study marks the result as a demonstration rather than an evaluation: the exon classifier's training data may include the 122 positions, so that workload is labelled a pipeline demonstration. Amendment 7 records in advance that REVEL's training data may include BRCA1 variants, and that CADD v1.7 and SpliceAI are not independent of each other.
facts.source_locator: protocol.md: Workloads, W2. amendment-007.md: Caveats stated in advance

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: 95% intervals from 2,000 grouped bootstrap resamples at seed 7 on every AUROC, and a paired bootstrap interval on each difference from a baseline, with no significance thresholds applied. Hardware variation is measured rather than assumed: the same 200 variants are rescored in a second process on each platform (maximum absolute difference 0.0 and Spearman 1.0 on all three), and cross-platform differences are reported against the reference platform. Each platform ran once, which the protocol says makes the timings receipts rather than a performance benchmark.
facts.source_locator: protocol.md: Metrics and uncertainty, Limitations. results.json: same_platform_repeat

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is a single nucleotide variant in BRCA1, scored in an 8,192 base pair window centred on it, with a functional class from the saturation genome editing assay. For the exon workload the unit is one genomic position out of 122, and for the memory probe it is one synthetic sequence of a given length.
facts.source_locator: protocol.md: Data, Workloads

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human, and one gene. All variants are in BRCA1 on human chromosome 17, GRCh37, and the exon positions come from the same human notebook data.
facts.source_locator: protocol.md: Data, Limitations. amendment-007.md: Inputs

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Saturation genome editing of BRCA1, from Findlay et al. 2018, which assigns each variant a functional class (FUNC, INT or LOF) used here as the label. No new experiment was performed; the study is computational and uses the published table.
facts.source_locator: protocol.md: Data, Workloads

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: DNA sequence only for the scoring workload: a reference window and the same window carrying the variant, 8,192 base pairs, scored with batch size 1 and mean reduction. The embedding workload reads the final-token embedding of layer blocks.26 for forward and reverse sequences. The baselines read precomputed columns (CADD, phyloP) or the annotated consequence, not sequence.
facts.source_locator: protocol.md: Workloads

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot for the variant scoring: no fitting to the BRCA1 labels, only the likelihood difference between the variant and reference windows. The exon workload is a linear-probe style setup using a separately trained classifier on frozen embeddings, and because that classifier may have seen the positions, the study treats it as a demonstration. No checkpoint is fine-tuned.
facts.source_locator: protocol.md: Workloads

strengths.text: The protocol was written and approved before the paid runs, with the platforms, workloads, metrics, bootstrap seed, tolerances, spend cap and stopping rules fixed in advance, and design changes recorded as numbered amendments needing renewed approval.
strengths.source_locator: protocol.md: Status, Analysis plan and stopping conditions, Budgets, Approval and amendments

strengths.text: Hardware is treated as part of the result rather than ignored. Identical H100 runs on two clouds, a different GPU model, and a same-machine repeat are all measured, which is what shows that the L40S changes individual scores while barely moving the AUROC.
strengths.source_locator: results.json: agreement_with_reference and same_platform_repeat. README.md: Main findings

strengths.text: Operational facts are published as receipts next to the scores: image digest, driver, instance type, region, event timestamps, per-workload timings, peak memory, throughput and the price source used for each cost.
strengths.source_locator: operations.json: environment, instance, events_utc, timings_s, cost. protocol.md: Metrics and uncertainty

strengths.text: The follow-up that could have embarrassed the headline was planned in advance and its negative answer is published on the front page: against current CADD v1.7 and SpliceAI the noncoding advantage is not detected.
strengths.source_locator: amendment-007.md: Date and Analysis. README.md: Main findings

limitations.text: This is Rewire's own study run with its own code, not an independent reproduction of a published score, and it makes no biological claim: the protocol states that the variant scores are not a calibrated clinical interpretation and that the BRCA1 and exon tasks say nothing about clinical validity, calibration or ancestry.

One gene, one checkpoint size and one run per platform. The 40B model is described from sources only, two of the four planned platforms came out unavailable, and AWS was deferred and remains untested.
limitations.source_locator: protocol.md: Limitations. results.json: platforms. README.md: Status and Choosing hardware

limitations.text: The score depends on the GPU model, so a result cannot be quoted without the hardware. The L40S gave a maximum per-variant difference of 1.3e-3 and Spearman 0.983 against the H100 reference, and the repository reports that at a threshold fixed on the H100, 72 of 3,893 variants change call on the L40S.
limitations.source_locator: results.json: agreement_with_reference P5. README.md: Main findings

limitations.text: The run receipts do not bind the scientific numbers. The protocol puts timings and costs in operations.json and says they are not compared, the AUROCs are computed afterwards from the committed scores, and the README records that the manuscript-bound verification stamp was not re-run after the text changed.

run_guide.summary: Prepare and verify the inputs offline, then run one platform's workloads from the pinned container image and let the launcher tear the machine down.
prerequisites: Local tools uv, jq, ssh, and the gcloud or aws CLI for those providers.
Provider access: Google Cloud quota of at least 1 preemptible H100, or Runpod prepaid credit; AWS needs On-Demand P and G instance quota and is untested in this study.
Credentials kept outside the repository, for example in ~/.config/evo2ops/env with mode 600.
At least 100 GB of disk: the image is about 25 GB unpacked and the two 7B checkpoints are 13.8 GB and 13.0 GB; the launchers use 200 GB.
Money: scoring cost USD 0.45 to 0.80 per 1,000 variants at October 2026 list prices, and the study's own cap was USD 150.
Licence terms: Evo 2 code and weights are Apache-2.0, the Findlay et al. BRCA1 function scores are free for nonprofit use only, and the study code's licence is stated as to be set at publication.

description: Rewire's own study: simulated rare-disease cases on the intellectual disability panel, ranking the inserted diagnostic variant among a person's rare variants by each score, baseline and combined model.

attributes.task: Rank the diagnostic variant first among a case's rare candidate variants
attributes.scope_note: Main analyses of the three studies, stratum all. The filter checks (bg1pct, nomoi, all1kg, heldout, evee), the frequency sweep, the diagnostic-group strata and the paired contrasts are not ingested.
limitations: gnomAD presence is only partly fixed (README.md, Limits): diagnostics keep their full gnomAD frequency by design and most are absent from gnomAD, while background variants rarely are, so a score that learned gnomAD presence could pick the diagnostic for that reason.
Simulated cases: a ClinVar pathogenic variant is inserted into the rare variants of a 1000 Genomes person in the panel's genes. Lists are short and the people are not patients.
One panel (PanelApp 285, intellectual disability). Consequence is taken over MANE Select transcripts only.
ClinVar diagnostics were partly classified with the same lookup scores, which favours the lookups and both baselines.
A run by the project with its own code. Evo 2 was added after every other result had been seen and is exploratory.

profile.summary: A Rewire study that tests variant scores on simulated rare-disease cases. Each case is one 1000 Genomes person's rare variants in the intellectual disability panel genes (PanelApp 285) plus one inserted ClinVar pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant; a score succeeds when it ranks that diagnostic first. It compares established lookups (CADD, SpliceAI, REVEL, AlphaMissense), a ClinGen rule-based ranking, and added scores such as AlphaGenome AVI, GPN-MSA, GPN-Star and Evo 2.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: opening, Design

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How often a score, a combined model or a baseline ranks the inserted diagnostic variant first among a case's rare candidate variants (top 1). The primary question is whether adding AlphaGenome AVI to the combined lookups raises top 1 on 500 locked replication cases by at least 5 points.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Findings, Design; PROTOCOL.md section 8

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Backgrounds are 1000 Genomes people's variants in the panel's MANE Select exons plus 20 bp, kept below 1% frequency, then filtered to grpmax below 0.1% using gnomAD v3.1.2 with the person and their family left out, and by the gene's mode of inheritance. ClinVar P/LP background variants are removed. Diagnostics are ClinVar P/LP variants with 2 or more review stars, drawn by class quotas. Three studies: 200 SNV cases and 120 indel cases on the first run's 50 people, and 500 replication cases on 50 new people with no diagnostic position reused. The median list on the 500 is 19 SNVs.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Design; PROTOCOL.md sections 1 to 5

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Models are cross-validated (5-fold, grouped by person) on the 200 and 120, and fitted once on the 200 and applied unchanged to the 500. The primary contrast has a 95% paired interval from 1,000 bootstrap resamples of people, read by a rule fixed in advance with a smallest gain of interest of 5 points; secondary scores use Bonferroni-adjusted intervals. A missing score ranks last. The README reports the primary gain as +1.8 points (-0.4 to +4.0), inside -5 to +5.
sections.source_locator: PROTOCOL.md sections 6, 8 and 11; README.md: Findings and Q1

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The README lists the scripts in order, run from rare-disease-v2 with uv and Python 3.12. Several inputs come from the first run's data folder and from sibling repositories, and CADD and REVEL scores are refetched because they are not committed.
sections.source_locator: README.md: How to rerun

facts.value: Three case sets: 500 replication SNV cases (50 new people), 200 SNV cases and 120 indel cases (the first run's 50 people).

name: ClinGen PP3/BP4 local posterior score calibration on held-out ClinVar missense SNVs (Rewire)
description: Rewire-designed CPU calibration benchmark applying Pejaver et al. 2022 and Bergquist et al. 2025 local posterior calibration across temporally held-out ClinVar missense SNVs and non-1000G allele-frequency controls.

attributes.task: Calibrate computational variant predictor scores to ACMG/AMP PP3 and BP4 evidence strength thresholds
attributes.scope_note: Nine score tracks across eight predictors calibrated on CPU from committed variant cohorts and score tables with 1,000 stratified bootstrap resamples.
limitations: Precomputed score tables on temporally held-out ClinVar >=2-star missense SNVs; does not evaluate indels, noncoding variants or predictors absent from public lookup tables.
EVEE (Zenodo 19701997) incorporates ClinVar supervision through 2026-03-20 and has direct target exposure on post_2023_12 and post_2025_03; withheld as a leaked descriptive control.

Earlier predictors (REVEL v1.3, CADD v1.7, AlphaMissense) predate or partially overlap older ClinVar releases; only variants without prior P/LP or B/LB assertions at the cutoff date enter each holdout.

gnomAD reference calibration uses 6,312 missense SNVs (5,155 ClinVar VUS with population AF and 1,157 gnomAD missense background SNVs) to solve the prior-matched local posterior equation with gft = 0.03.
attributes.source_locator: benchmarks/clingen-pp3-bp4/README.md

profile.summary: This is a Rewire-built calibration benchmark, not a published suite. It takes precomputed scores from eight variant predictors and foundation models and converts them into ACMG/AMP computational evidence thresholds (PP3 and BP4, from +1 to +8 and -1 to -8) using the Pejaver et al. 2022 local posterior method with the Bergquist et al. 2025 additions. The scoring set is ClinVar GRCh38 missense SNVs with at least two review stars that were not classified P/LP or B/LB in the 26 December 2023 ClinVar release (or the 30 March 2025 release for the sensitivity cohort). It runs on CPU from committed score tables.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: header and Method; receipt.json

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two things at once. First, how well each predictor separates pathogenic or likely pathogenic from benign or likely benign missense variants, reported as AUROC with a 95% interval and AUPRC. Second, and the point of the exercise, which ACMG/AMP evidence strengths each predictor's scores can actually support: the score value at which the local posterior probability of pathogenicity reaches the cutoff for supporting, moderate, intermediate, strong and very strong evidence, in both directions. Where a predictor's scores never reach a strength on a cohort, the table records that it was not reached.
sections.source_locator: README.md: header and Primary Results; calibration_tables.tsv header; calibration_summary.json posterior_cutoffs

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Variants come from the ClinVar GRCh38 VCF of 8 November 2026, restricted to clean missense SNVs with at least two review stars. Three cohorts are drawn. post_2023_12 is the primary one: 9,450 variants (5,508 pathogenic or likely pathogenic, 3,942 benign or likely benign), of which 4,188 are new since 26 December 2023, excluding every variant already classified P/LP or B/LB in the December 2023 release. post_2023_12_af001 restricts the same cohort to 8,141 variants whose gnomAD v3.1.2 non-1000G genome grpmax frequency is below 0.1%. post_2025_03 is a sensitivity cohort of 3,818 variants held out from 30 March 2025. A separate population reference set of 6,312 missense SNVs (5,155 ClinVar variants of uncertain significance with population frequency and 1,157 gnomAD background SNVs), disjoint from the evaluation cohorts, supplies the population term the calibration needs.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Method, Temporal holdouts; cohort_summary.json; download_manifest.json

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The calibration uses a disease prior alpha of 0.0441, c of 1124, a minimum of 100 points per local window and a population reference fraction gft of 0.03, following Pejaver et al. 2022. Bergquist et al. 2025 adds the +3 and -3 intermediate strengths and one-sided 95% conservative discounted thresholds from 1,000 bootstrap resamples, with seed 20261123. The posterior cutoffs that define each strength are recorded in the output (for example 0.0999 for supporting and 0.6073 for strong). The run took 173.51 seconds on CPU, and the receipt records the hash of every input score table and every output file.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Method; receipt.json; calibration_summary.json

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The calibration re-runs from the committed cohort and score tables with one command and no GPU, then the result hashes can be checked against the committed SHA256SUMS file. A test suite covers the calculation and the file integrity.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Reproduction

strengths.text: The output is in the units a clinical laboratory uses: a score threshold per ACMG/AMP evidence strength, rather than an AUROC alone.
Every run records its parameters, seed, environment and the hash of each input and output file, and the whole calibration re-runs on CPU in under three minutes.
Two leakage controls are applied and the one predictor with known target exposure is labelled and withheld rather than quietly included.

limitations.text: Missense SNVs only, from precomputed public score tables: indels, noncoding variants and predictors without a public lookup table cannot be evaluated.

EVEE is directly exposed to the held-out labels (ClinVar supervision through 20 March 2026) and is reported only as a descriptive leaked control. The files read do not assess exposure for the other predictors.
Thresholds move with the control set: under the rare-variant restriction AlphaGenome AVI loses its PP3 strong threshold and AlphaMissense loses its BP4 thresholds altogether.
This is Rewire's own study, not an external benchmark: there is no leaderboard and no independent review of the calibration.

name: RFD4-Proteina frozen project benchmark, October 9 2026 supplement
description: The frozen benchmark packet published with RFD4-Proteina, which scores design methods on four target sets with a common AlphaFold3 evaluation and reports pass rates and efficiency per GPU-hour.

limitations: Built and run by the RFD4-Proteina authors, who are also the authors of the best-performing method in it.
The published efficiency table counts computational passers, which the card states do not establish experimental activity.

Conditioning differs between some rows: protein binding compares RFD4 backbone conditioning with all-atom conditioning for several baselines, and DNA compares unfixed RFD4 inputs with fixed-DNA baselines.
Only three DNA targets are included.

The methods supplement records timing exceptions, including an approved backbone timing proxy with no measured AlphaFold3 cost for the historical protein-binding all-atom RFD4 arm, and batched remeasurements rather than batch-1 wall time for one comparator's fixed-small-molecule costs.
The exact schedule and checkpoint of each cohort are stated to come from its own native config, which the packet does not publish, so no row is tied to a named checkpoint file.
Not executable as published: the packet publishes summary and per-target rows, not a runner.
No wet-lab endpoint: every pass criterion is computational and is defined by the packet itself.

runner.note: No runner or harness is published with the packet; it publishes result tables and per-target rows.

split.note: An evaluation-only target set with no train or test split.

review.note: The SHA-256 the provenance file declares for summary.csv equals the hash of the retrieved summary.csv, so the packet is internally consistent.
review.reviewer_note: Claude (Opus 5) extraction agent; no human review claimed. Extraction only: a different agent reviews this batch, and nothing here is reproduced.

attributes.scope_note: Four target sets: 24 protein-binding targets, 77 small-molecule binding entries, 37 Atomic Motif Enzyme tasks and 3 DNA-binding targets. Each model, protocol and target has 200 original attempts, including native failures, with no replacement of rejected originals. The provenance file states the scope as 'Frozen project benchmark runs; not a new evaluation of every model Hub revision', and the methods supplement states the release uses frozen cohorts rather than every run in the live catalog, excluding antibody, HalluDesign, full-pipeline BindCraft and Genie3 search arms.

attributes.task: Conditioned biomolecular binder and enzyme-scaffold design, scored by a common AlphaFold3 evaluation and by efficiency per GPU-hour

profile.summary: This is the frozen benchmark packet published with RFD4-Proteina on Hugging Face: a set of result tables, not a runnable suite. It scores design methods on four target sets, 24 protein-binding targets, 77 small-molecule targets, 37 Atomic Motif Enzyme tasks and 3 DNA-binding targets, each model, protocol and target having 200 original attempts. Every attempt is judged by one common AlphaFold 3 evaluation with a pass criterion written per benchmark, and the headline number is efficiency: the mean over targets of structurally distinct passers per unit of GPU time, counting both generation and the AlphaFold 3 evaluation. The packet publishes a summary table of 52 rows, a per-target source table, a methods supplement with the criteria and timing rules, and a provenance file with digests. A reader comparing design methods on cost as well as hit rate can use it; it reports computational passers, which the packet says do not establish experimental activity.
profile.summary_source_locator: METHODS.md: Common accounting and timing, Common AF3 scoring; provenance.json; README.md: Measured design efficiency

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Not just whether a design method succeeds, but what each success costs. Two things are reported for every model, protocol and target: a rate, which is the share of 200 original attempts that pass the common AlphaFold 3 criterion, and an efficiency, which divides structurally distinct passers by the GPU time spent generating them plus the GPU time of the shared evaluation. The packet is explicit about what a pass is not: passers are computational, structural clusters are algorithmic rather than experimentally distinct proteins, and the whole release reuses existing evaluation outputs rather than running anything new.
sections.source_locator: METHODS.md: Common accounting and timing, Common AF3 scoring; README.md: Measured design efficiency

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Four target sets and a fixed number of attempts, with no train or test split: the sets are evaluation panels. The counts are printed in the criteria table, 24 protein-protein interface targets, 77 small-molecule targets, 37 Atomic Motif Enzyme targets and 3 DNA targets, and each model, protocol and target combination has 200 original attempts including native failures and unmatched required motifs, with no replacement of rejected originals. What goes into the release is a frozen selection rather than everything that was ever run: the cohorts come from an evidence freeze file, antibody, HalluDesign, full-pipeline BindCraft and Genie3 search arms are excluded, and the provenance file describes the scope as frozen project benchmark runs rather than a new evaluation of every model revision. Each model's recipe, including steps, checkpoints, sequence designers and input handling, is written out in a table in the methods supplement, which also says that the executed receipts rather than the current upstream README identify what each cohort actually ran.
sections.source_locator: METHODS.md: Supplement methods, Common accounting and timing, Model recipes and adaptations, Common AF3 scoring; provenance.json

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: One shared AlphaFold 3 evaluation decides every pass, with a criterion written per benchmark. Protein binders need binder pTM at least 80 on the native 0 to 100 scale, a minimum interface PAE of at most 1.5 Angstrom and a target-backbone-aligned binder backbone RMSD of at most 2.5 Angstrom, with CA-only RMSD for Genie3, and a target mutation at a hotspot or within 5 Angstrom of binder heavy atoms fails. Small-molecule binders need interface PAE at most 1.5 Angstrom, chain-of-interest ipTM at least 80 out of 100, protein backbone RMSD at most 1.5 Angstrom and ligand RMSD at most 5 Angstrom after protein-backbone alignment; a second, older DISCO criterion on the same 77 targets uses a 2 Angstrom backbone RMSD and a 2 Angstrom ligand centroid displacement with no PAE or ipTM cutoff, and the packet notes the two are not nested. Atomic Motif Enzyme tasks need backbone RMSD at most 2 Angstrom, motif all-atom RMSD at most 1.5 Angstrom and interface PAE below 1.5 Angstrom. DNA targets need interface PAE at most 1.5 Angstrom and a DNA-aligned binder backbone RMSD at most 8 Angstrom. From those verdicts, the ordinary rate is passing originals over 200 and the clustered rate is distinct clusters among passing originals over 200, with clusters computed inside each model, protocol and target by Foldseek at a TM threshold of 0.5 and never pooled. Efficiency is the arithmetic mean across targets of successes divided by generation plus AlphaFold 3 GPU seconds, which the provenance file expresses per GPU-hour and the methods supplement also reports in per-10-GPU-minute units; failed originals and the time they consumed stay in the denominator.
sections.source_locator: METHODS.md: Common AF3 scoring; provenance.json

sections.title: How the timings were taken
sections.body: The timing rules matter as much as the criteria, because efficiency is half the result. Generation time is the complete stored warm generation cost, including required sequence design and intrinsic folding or search, excluding setup, loading, warmup and compilation where those were measured separately, and it is not a diffusion-only timer. Batched costs are amortised across the batch, and the packet says batch shares are not individually measured latency and that the measured batch size is not a claim about maximal throughput. Component columns for MPNN and native folding are already inside the generation figure and must not be added again; a zero means the component did not run or used no GPU and a blank means it was not separately measured. Three exceptions are named rather than hidden: ODesign keeps an approved original-generation timing proxy, Complexa's fixed-small-molecule costs are batched remeasurements rather than batch-1 wall time, and the historical RFD4 protein-binding all-atom arm uses an approved backbone timing proxy and has no measured AlphaFold 3 cost. A configuration with a missing AlphaFold 3 cost drops out of inclusive efficiency comparisons but keeps its successes in rate comparisons.
sections.source_locator: METHODS.md: Common accounting and timing

sections.title: What the tables contain
sections.body: The packet is four files. summary.csv holds one row per panel, model, protocol and dataset, with columns for the criterion, the pass and clustered percentages, successes and unique clusters per 10 GPU-minutes, the number of targets, the number of attempts and a timing note; counting its rows in this pass gives 52, the number the provenance file also states, alongside 2,488 per-target criterion rows in the companion source data. provenance.json records the source release label, the paper commit and path, the metric definition and the SHA-256 digests of the two CSV files. METHODS.md carries the criteria, the timing rules and the per-model recipes. The model card's own efficiency table prints a four-row headline comparison in per-GPU-hour units, with a warning above it that the numbers were measured on the previous release pair in the October 9 2026 frozen benchmark, predate the current checkpoints and have not been remeasured.
sections.source_locator: summary.csv header and rows; provenance.json; README.md: Measured design efficiency

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Four target sets, with the counts printed in the criteria table: 24 protein-protein interface targets, 77 small-molecule targets, 37 Atomic Motif Enzyme targets and 3 DNA targets. The small-molecule set is scored twice, under the current sm_binder criterion and under the original DISCO criterion, on the same 77 targets. Each model, protocol and target has 200 original attempts, so a panel's attempt count in summary.csv is 200 times its targets, for example 7,400 for the 37 AME targets.
facts.source_locator: METHODS.md: Common AF3 scoring; summary.csv

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Inapplicable. These are evaluation-only target sets with no train, validation or test partition. The divisions that exist are by panel, by protocol, one-shot or native pipeline, and by conditioning mode, for example fixed and unfixed DNA inputs.
facts.source_locator: summary.csv, panel, protocol and dataset columns

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Three, all higher is better. The ordinary rate is passing originals over 200. The clustered rate is distinct clusters among passing originals over 200, with clusters computed within each model, protocol and target using Foldseek at TM threshold 0.5, alignment type 1 and minimum sequence identity 0, never pooled across targets or models. Efficiency, the headline, is the arithmetic mean across targets of successes divided by generation plus AlphaFold 3 GPU time; the provenance file writes it per GPU-hour and summary.csv carries it in per-10-GPU-minute columns for both successes and unique clusters.
facts.source_locator: METHODS.md: Common AF3 scoring and Common accounting and timing; provenance.json; summary.csv header

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Thirteen other design methods, each with its executed recipe written out in the methods supplement: RFdiffusion3, BoltzGen, Proteina-Complexa, DISCO, Genie3, BindCraft and BindCraft2 as single-backbone runs, Protein-Hunter, ESMFold2 inversion, RFdiffusion, RFdiffusion2, ODesign and AlphaProtein-novo. RFD4-Proteina itself appears in several arms, with low, medium and high thinking schedules and a search pipeline. The model card's headline table names the best comparator per benchmark: Proteina-Complexa for protein binders, BoltzGen for small molecules, AlphaProtein-novo Codesign for Atomic Motif Enzyme and BoltzGen with fixed DNA for DNA binders.
facts.source_locator: METHODS.md: Model recipes and adaptations; README.md: Measured design efficiency

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None in the train and test sense, because the packet evaluates released models on fixed target sets and trains nothing. Two things stand in its place. The evaluation is common: every arm is judged by the same reused AlphaFold 3 outputs and the same criterion, and no arm may select its outputs using that evaluation. And the clustering that produces the distinct-passer counts is kept inside each model, protocol and target so that clusters are not pooled between arms.
facts.source_locator: METHODS.md: Common accounting and timing, Common AF3 scoring

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: None reported. The packet prints no confidence intervals, standard errors or seed repeats; its sample is the fixed 200 original attempts per model, protocol and target, and the efficiency figure is an arithmetic mean across targets rather than a pooled total. For the DNA panel that mean is over three targets. The packet instead documents the conditions that make rows unequal: timing exceptions, differing conditioning between arms, and the caution that the conditioning panels show observed differences rather than isolated causal effects.
facts.source_locator: METHODS.md: Common accounting and timing, Supplement selection and conditioning comparisons; README.md: Measured design efficiency

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One original design attempt against one target, under one model and protocol. Attempts are counted whether or not they produced a usable output, since native failures and unmatched required motifs are included and rejected originals are not replaced. Results are aggregated to one row per panel, model, protocol and dataset in summary.csv.
facts.source_locator: METHODS.md: Common accounting and timing; summary.csv

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Not stated. The packet names its targets by panel and dataset label, such as the Atomic Motif Enzyme set from M-CSA and the protein, small-molecule and DNA target sets, and gives no species for them in the files read here.
facts.source_locator: summary.csv, dataset column

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: None. Every criterion is computational and is defined by the packet itself, from reused AlphaFold 3 outputs. The model card states plainly that computational passers do not establish experimental activity, and the methods supplement that structural clusters are algorithmic, not experimental successes.
facts.source_locator: METHODS.md: Common AF3 scoring; README.md: Measured design efficiency

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Whatever each method's native conditioning takes, and this differs between arms by design, which is why the packet warns about it. Protein targets are templated from propagated coordinate-conditioning information using stored coordinates, DNA alignment includes the target DNA in both conditioning modes, and the datasets column separates fixed from unfixed ligand and DNA inputs and all-atom from backbone protein conditioning. Per-model input handling, down to hotspot projection and bond-type treatment, is listed in the recipe table.
facts.source_locator: METHODS.md: Common AF3 scoring, Model recipes and adaptations, Supplement selection and conditioning comparisons; summary.csv dataset column

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Released models run under their own native configurations, with no training or fine-tuning in the packet. The supplement states that the exact schedule and checkpoint of each cohort comes from its own native config, and that executed receipts rather than the current upstream README identify what each cohort ran. The protocol column separates one-shot runs from native pipelines, which include a method's own intrinsic selection or search stages, and those stages count toward its generation cost.
facts.source_locator: METHODS.md: Common accounting and timing, Model recipes and adaptations; summary.csv protocol column

strengths.text: The accounting rules are written down in unusual detail: what generation time includes and excludes, that component columns are already inside it, what a zero and a blank mean, and that batch shares are amortised rather than measured latencies.

Exceptions are named rather than smoothed over. The supplement lists the three arms whose timings are proxies or batched remeasurements and says they are not disguised as direct per-design measurements.

The pass criteria are explicit numerical thresholds per benchmark, and where two criteria exist for the same 77 small-molecule targets the packet states that they are not nested and keeps their verdicts separate.

The release is internally checkable: provenance.json records the metric definition, the row counts and the SHA-256 digests of the result tables, and states that the scope is frozen project benchmark runs rather than a fresh evaluation of every model revision.

limitations.text: It was built and published by the authors of the method that wins every panel in it, and the comparator in each row is selected by the packet's own rule.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: Measured design efficiency; METHODS.md: Supplement selection and conditioning comparisons

limitations.text: Conditioning is not matched between arms. The model card states that protein binders compare RFD4 backbone conditioning with all-atom conditioning for several baselines, that the DNA comparison puts unfixed RFD4 inputs against fixed-DNA baselines, and that one comparator's small-molecule route uses fixed ligands.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: Measured design efficiency; METHODS.md: Supplement selection and conditioning comparisons

limitations.text: Every endpoint is computational and defined by the packet, and two of the panels are small: the DNA benchmark has three targets, so its efficiency mean is over three numbers.
limitations.source_locator: METHODS.md: Common AF3 scoring; README.md: Measured design efficiency

limitations.text: It is not executable and not current. The packet publishes summary and per-target rows with no runner, it launches no generation or rescoring of its own, each cohort's exact schedule and checkpoint comes from a native config the packet does not publish, and the model card warns that these numbers were measured on the previous release pair and have not been remeasured on the current checkpoints.
limitations.source_locator: METHODS.md: Common AF3 scoring, Model recipes and adaptations; README.md: Measured design efficiency

name: Virus profiler benchmark against a shared Virus Pathogen Database (Tisza et al. 2026)
description: EsViritu, Kraken2, Centrifuger, Metabuli and Sylph on positive controls, pathogen-free negative controls and mutated mock communities, all querying the same database.

attributes.task: Detect and profile vertebrate, plant and other pathogen viruses from metagenomic reads
attributes.source_locator: Results; Methods 'Tools and parameters', 'Positive controls', 'Negative controls', 'Mock communities'
attributes.scope_note: Only Supplemental Tables S2, S6 and S9 (headline settings) were extracted; per-sample and parameter-sweep tables (S5, S10, S22, S24), regression terms (S1, S3, S11, S12), statistical tests and timing (S15) were not.
limitations: Benchmark built and run by the developers of EsViritu.
All data are synthetic or pathogen-free libraries; no clinical specimen with a reference test.

profile.summary: This is the benchmark published with EsViritu, a virus taxonomic profiler, not an independent suite. Five profilers (EsViritu, Kraken2, Centrifuger, Metabuli and Sylph) are run over a sweep of their own sensitivity and specificity parameters, all querying the same Virus Pathogen Database, on three sets: synthetic reads from seven real virus genomes 75.9% to 95.6% identical to their closest reference, seven pathogen-free negative control libraries, and six mock communities of mutated virus genomes in a bacterial and human background. It measures what a reader of a metagenomic virus report needs to know: how few reads a tool needs to call a divergent virus, how often it calls something that is not there, and how close the profile is to the true composition.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods, Tools and parameters, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Three properties, each with its own set. Sensitivity to divergence and depth: how often a tool reports the right family from synthetic reads of a genome that sits well below the identity of anything in the database, at 1, 10, 100 and 1,000 reads. Specificity: how many false-positive reads and false species a tool reports on libraries that contain no pathogen. Profile accuracy: how close a tool's community profile is to the known composition of a mock community, by detection and by relative abundance, at every taxonomic rank. The authors' framing is that a profiler must do both halves at once, reporting a virus from a single read without ever reporting one that is absent.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Every tool builds its own index from the same genome sequences and the same NCBI taxonomy dump, which is the design feature that makes the comparison about algorithms rather than reference content. The database is Virus Pathogen Database v3.2.4 with one change: the taxonomic labels were taken only from the NCBI TaxDump of 1 June 2026, erasing the custom subspecies labels the standard version uses, and this modified v3.2.4b is deposited on Zenodo. The positive controls are reads synthesised with bbtools randomreads.sh from seven reference genomes spanning 75.9% to 95.6% identity to their closest database entry. The negative controls are seven pathogen-free libraries: human genome mock reads, mouse RNA, anaerobic digester, freshwater, marine water, hot springs and soil. The mock communities are six sets, three of 90 genomes drawn at random from the database and three of 60 genomes with at most one assembly per family, each mutated to a ladder of 80, 85, 90, 95, 98 and 100% identity, with 10,000 viral read pairs in total per community and a background of 100 random bacterial genomes plus the human genome at 50,000,000 reads (50,010,000 reads per community).
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Tools and parameters, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities, Virus Pathogen Database. Zenodo record: files and licence

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Each tool is run over a grid of the parameters that govern its sensitivity and specificity, and a single headline setting is then chosen per tool as the one that maximises specificity while keeping as much sensitivity as possible. Detection in the positive controls is modelled by Firth-penalised logistic regression of detection on tool, depth and genome, with EsViritu as the reference level and Benjamini-Hochberg correction on the tool contrasts, chosen because the most and least sensitive tools separate completely; each genome is summarised by its LD50, the depth at which detection reaches 50%. The negative controls are compared with Friedman tests, post-hoc Wilcoxon tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction and Kendall's W effect sizes. Mock community profiles are scored at every rank for F1, Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and correlation, with abundance calibration by Lin's concordance correlation coefficient in a pooled and a resolvable stratum, and under two definitions of ground truth: strict provenance lineage, and divergence-capped, which caps the rank a tool can be credited with by the genome's identity to its reference.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Tools and parameters, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities; Results

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: On the positive controls Metabuli was the most sensitive tool, reaching 50% detection at or near a single read for most genomes and detecting more often than EsViritu (odds ratio 127.6, p = 0.012); EsViritu held single-read sensitivity down to 85.05% identity, Kraken2 and Centrifuger at their headline settings detected nothing below 85% identity and reached single-read sensitivity only at 95%, and Sylph failed to reach 50% detection in six of the seven genomes at any depth. The negative controls reverse the order: EsViritu in short-read mode and Sylph at all parameters were effectively clean, each with a median of zero false species and EsViritu with one spurious call in total, while the settings that made the other tools competitive on sensitivity produced very high false-positive counts, Centrifuger going from near zero to hundreds of thousands of false hits per library depending on one parameter. On the mock communities the paper reports EsViritu as better than or equal to every other tool on virtually all communities, ranks and metrics, under both ground-truth definitions. The headline settings chosen were EsViritu sr, Centrifuger minimum hit length 100 with minimum score 0, Kraken2 confidence 0.5 with minimum hit group 2, Metabuli precision 1 with minimum score 0.15, and Sylph 10 k-mers per genome.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The benchmark's own inputs and results are deposited on Zenodo, including the modified database and the positive, negative and mock result archives, and the processing and analysis repository is released with a stable tag. The tool under test installs from Bioconda in two commands, needs its database downloaded from Zenodo (about 400 MB decompressed, with a published md5), and is run per sample with a reads file, a sample name and an output directory. Reproducing the comparison itself needs the other four tools built against the same database, which the paper describes but the sources read do not give as commands.
sections.source_locator: Repository: README.md, Installation and Running the tool. Paper: Code and data availability. Zenodo record: files

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Three sets, all synthetic or pathogen-free. Positive controls: synthetic read sets from seven real virus genomes at 75.9% to 95.6% identity to their closest database reference, at four depths with ten permutations each. Negative controls: seven pathogen-free libraries (human genome mock reads, mouse RNA, anaerobic digester, freshwater, marine water, hot springs, soil). Mock communities: six communities, three of 90 genomes and three of 60 genomes, each at 50,010,000 total reads. The shared reference is Virus Pathogen Database v3.2.4b, built from 63 virus families and described elsewhere in the paper as nearly 20,000 genomes.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities, Virus Pathogen Database; Discussion

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: There is no train and test split: none of the tools is trained here, and each is run on every sample. The structure is by experiment and by condition: read depth (1, 10, 100, 1,000) with ten permutations for the positive controls, background type for the negative controls, and the identity ladder (80, 85, 90, 95, 98, 100%) and community design (90 random genomes or 60 one-per-family) for the mock communities. Two ground-truth definitions are applied to the mock communities. The paper is inconsistent on where the divergence-capped metrics apply: the Methods say only the one-per-family communities were measured with them, while the Results say both strict and divergence-capped metrics are reported for all six communities in Fig. S2.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Positive controls and Mock communities; Results

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Per experiment. Positive controls: detection probability, higher better, and LD50, the depth giving 50% detection, lower better. Negative controls: false-positive read percentage and false species counts, lower better. Mock communities: F1 with precision and recall for detection, higher better, and Bray-Curtis dissimilarity, lower better, with Pearson and Spearman correlation to ground truth and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient for abundance calibration, all computed at every taxonomic rank.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities; Figure 3 caption; Results

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Four other profilers at pinned versions: Kraken2 v2.17.1, Centrifuger v1.1.1-r309, Metabuli v1.2.0 and Sylph v0.9.0, each run across a sweep of its own thresholds, for example Kraken2's confidence score from 0 to 0.5 and minimum hit group from 2 to 5. EsViritu v1.3.1 is the tool under test and was run in both its short-read sr and sensitive sense configurations.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Tools and parameters; Results

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The controls here are about reference content and divergence rather than training data. All five tools index the same genomes and the same taxonomy dump, so none has a richer reference than another; the custom subspecies labels were stripped so that no tool is credited or penalised for labels only one database version carries; the positive control genomes are deliberately 75.9% to 95.6% identical to anything in the database; and the mock community genomes are mutated away from their references on a ladder down to 80%. The divergence-capped ground truth caps the rank a tool may be credited with at a given identity, which stops a tool scoring for a species call it cannot support.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Tools and parameters, Positive controls, Mock communities; Results

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Replication and formal tests, but not intervals on most headline numbers. Ten independent permutations per genome and depth in the positive controls, feeding a Firth-penalised logistic regression with Benjamini-Hochberg corrected tool contrasts and reported odds ratios with p values; Friedman tests with post-hoc Wilcoxon tests, Benjamini-Hochberg correction and Kendall's W for the negative controls; six independent communities for the mock analysis, with results reported under both ground-truth definitions as a robustness check. Divergence is treated descriptively because it is confounded with genome, one genome per identity level.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities; Results

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: Depends on the experiment. Positive controls: one synthetic read set from one genome at one depth, scored as detected or not when the tool reports the corresponding family. Negative controls: one pathogen-free sequencing library, scored by the false-positive reads and false species in it. Mock communities: one community profile, compared with the known composition at each taxonomic rank.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Viruses of humans, animals and plants as the targets, drawn from the 63 families in the Virus Pathogen Database. The backgrounds are host and environmental: human, mouse, 100 random bacterial genomes, and environmental metagenomes from an anaerobic digester, freshwater, marine water, hot springs and soil. The database itself was screened against human, dog, mouse, cow, macaque, chicken, cat and rat genomes to mask host-derived regions.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Virus Pathogen Database, Negative controls, Mock communities

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: None in the wet-lab sense for the benchmark itself: the positive controls and mock communities are simulated reads, generated with bbtools randomreads.sh and with InSilicoSeq using log-normal abundance distributions and a NovaSeq error model. The negative controls are real sequencing libraries, but from pathogen-free host, synthetic and environmental material rather than from a clinical specimen with a reference test.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Sequencing reads and the shared reference database, nothing else. Each tool builds its index from the same FASTA and taxonomy dump and is given the read set; EsViritu takes a FASTQ (gzipped allowed), a sample name and an output directory, with paired, unpaired or interleaved input.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Tools and parameters. Repository: README.md, Running the tool

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: No training. Each tool is a reference-based classifier run at fixed parameter settings; the only tuning is the published parameter sweep, from which one headline setting per tool is chosen to maximise specificity while keeping as much sensitivity as possible. The sweep and the headline choice are made on the same benchmark data.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Tools and parameters; Results

strengths.text: The reference set is held constant. All five tools build their index from the same genomes and the same taxonomy dump, and the subspecies labels unique to one database version were removed so no tool is scored on labels another cannot see.

Each tool is swept across its own sensitivity and specificity parameters rather than run at one setting, which is what exposes that the settings making a tool competitive on detection are the ones that flood the negative controls.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Tools and parameters; Results

strengths.text: Sensitivity and specificity are tested on separate purpose-built sets, with replication and formal statistics: ten permutations per genome and depth with a regression that handles complete separation, and Friedman with post-hoc Wilcoxon tests on the negative controls.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Positive controls and Negative controls

strengths.text: Two ground-truth definitions are reported rather than one. The divergence-capped truth refuses credit for a species call on a genome too divergent to support it, and results under the strict definition are reported alongside as a robustness check.

limitations.text: The benchmark was built and run by the developers of the tool it favours, and EsViritu's own database is the shared reference, so the comparison is on home ground even though the content is identical for all tools.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Methods, Tools and parameters; Code and data availability

limitations.text: No clinical specimen is involved. Every positive signal is simulated and every negative is a pathogen-free library, so the benchmark says nothing about agreement with a reference diagnostic test on real patient samples.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities

limitations.text: The positive control panel is seven genomes, one per identity level, and the paper says identity is therefore confounded with genome and treats divergence descriptively. The headline parameter settings are also chosen on the same data they are then reported on.

One comparison is not like for like: Sylph reports a k-mer containment sequence abundance that the authors say was not readily comparable to the other abundance metrics, so its abundance results are not on the same footing.

The article is a preprint record under a non-commercial licence, and most per-tool numbers live in supplementary tables rather than the text, so the figures a reader can quote from the article itself are limited.

diagram.title: Tisza et al. virus profiler benchmark workflow
steps: one shared reference: Virus Pathogen Database v3.2.4b with NCBI TaxDump labels
each of five tools builds its own index from those sequences
three input sets: synthetic reads from seven divergent genomes, seven pathogen-free libraries, six mutated mock communities
each tool run across its parameter grid, then one headline setting chosen
detection probability and LD50, false-positive reads and species, F1 and Bray-Curtis per rank
Firth regression, Friedman and Wilcoxon tests, under strict and divergence-capped ground truth
diagram.caption: How the five profilers are compared on the same database.
diagram.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Tools and parameters, Positive controls, Negative controls, Mock communities

gaps: The supplementary tables that hold the per-tool, per-parameter numbers (including Tables S2, S6 and S9, which the three stored protocols are drawn from) were not fetched, so only the figures printed in the article text are recorded.
No per-tool F1 or Bray-Curtis value is printed in the article text; those appear in Figure 3B and the supplementary tables.
The benchmark's own processing and analysis repository is https://github.com/tiszalab/esviritu_benchmarks, release 2026-09-29a; its code was not saved or reviewed here.
The paper gives counts of genomes in the database only loosely (63 families, nearly 20,000 genomes in the Discussion), so no exact database size is recorded.

run_guide.summary: Install the tool under test from Bioconda, download and verify its database, and profile a read set; the benchmark's own inputs and results are on Zenodo.
prerequisites: conda, with mamba preferred for creating the environment.
About 400 MB of disk for the decompressed database, downloaded from Zenodo and checked against its published md5.
Reads in FASTQ format, gzipped allowed, as paired, unpaired or interleaved files.
The tool is MIT licensed and the benchmark data deposit is CC BY 4.0; the article itself is CC BY-NC 4.0.

Reproducing the full comparison also needs Kraken2 v2.17.1, Centrifuger v1.1.1-r309, Metabuli v1.2.0 and Sylph v0.9.0 built against the same database, which the sources read describe but do not give as commands.

name: SegmentNT human genome annotation
description: Fourteen genomic-element annotation tasks from the SegmentNT study, with complete per-nucleotide MCC and auPRC comparisons from Supplementary Tables 2 and 3. Each element and metric remains a separate comparison.

profile.summary: This is the human genome annotation evaluation from the SegmentNT paper. A model must label every nucleotide of a DNA sequence with 14 types of genomic element, from protein-coding genes and exons to splice sites, promoters, enhancers and CTCF-bound sites. Performance is measured per element and per nucleotide, as MCC and area under the precision-recall curve on held-out chromosomes 20 and 21. It is used to compare segmentation models and architectures on how precisely they place genomic features.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results and Methods; Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 captions

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Per-nucleotide localisation of 14 element types, split into gene elements (protein-coding genes, lncRNAs, 5' UTR, 3' UTR, exon, intron, splice acceptor and donor sites) and regulatory elements (poly(A) signal, tissue-invariant and tissue-specific promoters and enhancers, CTCF-bound sites). Each element is a separate binary mask over the sequence, so a model is judged on each element in turn rather than on one combined score.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Human genomic elements; Results

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Gene elements and poly(A) signals come from GENCODE V44, filtered to drop level three (automated) transcripts so every training annotation is human-curated; introns and splice sites were extracted with the HISAT2 script. Promoters, enhancers and CTCF-bound sites come from ENCODE's SCREEN database, with distal and proximal enhancers combined and each promoter or enhancer labelled tissue-invariant or tissue-specific using the Meuleman et al. vocabulary. The dataset is built by overlapping all 14 element tracks with every DNA sequence of the chosen length; sequences containing N are removed.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Human genomic elements

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The split is by chromosome: chromosomes 20 and 21 are the test set, chromosome 22 is validation and the rest is training. Test chunks containing genes homologous to genes on the training or validation chromosomes were removed using Ensembl BioMart annotations (accessed 8 May 2024). Validation and test sequences are fixed by sliding a window of the model's length over the chromosome. A model outputs 14 probabilities per nucleotide; the predictions are concatenated across sequences per element type and scored per nucleotide with MCC, auPRC, Jaccard similarity and F1, plus a region-level SOV score. The test set was sampled ten times with different window start positions to give a spread. The best checkpoint is chosen on the validation chromosome by average MCC over the 14 elements.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model training and evaluation; Supplementary Table 2 caption

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository ships inference code in Jax. Clone it, install the package, then load a pretrained segmentation model with get_pretrained_segment_nt_model, tokenise sequences and read the per-nucleotide probabilities for each of the 14 features. The published evaluation itself, including the test chromosome manifests, is not released as a script.
sections.source_locator: README.md: installation; docs/segment_nt.md: How to use

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One human segmentation dataset of 14 element types built from GENCODE V44 and ENCODE SCREEN annotations, instantiated at sequence lengths of 3 kb, 10 kb, 20 kb and 30 kb. Supplementary Table 4 splits all test-set nucleotides for SegmentNT-30kb into edge, interior and spurious classes; for each element these three counts sum to 72,960,000 nucleotides (for 3UTR, 103,780 plus 681,711 plus 72,174,509). This total is a sum derived for one model's windows; no other test-set count is stated in the parts read.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Human genomic elements; Model training and evaluation; SI: Supplementary Table 4

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: By chromosome: 20 and 21 for test, 22 for validation, the rest for training. Training sequences are randomly sampled; validation and test sequences are fixed sliding windows.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model training and evaluation

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Per-nucleotide MCC and auPRC per element are the reported comparisons (Supplementary Tables 2 and 3); Jaccard similarity, F1 and a region-level SOV score are also computed. Higher is better.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model training and evaluation; Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 captions

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Randomly initialised BPNet architectures (embedding 64 and 1,024), three SpliceAI architectures (embedding 32, 256 and 920), U-Net heads alone at 63M and 252M parameters, a U-Net with a linear up-projection, a randomly initialised SegmentNT, a head-only SegmentNT, and a SegmentNT whose backbone is NT v1 2.5B. SegmentEnformer and SegmentBorzoi appear in the same tables.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model ablations and baselines; Supplementary Table 2

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Chromosome-level split, plus removal of test chunks containing genes homologous to genes on the training or validation chromosomes. The authors note this does not remove homologous distal regulatory elements, which could still inflate performance in those regions.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model training and evaluation

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: The test set is sampled ten times with different sliding window start positions; results are means with standard deviations over those ten samplings.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods; Supplementary Table 3 caption

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One nucleotide within a DNA sequence, carrying a binary label for each of the 14 element types.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results; Methods

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human for this evaluation. The paper also builds a multispecies dataset, which is a separate evaluation.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Human genomic elements; Multispecies dataset

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: No direct assay: labels are curated annotations. Gene elements come from GENCODE V44, regulatory elements from ENCODE's SCREEN database, and the tissue-invariant or tissue-specific split from the Meuleman et al. vocabulary.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Human genomic elements

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: DNA sequence only. SegmentNT models tokenise as 6-mers and cannot take sequences containing N.
facts.source_locator: docs/segment_nt.md: How to use; Paper: Methods

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Supervised training of a segmentation head on top of a DNA encoder, trained end to end; the paper also reports head-only and randomly initialised variants as ablations.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results; Methods, Model ablations and baselines

strengths.text: Every element is scored separately at nucleotide resolution, so a model's strength on, say, splice sites is visible rather than averaged away.
The split is by chromosome and test chunks with genes homologous to training genes are removed, which is stricter than a random split.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model training and evaluation

strengths.text: Ten test samplings give a standard deviation for every reported number, and ablations include randomly initialised and head-only models.

limitations.text: Homologous distal regulatory elements are not removed from the test set, which the authors say could still inflate performance in those regions.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model training and evaluation

limitations.text: There is no released evaluation harness or test manifest: the repository gives inference code, not the benchmark pipeline, so another group cannot reproduce the exact test set from the sources read.
The code is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and the weights are released for research purposes, so commercial use is restricted.

Scores on CTCF-bound sites and tissue-specific promoters are low for every model: in Supplementary Table 2 (MCC) the best CTCF-bound score is 0.19 (SegmentEnformer-196kb) and the best tissue-specific promoter score is 0.33 (SegmentEnformer-30kb and SegmentBorzoi-524kb).

prerequisites: Python with the repository's dependencies, installed from the repository itself; Jax is used for inference.

SegmentNT inputs must not contain N, because sequences are tokenised as 6-mers.

steps.explanation: Creates a virtual environment and installs the local package, as the README's steps 2 and 3.

steps.title: Run the model on sequences
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import haiku as hk
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from nucleotide_transformer.pretrained import get_pretrained_segment_nt_model

jax.config.update("jax_platform_name", "cpu")
backend = "cpu"
devices = jax.devices(backend)
max_num_nucleotides = 8
parameters, forward_fn, tokenizer, config = get_pretrained_segment_nt_model(
    model_name="segment_nt",
    embeddings_layers_to_save=(29,),
    attention_maps_to_save=((1, 4), (7, 10)),
    max_positions=max_num_nucleotides + 1,
)
forward_fn = hk.transform(forward_fn)
apply_fn = jax.pmap(forward_fn.apply, devices=devices, donate_argnums=(0,))
sequences = ["ATTCCGATTCCGATTCCAACGGATTATTCCGATTAACCGATTCCAATT", "ATTTCTCTCTCTCTCTGAGATCGATGATTTCTCTCTCATCGAACTATG"]
tokens_ids = [b[1] for b in tokenizer.batch_tokenize(sequences)]
tokens = jnp.asarray(tokens_ids, dtype=jnp.int32)
random_key = jax.random.PRNGKey(seed=0)
keys = jax.device_put_replicated(random_key, devices=devices)
parameters = jax.device_put_replicated(parameters, devices=devices)
tokens = jax.device_put_replicated(tokens, devices=devices)
outs = apply_fn(parameters, keys, tokens)
logits = outs["logits"]
probabilities = jnp.asarray(jax.nn.softmax(logits, axis=-1))[...,-1]
print(f"Features inferred: {config.features}")
PY
steps.explanation: A shortened copy of the documentation's Python example (the device print, the length assert, the probabilities shape print and the intron lines removed), wrapped by Rewire in a shell heredoc so it runs as one command. It loads the human SegmentNT model, tokenises two short sequences and prints the feature names behind the per-nucleotide probabilities. Supported model names are segment_nt and segment_nt_multi_species.

outputs: Per-nucleotide probabilities for each of the 14 features, with the feature names printed from config.features. The documentation's full example also shows how to pull out the intron probabilities; the shortened step does not.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
This runs inference on example sequences; it does not reproduce the paper's test evaluation, for which no harness is released.
For sequences between 30 kb and 50 kb the documentation says a rescaling_factor argument must be passed.

name: TorchCraft 8-target cyclic peptide design benchmark
description: A computational comparison of cyclic peptide design methods over eight target systems in two cyclisation modes, scored by cyclisation integrity and TorchScore confidence.

limitations: Author-built and author-run: the method's developers defined the panel, the criterion and the comparators.
Scored by TorchScore, which uses the same pretrained AlphaFold 3 weights the TorchCraft designs were optimised against.
Printed only as a figure; no per-target or aggregate number is printed, so this batch records no result for it.
Pass rates are predictor-derived and are not experimental success rates.

split.note: A design panel, not a train and test split.

review.method_note: Every quotation and locator on this record was re-read in the refetched artifact named by retrieval_url. All seven pinned artifacts were re-retrieved by the reviewer on 2026-11-16T00:08Z. Six came back byte-identical to the hash on their source record. The Hugging Face page did not, and cannot: three consecutive fetches gave three different hashes. Normalising its per-request hf-sanitized CSS class hashes leaves one further per-request difference, window.requestId, and the page also prints a download counter; with those normalised the markup is identical. Its licence tag, gate text and dataset card matched the recorded quotations word for word, so the page is a per-retrieval stamp, not a changed page. The pdftotext -layout text layer of the refetched PDF hashes to 90f1da5f8a936766087beba0ade3f038f5b69504b9f581b42f2391f5640c5e6b, the value the extractor recorded.
review.reviewer_note: Claude (Opus 5) review agent, independent of the extractor; no human review claimed. Every pinned artifact was re-retrieved and hashed, and every stored value re-read against it. Nothing was reproduced: no design run, score, docking calculation or binding measurement was repeated, and no value was recomputed from source data.

attributes.scope_note: Eight target systems (MCL-1, MDM2, PD-L1, IL-23R, albumin, KEAP1, GABARAP and RagA:RagC) with peptide lengths of 12 to 18 residues. 100 designs per method per target in the head-to-tail setting. BoltzGen, RFpeptides and TorchCraft are compared, with TorchCraft also run in a disulfide-linked setting; results are printed only as the chart of Figure 4c.
