profile.summary: This is the in silico cyclic peptide design comparison published with TorchCraft. Eight target systems, listed with PDB entries, crops, hotspots and a peptide length range of 12 to 18 residues in Supplementary Table S6, are designed against by BoltzGen, RFpeptides and TorchCraft, with 100 designs per method per target in the head-to-tail cyclisation setting; TorchCraft is also run in a disulfide-linked setting. A design passes only if its predicted structure forms the intended cycle without chain breaks and its TorchScore pLDDT exceeds 70 and ipTM exceeds 0.5. Figure 4c prints the pass rates per target. The question it answers is which design method produces cyclic peptides that satisfy both the cyclisation geometry and a confidence threshold.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Section 2.4 and Figure 4c; Appendix A.4.3.3; Supplementary Table S6

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two things at once, which is what makes this panel different from the others: whether the predicted peptide is actually cyclic and intact, and whether the predictor is confident about the complex. The authors evaluate two cyclisation parameterisations, head-to-tail, which uses cyclic relative positional encoding so the termini are adjacent in sequence space, and disulfide-linked, which keeps linear encoding and fixes the two cysteine positions that define the linkage. Predicted structures are classified by whether they satisfy the intended cyclisation and the backbone-integrity criteria, with the breakdown of cyclised, intact but not cyclised and backbone-broken predictions reported in a supplementary figure.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 2.4; Supplementary Figure S6 caption

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: A target panel, not a dataset, and no split. Supplementary Table S6 lists eight target systems with a PDB entry, the target chains and residue crop, hotspot residues and a peptide length of 12 to 18 residues for each: MDM2, MCL-1, GABARAP, PD-L1, KEAP1, RagA:RagC, IL-23R and albumin, counted from its rows. In the head-to-tail benchmark each method generates 100 designs per target with its default settings. TorchCraft is additionally evaluated in the disulfide-linked setting, where all positions except the two cysteines may be redesigned in the polished variant.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Appendix A.4.3.3; Supplementary Table S6

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: For BoltzGen and RFpeptides the full peptide sequence of each generated structure is redesigned eight times with ProteinMPNN without fixing residues, each redesign is rebuilt with FlowPacker and scored with TorchScore, and the redesign with the highest pLDDT plus 100 times ipTM becomes that original design's score. TorchCraft head-to-tail outputs are scored raw and, optionally, after redesigning all peptide positions eight times with the same rebuild and selection procedure. In the disulfide-linked setting raw outputs are scored directly, or all positions except the two cysteines are redesigned eight times and then rebuilt and selected in the same way. The pass criterion has three parts that must all hold: the intended cycle must be formed, the backbone must have no chain breaks, and TorchScore pLDDT must exceed 70 with ipTM above 0.5. Rosetta interface scores for the same panel are reported separately as an orthogonal assessment.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Appendix A.4.3.3; Supplementary Figure S7 caption

sections.title: What TorchScore is
sections.body: The scorer every pass rate in this panel depends on is worth stating plainly, because it is not an independent evaluator. TorchScore is a score-only loading of the same TorchFold implementation used for design: given input coordinates it skips the diffusion structure module and runs the confidence pathway, returning pLDDT, pTM and ipTM. No separate scoring network is trained, and in this study it used the pretrained AlphaFold 3 weights, the same checkpoint the designs were optimised against. Sequences rebuilt with FlowPacker are scored from those coordinates and are not refolded from sequence.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Appendix A.4.2

strengths.text: The criterion includes a geometric check that cannot be gamed by confidence alone: a design fails unless the predicted structure actually forms the intended cycle with an unbroken backbone.

Cyclisation outcomes are reported in their own right, as fractions of cyclised, intact but not cyclised and backbone-broken predictions, so the failure modes are visible rather than folded into one rate.
Both cyclisation parameterisations are described concretely, down to the positional encoding and the fixed cysteines, and both are evaluated.
An orthogonal assessment of the same panel is published alongside, with Rosetta interface scores reported for the designs of Figure 4c.

limitations.text: Author-built and author-run: the developers of TorchCraft chose the eight targets, the criterion and the comparators and ran every method themselves.

The scorer shares its weights with the designer. TorchScore is the confidence pathway of the same pretrained AlphaFold 3 checkpoint TorchCraft optimises against, scoring supplied coordinates without refolding.
A pass is predictor-derived, not experimental. No binding or stability measurement enters this panel.

The results are printed only as the chart of Figure 4c, with no per-target numbers and no uncertainty, so no value can be recorded. The disulfide-linked TorchCraft arm also has no comparator: BoltzGen and RFpeptides are run head-to-tail only.

profile.summary: This is the in silico ligand-conditioned pocket design comparison published with TorchCraft. Ten chemically diverse small molecules, ALE, ATP, CHD, CMP, DLU, FAD, IAI, OQO, SAM and TRP, each serve as the ligand a design must build a pocket for. For each method and each ligand 500 designs are generated under that method's own default settings, and the two methods compared are BoltzDesign and TorchCraft. The paper states the 160-residue length and the absence of a supplied native scaffold for the TorchCraft designs. The designs are assessed in two ways: score distributions from AutoDock Vina and affinity predictions from Boltz-2, printed in Figure 5c and 5d, and separately a TorchScore pass rate for TorchCraft, where a design passes when its pLDDT exceeds 70 and its ipTM exceeds 0.7. Nothing here is measured experimentally.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a design method can produce a protein that forms a plausible pocket around a specified small molecule, across a chemically varied panel. The ligands span nucleotides, cofactors, metabolites and drug-like compounds, so the panel also asks how the answer changes with ligand chemistry; the paper reports that score distributions varied across ligands and methods. Three different computational views are used rather than one: a physics-based docking score, a learned affinity prediction, and a predictor confidence pass rate.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: No dataset and no split. The panel is the ten ligands named in Supplementary Figure S8, chosen for chemical diversity. For each method and each ligand, 500 designs are generated with that method's default settings. For TorchCraft the paper adds that the designs are 160-residue proteins generated without a supplied native scaffold; Appendix A.4.3.4, which covers both methods, gives neither a length nor a scaffold condition for BoltzDesign. Raw outputs are evaluated without post hoc sequence redesign or score-based preselection. The design procedure that produced them is described in the appendix as a staged schedule in which the ligand is added and the interface objective is weighted up gradually, separating fold formation from pocket optimisation, but the benchmark itself is defined by the ligand panel, the design count and the three scores.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 2.5; Appendix A.1.3 and A.4.3.4; Supplementary Figure S8 caption

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Two methods are compared, BoltzDesign and TorchCraft, and both are evaluated without sequence redesign in the arms that are compared directly. The score distributions of the resulting designs are assessed with AutoDock Vina and Boltz-2 and shown in Figures 5c and 5d. For TorchCraft alone, a TorchScore pass rate is also reported in Supplementary Figure S9: a design passes when TorchScore pLDDT exceeds 70 and TorchScore ipTM exceeds 0.7. A further TorchCraft variant is reported separately, in which ligand-interface residues are fixed, all other positions are redesigned eight times with LigandMPNN, the redesigned sequences are refolded with TorchFold, the structure with the highest pTM is kept, and that is then scored with AutoDock Vina and Boltz-2.

profile.summary: This is the in silico minibinder comparison published with TorchCraft. Twelve protein targets, each with a fixed crop and length-specific hotspot residues listed in Supplementary Table S4, are given to three design methods, TorchCraft, BoltzGen and RFdiffusion, at binder lengths of 75, 120, 160 and 200 residues, with 100 designs per method per length per target. Every design ends up scored by TorchScore, a score-only loading of the same AlphaFold 3 weights TorchCraft designs against, and counts as a pass when both its pTM and its ipTM exceed 0.7. Figure 2f prints the resulting pass rates aggregated over the four lengths. It is a comparison of computational pass rates between design methods on one target panel, not a measurement of binding.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a design method produces minibinders that a structure predictor is confident about, across a spread of targets and binder lengths. The quantity is a pass rate: the share of a method's designs for a target that clear a confidence threshold. The authors are explicit that this is predictor-derived rather than experimental, and they add Rosetta interface-score distributions in a supplementary figure for that reason. The length sweep is part of the question: pass rates are reported per target and per binder length before being aggregated, and the paper says they varied by both.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 2.2; Figure 2f caption

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: There is no dataset to download and no split. The panel is twelve target proteins, each listed in Supplementary Table S4 with a PDB entry, the target chain and residue crop used, and hotspot residues given separately for the 75, 120 and 160 or 200 residue settings: IL-7Ralpha, InsulinR, PD-L1, TrkA, CD3D, EGFRc, EGFRn, FGFR2, IGF1R, PDGFRbeta, Tie2 and VirB8, counted from the rows of that table. For each method, each length and each target, 100 designs are generated with that method's default settings, so each cell of the comparison rests on 100 original designs.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Appendix A.4.1 and A.4.3.1; Supplementary Table S4

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The two comparator methods and TorchCraft are not scored on identical pipelines, and the paper describes the difference. For each BoltzGen and RFdiffusion design the full binder sequence is redesigned eight times with ProteinMPNN without fixing residues, each redesigned sequence is rebuilt to all-atom side chains with FlowPacker, the eight rebuilt models are scored with TorchScore, and the redesign with the highest pTM plus ipTM becomes the final score for that original design. TorchCraft is reported in two settings: raw, which is the default procedure and is scored directly by TorchScore without redesign, and MPNN-polished, in which interface residues are fixed and the rest are redesigned eight times, then rebuilt and selected exactly as for the comparators. A design passes when TorchScore pTM and ipTM both exceed 0.7. Figure 2f aggregates the pass rates over the four binder lengths.

sections.body: The scorer every pass rate in this panel depends on is worth stating plainly, because it is not an independent evaluator. TorchScore is a score-only loading of the same TorchFold implementation used for design: given input coordinates it skips the diffusion structure module and runs the confidence pathway, returning pLDDT, pTM and ipTM. No separate scoring network is trained, and in this study it used the pretrained AlphaFold 3 weights, the same checkpoint the designs were optimised against. Sequences rebuilt with FlowPacker are scored from those coordinates and are not refolded from sequence.

facts.value: Inapplicable. This is a design panel evaluated in silico, with no train, validation or test partition.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: One: the computational pass rate, higher is better. A design passes when both TorchScore pTM and TorchScore ipTM exceed 0.7, and the pass rate is the share of a method's designs that pass, reported per target and aggregated over the four binder lengths. Rosetta interface scores are reported separately as an additional view, not as the criterion.

facts.value: Two other design methods, run by the TorchCraft authors with each method's default settings: BoltzGen and RFdiffusion. TorchCraft itself appears in a raw and an MPNN-polished setting.

strengths.text: The pass criterion is a stated numerical threshold on two named scores, so what counts as a pass can be checked rather than guessed.
The targets are pinned: Supplementary Table S4 gives a PDB entry, a chain and residue crop and hotspot residues for each target, separately for each binder length.

The comparators' handling is written out, including the eight ProteinMPNN redesigns, the FlowPacker rebuild and the selection rule, and TorchCraft is reported both raw and polished so the effect of the polish step is visible.
The authors state the weakness of their own criterion and add an orthogonal view, reporting Rosetta interface-score distributions because the pass rates are predictor-derived.

limitations.text: Author-built and author-run: the method's developers chose the targets, the lengths, the criterion and the comparators, and ran every method themselves.

The scorer is not independent of the designer. TorchScore runs the confidence pathway of the same pretrained AlphaFold 3 weights that TorchCraft optimises against, and the designs it scores are not refolded from sequence.
A pass is a predictor's confidence, not activity. No binding measurement enters this panel, and the paper's wet-lab results are separate campaigns against four targets.
The results are printed only as a figure. No per-target or aggregate number is given in text or table, so no value can be recorded from this panel, and no uncertainty is reported for any bar.

attributes.task: Design runtime measurement

profile.summary: This is a runtime measurement published with TorchCraft, not a scored benchmark of design quality. It reports how long one TorchCraft design takes at sequence lengths of 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 residues, on an Ascend 910B NPU with 64 GB with and without the fused attention operator, and on an A100 GPU with 80 GB with and without cuequivariance kernels. Runtime is given in minutes per design, obtained by halving the wall-clock time of a run at batch size 2, and the GPU numbers are the mean of three independent runs. Twenty cells are printed in Supplementary Table S9. Anyone planning capacity for a design campaign can use it to see how the cost scales with length and what the two optional acceleration paths are worth.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Supplementary Table S9; Appendix A.3.4 and A.3.5

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Wall-clock time per design, as a function of sequence length and of two optional kernel paths. The purpose is stated in the implementation appendix: TorchCraft optimises sequence logits through a frozen all-atom predictor, which is memory and compute heavy, and the authors describe the optimisations they applied, including a fused attention operator on the Ascend NPU and optional cuequivariance equivariant kernels on the GPU. Table S9 is where those optimisations are quantified. Nothing in this panel scores the designs themselves: it is a timing table.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Appendix A.3.4 and A.3.5; Supplementary Table S9

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: There is no dataset and no target panel. The table has five length columns, 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 amino acids, and four rows: NPU with fused attention, NPU without it, GPU with cuequivariance and GPU without it. The NPU rows are an Ascend 910B with 64 GB, the GPU rows an A100 with 80 GB. Batch size 2 is described as the recommended setting, and a cell's value is the total wall-clock time of a batch-size-2 run divided by 2. One cell is an exception: NPU without fused attention at 500 residues was run at batch size 1 because batch size 2 ran out of memory. The design task behind the timings is not stated anywhere in the table or its caption; only the sequence lengths are given.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Supplementary Table S9 and its caption and footnote

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The quantity reported is minutes per design, and lower is better. It is derived, not timed directly per design: a batch of two designs is run and the total wall-clock time is divided by two. On the GPU each configuration was run three times and the mean is printed; the caption does not say the NPU rows were repeated. No spread, standard deviation or interval is given for any cell. There is no submission process, no scoring criterion and no comparison with another method's runtime: the four rows are four configurations of the same implementation on two hardware platforms. The authors summarise the effect qualitatively, saying fused attention reduced runtime at several of the larger sequence settings and that its effect depended on length and batch size.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Supplementary Table S9 caption; Appendix A.3.4

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: No timing harness is published, but the design code the timings were taken from is. The TorchX repository the paper names holds the GPU tree on its main branch and an Ascend NPU tree on a separate branch, which is the division the table's two platforms follow. A user installs the base torchx environment first, then runs one of the TorchCraft task scripts for monomer, VHH or minibinder design and times it. The cuequivariance arm of the table corresponds to an optional install and a configuration change the README describes: install the pinned CUDA 12 requirements file, then set the triangle multiplicative and triangle attention options to cuequivariance in the TorchCraft base configuration, where the default is torch. The NPU fused attention arm belongs to the NPU branch, which the README lists as carrying the optional CANN fused attention extra.

run_guide.summary: Install the TorchX design stack at a pinned commit and run a TorchCraft design, optionally with the cuequivariance kernels that the GPU arms of the runtime table compare.
prerequisites: An NVIDIA GPU for the main branch, which the README calls the GPU tree; the Ascend NPU code is on a separate branch.
Conda or a virtual environment for the torchx base environment, which compiles C++ extensions and builds the CCD chemical data.
TorchFold weights from the Hugging Face dataset page, which the README describes as gated with access on request.

git clone https://github.com/Mingchenchen/TorchX
cd TorchX
git checkout --detach ebf9dc6676ecb1be505bc72f87de408995f0d8fd

cd torchx_gpu/torchx
# follow torchx_gpu/README.md

attributes.task: Binder design

profile.summary: This is the in silico VHH, or nanobody, design comparison published with TorchCraft. Fifteen protein targets, each with a PDB entry, a crop and hotspot residues in Supplementary Table S5, are designed against by four methods, TorchCraft, RFantibody, BoltzGen and Germinal, over five nanobody frameworks, with 100 designs per method per framework per target and CDR lengths fixed at 8 residues for HCDR1 and HCDR2 and 9 to 21 for HCDR3. A design passes only if it clears two thresholds: a TorchScore ipTM above 0.7 and an ESM2-150M sequence perplexity below 6.31, the second standing in as an expression proxy. Figure 3i prints the pass rates per target and Supplementary Figure S5 splits them by framework.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Section 2.3 and Figure 3i; Appendix A.4.3.2; Supplementary Table S5

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a method can design nanobody CDR loops, on a fixed framework, that a structure predictor is confident bind the target and that a protein language model considers likely to express. The second part is unusual and deliberate: the pass criterion pairs a structural confidence threshold with a sequence perplexity threshold the authors calibrated against expression data. The framework-stratified figure asks a further question, how much the result depends on which of the five scaffolds is used, with the same target panel and criterion.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 2.3; Appendix A.4.3.2; Supplementary Figure S5 caption

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: No dataset and no split: a target panel. Supplementary Table S5 lists fifteen targets with a PDB entry, the target chain and residue crop and hotspot residues for each: IL13, HNMT, 1433E, BHRF1, EFNA1, CCL2, IL20, CSF1, MZB1, LIF, XIAP, RSPO1, FCGR3B, UNG and DAF, counted from its rows. Its caption fixes the CDR lengths for all designs at HCDR1 of 8 residues, HCDR2 of 8 and HCDR3 of 9 to 21. Five nanobody frameworks are used, named in Appendix A.5.2.1 as 7EOW (caplacizumab), 8Z8V (ozoralizumab), 5JDS (envafolimab), 7XL0 (vobarilizumab) and 8COH (gefurulimab), the same five identifiers that label the per-framework panels of Supplementary Figures S3 and S5. For each method, each framework and each target, 100 designs are generated with that method's default settings. The expression proxy threshold was built separately: public nanobody expression measurements were combined with accumulated TorchCraft expression data, designs expressing at least 0.08 mg were labelled high expression, and ESM2-150M perplexity was swept as a one-dimensional classifier with the threshold chosen to maximise the Matthews correlation coefficient.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Appendix A.4.3.2; Supplementary Table S5 and Figure S5 captions

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The four methods are handled differently before scoring, and the paper sets out how. For BoltzGen and RFantibody the full designed sequence is redesigned eight times with AbMPNN without fixing residues; for Germinal the original pipeline is followed, fixing CDR residues that contact the interface and applying AbMPNN only outside the CDRs. Each redesigned sequence is rebuilt to all-atom side chains with FlowPacker, the eight rebuilt models are scored with TorchScore, and the one with the highest ipTM becomes that original design's score. TorchCraft is reported raw, scored directly without redesign, and in an MPNN-polished setting where its interface CDR residues are fixed and the rest redesigned eight times with AbMPNN before the same rebuild and selection. The pass criterion is both thresholds together: TorchScore ipTM above 0.7 and ESM2-150M perplexity below 6.31. Rosetta interface-score distributions are reported separately as an additional assessment.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Appendix A.4.3.2; Section 2.3

sections.title: What TorchScore is
sections.body: The scorer every pass rate in this panel depends on is worth stating plainly, because it is not an independent evaluator. TorchScore is a score-only loading of the same TorchFold implementation used for design: given input coordinates it skips the diffusion structure module and runs the confidence pathway, returning pLDDT, pTM and ipTM. No separate scoring network is trained, and in this study it used the pretrained AlphaFold 3 weights, the same checkpoint the designs were optimised against. Sequences rebuilt with FlowPacker are scored from those coordinates and are not refolded from sequence.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Appendix A.4.2

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One target panel, not a dataset: fifteen protein targets with PDB entries, crops and hotspots in Supplementary Table S5, crossed with the five nanobody frameworks 7EOW, 8Z8V, 5JDS, 7XL0 and 8COH named in Appendix A.5.2.1, at 100 designs per method per framework per target. CDR lengths are fixed for all designs at HCDR1 of 8 residues, HCDR2 of 8 and HCDR3 of 9 to 21.

facts.value: None reported. The panel prints no replicate runs, seeds, confidence intervals or standard errors; the spread that is shown is the distribution over the fixed number of designs per target, 100 per method per framework per target.

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One designed VHH for one target on one framework: a designed CDR sequence set in a fixed framework with its predicted all-atom complex, scored as one original design after the eight-way redesign selection where that applies.

facts.value: Not stated as such. The fifteen targets are named proteins with PDB entries in Supplementary Table S5, including human interleukins and an Epstein-Barr virus protein, BHRF1, but the table gives PDB entries, chains and residue ranges rather than species.

facts.value: None in this panel. Every criterion is computed by a predictor. The paper reports wet-lab binding measurements elsewhere in the study, for minibinders and VHHs against four targets each, but those campaigns are separate from this comparison.

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The target crop and hotspots from Supplementary Table S5, the nanobody framework sequence, which is held fixed, and the CDR length settings. facts.source_locator: Paper: Appendix A.4.1; Supplementary Table S5

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: No training or fine-tuning. Each method runs with its default settings, and TorchCraft optimises sequence logits through frozen pretrained AlphaFold 3 weights; the paper states that all designs reported in the study used pretrained AF3 weights.

strengths.text: The pass criterion is two stated thresholds, and the second one was calibrated rather than asserted: the perplexity cut-off of 6.31 comes from a retrospective expression analysis with a stated labelling rule and selection objective.
The framework dependence is reported, not averaged away: Supplementary Figure S5 splits the same panel and criterion across the five nanobody scaffolds.
Each comparator's redesign path is written out, including the Germinal-specific rule of fixing interface-contacting CDR residues, and TorchCraft is reported both raw and polished.

limitations.text: Author-built and author-run: the developers of TorchCraft chose the targets, frameworks, criterion and comparators and ran all four methods themselves.

The scorer shares its weights with the designer. TorchScore is the confidence pathway of the same pretrained AlphaFold 3 checkpoint TorchCraft optimises against, and scores supplied coordinates without refolding the sequence.

The expression half of the criterion is a proxy with a calibration that is not public here: the threshold was fitted partly on accumulated TorchCraft expression data, which the paper does not release, so it cannot be re-derived independently.
The results are printed only as figures. Neither Figure 3i nor Supplementary Figure S5 is accompanied by per-target numbers or any measure of uncertainty, so no value can be recorded from this panel.

profile.summary: A small evaluation from the CIViC MCP paper: can a large language model say which CIViC clinical significance labels are supported for a (molecular profile, cancer type, therapy) triplet? GPT-5 was tested alone, with the CIViC MCP server, and in Agent Mode on 100 randomly sampled CIViC triplets. It is relevant to people judging LLM tools for retrieving curated cancer variant evidence; it is one paper's study, not a maintained benchmark.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Section 3

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether an LLM retrieves current CIViC evidence correctly. For each triplet and each candidate clinical significance, the model answers supports, does not support, or no evidence. The authors frame it as a test of retrieval through the MCP server against recall from pretraining or web browsing.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Section 3

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: 100 triplets were randomly selected from CIViC Evidence Items; expected answers come from CIViC. The README describes QA_triplet_dataset.csv as holding the triplets and expected answers. The scoring script reads a CIViC evidence extract dated 2_27_26 in its file name. The illustrative example in the paper was chosen separately and is not in the 100.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sections 2.1 and 3; README.md: Evaluation Scripts; eval_one_shot.py: CONFIG

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: GPT-5 is prompted zero-shot at temperature 1. Scoring is at the significance-label level, micro-averaged within each Evidence Type, with the common no-evidence label excluded. Reported metrics are overall accuracy and micro-F1, plus mean response time with a 95% confidence interval; the script uses 10,000 bootstrap resamples. The paper reports GPT-5 with MCP at 0.95 accuracy and 0.98 micro-F1, GPT-5 alone at 0.30 and 0.46, and Agent Mode at 0.83 and 0.91.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository ships the model outputs and the scoring script. Clone it at the pinned commit, install the Python requirements, and run eval_one_shot.py from the eval_QA_experiment folder; it rescores the no-MCP, MCP and Agent Mode outputs and writes summary CSVs. Generating new model answers needs an OpenAI API key and the separate one_shot scripts, which are not covered here.

profile.summary: This record covers the evaluation reported in the ENIGMA BRCA1 and BRCA2 Variant Curation Expert Panel's 2024 specification paper. The panel reviewed every ACMG/AMP classification criterion for its relevance to BRCA1 and BRCA2, used statistical methods to calibrate how strong each data type's evidence is, and then tested the resulting specifications on a pilot set of 40 variants that already had ClinVar classifications. The measure of success is how many of those variants the specifications resolve or classify with more confidence. It is useful to anyone who wants to know how a gene-specific ACMG/AMP specification is built and validated, rather than to anyone comparing computational predictors.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Summary

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two things. First, whether each ACMG/AMP criterion can be applied to BRCA1 and BRCA2 at all, and at what strength: the panel found that the original descriptions of 13 evidence codes were non-applicable or overlapped other criteria, and that eight codes needed their scenario of use extended or repurposed. Second, whether the resulting specifications change classification outcomes in practice, tested on variants whose existing ClinVar status was known.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Summary

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The panel is a ClinGen Variant Curation Expert Panel that grew out of an ENIGMA BRCA1 and BRCA2 classification sub-group formed in 2015 as a ClinGen external expert panel, and became an internal panel to fit the Food and Drug Administration recognised process for ClinVar submissions. The pilot set is 40 variants chosen by their pre-existing ClinVar classification: 13 of uncertain significance or conflicting, 14 pathogenic or likely pathogenic and 13 benign or likely benign. How the calibration itself was done, and how the pilot variants were selected within each class, is in the article body, which is not in the record read.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Summary

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The pilot is scored by classification outcome, not by a continuous metric: for each of the 40 variants, whether applying the specifications resolved an uncertain or conflicting classification, and whether confidence in an already classified variant was retained or improved. The headline result is that 11 of the 13 uncertain or conflicting variants were resolved. Alongside this, the calibration step assigned evidence strengths and weights to every code using statistical methods, and the documentation was revised after the pilot for clarity and ease of use. The statistical method, the thresholds it produced and the tables holding them are in the article body and were not readable here.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Summary

strengths.text: Evidence strength was calibrated statistically rather than assigned by convention, and the panel reports that this calibration was what justified the utility and strength of each data type for gene-specific use.

The specifications were piloted before release, on a deliberately mixed set of 40 variants spanning uncertain or conflicting, pathogenic and benign prior classifications, and the documentation was revised in response.

The review was willing to find fault with both inputs: it reports gaps in the panel's own pre-existing research process as well as in the baseline ACMG/AMP criteria, and judged 13 evidence codes non-applicable or overlapping.

limitations.text: The pilot is 40 variants, two genes and one expert panel, so the reported resolution rate rests on 13 uncertain or conflicting variants. It is a demonstration that the specifications work, not a measurement of how often they resolve uncertainty at scale.

The panel evaluated its own specifications on variants whose prior ClinVar classifications were known, and the record read says nothing about blinding or about whether the pilot variants were independent of the calibration data.

Nothing here is reusable as a benchmark: there is no score, no held-out set, no code and no released evaluation data. The outcome is a written specification, which the authors describe as publicly accessible protocols for genetic diagnosis.

The article is not open access. The copyright line reserves all rights, including for text and data mining and AI training, and no open full text could be retrieved, so this page rests on the Summary alone.

profile.summary: This is the evaluation published with OncoVI, a Python tool that automates the ClinGen, CGC and VICC oncogenicity guidelines for somatic variants. OncoVI's classifications are compared against four reference sets: 93 variants supplied by the guideline authors, 7,802 real-world variants from the Erlangen Molecular Tumor Board, 691 ClinVar variants with curated oncogenicity classifications, and a 135-variant subset of the tumour board variants that three expert cancer biologists reclassified under the guidelines. Every comparison is a three-class agreement rate between OncoVI and the reference. It shows how far an automated reading of the guidelines matches guideline authors, a tumour board and ClinVar.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Materials and Methods, the four data set sections; Results

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether software can apply the oncogenicity guidelines and reach the same class a human assessor would. For each variant OncoVI collects evidence from public resources, decides which of the 11 oncogenic and five benign criteria are triggered, sums their points and maps the total to a class: 10 or more is oncogenic, 6 to 9 likely oncogenic, 0 to 5 a variant of uncertain significance, minus 1 to minus 6 likely benign, and minus 7 or lower benign. The comparisons then ask how often that class matches the guideline authors' own classification, a tumour board's assessment of protein function, ClinVar's curated oncogenicity call, and a blinded expert reclassification under the same guidelines.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, first paragraph. Repository: README.md, figure caption

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Four sets, each with a different reference. The standard operating procedure set is 93 variants taken from Supplementary Tables 1 and 3 of the guideline paper, with the triggered criteria, scores and classifications as the authors published them; genomic coordinates for 23 of them had to be derived by hand from the DNA change. The tumour board set is 7,802 unique somatic variants across 489 genes from 557 people seen by the Comprehensive Cancer Center Erlangen-EMN tumour board between February 2022 and February 2024, sequenced from formalin-fixed tissue with the TruSight Oncology 500 assay and classified into five classes by three expert cancer biologists. The ClinVar set is the 691 somatic variants, out of 6,113, that had an NCBI-curated oncogenicity classification as of 12 April 2025. The validation set is 135 tumour board variants chosen after the fact from the confusion matrix, taking every strong disagreement plus random variants from selected cells, which the same three experts then reclassified under the guidelines while blinded to how OncoVI implements the criteria.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Standard Operating Procedure Data Set, Molecular Tumor Board Data Set, Validation Data Set, ClinVar Data Set; Results

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Variants are annotated by a Python pipeline built on Ensembl VEP version 111.0 against GRCh38, with the dbNSFP 4.5a and SpliceAI plugins, keeping only coding consequences, dropping variants with a global gnomAD frequency of 0.025 or more, and preferring the MANE canonical transcript. OncoVI then queries the knowledgebases behind each criterion and produces a class. For scoring, the five classes are collapsed to three (oncogenic or likely oncogenic, uncertain, benign or likely benign) and compared with the reference as accuracy or concordance, with per-class sensitivity, confusion matrices, and stratification by gene class and by functional consequence. Scores assigned by OncoVI and by the reference are compared by correlation on the variants where the classes agree.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Variant Annotation via the VEP-Based In-House Pipeline and Data Analysis and Statistical Analysis; Results

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: On the guideline authors' 93 variants OncoVI reached 81% accuracy (75 of 93), with sensitivity 88% (38 of 43) for oncogenic or likely oncogenic and 83% (10 of 12) for benign or likely benign, and the scores correlated with the guideline authors' at r = 0.87. On the 7,802 tumour board variants the three-class concordance was 78% (6,060 of 7,802), which breaks down as 97% for uncertain variants (3,955 of 4,092) but 43% for benign or likely benign (961 of 2,261). On the 691 ClinVar variants it was 83% (573 of 691), with sensitivity 84% (362 of 431) for oncogenic or likely oncogenic and no variant crossing between the oncogenic and benign extremes. The validation set is the striking one: the experts' guideline-based reclassification agreed with the earlier tumour board assessment for only 34% of the 135 variants (46 of 135), and OncoVI agreed with the tumour board on 22% (30 of 135) but with the experts' reclassification on 80% (108 of 135).
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Performance on the SOP, MTB and ClinVar data sets and Comparative Analysis with Expert Re-Assessment

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: OncoVI is distributed as a repository with a conda setup, a resource preparation script, a VEP installation path and an example input. It supports GRCh38 only, takes variants as text or VCF, and writes a tab-delimited Excel file holding the annotation fields, the variant-specific score, the classification and the triggered criteria. The repository also ships OncoVI_mod, a version that avoids the licensed OncoKB resource by defining oncogene and tumour suppressor roles from COSMIC instead.
sections.source_locator: Repository: README.md, Get started, Test OncoVI on an exemplary set of variants and OncoVI_mod. Paper: Results

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Four. SOP set: 93 somatic variants from the guideline authors, classified by them as 14 oncogenic, 29 likely oncogenic, 38 uncertain, 6 likely benign and 6 benign. Molecular Tumor Board set: 7,802 unique somatic variants across 489 genes from 557 individuals. ClinVar set: 691 somatic variants across 227 genes with an NCBI oncogenicity classification, out of 6,113 candidates, comprising 1 benign, 1 likely benign, 373 likely oncogenic, 58 oncogenic and 258 uncertain. Validation set: 135 tumour board variants across 104 genes, reclassified by three experts.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, the four data set sections; Results

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: None in the machine learning sense: OncoVI is a rule implementation, so every variant in every set is scored and compared, with no training or held-out portion. The only derived subset is the 135-variant validation set, which was selected after the fact from the tumour board confusion matrix: all variants with the strongest disagreement plus randomly chosen variants from the cells where OncoVI said uncertain or oncogenic.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Validation Data Set; Results

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Three-class agreement, higher better: accuracy or concordance between OncoVI's class and the reference's, reported as a percentage with the counts, plus per-class sensitivity and a confusion matrix. Correlation between OncoVI's variant-specific score and the reference's score is reported for the variants where the classes agree. Agreement is also stratified by gene class (oncogene against tumour suppressor) and by functional consequence.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results; Figure 2, 3 and 4 captions

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: No other software is compared. The reference points are human: the guideline authors' own published classifications, the tumour board's five-class assessment of protein function, ClinVar's NCBI-curated oncogenicity classification, and three expert cancer biologists reclassifying under the guidelines. The repository adds an internal comparison between OncoVI and OncoVI_mod, which drops the licensed OncoKB resource, reported in a separate document rather than in the paper.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, the data set sections; Results. Repository: README.md, OncoVI_mod

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Blinding on the one comparison where it applies: the three experts reclassified the 135 validation variants while blinded to how OncoVI implements the criteria, although they were given the list of resources OncoVI uses for each criterion and had themselves produced the original tumour board classification. For the other three sets no control applies, because OncoVI is a rule implementation with no training data. The criteria were, however, interpreted by the OncoVI authors where the guideline text was unclear, and resources were chosen by them where the guidelines suggested none.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Validation Data Set; Results

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: No intervals on the agreement rates. The paper reports counts behind every percentage, correlation coefficients with p values for the score comparisons, and Fisher exact tests for the association between triggered criteria and correct classification, with significance at p of 0.05 or below. There are no replicates: the classifications are deterministic given the resources, and resource versions are pinned in the methods rather than varied.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Data Analysis and Statistical Analysis; Results

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One somatic variant in a human tumour, given as genomic coordinates with reference and alternate alleles, carrying a human-assigned oncogenicity or pathogenicity class. Across the sets the variants are mostly missense and truncating, with splice site, in-frame, synonymous, untranslated region and upstream changes also present.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, ClinVar Data Set; Results

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human only. The variants come from human tumour samples and public human variant databases, and the tool accepts only genome assembly GRCh38.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Molecular Tumor Board Data Set. Repository: README.md

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Targeted tumour sequencing for the real-world sets: formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue on a NextSeq500 with the TruSight Oncology 500 assay covering 523 cancer-related genes, processed with the vendor Local App version 2.2 to call small variants, copy number variants, fusions and splice variants. The labels themselves are expert or curator judgements, not assay readouts; the SOP and ClinVar sets carry no assay of their own.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Molecular Tumor Board Data Set

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Genomic coordinates on GRCh38, as a text table or a VCF, and whatever the integrated public resources return for them. The pipeline uses VEP annotation with dbNSFP and SpliceAI scores, gnomAD frequencies, ClinVar, COSMIC and, in the default configuration, the licensed OncoKB; no sequence model or structure is involved.
facts.source_locator: Repository: README.md, Input data and OncoVI_mod. Paper: Materials and Methods, Variant Annotation via the VEP-Based In-House Pipeline

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: None. OncoVI is a deterministic rule engine: each criterion is coded as IF-ELSE logic over the resources, points are summed and the class follows from fixed thresholds. Nothing is trained, fitted or tuned on any of the four reference sets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, first paragraph. Repository: README.md, figure caption

strengths.text: The reference sets are of different kinds and the weak spots show up differently in each: guideline authors' own variants, a real tumour board cohort, ClinVar curation and a blinded expert reclassification.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, the four data set sections; Results

strengths.text: Disagreements are followed up rather than left as a percentage. The validation set deliberately includes every strongest disagreement, and the paper traces where the score sat relative to a class threshold, for example that 55% of the oncogenic variants OncoVI called uncertain scored four or five, just under the cutoff.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Validation Data Set; Results, Performance on the ClinVar Data Set

strengths.text: Every percentage is reported with its counts, so each figure can be traced to the exact set it belongs to, and the resource and tool versions behind the annotation are pinned in the methods.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results; Materials and Methods, Variant Annotation via the VEP-Based In-House Pipeline

strengths.text: The code is public with a documented setup, and a variant that avoids the licensed OncoKB resource is provided so the tool can be run without it.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results. Repository: README.md, Get started and OncoVI_mod

limitations.text: The references disagree with each other more than the tool disagrees with them. On the 135 validation variants the experts' guideline-based reclassification matched the same experts' earlier tumour board assessment for only 34%, so an agreement rate against the tumour board (22% here, 78% over the full cohort) measures the reference as much as the tool.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results, Comparative Analysis with Expert Re-Assessment

limitations.text: The 80% agreement on the validation set is not an independent estimate. That set was chosen after seeing the confusion matrix, it is enriched for disagreements, and the experts were given the resources OncoVI uses for each criterion before reclassifying.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Validation Data Set

limitations.text: Agreement is uneven across variant kinds in a way the headline figures hide: on the tumour board set the benign and likely benign class agrees at 43% against 97% for uncertain, and truncating alterations agree at 49.4% against 78.2% for missense.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results, Performance of OncoVI on the Molecular Tumor Board Data Set

limitations.text: Results depend on resources that move and on one that is licensed: the default configuration uses OncoKB, ClinVar was read on 12 April 2025, and the criteria rest on the authors' own reading of the guideline text where it was unclear. The README states that an MIT licence applies to the scripts in the repository, while resources it uses such as OncoKB and COSMIC need separate licence agreements.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, ClinVar Data Set; Results. Repository: README.md

run_guide.summary: Install OncoVI in a conda environment, prepare its resources and VEP cache, and classify the example variant set.
prerequisites: conda 24.11.1 or later and Python 3.8.8 or later, as the README's requirements list them.
The Ensembl VEP conda package at version 111 or later, with the dbNSFP and SpliceAI plugin data.
Variants on GRCh38 only, as text or VCF.
Access to the resources OncoVI queries; the default configuration includes the licensed OncoKB, and OncoVI_mod is provided for users without it.
The README states that the MIT licence applies only to the scripts in the repository; OncoKB and COSMIC need their own licence agreements.

profile.summary: This is the evaluation published with Talos, an open-source tool that automates variant prioritisation for rare disease reanalysis. It is not a reusable suite: the reference is the set of diagnoses already known in two cohorts, 401 Acute Care Genomics probands and 688 Rare Genomes Project families, each reprocessed through one standardised calling pipeline. The measures are how many known diagnoses Talos returns and how many candidate variants a human must read to find them, reported separately for trios, singletons and the whole cohort and under default and strict filtering. A paired comparison against Exomiser and a prospective deployment on 4,735 undiagnosed individuals are reported alongside.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, Assessing Talos performance; Table 1

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two quantities in tension. Sensitivity: of the diagnoses already known in a cohort, how many does the tool put in front of an analyst. Workload: how many candidate variants the analyst has to read, per proband and per diagnosis. The cohorts were chosen so that the tool could be measured against manual analysis and with and without parental data, which is why every figure is reported separately for trios, singletons and the full cohort. The design question behind it is whether automated reanalysis can be run often enough to be sustainable, which is why the burden per case matters as much as the recall.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, Assessing Talos performance; Table 1

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Both cohorts were reprocessed from raw sequencing data through one pipeline, GATK for short variants, GATK-SV for structural variants in genomes and GATK-gCNV for copy number variants in exomes, and Talos was evaluated against the variants that pipeline detected. That matters for the denominator: of 208 known diagnoses in the ACG trios, 196 (94%) were detectable by the pipeline, and of 57 in the RGP trios, 54 (95%) were. The ACG cohort is 401 critically ill infants and children given ultra-rapid clinical genomic testing in Australia between 2018 and 2022, 115 exomes and 286 genomes, 94% trios, with a prior manual diagnostic yield of 55%. The RGP cohort is 688 families recruited remotely across the United States and sequenced at the Broad Institute before September 2022, 298 singletons and 390 trios, prior yield 15.4%, median proband age 26 years.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Assessing Talos performance, Acute Care Genomics cohort, Rare Genomes Project cohort; Table 1

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Talos is run on the reprocessed call sets and its returned candidates are compared with the known diagnoses. Two filtering settings are reported: default, and strict, which requires a phenotype match. Each cell of Table 1 gives the diagnoses found with the percentage of detectable diagnoses, the total candidate variants, candidates per proband and candidates per diagnosis. Success for Talos is simply that the causative variant is returned under default settings, since Talos returns an unranked set rather than a ranking. Against Exomiser, success is defined by rank position (top 1, top 5, top 10, or unconstrained), and because the two tools run on the same families the comparison uses McNemar's exact test on the discordant pairs with two-sided p values. The tool is described as deterministic and automated, so its output does not depend on the investigator, although prior diagnoses were known at evaluation time.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Methods, Exomiser comparison and Statistics and reproducibility

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: In the ACG trios Talos returned 177 of the 196 detectable diagnoses (90%) from 487 candidate variants, 1.3 per proband and 2.8 per diagnosis; across the full ACG cohort 186 of 208 (89%) from 523 candidates. Singletons cost more per diagnosis: 170 of 208 (82%) from 729 candidates, 4.3 per diagnosis. In the RGP cohort the trios gave 47 of 54 (87%) at 1.3 candidates per proband but 11.0 candidates per diagnosis, and the full cohort 80 of 93 (86%) at 13.7 per diagnosis. Strict filtering lowers both: for example 164 of 196 (83%) in ACG trios at 2.5 candidates per diagnosis. Against Exomiser on 194 ACG trio families with SNV or indel diagnoses, Exomiser found 172 (89%) with all variants considered, 164 (85%) in its top 10, 157 (81%) in its top five and 127 (65%) at rank one; McNemar's test found no difference at all-variants or top 10 and favoured Talos at top five and top one. In the prospective cohort of 4,735 undiagnosed individuals, Talos output led to 241 new diagnoses in 238 individuals, a 5.1% additional yield, all later classified pathogenic or likely pathogenic by accredited laboratories; across 29 monthly cycles, 92% of those diagnoses came in a cohort's first cycle and later cycles returned an average of five new candidate variants per 1,000 cases.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Results, Acute Care Genomics cohort, Rare Genomes Project cohort, Comparison with other tools, Iterative reanalysis in research and clinical datasets

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Talos is a Nextflow workflow with its dependencies in Docker, run locally or on a cluster. Build the image, download the external annotation resources into a large_files directory, run the preparation workflow that formats ClinVar, PanelApp and AlphaMissense into Hail tables, then run the combined annotation and analysis workflow from a single input TSV naming the cohort, its VCF, the data type, a pedigree and a config file. The annotation workflow is run once per dataset and only the prioritisation workflow is rerun for later reanalysis. Output is a JSON of candidate variants per proband with variant-level and gene-level evidence, inheritance checks and phenotype match tags, plus optional HTML reports and a simplified TSV.
sections.source_locator: Repository: README.md, Quick Start, Download Annotation Resources, Run Preparation Workflow, Run Annotation and Talos Combined Workflow, Outputs. Paper: Methods, Talos input requirements

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Two evaluation cohorts and one prospective deployment. ACG: 401 probands, 208 known diagnoses in the full cohort and 377 trios. RGP: 688 families (298 singletons, 390 trios), 93 known diagnoses in the full cohort, 106 prior diagnoses in the cohort overall. Prospective: 4,735 undiagnosed or partially diagnosed individuals, 3,739 exomes and 996 genomes, of whom 3,737 were analysed as singletons. The abstract describes the validation as 1,089 individuals, which is the 401 plus 688.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Abstract; Results, Iterative reanalysis in research and clinical datasets

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No train and test split: Talos is a rule and evidence pipeline, not a trained model, so every case in a cohort is analysed. The reported partitions are by family structure (trio only, singleton, full cohort) within each cohort, and by filtering setting (default or strict with phenotype matching). The denominator for sensitivity is the diagnoses detectable by the standardised calling pipeline, not all prior diagnoses.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1 and its footnote; Methods, Statistics and reproducibility

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Diagnoses recovered, as a count and a percentage of the detectable known diagnoses, higher better; and review burden as candidate variants in total, per proband and per diagnosis, lower better. For the prospective cohort the measure is additional diagnostic yield as a percentage of individuals. The Exomiser comparison adds rank-budget recall at top 1, top 5, top 10 and unconstrained, with McNemar's exact test p values on the discordant pairs.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Methods, Exomiser comparison; Results

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Two kinds. The manual clinical and research analysis that produced the known diagnoses in each cohort is the reference standard. Exomiser v.14 in its default configuration is the one competing tool, run on the same ACG trio SNV and indel call sets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Comparison with other tools; Methods, Exomiser comparison

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Weak, and the paper says so plainly: the investigators were not blinded and the prior diagnoses were known at evaluation time, which was necessary to benchmark against manual analysis. The protections are that Talos is deterministic and produces its output without investigator input, that both cohorts were reprocessed through one standardised pipeline so the tool is measured against a fixed call set, and that Exomiser ran on the same families. There is no held-out cohort and no prespecified threshold.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Statistics and reproducibility; Results, Assessing Talos performance

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Little. Counts and percentages are reported without confidence intervals, and no statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. The only inferential statistics are the McNemar exact test p values for the paired Talos against Exomiser comparison at each rank budget. Reproducibility rests on the pipeline being deterministic and on versioning the external annotation sources at run time, which the authors say allows exact reproduction of a given reanalysis cycle.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Statistics and reproducibility and Exomiser comparison

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A case: one proband, with or without parents, and the variant calls for that family. Success or failure is per family (did the known causative variant come back), and the burden measures count candidate variants per proband and per diagnosis.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Methods, Exomiser comparison

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human. All three cohorts are people with rare disease: critically ill infants and children in Australia, families recruited across the United States and Puerto Rico, and patients referred for genomic testing in Australia.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Acute Care Genomics cohort, Rare Genomes Project cohort, Iterative reanalysis

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Clinical exome and genome sequencing, reprocessed from raw data with GATK for short variants, GATK-SV for structural variants and GATK-gCNV for copy number variants. The labels are not assay readouts but clinical diagnoses: the variants previously reported for each case, and for the prospective cohort, variants later classified pathogenic or likely pathogenic by accredited laboratories and submitted to ClinVar.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Assessing Talos performance and Iterative reanalysis; Data availability

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Variant calls and family and phenotype metadata, not sequence. Mandatory: SNV and indel calls as single-sample or multi-sample VCF, a pedigree in PED format and a TOML configuration. Optional: structural and copy number variant calls, Human Phenotype Ontology terms per individual, and a previous results JSON to keep first-seen dates. The paper asks that input variants not be prefiltered beyond standard quality control so that Talos's own filtering applies consistently. Talos also draws on external resources: PanelApp Australia, ClinVar through ClinvArbitration, gnomAD and AlphaMissense.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Talos input requirements; Methods, Statistics and reproducibility. Repository: README.md, inputs and annotation resources

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: None of the machine learning kind. Talos applies logic modules, inheritance-aware filtering, allele frequency filtering and phenotype matching against versioned external evidence; nothing is trained on these cohorts. The only setting varied in the evaluation is default against strict filtering, and Exomiser was run at its default configuration.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Table 1; Methods, Exomiser comparison

strengths.text: Sensitivity and review burden are reported together, per family structure and per filtering setting, so the cost of each gain is visible: the ACG trios return 90% of detectable diagnoses at 1.3 candidates per proband, while RGP singletons return 87% at 18.4 candidates per diagnosis.

The denominator is honest about what the calling pipeline can see. Diagnoses due to variant classes the pipeline does not capture reliably, such as repeat expansions and low-level mosaics, are kept in the cohort and reported as missed, and the detectable subset is stated (196 of 208 in ACG trios, 54 of 57 in RGP trios).
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results, Acute Care Genomics cohort and Rare Genomes Project cohort; Methods, Statistics and reproducibility

strengths.text: The comparison with Exomiser is paired and analysed as such, with McNemar's exact test on discordant families and a stated reason why unpaired tests would be wrong, and it is reported at several review budgets rather than at one flattering cut.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Exomiser comparison; Results, Comparison with other tools

strengths.text: The tool is open source, containerised and reproducible by design: Docker and Nextflow with the study's configuration files published, and the external evidence sources versioned at run time.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Statistics and reproducibility; Code availability. Repository: README.md, Quick Start

limitations.text: The evaluation was run by the tool's own developers on cohorts whose diagnoses were already known, without blinding or randomisation, so the recall figures are not an independent prospective estimate.

No uncertainty is attached to the headline numbers. Every diagnosis count, percentage and candidates-per-case figure in Table 1 is a point estimate with no interval, and the only p values in the study are for the Exomiser comparison.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Table 1; Methods, Statistics and reproducibility

limitations.text: The cohorts cannot be downloaded openly, so a third party can rerun the benchmark only after gaining controlled access. The RGP data are under controlled access via dbGaP (phs003047). The Australian Genomics data, including genome and exome sequencing data, are available for ethically approved secondary health and medical research use, subject to participant consent, on application to the cohort's data access committee with evidence of ethics approval. What is public without application is the tool and its configuration.

Results depend on moving evidence sources and on local gene panels. Candidates during iterative reanalysis are returned only when the supporting evidence has changed, and the annotation sources are PanelApp Australia, ClinVar and gnomAD at whatever version was current, so a reanalysis elsewhere or later will not give the same output.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results, Iterative reanalysis; Methods, Statistics and reproducibility

limitations.text: The article itself is under a non-commercial, no-derivatives licence, so the text and tables cannot be redistributed or adapted freely, although the code is MIT.

gaps: Extended Data Table 5 (cost estimates), Extended Data Fig. 1 (which variants each tool found) and Supplementary Table 1 (the new diagnoses) were not fetched, so only the figures printed in the article text are recorded.

run_guide.summary: Build the Talos container, prepare its annotation resources, and run the annotation and analysis workflow over a cohort's VCF and pedigree.
prerequisites: Nextflow and Docker, as the README's requirements list them.

The external annotation resources (reference genome, gnomAD, AlphaMissense, phenotype data) downloaded into a large_files directory, plus up-to-date ClinVar and PanelApp dumps prepared by the preparation workflow.
A cohort VCF (single-sample or multi-sample), a pedigree in PED format and a TOML config; optional structural variant calls, HPO terms per individual and a previous results JSON.
A single machine is enough: the study's analyses ran on one virtual machine with 16 cores and 64 GB of memory.
The code is MIT licensed. The study's own cohorts are not public.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/populationgenomics/talos.git
cd talos
git checkout --detach d279709d4c8b601b2280ccf3fe5edb480f7a77f6
steps.explanation: The repository address is the one the paper's code availability statement gives; the checkout line was added here to pin the commit these steps were read from.

steps.title: Build the container
steps.shell: docker build -f docker/Dockerfile -t talos:12.3.2 .
steps.explanation: The README's build command. It notes that Talos uses Hail, which has been validated only on Java 11 and Python 3.10 and 3.11, so the default base image is an older one; a modern base can be chosen with build arguments at the user's own risk.

steps.title: Prepare the annotation resources
steps.shell:
bash large_files/gather_files.sh
nextflow \
    -c nextflow.config \
    run preparation.nf \
    --processed_annotations <static path for prepared files> \
    --large_files <path to the downloaded resources>
steps.explanation: The README links to a script, large_files/gather_files.sh, that performs the initial download of the required resources but gives no command for it; the bash line above was written here from that link. The README gives the preparation workflow command that formats ClinVar and PanelApp into Hail tables and reformats AlphaMissense. The two paths are placeholders; processed_annotations should be a static directory reused by later runs.
steps.source_locator: Repository: README.md, Download Annotation Resources and Run Preparation Workflow

steps.title: Run the annotation and analysis workflow
steps.shell:
nextflow \
  -c nextflow.config \
  run main.nf \
  --input_tsv nextflow/inputs/test.tsv \
  -output-dir <path_to_output_dir>
steps.explanation: The README's run of the combined workflow, using the example input TSV it ships. Each row of that TSV names a cohort, its VCF, the data type, a pedigree and a config, with optional columns for history and more. The annotation stage needs running only once per dataset; later reanalyses rerun only the prioritisation stage.

outputs: A JSON file of candidate variants per proband with variant-level and gene-level evidence, inheritance checks and phenotype match tags, written under a path of the form {workflow.outputDir}/{cohort}_outputs.

Reanalysis metadata per variant: first_seen and evidence_last_updated.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
They run the tool; they do not reproduce the paper's evaluation, which needs the ACG and RGP cohorts and their known diagnoses, neither of which is public.
The resource download and the two path arguments are site-specific, and the external evidence sources change over time, so the same command will give different candidates on a different date.

profile.summary: A single-laboratory study that reclassified 121 BRCA1 and BRCA2 variants of uncertain significance (VUS) from 120 patients in two steps: first with the standard ACMG/AMP system, current SVI recommendations and new data, then with the ClinGen ENIGMA expert panel specifications on the same data. It reports how many VUS each step moved to benign or likely benign. It is relevant to clinical variant scientists choosing classification rules for BRCA1 and BRCA2, not to model comparison.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Materials and Methods, 'Patients and variant data'

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How far gene-specific expert panel rules change the classification of existing VUS compared with the general ACMG/AMP rules, when both are applied to the same up-to-date evidence. The endpoint is the share of VUS reclassified, and in which direction.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Introduction

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: 121 VUS (40 in BRCA1, 81 in BRCA2) classified between January 2018 and November 2023 were taken from the laboratory's internal database. These were reclassified in two steps (t2 and t3) from the original classification (t1). All reclassifications were done by one experienced variant analyst. Both steps used the Tavtigian point-based scoring system, but the ENIGMA rules require -2 points for likely benign.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Step t2 applies the standard ACMG/AMP system with SVI recommendations as of November 2023 to the latest annotations. Step t3 applies the ENIGMA specifications version 1.1.0 to the same new data. The study counts VUS moved to likely benign or benign at each step: 20% (n = 24) at t2 and 83.5% at t3, with none moved to likely pathogenic or pathogenic. There is no external truth set; the authors attribute most of the difference to the ENIGMA BP1_STR code, applied to 93 variants.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods; Results

strengths.text: Both rule sets are applied to the same new evidence, which separates the effect of the rules from the effect of new data.
A single experienced analyst did every reclassification, removing differences between analysts.

limitations.text: There is no truth set: a higher reclassification rate is not shown to be more accurate. No variant was reclassified as likely pathogenic or pathogenic under either rule set.

profile.summary: A study that combines two saturation genome editing (SGE) screens of the BRCA2 DNA binding domain into four composite functional models, checks each against known pathogenic and benign variants, and then feeds the best one (the Integrated VarCall model) into ClinGen BRCA1/2 expert panel classification rules. It reports sensitivity and specificity against ClinVar and HDR assay standards, and the share of 6383 variants that could be classified. It is relevant to clinical variant scientists using BRCA2 functional data.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two things. First, how accurately each functional model (two original SGE studies, a concordance model, an Integrated VarCall model, an Integrated GMM model and a secondary concordance model) separates known pathogenic from benign variants. Second, how many BRCA2 variants can be classified as pathogenic or benign once the best functional model's evidence is added to the ClinGen rules.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: 6383 SNVs were scored in both SGE studies (HAP1 cells and humanised mouse ES cells); 1041 of them had discordant results. The Integrated VarCall model pools raw scores from both studies in a Bayesian hierarchical model with batch effects; silent variants are assumed benign and nonsense variants pathogenic, and the prior probability of pathogenicity is 0.2. Reference standards are 158 ClinVar P/LP and B/LB missense variants not influenced by SGE results and common to all six models, and 316 HDR assay missense standards.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results; Methods, 'Integrated VarCall model'; Figure 1 legend

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Because all models reach close to 100% when every pathogenic or benign category is counted, the comparison uses only the Pathogenic_Strong and Benign_Strong/Moderate categories: sensitivity against P/LP standards (or HDR abnormal) and specificity against B/LB standards (or HDR normal). The Integrated VarCall model reaches 98.9% sensitivity and 100% specificity on the ClinVar standards, and 97% and 100% on the HDR standards. Its functional calls are then combined with other evidence under ENIGMA specification version 1.2.0 and the classification yield is counted. A separate case-control analysis tests whether Pathogenic_Strong missense variants raise cancer risk: odds ratios from logistic regression adjusted for age and ancestry, 5.46 (95% CI 4.07 to 7.48) for breast cancer and 6.83 (95% CI 4.51 to 10.40) for ovarian cancer, using Ambry Genetics cases and AllofUs controls.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results; Figure 1 legend; Methods, 'ClinGen/ACMG/AMP classification'

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository provides the VarCall analysis in R with JAGS. Clone it, install JAGS and the listed R packages, then run runRtex.R in the VarCall folder. This reproduces the functional probabilities, not the comparison against ClinVar and HDR standards, for which no script is described.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Installation Guide; Test and Run

facts.source_locator: Paper: Results; Figure 1 legend

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No train and test split in the usual sense. The VarCall model is calibrated with silent variants as benign and nonsense variants as pathogenic, and scored on missense standards.

strengths.text: ClinVar standards exclude variants influenced by the SGE screens, and a second, assay-based standard set (HDR) is used.
All six models are compared on the same common standard sets.
Code is public, and the authors state that data are in GEO.

limitations.text: The standard sets are small (158 and 316 common variants) and no confidence intervals are given, so differences between models of one or two variants are hard to judge.
Only the strongest functional categories are scored; with all categories, every model is close to 100%.
Classification yield is not accuracy, and 242 of 964 functionally Pathogenic_Strong variants could not be classified for lack of other evidence.
BRCA2 DNA binding domain only. The repository has no licence that GitHub detects; its README states the MIT licence.

profile.summary: A single-centre study that reclassified 450 BRCA1 missense variants with conflicting ClinVar interpretations (ClinVar accessed 20 December 2022) with two methods: the automated VarSome tool and manual curation under the CanVIG-UK BRCA1/BRCA2 gene-specific guidance. It reports how often the two agree on a three-class scale, and how each matches ClinVar submitters and the 17 variants that later reached a ClinVar consensus. It is relevant to clinical variant scientists choosing between automated and gene-specific classification.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: How much an automated ACMG classifier (VarSome premium v11.5) and gene-specific manual curation (CanVIG-UK BRCA1/BRCA2 guidance v1.17) agree on BRCA1 missense variants that ClinVar submitters disagree about, and how each relates to ClinVar submitter calls and later ClinVar consensus.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Of 12,719 BRCA1 variants in ClinVar on 20 December 2022, 654 had conflicting interpretations, and the 450 missense variants among them were analysed. CanVIG-UK classifications were made by one genetic specialist and cross-checked by a second; VarSome results were used as produced, with no manual change. The same 450 variants were re-extracted from ClinVar on 1 May 2024 to find any that had reached consensus.

The main result is overall concordance between the two methods: 58.9% (95% CI 52.0 to 66.4%; 265/450), with no PV/LPV versus BV/LBV disagreements. Secondary analyses compare each method's calls with the share of ClinVar submitters calling a variant pathogenic or benign, and with the 17 variants (3.8%) that had a ClinVar consensus by May 2024; each method disagreed with that consensus on one variant.
