profile.summary: This was a public competition, hosted with Topcoder, on predicting what happens to mouse CD8 T cells in a tumour when a single gene is knocked out. The organisers generated an in vivo Perturb-seq data set of 73 gene knockouts in T cells transferred into a melanoma model, annotated each cell as one of five states, and asked teams to predict the five cell state proportions for held-out knockouts, to rank all expressed genes by two therapy-motivated objective functions, and to propose a new objective function. The top-ranked nominations were then knocked out in a second experiment, so submissions were scored against a prospective screen as well as held-out data. The record is useful to anyone comparing methods that predict perturbation effects on cell state composition rather than full expression profiles.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Machine learning competition section, Methods (Challenge setup and results); README.md: Code for Paper, Contents of this Repository

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: The biological question is which gene knockout shifts tumour-infiltrating CD8 T cells away from terminal exhaustion and towards progenitor and other useful states, which matters for checkpoint blockade and CAR T therapies. The challenge turns that into three tasks. Challenge 1 measures accuracy: predict the five-dimensional vector of cell state proportions for knockouts that were measured but withheld. Challenge 2 measures usefulness for picking targets: predict proportions for every expressed gene, rank the untested genes by two objective functions, and be scored against a new experiment that knocked out the nominated genes. Challenge 3 measures the objective function itself: propose a score that ranks perturbations by how close they bring the cell state distribution to a desired one. The organisers point out that most existing benchmarks look like Challenge 1 alone, and that Challenge 2 tests the methods for biological efficacy.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Machine learning competition section; Methods (Challenge setup and results)

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The training data come from an in vivo pooled CRISPR knockout screen. Naive CD8 T cells from OT-1 TCR transgenic mice were transduced with a guide library and adoptively transferred into congenic recipient mice, which were injected subcutaneously with B16-OVA melanoma cells one day after the transfer; the tumour-infiltrating T cells were collected 14 days later and sequenced. Screen 1 targeted 73 genes; after merging lanes it held 71,393 cells, and 31,009 remained after quality control for single-guide assignment and mitochondrial content. Leiden clustering gave five populations, annotated as progenitor, effector, terminal exhausted, cycling and other, and each perturbation is summarised by the proportions of those five states. A second experiment, Screen 2, targeted 59 genes, gave 75,227 cells and 25,738 after quality control, and served as the validation screen for Challenge 2. Perturbations with very few cells were dropped, with a cutoff of 32 cells for Screen 1 and 10 for Screen 2, leaving 59 perturbations for Screen 1 and 50 for Screen 2. A published screen of 180 transcription factors in the same mouse model was reannotated with the same five states and used as a third data set, with 173 perturbations after preprocessing. That screen activated the T cells before transfer and harvested them after 7 days rather than 14, and when the five cell states were mapped onto it some clusters could not be assigned. The two example objective functions were defined on the proportion vectors, with the unperturbed Screen 1 proportions as the reference point.
sections.source_locator: Paper: In-vivo single-cell CRISPR screens section, Methods (Data preprocessing and normalization, Cell state annotation, Challenge setup and results); README.md: Contents of this Repository

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: In Challenge 1 a submission is a five-number proportion vector per held-out knockout. Seven knockouts were withheld; three of them, Aqr, Bach2 and Bhlhe40, formed a validation set with up to three submissions and feedback, and the final ranking used the average absolute error over the remaining four, with one final submission. The error is the sum of absolute differences across the five states, so lower is better. In Challenge 2 the predicted proportions for all untested genes are turned into two ranked lists with the ICB and CAR T objective functions. The top-ranked genes from the Challenge 1 winners were knocked out in Screen 2, the measured genes were ranked by the same objectives, and each submission was scored by an area under the curve comparing its predicted ranking with the measured one. That score lies between 0 and 1 and a random ranking is expected to give 0.5. Scores were computed on both the filtered and the unfiltered Screen 2, averaged within each, and the final score was the smaller of the two averages. Challenge 3 submissions were written reports, ranked by single-blind peer review among participants, averaged over reviewer ranks, then reviewed by the organisers. For the follow-up benchmarking of the top 20 methods, the organisers reimplemented them and used cross-fold validation instead of the seven held-out perturbations alone: perturbations were partitioned at random into 6 folds for Screen 1 and the public screen and 5 folds for Screen 2, each fold held out in turn, and the whole procedure repeated 5 times to give a standard deviation.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Challenge setup and results, Benchmark on prediction error, Benchmark on ranking genes); run_exp.py

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository holds the organisers' own benchmarking code, not a submission server. Create the conda environment from environment.yml, get the split data files, and run the per-method scripts in the folder for the screen you want. The baseline script for Screen 1 loads a single AnnData file holding the internal splits, loops over six splits and five repeats for three predictors, nearest neighbour, kernel regression and bagged kernel regression, and prints the mean and standard deviation of the average error. Some data files are not in the repository and have to be downloaded from a Google Drive folder the README links.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Environment setup, Contents of this Repository, Notes; run_exp.py

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: Three Perturb-seq data sets of CD8 T cells. Screen 1, the training and Challenge 1 data, 73 targeted genes, 71,393 cells merged and 31,009 after quality control, 59 perturbations passing preprocessing. Screen 2, the validation screen for Challenge 2, 59 targeted genes, 75,227 cells and 25,738 after quality control, 50 perturbations passing preprocessing. A published screen of 180 transcription factors in the same mouse model, with T cells activated before transfer and harvested after 7 days, reannotated with the same cell states except for some clusters that could not be assigned, 173 perturbations passing preprocessing. Challenge 2 also required predictions for the expressed genes measured in Screen 1 that were not among the targets already tested, out of 15,077 measured genes.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Data preprocessing and normalization, Benchmark on prediction error, Challenge setup and results); Prediction on a public T cell perturbation dataset; README.md: Contents of this Repository

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Held-out perturbations, and a second experiment. Challenge 1 withheld seven randomly selected knockouts, of which three were a feedback validation set and the final ranking used the other four. Challenge 2 was scored on genes that had never been tested when the submissions were made, knocked out afterwards in Screen 2. The organisers' later benchmark instead used random cross-fold splits over perturbations, 6 folds for Screen 1 and the public screen and 5 for Screen 2, with every perturbation held out once, and for the Screen 1 to Screen 2 transfer they trained on all Screen 1 perturbations and predicted the Screen 2 ones.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Challenge setup and results, Benchmark on prediction error, Benchmark on ranking genes)

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Challenge 1: the average absolute error, the sum of absolute differences between predicted and measured proportions across the five cell states, averaged over the held-out knockouts, lower is better. Challenge 2: an area under the curve comparing the predicted ranking of the validated genes with their measured ranking, between 0 and 1 with 0.5 expected at random, higher is better, taken as the minimum of the averaged filtered and unfiltered Screen 2 scores. Challenge 3: averaged reviewer rank from single-blind peer review, lower is better. The follow-up benchmark also reports the absolute error on key states such as progenitor and cycling.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Challenge setup and results); Benchmarking top participating methods section

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Two simple baselines in the organisers' benchmark: predict the cell state proportions of the non-targeting control cells, and predict the average proportions over all training perturbations. The paper reports that no other prediction method was significantly better than the averaged perturbation baseline on Screen 1. The 246 team submissions themselves, and the 20 top methods reimplemented by the organisers with nearest neighbour, kernel regression and bagging predictors, are the other reference points.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Benchmarking top participating methods section; Machine learning competition section; run_exp.py

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: The held-out knockouts were withheld from the data given to participants, and Challenge 2 was judged against genes that had not been measured anywhere when the submissions were made, so a prediction could not be copied from the ground truth. The organisers do not describe any control on the external data a team may use for gene features, and the winning methods did draw on public databases and other genome-wide Perturb-seq data sets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Machine learning competition section; Methods (Challenge setup and results)

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: In the competition itself, one final submission was scored per team, with no replicates. In the organisers' later benchmark each cross-fold procedure was repeated 5 times to get a standard deviation of the accuracy, and each method was run 5 times for the ranking score. The winning Challenge 3 objective function adds a lower confidence bound term derived from the Hoeffding inequality that accounts for how few cells a perturbation has.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Benchmark on prediction error, Benchmark on ranking genes, Challenge setup and results)

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A single-gene knockout. Each example is one perturbed gene, summarised by a five-dimensional vector of cell state proportions over progenitor, effector, terminally exhausted, cycling and other cells, computed from the single cells carrying a guide for that gene.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Challenge setup and results, Implementation of top methods)

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Mouse. The screens used naive CD8 T cells from OT-1 TCR transgenic mice transferred into congenic mice that were then injected with B16-OVA melanoma cells, and the public screen used the same mouse model.
facts.source_locator: Paper: In-vivo single-cell CRISPR screens section; Prediction on a public T cell perturbation dataset

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: In vivo pooled CRISPR knockout screens with single-cell RNA sequencing. Guides were delivered by lentivirus to naive CD8 T cells, the cells were transferred into congenic mice that were injected with B16-OVA melanoma cells one day later, tumour-infiltrating T cells were collected after 14 days, and the reads were processed with Cell Ranger. Cell states come from Leiden clustering of the normalised data annotated with known T cell markers, with Screen 2 and the public screen annotated by transfer from Screen 1 after Harmony batch correction.
facts.source_locator: Paper: In-vivo single-cell CRISPR screens section; Methods (Data preprocessing and normalization, Cell state annotation)

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Anything, including outside data. A method has to map a gene identity to a proportion vector, and the organisers describe the top methods as first building a gene feature representation from the provided Perturb-seq data, from public databases such as STRING, NCBI and gene ontology, or from other genome-wide Perturb-seq data sets, then fitting a map from those features to proportions.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Benchmarking top participating methods section; Methods (Implementation of top methods)

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Fitting on the provided screen. A model is trained on the measured perturbations of Screen 1 and applied to genes it has not seen, with hyper-parameters chosen by cross validation on the training set. The organisers' reimplementations pair each of 15 gene feature sets with a predictor, nearest neighbour, kernel regression or bagging, so the feature source and the predictor can be varied separately.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Benchmarking top participating methods section; Methods (Implementation of top methods); run_exp.py

strengths.text: Submissions were tested prospectively. The genes the methods nominated were knocked out in a second experiment and the measured ranking was used to score every Challenge 2 submission, which is more than a held-out split can show.

The top 20 methods were reimplemented by the organisers in a common two-step form, so the contribution of the gene features can be separated from the contribution of the predictor, and the same predictor can be compared across 15 feature sets.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Implementation of top methods); Benchmarking top participating methods section

strengths.text: The comparison includes two baselines that are easy to beat by accident, the non-targeting control proportions and the average over training perturbations, and the organisers report that on Screen 1 no other method was significantly better than the averaged perturbation baseline.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Benchmarking top participating methods section

strengths.text: The same methods were also run on an independent published screen in the same mouse model, reannotated with the same cell states, and the organisers report that the ranking of the feature sets was largely preserved.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Prediction on a public T cell perturbation dataset

limitations.text: The competition scored very few test perturbations. The final Challenge 1 ranking rested on four held-out knockouts, which is why the organisers moved to repeated cross-fold splits for their own analysis.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Challenge setup and results, Benchmark on prediction error)

limitations.text: The signal the metric can show is limited. The organisers report that the gap between the best and worst performing feature sets was 7.5%, and that the error per gene tracks how far that perturbation sits from the average training perturbation, so a method can look good mainly by predicting the mean effect.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Benchmarking top participating methods section

limitations.text: It is one mouse model, one tumour and one cell type, with a restricted T cell receptor repertoire, and the cell state labels are clusters the organisers defined and then transferred to the other screens, so both the task and the labels are specific to this study.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: In-vivo single-cell CRISPR screens section; Methods (Cell state annotation)

limitations.text: Reuse is awkward. The paper is under a Creative Commons licence that forbids commercial use and derivatives, no licence is stated for the code, some data files are only on a Google Drive folder rather than in the repository, and the competition is closed, so there is no live leaderboard to submit to.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: licence statement in the PMC record; README.md: Notes (no licence section in the README)

profile.summary: FoldBench is a low-homology benchmark for all-atom biomolecular structure prediction: 1522 biological assemblies from the PDB, organised into nine tasks covering protein, RNA and DNA monomers and six interface types (protein-protein, antibody-antigen, protein-ligand, protein-peptide, protein-RNA and protein-DNA). Targets were deposited after the AlphaFold 3 validation cut-off of 13 January 2023 and filtered against a reproduction of the AlphaFold 3 training set, so a single benchmark can be used to compare co-folding models across molecule classes. Interfaces are scored by success rate (DockQ at least 0.23, or ligand RMSD below 2 angstroms with LDDT-PLI above 0.8 for ligands), monomers by LDDT. The targets, the evaluation code and reference results are published under the MIT licence.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Methods, Data curation procedure; README: FoldBench Targets, Leaderboard

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether an all-atom co-folding model can build the correct structure of a whole biological assembly, and in particular the correct interface between its parts, on targets it is unlikely to have memorised. The nine tasks separate the question by molecule class and interaction type, because the authors treat antibody-antigen interfaces, protein-ligand complexes and nucleic acids as the hard cases. Beyond raw accuracy, the benchmark measures how accuracy depends on similarity to the training set: protein-ligand results are split into an unseen-protein subset and an unseen-ligand subset, and success rate is plotted against ligand similarity to the training data.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Results, Benchmarking protein-ligand co-folding performance

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The authors first reproduced the AlphaFold 3 training set at its 2021-09-30 cut-off, then took PDB entries deposited after 13 January 2023 and before 1 November 2024. Entries must be non-NMR with resolution better than 4.5 angstroms, fewer than 300 polymer chains and between 10 and 2560 tokens under the AlphaFold 3 tokenisation, and the first bioassembly of each entry is the target. Assemblies are cleaned: water removed, chains with fewer than 4 resolved residues or all-unknown residues removed, protein chains with a C-alpha gap over 10 angstroms removed, and clashing chains dropped by a stated rule. Targets are then split into monomers (one polymer chain, below 40 per cent identity to the training set) and interfaces (chain pairs with any heavy atoms within 5 angstroms), each with its own homology rule: a polymer-polymer interface is dropped if both chains exceed 40 per cent identity to two chains of one training complex, protein-protein interfaces are further filtered with Foldseek-Multimer at TM-score below 0.5, a protein-ligand interface is dropped if the protein exceeds 40 per cent identity and the ligand exceeds 50 per cent Tanimoto similarity to a ligand in the same training complex, and protein-peptide interfaces require the protein below 40 per cent identity. What remains is clustered at 40 per cent identity for proteins and 100 per cent for nucleic acids and peptides, keeping the highest-resolution member, under per-task resolution limits.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data curation procedure

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Inputs are generated once from the mmCIF of each bioassembly as AlphaFold 3 JSON, with bond information removed, and then converted to each model's own format. Every model predicts with a 5 by 5 sampling strategy, five seeds by five samples, with 10 recycles, and unless stated otherwise the reported result is the structure with the highest ranking score. Scoring uses OpenStructure v2.8 as the main tool, for LDDT, TM-score and GDT-TS on monomers and for DockQ on most protein interfaces; protein-nucleic acid interfaces are scored with the DockQ v2 program because OpenStructure does not support them. An interface counts as a success at DockQ at least 0.23, and DockQ is also binned into incorrect, acceptable, medium and high. Protein-ligand interfaces use binding-site superposed, symmetry-corrected ligand RMSD, with success defined as ligand RMSD below 2 angstroms and LDDT-PLI above 0.8. Antibody CDR H3 loop RMSD is computed separately after Chothia renumbering through AbNum and PyRosetta4. Monomer tasks report LDDT rather than a success rate. Inference ran on NVIDIA H800 80GB GPUs.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model Inference and Evaluation and metrics; README: Leaderboard note

sections.title: Leaderboard and the training cut-off problem
sections.body: The repository keeps a leaderboard with two target sets: the full set of targets released after 2023-01, and a subset released after 2024-01. On the full set AlphaFold 3 leads at 72.93 per cent on protein-protein, 47.90 per cent on antibody-antigen and 64.90 per cent on protein-ligand, with antibody-antigen the weakest task for every model. The readme marks Boltz-2 and RosettaFold3 with an asterisk because their training cut-off is later than FoldBench's reference date of 2023-01-13: the low-homology guarantee holds only against PDB data before that date, so those models may have seen the targets, and the readme says their results are for reference only and should not be compared directly with the valid models. Two further caveats are printed: nucleic acid monomer results are omitted from the 2024-01 set for want of targets, and one model's protein-RNA row is blank because of inference or evaluation errors.
sections.source_locator: README: Leaderboard and its footnotes

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository is cloned, a conda environment is created from environment.yml, and scoring runs in two steps. The first, evaluate.py, reads a prediction_reference.csv for the named algorithm and, for each requested target type, merges the target table with the prediction table on PDB identifier and scores every prediction against its ground truth with OpenStructure; for the protein-DNA and protein-RNA interface types it additionally scores with DockQ v2. The second, task_score_summary.py, aggregates those per-target scores into success rates or LDDT per task and writes a summary table. Running on more than the bundled examples needs the target CSV files edited and the referenced ground-truth CIF files downloaded from a link the readme gives, and a model's predictions registered in prediction_reference.csv.
sections.source_locator: README: Getting Started, Evaluation; evaluate.py

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: 1522 biological assemblies from the PDB, in nine task sets. The paper's Methods give 334 protein monomers (after removing 7 de novo designed proteins), 14 DNA monomers, 15 RNA monomers, 558 protein-ligand interfaces, 172 antibody-antigen interfaces, 279 general protein-protein interfaces (antibody-antigen excluded), 51 protein-peptide interfaces, 70 protein-RNA interfaces and 330 protein-DNA interfaces. The repository readme lists the same counts except for protein monomers, where it says 330 structures. The protein-ligand set is further split into an unseen-protein subset of 76 targets and an unseen-ligand subset of 482 targets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, final clustering and resolution cut-offs; Results, protein-ligand; README: FoldBench Targets

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Evaluation only: there is no training split, and every target is scored. The separation from training data is by deposition date and by homology to a reproduced AlphaFold 3 training set, with a per-task homology rule, followed by clustering at 40 per cent identity for proteins and 100 per cent for nucleic acids and peptides. The leaderboard reports two nested evaluation sets, targets released after 2023-01 (the full set) and the subset released after 2024-01, and the protein-ligand task is additionally reported on its unseen-protein and unseen-ligand subsets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data curation procedure; README: Leaderboard

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Interfaces are scored by success rate, higher is better: DockQ at least 0.23 for protein-protein, antibody-antigen, protein-peptide, protein-RNA and protein-DNA, and ligand RMSD below 2 angstroms together with LDDT-PLI above 0.8 for protein-ligand. Monomer tasks report LDDT, higher is better. DockQ is also binned as incorrect below 0.23, acceptable 0.23 to below 0.49, medium 0.49 to below 0.80, high 0.80 and above. Further measures reported beside these are TM-score and GDT-TS for monomers, LDDT-LP for the ligand pocket, and CDR H3 loop RMSD for antibodies, lower being better for the RMSD measures.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Evaluation and metrics; README: Leaderboard note

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The paper evaluates five all-atom predictors: AlphaFold 3, Boltz-1, Chai-1, HelixFold 3 and Protenix. The repository leaderboard adds OpenFold 3 (preview) to the same set, and lists Boltz-2 and RosettaFold3 separately as models whose training cut-off is later than the benchmark's reference date. There is no classical docking or template-based reference method.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; README: Leaderboard

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: This is the benchmark's main design feature. Targets must be deposited after 13 January 2023, the AlphaFold 3 validation cut-off, and before 1 November 2024. The authors reproduced the AlphaFold 3 training set at its 2021-09-30 cut-off and filtered against it with a rule per task: monomers below 40 per cent sequence identity; a polymer-polymer interface removed when both chains exceed 40 per cent identity to two chains of one training complex; protein-protein interfaces additionally filtered by Foldseek-Multimer at TM-score below 0.5; a protein-ligand interface removed when the protein exceeds 40 per cent identity and the ligand exceeds 50 per cent Tanimoto similarity to a ligand in the same training complex; protein-peptide interfaces requiring the protein below 40 per cent identity. Remaining similarity is then measured rather than assumed, by reporting accuracy against training-set similarity. The limit is stated plainly in the readme: the guarantee holds against PDB data before 2023-01-13 only, so models with a later training cut-off are flagged and set aside. The readme also says the authors developed an algorithm to identify and prevent overfitting of models on FoldBench, without describing it.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data curation procedure; Results; README: Leaderboard footnotes

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Sampling variation is handled by generating 25 structures per target for every model (five seeds by five samples, 10 recycles) and reporting the one with the highest ranking score, with best-of-25 comparisons shown separately. Figures carry 95 per cent confidence intervals on mean success rates and mean DockQ scores, and box plots show medians and interquartile ranges. The leaderboard tables in the repository carry no interval.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model Inference; Figure 3 and Figure 4 captions; README: Leaderboard

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: One example is either a single polymer chain (a protein, RNA or DNA monomer) or one interface, a pair of chains whose closest heavy atoms are within 5 angstroms, extracted from a predicted full biological assembly. For the protein-ligand task the example is a protein and ligand interface, with one interface chosen at random per ligand. Each target comes from the first bioassembly of a PDB entry.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data curation procedure

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Unreported. Targets are PDB biological assemblies selected by date, resolution, size and homology; the paper and the readme report molecule class, chain counts, token counts and oligomeric state but give no species composition.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Overview of the benchmark; Figure 2 caption

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Experimental structure determination, with NMR excluded. Entries must be non-NMR with resolution better than 4.5 angstroms, and the per-task limits are tighter: below 2.0 angstroms for general protein-protein interfaces, below 2.5 angstroms for antibody-antigen, protein-RNA and protein-DNA interfaces, and no further limit for protein-peptide interfaces. No binding or activity assay is involved.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Data curation procedure

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The full specification of the assembly: sequences and chemical components of every entity, generated from the mmCIF of the bioassembly as AlphaFold 3 JSON with bond information removed, then converted to each model's own input format. Each model uses its own multiple sequence alignment and template pipeline, which the paper notes is not uniform: AlphaFold 3 and HelixFold 3 search RNA alignments and templates locally while the other three do not, and the commit and alignment source of each method are listed in a supplementary table.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model Inference

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Zero-shot inference from released checkpoints. No model is trained or fine-tuned for the benchmark; each is run at a pinned commit with the stated sampling strategy. The repository invites a contributor to submit an algorithm for the maintainers to run, through a packaging guide, rather than submitting scores.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model Inference; README: Integrating a New Model into FoldBench

strengths.text: One target set and one scoring pipeline cover nine tasks across proteins, nucleic acids and ligands, so results for different molecule classes come from the same construction rules rather than from separate task-specific datasets.

The homology filter is explicit and per task, built against a reproduction of the AlphaFold 3 training set, and includes a structural filter (Foldseek-Multimer at TM-score below 0.5) for protein-protein interfaces rather than sequence identity alone.

The benchmark reports how accuracy depends on similarity to training data instead of only reporting a single number, including a ligand-similarity breakdown that the authors read as evidence of memorised binding modes.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results, Benchmarking protein-ligand co-folding performance

strengths.text: Targets, evaluation code and reference results are released under the MIT licence, with a documented path for a new model to be run by the maintainers and a maintained leaderboard that is updated when new models are evaluated.
strengths.source_locator: README: Updates, License, Integrating a New Model; LICENSE; Paper: Code availability

limitations.text: The low-homology guarantee is dated. It holds only against PDB data before 2023-01-13, so any model trained after that date may have seen the targets; the readme flags Boltz-2 and RosettaFold3 on that ground and says their numbers should not be compared with the valid models.

Some tasks are too small to carry much weight: 14 DNA monomers, 15 RNA monomers and 51 protein-peptide interfaces, and the nucleic acid monomer results are omitted from the 2024-01 set altogether for want of targets.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, final counts; README: Leaderboard footnotes

limitations.text: The models are not run through identical pipelines. The authors had to modify several of them to get predictions at all, remove glycans for Boltz-1, drop modified residues for HelixFold 3, patch an AlphaFold 3 error and work around a Chai-1 token limit, and the alignment and template search differs between methods.

Not every model produces a score for every target, so the denominators differ: the final counts of predictable and assessable targets per task and model are given in a supplementary table, and one leaderboard cell is blank because of inference or evaluation errors.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Evaluation and metrics; README: Leaderboard footnotes

limitations.text: The two counts published for the protein monomer task do not agree: the paper's Methods give 334 targets, the repository readme 330 structures. Neither source explains the difference.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, final clustering and resolution cut-offs; README: Monomeric Structures

run_guide.summary: Clone the benchmark, build its conda environment, score a model's predictions per target and aggregate them into success rates and LDDT per task.
prerequisites: conda, to create the environment from the repository's environment.yml.
A model's predicted structures, registered in prediction_reference.csv for that algorithm with its ranking scores and file paths.
The ground-truth CIF files: the bundled examples come with four, and the full referenced set is a separate download the readme links.
The evaluation code is MIT licensed.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/BEAM-Labs/FoldBench.git
cd FoldBench
git checkout --detach 4273f6877d82bd0b2fa476d1b2f34d121cbccc70
steps.explanation: The readme's clone command, with a checkout line added so the steps below run against the same commit as the saved readme and script.

steps.title: Create the evaluation environment
steps.shell:
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate foldbench
steps.explanation: Builds the environment the scoring scripts need, which includes OpenStructure and DockQ.

steps.title: Score each prediction against its ground truth
steps.shell:
python evaluate.py \
  --targets_dir ./examples/targets \
  --evaluation_dir ./examples/outputs/evaluation \
  --algorithm_name Protenix \
  --ground_truth_dir ./examples/ground_truths
steps.explanation: The readme's first evaluation step, run here on the bundled Protenix example. Reading evaluate.py, it loads prediction_reference.csv from the algorithm's evaluation directory, and for each target type merges the target CSV with that table on pdb_id and scores it with OpenStructure, adding DockQ v2 scoring for the protein-DNA and protein-RNA interface types.

steps.title: Aggregate the scores into the task table
steps.shell:
python task_score_summary.py \
  --evaluation_dir ./examples/outputs/evaluation \
  --target_dir ./examples/targets \
  --output_path ./examples/summary_table.csv \
  --algorithm_names Protenix \
  --targets interface_protein_ligand interface_protein_dna monomer_protein \
  --metric_type rank
steps.explanation: The readme's second step. It summarises the per-target scores for the named models and task types into the final success rates and LDDT values and writes them to the given path.

outputs: Per-target score files under the algorithm's evaluation directory, as the bundled example's OpenStructure and DockQ v2 JSON files show.
A summary table at the path given to the second step, holding the success rate or LDDT per task for the named models.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
They score predictions only. Generating the predictions needs each model run separately, which the repository supports through per-algorithm containers rather than these steps.
Going beyond the bundled examples needs the target CSV files edited, the referenced ground-truth CIF package downloaded from an external link, and prediction_reference.csv updated by hand.

profile.summary: The MPRabc paper's evaluation of enhancer-gene link predictors on K562 cells. Predicted links are scored against a gold-standard set of 10 356 CRISPRi perturbations (471 positive, 9885 negative) using the benchmarking pipeline of Gschwind et al., with area under the precision-recall curve as the main metric. It is useful to regulatory genomics researchers comparing enhancer-gene models, but it is one paper's run on one cell line.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Methods, 'Benchmarking'

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a model can tell which candidate enhancers regulate which genes in K562 cells. The truth set is enhancer-gene pairs tested by CRISPR interference: a pair is positive when perturbing the enhancer significantly reduced the gene's expression. The paper uses the systematic benchmarking pipeline of Gschwind et al., which pools CRISPR perturbation results into a gold standard and asks how well model scores recover them.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction; Methods, 'ENCODE-rE2G' and 'Benchmarking'

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Candidate enhancers are DNase-seq peaks called with MACS2, resized to 500 bp, keeping the top 150 000 by read count; every candidate within 5 000 000 bp of a gene's TSS forms a candidate pair. DNase-seq, H3K27ac ChIP-seq and Hi-C come from ENCODE. Models are evaluated on predefined CRISPRi datasets from Gschwind et al., and the paper reports the K562 set of 10 356 perturbations. MPRabc itself was trained on K562 CRISPRi-labelled pairs, as Gschwind et al. recommend.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, 'Dataset', 'ENCODE-rE2G' and 'Benchmarking'

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Model scores are intersected with the labelled pairs and AUPRC is computed; precision at 70% recall is the secondary metric, using the pipeline's default operating point. Uncertainty comes from 10 000 bootstrap replicates of the labelled pairs, with 95% percentile intervals. The paper reports MPRabc at AUPRC 0.707 (95% CI 0.663 to 0.746), against the ABC model at 0.612 and ENCODE-rE2G at 0.634, and ablations that drop the MPRALegNet or Sei features.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, 'Benchmarking'; Results; Table 3

profile.summary: This is the cell type annotation evaluation published with scTab. A classifier is trained on a corpus built from the CELLxGENE census release 2023-05-15, 22.2 million human cells from 5,052 donors, 56 tissues and 164 cell type labels, and is scored on cells from donors it has never seen. The score is the macro-averaged F1, with a correction from the Cell Ontology so that predicting a finer label than the author annotated is not punished, while predicting a coarser one is. The paper reports this for linear, tree-based and deep models and for three single-cell transformer models, several of them refitted by the authors, and it publishes the processed data with fixed splits and tuned reference models so that others can reuse the same comparison.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Results, A dataset and evaluation metric section; Methods, Dataset preparation and Ontology-corrected cell type classification

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a classifier can name the cell type of a single cell across the whole human body, not within one tissue, and whether it still does so for donors it has not seen. The authors frame the difficulty as a labelling problem: public corpora annotate at different levels of detail, so an evaluation that treats 164 ontology labels as mutually exclusive rewards a model for copying each study's annotation granularity rather than for telling cell types apart. Their fix is to judge a prediction against the Cell Ontology, which turns the task into predicting a label at least as specific as the author's. A second question the evaluation covers is whether a model knows when it is wrong: uncertainty scores from a deep ensemble are tested for separating correct predictions from incorrect ones, and from cells whose type was never in training.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, A dataset and evaluation metric section; Methods, Ontology-corrected cell type classification and Uncertainty quantification

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The corpus starts from the CELLxGENE census release 2023-05-15, restricted to human data on the 19,331 human protein-coding genes. Five filters follow: only primary data, so that the same cell in an atlas metastudy cannot appear on both sides of the split; only 10x-based assays; the label must be a subtype of the native cell term; each cell type needs at least 5,000 cells and at least 30 donors; and each cell type needs at least seven parent nodes in the ontology, a heuristic to drop very broad labels, which the authors note does not remove all coarse labels. Counts are normalised to 10,000 per cell and log transformed. The result is 22,189,056 cells, 164 cell types, 5,052 donors and 56 tissues, split by donor 70, 15 and 15 per cent into 15,240,192 training, 3,500,032 validation and 3,448,832 test cells. Subsampled training sets are also defined for the scaling experiments, both random and donor-based, from 15 to 100 per cent. The processed corpus is published as a 164 GB download in Merlin dataloader format, with a 0.5 GB minimal subset and the trained checkpoints.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset preparation and Subsampled datasets; Results; README.md: Model checkpoints and training data

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A model outputs one label per cell from the 164, and the score is the macro average of the per-class F1 on the held-out donors, so every cell type counts equally regardless of how many cells it has. The ontology correction decides right from wrong: the same label as the author is right, a subtype of the author's label is also right, a parent of the author's label is wrong, and anything else is wrong, with child relations looked up in the Cell Ontology. The paper reports each model as a mean and standard deviation over several fits with different random initialisations, and the supplementary information gives a second version of the same table with bootstrapping across test donors added, which widens the intervals by about an order of magnitude, for example scTab 0.8295 plus or minus 0.0007 over seeds against 0.8300 plus or minus 0.0069 with donor bootstrapping. A separate evaluation aggregates the fine-grained predictions to 31 coarse labels without retraining. Uncertainty is scored by averaging the predicted probabilities of 5 independently trained models, taking one minus the maximum probability as the uncertainty, then measuring the ROC-AUC for separating correct predictions from incorrect ones and from cells of types absent from training, where 1.0 is perfect separation and 0.5 is none. Training and inference cost are reported too, on named hardware.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Ontology-corrected cell type classification, Performance evaluation on coarse cell type labels, Uncertainty quantification; Supplementary Tables 1 and 2

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Download the processed corpus, or the 0.5 GB minimal subset for a first try, and the checkpoints. Install the cellnet package from the repository, either inside the Merlin PyTorch container the authors used or with pip plus the GPU requirements file. The repository holds the data loading code, training scripts, and notebooks for training, for creating the data store and for all the evaluation in the paper, with tutorial notebooks for loading data and for running a trained model. A modern GPU is needed; the authors state that on a desktop without GPU acceleration the runtime will probably exceed several days.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Model checkpoints and training data, Project structure, Installation, Hardware requirements

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: One corpus, built from the CELLxGENE census release 2023-05-15: 22,189,056 human cells, 164 cell types, 5,052 donors, 56 tissues and 249 datasets, on 19,331 protein-coding genes. The test set is 3,448,832 cells, the validation set 3,500,032 and the training set 15,240,192. Subsampled training sets at 15, 30, 50, 70 and 100 per cent, by cells and by donors, are defined for the scaling experiments.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset preparation and Subsampled datasets; Figure 1 caption

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: By donor, fixed and published. 70 per cent of donors go to training and 15 per cent each to validation and test, so a donor appears in exactly one split. The authors chose this over a random cell split, which leaks similar cells, and over a study-based split, which leaves cell types missing from one side. Because every cell type is present in at least 30 donors, each type has 4 to 5 donors in the validation and test sets.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset preparation; Results, A dataset and evaluation metric section

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Macro-averaged F1 over the 164 cell types, higher is better, computed after the ontology correction. For the uncertainty evaluation, the ROC-AUC for separating the uncertainty scores of two groups of cells, higher is better, with 0.5 meaning no separation. The coarse-label evaluation uses the same macro F1 over 31 aggregated labels.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Ontology-corrected cell type classification, Uncertainty quantification, Performance evaluation on coarse cell type labels

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Nine reported models, all refitted or run by the authors on this corpus. Macro F1 over seeded fits: scTab 0.8295 plus or minus 0.0007, XGBoost 0.8127 plus or minus 0.0005, MLP 0.7971 plus or minus 0.0012, an optimised linear model 0.7848 plus or minus 0.0001, CellTypist retrained on a 1.5 million cell subsample 0.7304 plus or minus 0.0015, scGPT zero-shot 0.7301 plus or minus 0.0035, UCE zero-shot 0.7611 plus or minus 0.0018, scGPT fine-tuned 0.749 from a single run, and CIForm on a 750,000 cell subsample 0.766 from a single run. Tuning matters: with default hyper-parameters XGBoost scores 0.5855 plus or minus 0.0112 and CellTypist 0.6258 plus or minus 0.0036.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Cross-tissue cell type classification requires nonlinear models and Robust benchmarks section; Supplementary Tables 1 and 6

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Three. Only primary data are used, so a cell duplicated into an atlas metastudy cannot appear in both training and test. The split is by donor, not by cell, so no cell from a test donor is seen in training. The ontology correction stops a model from being rewarded for mimicking one study's annotation granularity. The authors give no sequence or expression similarity cut-off beyond this, and note their broad-label filter is only a heuristic, leaving some coarse labels in the corpus.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, A dataset and evaluation metric section; Methods, Dataset preparation

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: Repeated fits with different random initialisations, 4 or 5 runs per model, reported as mean and standard deviation, and a second version of the table that also bootstraps across test donors, which gives much wider intervals, for example scTab 0.8300 plus or minus 0.0069 against 0.8295 plus or minus 0.0007 over seeds alone. The two single-run entries, fine-tuned scGPT and CIForm, carry no interval. Model uncertainty itself is estimated with a deep ensemble of 5 networks.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Uncertainty quantification and Statistics and reproducibility; Supplementary Table 1

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A single cell. One example is one cell's expression vector over 19,331 protein-coding genes, labelled with the author-provided Cell Ontology term, and the prediction is one of the 164 labels.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset preparation; Results, A dataset and evaluation metric section

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human only. The corpus is the human part of the CELLxGENE census, across 56 tissues.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset preparation

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Single-cell RNA sequencing, restricted to the 10x Genomics family of assays, which the authors list as 10x 5 prime v2 and v1, 10x 3 prime v3, v2 and v1, and the two 10x transcription profiling terms. The labels are the cell type annotations supplied by the original authors and mapped to Cell Ontology terms by the CELLxGENE schema.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset preparation; Results

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: The expression vector alone. Models take the normalised, log transformed counts over the 19,331 protein-coding genes; no tissue, donor or assay metadata is described as an input. The published corpus is distributed in the Merlin dataloader format for exactly this input.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Dataset preparation and Data loading infrastructure; README.md: Model checkpoints and training data

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: All three settings appear. Most models are trained from scratch on the training split, including scTab, XGBoost, the MLP and the optimised linear model. CellTypist and CIForm were retrained on subsamples because of memory limits. The transformer models were used both zero-shot, by fitting a logistic regression on frozen embeddings, and fine-tuned, in the case of scGPT on 150,000 cells.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Cross-tissue cell type classification requires nonlinear models; Methods, Model details; Supplementary Table 1

strengths.text: The split is by donor and the data are deduplicated to primary records, which removes the two easiest ways to flatter a cell type classifier.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results, A dataset and evaluation metric section; Methods, Dataset preparation

strengths.text: The metric handles the annotation granularity problem explicitly. A finer prediction than the author's label counts as correct and a coarser one as wrong, with the relations taken from the Cell Ontology, so the score is less a test of copying one study's labelling habits.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Ontology-corrected cell type classification

strengths.text: It is published as a reusable benchmark, not only as a result: the processed corpus with fixed splits, a small subset, the trained checkpoints and the data loading code are all downloadable, and the paper argues that tuned reference models matter by showing XGBoost rising from 0.5855 to 0.8127 with tuning.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Results, Robust benchmarks section; README.md: Model checkpoints and training data

strengths.text: The supplementary information reports the same comparison twice, over seeds alone and with bootstrapping across test donors, which shows how much of the apparent precision comes from fixing the test donors.
strengths.source_locator: Supplementary Table 1, parts a and b

limitations.text: The label set is a filtered slice of the ontology, chosen by thresholds the authors describe as data dependent: at least 5,000 cells and 30 donors per type, and at least seven parent nodes. Rare cell types are therefore absent by construction, and the authors say coarse labels remain despite the heuristic.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results, A dataset and evaluation metric section; Methods, Dataset preparation

limitations.text: Every comparison number was produced by the scTab authors, and several competitors were handicapped by memory limits: CellTypist was retrained on 1.5 million cells, CIForm on 750,000, and the fine-tuned scGPT on 150,000, with those two reported from a single run and no interval.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results, Cross-tissue cell type classification requires nonlinear models; Supplementary Table 1

limitations.text: Scores depend on how fine the labels are, so they are not comparable across label sets. The same scTab predictions give 0.897 on 31 coarse labels against 0.830 on the fine-grained ones, and the authors tie the model's advantage to parts of the ontology, mainly immune cells, that happen to be finely resolved.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results, Cross-tissue cell type classification requires nonlinear models

limitations.text: Reproducing it is expensive and tied to specific infrastructure. The processed corpus is a 164 GB download, the repository states a modern GPU is required and that a desktop run would probably exceed several days, and training times in the supplementary table run from about 10 to 33 hours on A100 class hardware.
limitations.source_locator: README.md: Model checkpoints and training data, Hardware requirements; Supplementary Table 2

name: Livesey and Marsh variant effect predictor benchmark (2025 edition)
description: Ranks missense variant effect predictors by pairwise comparisons of their Spearman correlation with human deep mutational scanning data, and separately by pairwise AUROC on ClinVar pathogenic versus gnomAD missense variants.

attributes.version: Genome Biol 2025;26:104 (third edition, after Mol Syst Biol 2020 and 2023)
attributes.task: Missense variant effect prediction, ranked against functional assays and clinical labels
attributes.scope_note: 97 VEPs on 36 human DMS datasets (one score set per protein, at least 1000 single amino acid substitutions after removing ClinVar and gnomAD variants); 83 VEPs on 819 proteins with at least 10 ClinVar pathogenic or likely pathogenic and 10 gnomAD v4.1 missense variants. Rank score is each VEP's average pairwise win rate against all other VEPs.
attributes.source_locator: Results 'New DMS datasets and VEPs', 'Comparison of VEP performance using DMS data', 'Performance of VEPs on clinical variant classification'; Methods
limitations: Rank scores are relative: they depend on which other VEPs are in the comparison and are not a per-VEP correlation or AUROC.
The earlier editions (Mol Syst Biol 2020;16:e9380 and 2023;19:e11474) used other DMS sets, VEP sets and, in 2020, another ranking method; they are not extracted here.

profile.summary: This is the third edition of the Livesey and Marsh benchmark of missense variant effect predictors. It ranks 97 predictors by how well their scores correlate with deep mutational scanning measurements in 36 human proteins, and separately ranks 83 predictors by how well they separate ClinVar pathogenic from gnomAD population missense variants in 819 proteins. Rankings are pairwise: each predictor's score is its average win rate against every other predictor on the variants both of them score.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Results, Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 legends

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two things. First, agreement between a predictor's scores and experimental fitness measurements from deep mutational scanning, using absolute Spearman correlation, because only a monotonic relationship is needed. Second, discrimination between pathogenic and population missense variants in clinical data, using AUROC per protein. The authors' premise is that a predictor consistent across many functional assays is the most useful one, and they report that relative performance on the assay benchmark predicts relative performance on the clinical one for predictors not trained on human clinical variants.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Comparison of VEP performance using DMS data; Abstract

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The assay set starts from the 26 datasets of the previous edition, removes every variant also present in the authors' ClinVar and gnomAD sets, then keeps only datasets with at least 1000 scored amino acid variants. Datasets measuring antibody binding or unrelated binding affinity, and those without methodological details, were excluded; 13 new datasets, mostly from MaveDB, were added, giving 36 proteins and 207,460 single amino acid variants. One score set per protein is used, chosen as the one with the highest median Spearman correlation across all predictors. The clinical set takes ClinVar missense variants (downloaded 06/08/2024) labelled pathogenic, likely pathogenic or pathogenic/likely pathogenic, drops 0-star entries and entries with conflicting interpretations, and uses gnomAD v4.1 missense variants that pass the genomes or exomes filters as a putatively benign class. Proteins with at least 10 of each class qualify, giving 819 proteins.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods; Results, New DMS datasets and VEPs; Performance of VEPs on clinical variant classification

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: For each protein, the absolute Spearman correlation with the assay is computed for every pair of predictors using only variants all three (assay and both predictors) score. The predictor with the higher correlation wins the comparison. Win rates are pooled over proteins and the rank score is the average win rate against all other predictors. The clinical ranking uses the same pairwise procedure with AUROC in place of Spearman, and a parallel version uses AUPRC. Predictors that score low for pathogenic are inverted by subtracting from 1. Error bars on the assay ranking are the standard deviation of the rank score over 1000 bootstraps resampling 36 protein datasets with replacement; error bars on the clinical ranking are the standard error across comparisons.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Spearman's correlation and rank score; AUROC and AUPRC; Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 legends

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: Download the prediction files and the scripts from the three figshare records and run the two Python scripts. Figures_1_and_2.py rebuilds the assay benchmark from the per-protein prediction CSVs, the DMS summary, the ClinVar and gnomAD variant files and the renaming and inversion rules; Figure 3.py rebuilds the clinical ranking from the variant score file. Paths at the top of each script must be set first.
sections.source_locator: Figures_1_and_2.py: header and paths; figshare record 28295408

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: 36 human deep mutational scanning datasets covering 207,460 single amino acid variants (one score set per protein), and a clinical set of ClinVar pathogenic or likely pathogenic versus gnomAD v4.1 putatively benign missense variants across 819 proteins.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: No train, validation or test split: all data are evaluation data, and the predictors are external tools. Variants present in ClinVar or gnomAD are removed from the assay benchmark, and datasets were excluded for predictors trained on that assay data.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Comparison of VEP performance using DMS data

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Assay benchmark: pairwise win rate on absolute Spearman correlation (higher is better). Clinical benchmark: pairwise win rate on AUROC, with an AUPRC version in the supplement (higher is better).
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: The predictors are the comparison set: 97 in the assay benchmark and 83 in the clinical one, grouped as clinical-trained (46), population-free (31) and population-tuned (6). 27 came from dbNSFP 4.2; the rest were run locally, downloaded, taken from web interfaces or from ProteinGym.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, VEPs; Results

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: For the assay benchmark: all ClinVar and gnomAD variants are removed, and proteins are excluded for predictors trained on that assay. For the clinical benchmark: none. The authors state they made no effort to exclude training variants there and that clinical-trained predictors are likely inflated by circularity.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: 1000 bootstraps resampling the 36 protein datasets with replacement give the standard deviation of each assay rank score; the clinical ranking reports the standard error across pairwise comparisons.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 legends

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A single amino acid substitution in a human protein, with either an assay fitness score or a clinical or population label.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, New DMS datasets and VEPs

facts.label: Organisms
facts.value: Human proteins. Some assays are carried out in other systems, for example yeast complementation assays.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Table 1

facts.label: Assays
facts.value: Deep mutational scanning, classified as direct (measuring the protein's own function) or indirect (for example growth or complementation). Clinical labels come from ClinVar assertions and gnomAD allele observations, not assays.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Fig. 1 legend; Table 1

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: Inapplicable: the benchmark scores whatever each published predictor produces and does not restrict inputs. Coverage differs between predictors, with some scoring only substitutions reachable by a single nucleotide change.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Results, Comparison of VEP performance using DMS data

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: None: published predictors are used as they are, with no fine-tuning or retraining by the benchmark authors.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Methods, VEPs

strengths.text: Pairwise comparison on shared variants removes the advantage a predictor could gain from scoring only an easy subset, which the authors show can otherwise produce outliers.
The assay benchmark removes ClinVar and gnomAD variants, which the authors say offsets the advantage predictors gain from training on those databases.
Predictions, clinical labels and the analysis scripts are deposited on figshare, the data under CC BY 4.0 and the scripts under MIT.

limitations.text: A rank score is relative, not absolute: it depends on which other predictors are in the comparison and is not a correlation or an AUROC.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Spearman's correlation and rank score

limitations.text: The clinical ranking excludes no training variants, so the authors say clinical-trained predictors are likely inflated there by circularity.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results, Performance of VEPs on clinical variant classification

limitations.text: The negative class is gnomAD population variants, which the authors accept will contain some pathogenic variants not yet classified, especially in recessive and incompletely penetrant genes.
Each protein is represented by one assay score set, chosen as the one correlating best with the predictors on average, so the choice depends on the predictors being tested.
limitations.source_locator: Paper: Results, New DMS datasets and VEPs

name: ClinGen SVI calibration of computational predictors for PP3/BP4
description: Local posterior probability calibration of missense predictor scores to ACMG/AMP evidence strengths (PP3 for pathogenicity, BP4 for benignity), on ClinVar missense variants with a prior probability of pathogenicity estimated from gnomAD.

attributes.version: Pejaver et al. 2022 (13 tools) and Bergquist et al. 2025 (3 further tools, point-based intervals)
attributes.task: Calibrate predictor score thresholds to ACMG/AMP evidence strengths for missense variants
attributes.scope_note: Calibration on the ClinVar 2019 set (11,834 missense variants, 1,914 genes, rare in gnomAD, training variants of the tools removed where available); prior probability of pathogenicity 4.41% from the gnomAD set by DistCurve; thresholds where the one-sided 95% bootstrap bound of the local positive likelihood ratio reaches 2.406, 5.790, 33.53 and 1,124 (Supporting to Very Strong).
attributes.source_locator: Pejaver et al. 2022 Methods and Table 1; Bergquist et al. 2025 Materials and Methods
limitations: Genome-wide calibration; evidence strength varies between genes (Tejura et al. 2024).

Several authors of Pejaver et al. 2022 developed calibrated tools: B.-J. Feng (BayesDel; reference 13 is Feng's PERCH paper), V. Pejaver, K.A. Pagel, S.D. Mooney and P. Radivojac (MutPred2, reference 19), V. Pejaver (REVEL, reference 23), R. Karchin (VEST4, reference 25) and A. O'Donnell-Luria (MPC, reference 18).

profile.summary: A ClinGen Sequence Variant Interpretation calibration that turns missense predictor scores into ACMG/AMP evidence strengths: PP3 (supporting to very strong for pathogenicity) and BP4 (for benignity). Pejaver et al. 2022 calibrated 13 tools on 11,834 ClinVar missense variants using a 4.41% prior from gnomAD; Bergquist et al. 2025 applied the same method to AlphaMissense, ESM1b and VARITY. Clinical laboratories and tool developers use it to set score thresholds for variant classification.
profile.summary_source_locator: Pejaver 2022: Summary, Data sets, Prevalence; Bergquist 2025: Abstract

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: For each tool, the score intervals at which the local posterior probability of pathogenicity, or the local positive likelihood ratio, reaches each ACMG/AMP evidence level. The method estimates a local positive predictive value and can in principle calibrate any continuous score. Bergquist et al. 2025 also map evidence levels to points in the Bayesian adaptation of the guidelines.
sections.source_locator: Pejaver 2022: Summary; Bergquist 2025: Introduction

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The ClinVar 2019 set holds pathogenic, likely pathogenic, likely benign and benign missense variants with gnomAD allele frequency below 0.01, in genes with at least one pathogenic variant; VUS, zero-star and conflicting entries and known training variants of the tools were removed, leaving 11,834 variants in 1,914 genes. The gnomAD set (363,894 variants, 3,640 genes) is used to estimate the prior and how often each evidence level would be assigned; gnomAD variants found in ClinVar were removed. The ClinVar 2020 set (9,114 variants, 2,197 genes) holds variants added after December 2019 and is used for validation.
sections.source_locator: Pejaver 2022: Materials and methods, Data sets

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: The prior probability of pathogenicity was estimated at 4.41% with DistCurve on the gnomAD set. Evidence thresholds correspond to positive likelihood ratios of 2.406, 5.790, 33.53 and 1,124 for supporting, moderate, strong and very strong. A score threshold is set where the one-sided 95% confidence bound of the local likelihood ratio, from 10,000 bootstrap iterations, reaches the required value. Thresholds are then checked on the ClinVar 2020 set. Bergquist et al. 2025 reused the same data sets, parameters and cut-offs.

facts.label: Datasets
facts.value: ClinVar 2019 set (11,834 variants, 1,914 genes) for calibration, gnomAD set (363,894 variants, 3,640 genes) for the prior and coverage, ClinVar 2020 set (9,114 variants, 2,197 genes) for validation.
facts.source_locator: Pejaver 2022: Data sets

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: Time split: calibrate on ClinVar variants up to December 2019, validate on variants added to ClinVar after December 2019.
facts.source_locator: Pejaver 2022: The ClinVar 2020 set

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Local positive likelihood ratio (equivalently local posterior probability) per score; thresholds at 2.406, 5.790, 33.53 and 1,124 for the four evidence levels. A higher ratio means stronger pathogenic evidence; for BP4 the reciprocal applies.
facts.source_locator: Pejaver 2022: Table 1

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: No baseline in the usual sense; 13 tools were calibrated in 2022 (BayesDel, CADD, EA, FATHMM, GERP++, MPC, MutPred2, PhyloP, PolyPhen-2, PrimateAI, REVEL, SIFT, VEST4) and AlphaMissense, ESM1b and VARITY in 2025.
facts.source_locator: Pejaver 2022: In silico tools considered; Bergquist 2025: Abstract

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Known training variants of the tools (and of constituent tools of meta-predictors) were removed where available; gnomAD variants in ClinVar were removed; validation uses later ClinVar entries. For VARITY, scores came from model versions that did not train on each variant.
facts.source_locator: Pejaver 2022: Data sets; Bergquist 2025: Selection of computational tools

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: One-sided 95% confidence bounds from 10,000 bootstrap iterations set the thresholds.

facts.label: Entity type
facts.value: A missense variant with a predictor score.

facts.label: Assays

facts.value: Any tool's precomputed or generated score for each variant; the method needs only the score.

facts.value: Not applicable as a model training regime: tools are calibrated as published, without retraining.

strengths.text: Gives each tool evidence-level thresholds tied to a quantitative Bayesian framework instead of developer-chosen cut-offs.
Training variants of the tools are removed where available, and thresholds are validated on later ClinVar entries.
Data sets and results are on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0 and the code is MIT-licensed.

limitations.text: Calibration is genome-wide across known disease genes; the authors say single-gene laboratories may need their own calibration.
ClinVar classifications may already have used these tools, and the authors call for better cataloguing to avoid circularity.
Some high evidence levels are reached by few variants, as Bergquist et al. note for the newer tools.
Missense variants only, and intended for use within the ACMG/AMP rules.
